en: Now begins the second chapter. Salutations to Kṛṣṇa, whose form is existence, consciousness, and bliss; who acts without effort; who is known through the Vedānta; who is the Guru and the witness of the intellect. (1)

I worship the Lord of Jānakī, who follows the established tenets of Vedānta and is unshaken by the arguments of the Sāṃkhya and other Smṛtis; who is not known through various rootless scriptures as having an origin and dissolution like space and other elements; who is devoid of birth and end, whose body is consciousness, who is all-pervading, and who, though designated by a subtle body (liṅga) as a "doer," is in truth devoid of a physical form. 2.
START BsRp_2,1.1.1:
If it be argued that there would be the fault of leaving no room for the Smṛtis, we say no, because that would entail the fault of leaving no room for other Smṛtis.

According to the Śruti, "I shall manifest name and form," the creator of names and bodies (the *nāmatanukṛt*), who is also the fashioner of names and forms (*saṃjñāmūrtivyākarta*), [acts] by means of the adjunct of the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*).

The meaning is: "I worship Him"—the Supreme Self, who is celebrated and well-known as the "Agent" and the "Part," who is non-different from the inner self (pratyak), and who is the controller of primordial nature (mūlaprakṛti).
In connection with the Smṛti, he recounts what has preceded in order to state the relationship between the subject matter of the preceding and following chapters:
"In the first chapter... and so forth.
The meaning is as follows: beginning with the *janmādi-sūtra*, it has been established that Brahman is the cause of the origin and so forth of the world;
in sūtras such as "But by the vision of the scripture" (*śāstradṛṣṭyā tu*), it is stated that He alone is the non-dual Self of all;
and by the sūtra beginning with "That which is inferable" (*ānumānikam*), it is shown that any other cause is not based on the Vedas.

Having thus restated the subject matter of the first chapter, he briefly explains the subject matter of the second chapter— which concerns the removal of contradictions regarding that same topic— chapter by quarter, beginning with the words "Now" (*idānīm*).
Here, in the first quarter (*pāda*), the removal of contradictions against the concordance (*samanvaya*) [of the Vedas] with the Smṛtis and arguments of the Sāṃkhya and other schools is effected.
In the second pāda, it is stated that the scriptures of the Sāṃkhya and other schools are rooted in error, for the sake of non-contradiction [with the Vedas].

In the third pāda, non-contradiction is established by explaining the order of the birth and dissolution of the great elements, such as space, as well as the creation and individual self (jīvātman) according to each Vedānta text.
The meaning of the fourth pāda is the non-contradiction of the scriptures concerning the subtle body (liṅgaśarīra).
This is the very same point;
for the sake of easy understanding, it is summarized in verse: "In the second [chapter], there is no contradiction with memory and reasoning, nor is there any fault in the other [arguments];
there is likewise no contradiction with the scriptural texts concerning the enjoyer of the elements and the scriptural texts concerning the subtle body."
Thus,

since it is impossible to resolve doubts regarding contradiction when the subject matter is not yet known, it is logical that the chapter on non-contradiction (*avirodhādhyāya*) follows immediately after the chapter on systematic harmony (*samanvayādhyāya*).
Regarding this, he states the purport of the first section (*adhikaraṇa*):
Regarding the word "first":

since this section (pāda) is intended to remove contradictions regarding the scriptural harmony (*śrauta-samanvaya*), it connects with the scripture (*śruti*), the treatise (*śāstra*), and the chapter (*adhyāya*). Because all the topical discussions (*adhikaraṇas*) consist of establishing one's own position, they are connected to this section.
Here, in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the result is the non-establishment of the stated harmony due to contradiction with Smṛti.

The distinction is that its establishment occurs in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*). In this regard, the subject matter (*viṣaya*) is the concordance (*samanvaya*) of the Vedānta texts with Brahman as previously stated.

Since there is doubt—arising from whether the authority of Smṛti is valid or invalid—as to whether that [concordance] is contradicted by the Sāṃkhya Smṛti or not, he states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*):
Regarding what was said:
*tantra* is that by which principles (*tattva*) are woven or explained; it refers to the scripture spoken by Kapila and others spoken by Pañcaśikha and so forth.
The meaning is that this being so, the Vedāntas would be purposeless with respect to the systematic presentation (*samanvaya*) of non-dual Brahman.
To the objection that there is no contradiction because those [Vedic injunctions] also have Brahman as their sole purpose, he says:
"For in them... (*tāsu hi*).

Now, one might object: "If, for the sake of establishing the authority of the Sāṃkhya Smṛti, one accepts the doctrine of Pradhāna, would it not follow that the Smṛtis of Manu and others lose their authority? Anticipating this, he says "Manvādi... [etc.], meaning that those [Smṛtis] possess authority because they have scope regarding dharma. If that is so, then let the Smṛtis of the Sāṃkhyas and others also possess authority with respect to dharma through their primary purport.
Since there is no contradiction in the fact that reality is indeed Brahman itself, he says "not so";
for since conceptualization is impossible regarding reality, it is appropriate to explain the Śruti in accordance with the Smṛti, which leaves no room for alternative interpretations.
He says "Therefore" because of the principle that between that which has scope and that which lacks scope, the one lacking scope is stronger.
He raises an objection, suggesting that the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is not tenable because it is accepted that scripture (smṛti) lacks authority when it contradicts direct revelation (śruti).
How so?

He says: this prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) would not occur to those who are capable of understanding the meaning of the scripture independently; however, it would indeed occur to those who have faith in the elder Sāṃkhya teachers.
Thinking, "It might be so," [the author] says,
"And [regarding] Kapila and others," because one would have faith in them due to their possession of knowledge of supersensuous objects.
One should behold him as the Supreme Lord, who in the beginning brought forth the sage Kapila as he was being born, and who sustained him with his knowledges once he was produced.
This is the interpretation of the scriptural passage.

Just as you assert that the doctrine of Brahman must be abandoned because it contradicts the Sāṃkhya Smṛti, so too do I maintain that the doctrine of Pradhāna must be abandoned because it contradicts other Smṛtis; thus he establishes the final conclusion with the words, "the resolution of that."

Therefore, from that Brahman, the unmanifest— which is to say, the world in its subtle form— is dissolved into Māyā. Having thus stated the words of the Itihāsas, he now cites the consensus of the Purāṇas:
Regarding the phrase "and therefore":
that from which something originates is its source (*prabhava*), meaning the cause of birth;
that in which something dissolves is its dissolution (*pralaya*), meaning the substratum of absorption.
Therefore, from the Lord as the agent, Brahmā and the others arise;
He alone is the root material cause. Is He transformative? No.
It is eternal and immutable;
therefore, the meaning is that it is permanent.
Now, why was the contradiction with scripture not mentioned? To this he says:
Regarding the phrase "by the power of Smṛti": since there are mutual contradictions among the Smṛtis, how can there be a determination of the truth? To this, he says:
"But it has been shown," and so forth.
The meaning is that the determination of reality is achieved by the Vedas alone.
To the question, "What then is the status of the Smṛtis?", he says: "And in case of conflict... [vipratipattau ca].

The meaning is that when there is a mutual contradiction among Smṛtis regarding the true nature of reality, since an option (*vikalpa*) is impossible with respect to an objective fact, those Smṛtis whose basis is an established Śruti are authoritative, whereas others, whose basis is a merely inferred Śruti, are not authoritative. Regarding the point that a Smṛti is not authoritative when it contradicts an established Śruti, he states the reasoning of Jaimini:
Regarding the phrase "so it has been said":

there arises a doubt as to whether the Smṛti rule, "The Audumbarī post must be entirely covered," which contradicts the direct Vedic Śruti, "One should chant the Udgītha while touching the Audumbarī," is authoritative or not.

Having reached the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) that it is authoritative because one can infer a foundational Śruti for it, the established conclusion (siddhānta) is: when there is a contradiction with an already established Śruti, the authority of the Smṛti is *anapekṣam*, meaning devoid of expectation [of a corroborating Śruti].

The meaning is as follows: "to be abandoned" refers to the fact that while an inference based on scripture (*śruti*) occurs when there is no contradiction, here, because there is a contradiction, an inference from scripture is impossible; thus, due to the absence of its source, the Smṛti rule regarding the total wrapping [of the sacrificial post] is invalid.
Let it be granted that the Sāṃkhya Smṛti is based on perception; to this he says: "And not...
It is being questioned whether the knowledge of supersensuous objects can be possible for yogins by virtue of the greatness of their supernatural powers (siddhi).
Regarding the word "possible" (*śakyam*):
It is said that Kapila and others first ascertained the authority of the Veda and then achieved perfection through the practice of *dharma*, which is its meaning;

by that perfection, it is argued that it is not proper to violate the beginningless *Śruti* according to the *Smṛtis* they composed, because that would contradict what must be relied upon (*upajīvya*). To this, he replies: "No."
"Even from the perspective of established proof" (*siddherapi*) means "to entertain excessive doubt.
The meaning is that it is impossible to suspect that the Vedas have abandoned their primary sense (*mukhyārtha*) and possess only a figurative sense (*upacaritārthatva*).
If it is argued that the Veda is not dependent [on other means of knowledge] because it is self-established (*svataḥsiddha*), we say no;
for there is no evidence for the self-establishment of one who is not God (*anīśvara*). Even granting this for the sake of argument, he says:
Regarding the term *siddha*:

even when the meaning of the Vedas is being determined by relying on the statements of the *siddhas*, if there is mutual contradiction among those statements of the *siddhas*, it is proper that the determination of the Vedic meaning be made through the reasoning of Manu and others based upon the Śruti.
This is the sense. The literal meaning is that the mere words of the *siddhas*, without having the Śruti as their foundation, are not the cause for determining the ultimate truth.
Now, one might ask: "How can the mind of a person of dull intellect, who has faith in the Sāṃkhya tradition, be brought onto the path of Vedānta?
To this, he says: "By that which is dependent on another," and so forth.
Furthermore, one might object: "Since the Śruti declares Kapila to be omniscient, faith in his doctrine is difficult to ward off. To this, he says:
As for the phrase "But that which..."—
the delusion that the author of Sāṃkhya is mentioned in the Śruti merely by the word "Kapila" is incorrect,
because it is impossible for that proponent of dualism to be omniscient.
And here, Kapila, who is known as such because he is endowed with all knowledge, is indeed a portion of Vāsudeva;
for the sense is that he is "all-knowing" (sarvajña) because he teaches the Vedic Sāṃkhya, which is the knowledge of the self-nature of all things.
[The term] *prataptuḥ* means of the one who causes burning.
Furthermore, it is enjoined that "one should see that Lord who sustains Kapila through his knowledges.

Thus, the mention of Kapila’s omniscience—which serves another purpose as a subordinate element to the realization of the Lord—is a mere restatement (*anuvāda*). Since such a quality is not established by any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it cannot serve to establish its own object; therefore, omniscience is not proven by a mere restatement.
This is what he means by saying "anyārtha" (for another purpose).
Having refuted the scriptural authority of Kapila, the proponent of dualism, he states that Manu, the proponent of Brahman, possesses scriptural authority with the words "And it occurs...
He further states that even in the Itihāsas, non-duality is demonstrated by means of a censure of the Kāpila doctrine.
"In the Mahābhārata as well" means:
the purpose of the inquiry is whether the individual selves (*puruṣas*) are in reality distinct, or whether they are the one inner self (*pratyagātman*) of all objects of perception.

Just as there is a single source or material cause for many bodies in the form of persons—namely, the earth—so too that Person, the Self, is the universe, consisting of all things as the material cause of everything, and is characterized by qualities such as omniscience.
I shall explain this fully.
He is "Viśvamūrdhā" (the one whose head is the universe) because he alone is the head of all—the gods, animals, humans, and so forth—well-known throughout the world;
for he has entered into every single field by way of being a reflected image.
Thus is the application of the term "connected with the universe" (*viśvayuj*) and so forth.
He moves through and understands all beings;
the meaning is "everywhere."
"Moving according to his own will" means independent;
he has no one who restrains him;
the meaning is that he is the Lord of all.
"At one's ease" means,
in other words, "having the nature of sorrowless bliss.
Having stated the contradiction of the Sāṃkhya system with the Smṛtis rooted in the Veda, he now states its direct contradiction with the Veda itself:
"And [there is] scripture" (śrutiśca).

The connection is as follows: it is established that at the time of such a cognition, not only is there something contrary to the Veda through the mere postulation of an independent *prakṛti*, but also through the postulation of a plurality of selves.
To the objection—"In the case of conflict with *smṛti*, why should the Veda itself not be rendered invalid?"—he says:
Regarding the phrase "for the Veda":
the authority of the Veda is self-established because it is not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*).

In the case of human statements, their authority must be known through the postulation of a memory of their own meaning and the experience that is its source; thus, there is a remoteness consisting in "extrinsic validity" (*parataḥ-prāmāṇya*) due to this mediation.
The literal meaning is that there is a distinction between Śruti and Smṛti.
For when two equal authorities conflict, that which has no scope (the one with no room for application) sublates that which has scope;

however, here, due to the disparity between intrinsic validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*) and extrinsic validity (*parataḥ-prāmāṇya*), the Vedic sentence—which possesses immediate certainty of validity and whose contradiction has not yet arisen—sublates the conflicting Smṛti. This is the intended sense.
"Therefore" means "because of the distinction"; the sense is that it is possible for [the opponent's position] to be rooted in error. //1//
And because others are not perceived. (BBs 2.1.2)

Since the Great Principle (mahat) and the I-principle (ahaṅkāra) are not established [as real], and since the subtle elements (tanmātrāṇi) are also unestablished because they have the I-principle as their material cause, one cannot even remember them; thus he says:
"And of the others... (itareṣāṃ ca).
Now, one might object that "the Great" (mahat) and the other principles are well-known from the scripture stating, "Beyond the Great is the Unmanifest" (mahataḥ param avyaktam);
therefore, he says, "And even that which...
He states the intended meaning of the Sūtra as follows:

"Is to be rejected": the meaning is that it is determined that the Sāṃkhya Smṛti possesses no authority with respect to the Pradhāna, just as it lacks authority regarding the Mahat and other principles.
To the question, "Even if the Sāṃkhya Smṛti is sublated, how is there a sublation of the arguments stated therein?", he says:

He reflects. //2// START BsRp_2,1.2.3ḥThe Blessed One said: "Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? Here, monks, one person dwells contemplating the body in the body internally; another dwells contemplating the body in the body externally; another dwells contemplating the body in the body both internally and externally; and another dwells contemplating the nature of arising in the body, or dwells contemplating the nature of passing away in the body, or dwells contemplating the nature of both arising and passing away in the body. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. //3//The Blessed One said: "Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? Here, monks, one person dwells contemplating the body in the body internally; another dwells contemplating the body in the body externally; another dwells contemplating the body in the body both internally and externally; and another dwells contemplating the nature of arising in the body, or dwells contemplating the nature of passing away in the body, or dwells contemplating the nature of both arising and passing away in the body. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. //3// Furthermore, monks, how does a person dwell contemplating the body in the body internally? Here, monks, a certain person, having gone to the forest, or to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut, sits down; having folded his legs crosswise, set his body erect, and established mindfulness in front of him, ever mindful he breathes in, mindful he breathes out. Breathing in long, he knows: "I breathe in long"; or breathing out long, he knows: "I breathe out long. Breathing in short, he knows: "I breathe in short"; or breathing out short, he knows: "I breathe out short. He trains thus: "Experiencing the whole body, I shall breathe in"; he trains thus: "Experiencing the whole body, I shall breathe out. He trains thus: "Tranquillizing the bodily formation, I shall breathe in"; he trains thus: "Tranquillizing the bodily formation, I shall breathe out. Just as a skilled turner or his apprentice, when making a long turn, knows: "I make a long turn," or when making a short turn, knows: "I make a short turn"—even so, monks, a bhikkhu, breathing in long, knows: "I breathe in long"; or breathing out long, he knows: "I breathe out long. Breathing in short, he knows: "I breathe in short"; or breathing out short, he knows: "I breathe out short. He trains thus:

"Experiencing the whole body, I shall breathe in"; he trains thus: "Experiencing the whole body, I shall breathe out. He trains thus: "Tranquillizing the bodily formation, I shall breathe in"; he trains thus: "Tranquillizing the bodily formation, I shall breathe out. In this way, monks, a person dwells contemplating the body in the body internally. Furthermore, monks, how does a person dwell contemplating the body in the body externally? Here, monks, a certain person, with regard to the bodies of others—whether those of the noble ones or those of commoners, whether beautiful or ugly, whether far or near—he contemplates the body in those bodies, considering: "This body, too, is of the same nature, of such a nature, not exempt from such a condition. In this way, monks, a person dwells contemplating the body in the body externally. Furthermore, monks, how does a person dwell contemplating the body in the body both internally and externally? Here, monks, a certain person, with regard to his own body and the bodies of others—whether those of the noble ones or those of commoners, whether beautiful or ugly, whether far or near—he contemplates the body in those bodies, considering: "This body, too, is of the same nature, of such a nature, not exempt from such a condition. In this way, monks, a person dwells contemplating the body in the body both internally and externally. Furthermore, monks, how does a person dwell contemplating the nature of arising in the body? Here, monks, a certain person contemplates the body as it arises: "Such is the nature of this body, namely, arising. In this way, monks, a person dwells contemplating the nature of arising in the body. Furthermore, monks, how does a person dwell contemplating the nature of passing away in the body? Here, monks, a certain person contemplates the body as it passes away: "Such is the nature of this body, namely, passing away. In this way, monks, a person dwells contemplating the nature of passing away in the body. Furthermore, monks, how does a person dwell contemplating the nature of both arising and passing away in the body? Here, monks, a certain person contemplates the body as it arises and passes away: "Such is the nature of this body, namely, arising and passing away. In this way, monks, a person dwells contemplating the nature of both arising and passing away in the body. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. //4// Furthermore, monks, there are these four foundations of mindfulness. What four? Here, monks, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. He dwells contemplating mind in mind, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. He dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. These, monks, are the four foundations of mindfulness. //5// Furthermore, monks, how does a bhikkhu dwell contemplating the body in the body? Here, monks, a bhikkhu, having gone to the forest, or to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut, sits down; having folded his legs crosswise, set his body erect, and established mindfulness in front of him, he abides contemplating the body in the body internally, or he abides contemplating the body in the body externally, or he abides contemplating the body in the body both internally and externally. Or else, he abides contemplating the nature of arising in the body, or he abides contemplating the nature of passing away in the body, or he abides contemplating the nature of both arising and passing away in the body. Or else, he contemplates the body as far as the soles of the feet, bounded by the skin on the outside, filled with various impurities: "In this body there are head-hairs, body-hairs, nails, teeth, skin; flesh, sinews, bones, bone-marrow, kidneys; heart, liver, midriff, spleen, lungs; intestines, mesentery, stomach, excrement; bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat; tears, grease, spittle, snot, oil-of-the-joints, urine. Just as a sack containing various grains might be opened, and one would see rice, paddy, mung beans, kidney beans, sesame seeds, husked rice, and so forth—even so, monks, a bhikkhu contemplates the body as far as the soles of the feet, bounded by the skin on the outside, filled with various impurities: "In this body there are head-hairs... and urine. Or else, monks, a bhikkhu reviews this very body, however it is placed, however disposed, as consisting of elements: "In this body there are the earth-element, the water-element, the fire-element, and the air-element. Just as a skilled butcher or his apprentice, having slaughtered a cow and divided it into portions, should sit at a crossroads—even so, monks, a bhikkhu reviews this very body, however it is placed, however disposed, as consisting of elements: "In this body there are the earth-element, the water-element, the fire-element, and the air-element. Or else, monks, a bhikkhu, as if seeing a corpse thrown aside in a charnel ground—one day dead, two days dead, three days dead, bloated, livid, and oozing with matter—compares this very body with that: "This body, too, is of the same nature, of such a nature, not exempt from such a condition. Or else, monks, a bhikkhu, as if seeing a corpse thrown aside in a charnel ground, being devoured by crows, hawks, vultures, dogs, jackals, or various kinds of worms, compares this very body with that: "This body, too, is of the same nature, of such a nature, not exempt from such a condition. Or else, monks, a bhikkhu, as if seeing a corpse thrown aside in a charnel ground, a skeleton with flesh and blood, held together by sinews... a fleshless skeleton smeared with blood, held together by sinews... a skeleton without flesh and blood, held together by sinews... disconnected bones scattered in all directions: here a hand-bone, there a foot-bone, here a shin-bone, there a thigh-bone
By this, Yoga is refuted.

(Sūtra 2.1.3) — Regarding the doubt as to whether the concordance established with respect to Brahman is contradicted by the Yoga-smṛti of the proponents of Pradhāna or not, he extends the previous reasoning:
"By this, Yoga is refuted."
Because this is an extended application (*atideśa*), the connection (*saṃgati*) and so forth should be understood as being the same as before.
He states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), which refutes what was not mentioned previously, with the words: "For there is here... (*asti hy atra*).
Nididhyāsana is yoga.

That body in which the three—the chest, the neck, and the head—are elevated is called "trirunnata" (threefold-elevated); if the reading is "trirunnatam," it is Vedic (chāndasa). The word "yuñjīta" (one should join) is to be supplied as the verb.
He states, "And the indicative marks," to show that there is not only an injunction regarding yoga, but also explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) that serve as indicators of yoga:
"Those who know yoga consider that aforementioned concentration (*dhāraṇā*) to be yoga, the supreme austerity."

The connection is as follows: having received this knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā), the method of yoga (yogavidhi), and the manner of meditation (dhyānaprakāra) through the grace of Death, Naciketas attained Brahman.

This means that since even the portion concerning the principles such as Pradhāna is accepted as authoritative by those who follow the Smṛti, it is so called because its yogic aspect—a portion of its meaning—is established as authoritative.

In the *Pramāṇalakṣaṇa* (the section on the means of valid knowledge), it was stated that Smṛtis such as "The Aṣṭakā rites must be performed" and "The teacher must be followed" possess authority because they do not contradict the meaning of the Veda, and thus their source is inferred to be Śruti.

Similarly, having restated the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that the Yoga-smṛti possesses authority regarding yoga—and by extension, authority regarding the categories of reality (*tattva*)—the author establishes the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) with the words "This [is... (*iyam*).
Now, one might ask: "Why are the Smṛtis of the Buddhists and others not refuted here? To this he says:
"Even though they exist.

The intention is that these are disregarded here because they are notorious for being deceptive, because they have been accepted by those who are unrefined and akin to cattle, and because they stand outside the Veda.
Regarding the phrase "the cause of that":

having known the God who is the cause of those aforementioned desires—one who is reached through Sāṃkhya and Yoga, that is, through discernment and meditation—and attained as one's own inner self (pratyaktayā), one is released from all fetters such as ignorance;
this is the meaning.
To the question, "Why has the refutation of both Smṛtis been performed as if they were rooted [in the Veda]? he says:
"But the refutation..."—for this reason.
The word "done" (*kṛtam*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
Regarding the phrase "due to proximity" (*pratyāsatter*):
this means that the words *sāṃkhya* and *yoga* found in the revealed scripture (*śruti*) must be understood according to meanings of the same class as those [words] occurring in the scripture.
Is the lack of authority of Smṛti in all its parts? No; he says: "by whichever part...
Anticipating an objection regarding the contradiction of the doctrine of Brahman with the views of Kaṇabhakṣa and others, he extends [the argument] by saying:
"By this" means by way of contradiction with scripture (*śruti*).

Having raised the objection that the sublation of that which is beneficial (*upakāraka*) is not logical, he states that the part which is beneficial is not to be sublated, but rather the part concerning reality (*tattva*): [he says].
"Those too" refers to:
reasoning (*tarka*) is inference (*anumāna*); the supporting argument (*yukti*) is the means of establishing it (*upapatti*). //3//
[The opponent objects:
"Because this [world] has different characteristics, it cannot be of that nature; moreover, so it is from scripture. (BS 2.1.4)

Since the Smṛtis lack authority, there is no contradiction with the concordance [of the Vedas] established by them; thus, stating the conclusion (*siddhānta*), he declares the purport of this section (*adhikaraṇa*) by way of a summary of what has preceded: "Brahmāsya...
He then challenges the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*):
"How much less so?"—this provides the reason for the lack of opportunity:
"Is it not just like the case of Dharma? etc.
Since Brahman is to be known solely through the Veda and is independent of other means of knowledge, there is no scope for inference-based reasoning (*tarka*) to enter therein.
Therefore, there is no room for an objection, because reasoning and the Veda have different objects; this is the meaning.

[The author] supports the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) by arguing that since what is already established is accessible through other means of knowledge, there is a contradiction due to the identity of their object.
"This might be so"—this is the supporting illustration (*avaṣṭambha*).

Now, one might object: "Even if there is a contradiction due to having the same object, let the other means of knowledge (*mānāntara*) alone be sublated because of its contradiction with scripture (*śruti*. To this, he says:

The phrase "and just as" means that it is proper to interpret a scriptural passage with a secondary figurative sense (*lakṣaṇāvṛtti*)— which has scope [for interpretation]— by means of another internal [textual] element that lacks scope [for literal application], just as a weak scriptural statement is sublated by a stronger one. Furthermore,

since reasoning (*tarka*) is an internal auxiliary to the direct realization of Brahman— which is the cause of liberation— it possesses an object that is immediate (*aparokṣa*), just like the primary [realization], because its domain consists of immediate examples.
But since verbal testimony concerns objects beyond the reach of the senses, it is extrinsic and is therefore sublated by reasoning; thus he says:
"perceived," etc.—by mere tradition.
The phrase "by way of being beyond perception" means this very point.
He demonstrates the primacy of direct experience with the words:
"and that which culminates in direct experience."

Fearing that the statement "This realization is not [attained] by logic" might be taken as a prohibition of reasoning (*tarka*) due to its being an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), he says "The Śruti also... to show that this is not so, because it would contradict an injunction.
Having thus raised the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), the systematic concordance (*samanvaya*) of the Vedānta texts—which maintain that the conscious Brahman is the cause—is established.

In the doubt as to whether [the proposition] "earth and so forth do not have consciousness as their material cause, because they are effects that are substances, like a jar" contradicts the logic of Sāṃkhya and Yoga or not— given that Smṛti is weak due to the absence of a source, while inference is stronger because it is rooted in pervasion (vyāpti)— it is indeed contradicted by that [inference].
Thus, he presents the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) by means of a counter-example:
"Not so, because of the difference in nature" (na vilakṣaṇatvāt). In this way, the establishment of the concordance (samanvaya) between the preceding and succeeding positions [is challenged].
And the establishment of that [point] results in the same consequence as before:
the world does not have Brahman as its material cause,
because it possesses characteristics different from that [Brahman].
Whatever is of a different character than something else is not of that same material cause; for example, necklaces and the like, which are of a different character than clay.
Pleasure, pain, and delusion are [the qualities of] *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* respectively.
And likewise, the world—consisting of pleasure, pain, and delusion—has a common nature as its material cause, because it is permeated by that [nature];
for whatever is thus [permeated] is so [in its cause], just as jars and other objects are permeated by clay; thus he says:
"By clay alone," etc.,
establishes its dissimilarity;
"and its dissimilarity from Brahman," etc., does the same.
For just as a single female body produces pleasure, distress, dejection, and so forth for her husband, co-wives, and paramours,
so too should other phenomena be understood.
In this context, "pleasure" (prīti) is happiness (sukha).
Paritāpa is grief;
viṣāda is delusion;
by the word "etcetera," passion and so forth are included.

One might object that it is incorrect to claim there can be no relationship of benefactor and beneficiary because both are equal in being conscious, since such a relationship is seen to exist between a master and a servant despite both being conscious; thus he raises the objection: "But even though [the self] is conscious... and so forth.
He states with the words beginning "no," etc., that there is no deviation [from the rule] because the body of a servant indeed benefits the consciousness of the master.
He further states that because conscious beings are devoid of increase or decrease, they do not stand in a relationship of mutual benefit.
"Unsurpassed" means because of its being a benefactor.
By the force of the fact that the world has consciousness as its material cause, as heard in scripture, he sets forth the view of a certain school: that the world is indeed conscious.
Regarding the phrase "even that which":
since the sentience of jars and the like is sublated by non-perception, he says: "But the non-apprehension... etc.
The meaning is that consciousness (caitanya), although existing, is not perceived because the internal organs (antaḥkaraṇa) have not undergone modification (pariṇāma).
The point is that the manifestation of consciousness occurs only when there is the coloring by a mental modification (vṛttyuparāga) from something other than the internal organ, and not otherwise.
As for the illustration regarding the non-manifestation of consciousness in the absence of a mental modification:
Regarding the word "yathā" (as):
since both the self and the non-self are conscious, from what cause does the relationship of owner and owned arise? To this, he says:
"Precisely from this."
Even though they are equal, there is an illustration for their status as that which is to be served (śeṣitva) based on the specific distinction of their individual natures—
namely, "just as" (yathā ca).
To the question of how the distinction between the conscious and the unconscious [can exist], he says:
"By distinction" means by the manifestation or non-manifestation of consciousness.
Having accepted the position of a certain partisan that everything is conscious, the Sāṃkhya offers this rebuttal:
He also addresses this by saying "in some way," and having abandoned his initial admission, he refutes it with the remainder of the sūtra,
beginning with "And not... and so forth.
Furthermore, the meaning of the word *tathātva* (suchness) is the distinction consisting in being conscious or unconscious;
the sense is that presumptive testimony (*śrutārthāpatti*) is sublated by the verbal testimony (*śabda*). //4//
But there is a designation of the presiding deity, on account of distinction and following after. (BS 2.1.5)
He raises an objection—intended as the point to be refuted by the subsequent sūtra—to the effect that [the Smṛti] is not contradicted because it is supported by Śruti:
"But surely...
Since the Śruti passages concerning clay and so forth refer to the presiding deities (abhimānin) of those elements, [they do not contradict the Smṛti].

To this, the Sāṃkhya replies— stating "the conceited one"— that it is not proper for the expression "consciousness and unconsciousness" (*vijñānaṃ cāvijñānaṃ ca*) to have a figurative meaning when it denotes the distinction between the conscious and the unconscious;
for "conversing" means disputing.
The meaning is that neither mere elements (*bhūta*) nor mere sense-faculties (*indriya*) are designated as conscious,
because that would contradict the distinctions well-established in common worldly usage and the Vedas.
He states another meaning for the word "particular" (*viśeṣa*):

The phrase "api ca" (furthermore) means that because the vital breaths (*prāṇas*)— previously described as "disputing for their own respective excellence for the sake of self-superiority"— are qualified by the term *devatā*, which denotes sentient beings, the words "prāṇa" and so forth refer to the presiding deities (*abhimānin*).
The meaning is that, having recognized the highest good (*niḥśreyasa*), that is, preeminence (*śraiṣṭhya*), in the vital breath, they became dependent upon the vital breath.
He explains "anugati" in various ways— as "anugatāśca" (and those that have followed)—
for the sake of that vital breath.

The offering of oblations (*baliharaṇa*) by means of speech and so forth was performed as a surrender of one's own qualities, such as being Vasiṣṭha; however, the observation of "splendor" (*tejas*) and so forth must be understood as having been explained by you yourself in the *Īkṣatyadhikaraṇa* as residing in a conscious being—this is the meaning.
"Since the world lacks consciousness, therefore... is the conclusion of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*). //5//
But it is indeed seen. (BBs 2.1.6)
Is it any kind of dissimilarity that serves as the reason, or is it a great dissimilarity?
Regarding the first case, he states an instance of deviation (vyabhicāra):
"This is not an absolute rule;
for it is observed [otherwise].
He raises the following objection: "Since the reason (hetu) is non-existent, there is no deviation (vyabhicāra)."
Regarding the word "nanu":
since there is some slight difference [between the two], he states "it is said" to show that there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*).
The meaning is that there exists a distinction between the body and its hair and so forth, characterized by being sentient and non-sentient respectively.
Regarding the second [reason] as well, he points out a deviation (vyabhicāra) in that very same context with the words "the Great [Self]" (mahān).
The transformative [cause] means that hair and so forth consist of a transformation inherent within themselves. Furthermore,
regarding those two things between which there is a relationship of material cause and effect, one who asserts their similarity must state whether that similarity is absolute or merely partial.
He states the fault in the first case with the words "absolutely" (*atyanta*).
Having raised the second objection, he says that since both Brahman and the world possess that existence, their relationship as material cause and effect (*prakṛti-vikṛtitva*) is established.
With the words beginning with "atha" (now),
having analyzed the state of being dissimilar, he states another refutation with the words beginning with "vilakṣaṇatvena" (by way of dissimilarity).

In the position that the world is not an effect of Brahman because it does not follow the nature of Brahman—such as consciousness and so forth—and yet everything is identical [to it], it would be asserted that there is a relationship of material cause and modification (*prakṛti-vikāra-bhāva*) despite total similarity; to show that this is inconsistent, he says:
"First... (prathama iti).
Regarding the third [point], however, there is an absence of an illustrative example (dṛṣṭānta).
Nor should it be argued that there exists an illustrative example such as "the world does not have Brahman as its material cause because it is insentient, like ignorance" (avidyāvat);
for [insentience] is a limiting adjunct (upādhi) due to its being beginningless (anāditva).

Nor is there a lack of pervasion of the probandum (*sādhya*) by destruction (*dhvaṃsa*), because that too, being of the nature of an effect and a latent impression (*saṃskāra*), is an entity (*bhāva*) and thus has Brahman as its material cause; furthermore, if it is not grasped as a non-entity (*abhāva*), then "being an eternal entity" (*anādibhāvatva*) serves as the limiting condition (*upādhi*). Now, he states the defect common to all three alternatives:
He introduces [the next section] by restating what was previously said; he states that there can be no objection based on reasoning because Brahman cannot be the object of dry logic,
beginning with the words "As for what was said," and so forth.

Because it lacks the grounds for application such as a characteristic mark (*liṅga*), similarity (*sādṛśya*), or a word's primary denotation (*padapravṛttinimitta*), Brahman is not within the scope of inference, comparison, or verbal testimony;
the meaning is that Brahman is to be known solely through the Veda by way of indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
This understanding regarding Brahman is not to be removed by independent reasoning, nor is it to be produced [by it].
Or rather, it should not be subverted by fallacious reasoning;
the understanding taught by a teacher who knows the Veda—other than a mere sophist—leads to right knowledge, to experience, and to its fruit.
"O dearest one," "O most beloved one"—these are the words of Death addressed to Naciketas.
Who indeed knows directly—that from which this manifold creation has come forth on all sides? Let alone knowing it; who here in this world has declared it, who has proclaimed it?
The lengthening and elision [of vowels] are Vedic;
the meaning is that there is not even one who can describe me as I truly am. They do not know my origin (prabhavam), because, being the source of all, I have no birth.
"Under the guise" means under the pretext of the method of reflection.
"Dry" means independent of the sacred revelation (śruti).

When the reality has been ascertained through the sacred revelation, that which is subsequently adopted for the purpose of removing doubts regarding human defects and the like is "supported by the sacred revelation."
Regarding this, he says: "In the state of dream" (*svapnānte*).

It is impossible for the individual soul (*jīva*), which possesses various states and is joined with the manifold world (*prapañca*) of the body and so forth, to attain identity with Brahman, who is devoid of all manifoldness.

When there arises a lack of conviction regarding the meaning of the Śruti— namely, that the non-duality of Brahman is untenable because it contradicts the validity of the means of knowledge that apprehend duality—
in order to dispel that [doubt], [the text shows] that the Self, which persists through all its states, is not followed by and is untouched by those fluctuating states;

for if the states were inherent, they could not fail to deviate from the Self, just as heat cannot fail to deviate from fire, and thus the absence of the illusion of the phenomenal world in deep sleep would be impossible if [the world] were non-existent.

The meaning is as follows: when [the teacher] says "My dear," the possibility of identity with Brahman, which is devoid of phenomenal expansion (*niṣprapañca*), arises from the perception of non-difference;
thus, reasoning such as "just as jars and other objects are non-different from clay, so too the world is non-different from Brahman because it is born from it" is resorted to.
The point is that since no other kind of reasoning enters into this matter of Brahman, and since this [kind of reasoning] is favorable, there is no room for an objection based on reasoning.
He states that dry logic has no access to Brahman and that [the teaching] is in accord with the Sūtras by saying:
"Because reasoning is unestablished."
Deceptiveness means the state of not being a means of valid knowledge.

As for the objection raised by the Sāṃkhya against the proponent of a single school (ekadeśin)— namely, that if it were asserted that the entire world is conscious, the scriptural teaching of differentiation would be untenable—
that is not correct.
In that regard, for that partial proponent (ekadeśin), it is possible to reconcile the scriptural mention of a distinction between consciousness and its manifestation or non-manifestation.

However, for the Sāṃkhya, this objection becomes like an adamantine coating (vajralepa), because if everything were an effect of the Pradhāna, all would be insentient, and thus a distinction between sentient and insentient effects would be impossible; thus he says:
With the words "Even he who... and so forth, [the author] addresses the question:
"If, in the established doctrine (siddhānta), a distinction between the conscious and the unconscious is admitted, how can Brahman be the material cause (prakṛti)? To this, he says:
"Because it has already been refuted."
The meaning is that [the objection] has been refuted by the two reasons of being non-conclusive and being deviant. //6//
If it be argued that [the world] is non-existent, we say no, because [the scripture] is merely a negation. (BS 2.1.7)

Anticipating the objection that the effect must be non-existent prior to its production because it is impossible for it to exist in the form of its own contradictory cause— which would result in the fallacy of contradicting one's own tenets— he provides the following resolution, beginning with the words "If it be argued that it is non-existent," etc.: since the effect is illusory (mithyā), its existence in the form of the cause throughout the three periods of time is not contradictory.
The meaning is that the negation of existence [expressed by] "because it is non-existent" is purposeless.
To show that there is no reality in the effect, he cites scripture: "All that... [etc.].
Having restated the doubt of one who does not understand falsity (*mithyātva*), he refutes it with the words beginning "nanu" and so forth;
and this has been explained at length.
The meaning is "falsehood. //7//
At the time of reabsorption, [the world] would follow the same [consequences] as that; therefore, [the doctrine] is inconsistent. (BS 2.1.8)

He explains the sūtra that raises an objection for the sake of establishing the theory of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*), namely that if the cause is non-different from the effect, it would follow that the cause is also impure and so forth, just like the effect— introducing it with "here he says.
This is the explanation of the term *pratisaṃsṛjyamāna*.
Regarding the word "kāraṇe" (in the cause):
the meaning is that it is just as a substance of salt, when dissolving in water, vitiates the water.
He states another interpretation of the Sūtra:
"Moreover" (apica): the meaning is that upon the dissolution of every effect, there would follow the consequence of its becoming uniform in nature, like its cause.
He states another point:

"Moreover" (api ca): the meaning is that since the causes of production—such as karma and so forth—exist even during dissolution, there would follow the undesirable consequence that liberated beings, like those who are still experiencing [karma], would also be produced upon rebirth.
He states another interpretation preceded by a doubt:

Regarding the word "atha": if the effect were distinct from the cause even at the time of dissolution, then—just as during the period of maintenance—there would follow the consequence of the absence of dissolution, and because of the resulting duality with the effect, this view would be inconsistent. This is the meaning. //8//
But it is not so, because of the existence of examples. (BBs 2.1.9)

He explains the sūtra of the established conclusion (*siddhāntasūtra*), which states: "Upon dissolution, the world does not defile its own cause, because it is merged within that cause, just as blue pots and the like do not defile clay and the like."
By the words "naiva" and so forth: "apigacchat" means dissolving;
the state of differentiation is the period of persistence.
Regarding the phrase "of your position":
the statement that sweet water is not a cause for saltiness is not a valid example.
Furthermore, he says that if it were a defecting factor, the effect would persist like salt.
"Or rather, it is non-existence itself.

The meaning is that when the effect does not exist, a connection of the cause with its properties is not possible; for when the substratum (dharmin) is absent, its properties (dharmas) are also absent.

Now, one might object that in the theory of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*), even during dissolution, the effect exists as non-different from its cause, and thus [the objection] would remain a defect; to this he says:
"Even though there is non-difference" (*ananyatve ’pi*).

The meaning is this: while the superimposed [effect] possesses the attributes of its substratum due to their non-difference, the substratum does not possess the attributes of the superimposed effect, because the substratum has an existence distinct from the effect.
He answers by means of a counter-objection, stating that even so, the qualification "even though" (kiñcāpi) is redundant:
"And it is too little," etc.
Having explained the example of transformation (pariṇāma), he explains the example of illusory appearance (vivarta).
Regarding the phrase "asti ca":
because he is dissatisfied with the notion that illusion has no material cause (*anupādāna*), he states another example,
beginning with "yathā" (just as).
Since there is indeed a perceived contact during the time of dreaming, he says "upon awakening" (*prabodha*).
The meaning is that because the self is untouched by the dream both in the waking and deep-sleep states, it is likewise untouched at that [dream] time.

If there is no contact with the states of the individual soul (jīva) during sacrifice, then what need is there to speak of the Omniscient One? Thus he states the point of application (*dārṣṭāntika*) with the word "evam" (thus).
Alternatively, the three states of the Lord (*īśvara*) are the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the waking world.
Regarding that state of non-attachment, he cites the consensus of the elders, saying:
"It is said here.

The meaning is that when one awakens at the time of the instruction "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*) and abandons the sleep of *māyā*, one then experiences the Lord as one's own Self—non-dual and devoid of the states of birth, dissolution, and persistence.
He states the conclusion with the word "therein" (tatra).
Having restated the second inconsistency, he refutes it by means of that very same Sūtra:
Regarding the phrase "yatpunar" (as for what more):
he states the scriptural authority (*śruti*) for the existence of ignorance during deep sleep (*suṣupti*) and for the subsequent arising of differentiation, with the words "and scripture."
The statement that they "do not know" while Brahman exists as one is an expression of ignorance (*ajñāna*).

The statement regarding their differentiation refers to the fact that prior to deep sleep (*suṣupti*) and upon awakening, they become divided by means of birth and so forth, and at the time of subsequent rising, they become exactly as they were before.

Now, one might ask: even if the power of differentiation and ignorance exist during deep sleep, how can their existence be established in the case of the universal dissolution (*sarvapralaya*)? To this, he says:
Regarding the phrase "just as":

just as in deep sleep, even though all effects are undifferentiated within the Supreme Self, there exists the power of ignorance which is the cause for their subsequent differentiation; so too, even during the dissolution—the great pralaya—one may infer the power for the differentiation of creation again, due to the connection with illusory ignorance.
Since the conventional practice of differentiation, which is the effect of false knowledge, remains now uncontradicted— like a dream— due to the absence of the awakening to reality,
the meaning is that the existence of the cause is established by the observation of its effect.

The underlying sense is that because the power of ignorance (avidyā-śakti) persists even during the great dissolution (mahāpralaya), there is a necessity for the rebirth of ignorant individual souls (jīvas).
"By this" means by the absence of the power of knowledge that serves as the cause of birth. //9//
And because of the faults in one's own position. (BBs 2.1.10)
He states that "since defects such as heterogeneity (vailakṣaṇya) and so forth apply even to the Sāṃkhya position, we need not exert ourselves to refute them" by saying "svapakṣa...
He then explains the sūtra:
"His own" means they would become manifest;
"for this very reason."

It should be understood that this fault belongs only to the Sāṃkhya, for whom the effect is real, because it is impossible for that which is real to exist in the form of a cause opposed to it; it does not belong to the proponent of the falsity of the effect (*kāryamithyātvavādin*).
He states the fourfold fault mentioned in the Sūtra "apītau" (at the time of reabsorption) with the words:
"tathāpītāv" (likewise at the time of reabsorption).
It follows that the Pradhāna, like its effects, would possess form and other qualities;
there would be no restriction as to which karma and so forth constitute its material cause or what is to be enjoyed by it;
and the distinction between the bound and the liberated would be untenable.

If it is argued that for the sake of establishing distinctions, the specific aggregates of the liberated dissolve into the Pradhāna while the distinctions of the bound do not dissolve, then the consequence is that those which have not dissolved would lack the status of being effects, just like the Puruṣa;
this is the meaning. //10//
Because reasoning is not firmly established, if it is argued that the object can be inferred otherwise, even so, there follows the consequence of the impossibility of liberation. 2.1.11.
Furthermore, since reasoning (*tarka*) is subject to the possibility of error, the faultless systematic harmony (*samanvaya*) of the Vedānta is not sublated by it; thus he says:
"Also because of the instability of reasoning.
He raises an objection, suggesting that even though human intellects are diverse, one might place trust in the reasoning of Kapila because of his omniscience:
Regarding the word "atha":
he offers a rebuttal according to the maxim, "If Kapila is omniscient, what proof is there that Kaṇāda is not?"—
namely, "even so."
He explains the portion of the doubt situated within the Sūtra with the words, "Now it might be said" (*athocyeta*).

The meaning is that even if reasoning (*tarka*) based on dissimilarity (*vilakṣaṇatva*) and so forth is unstable, some reasoning endowed with both pervasion (*vyāpti*) and presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) will be established; by that [reasoning], the Pradhāna can be inferred.

[Objection: But surely that [inference] is also non-conclusive (apratiṣṭhita), because it belongs to the class of reasoning (tarka), just like [the arguments concerning] being of a different nature and so forth.
To this he says: "Not so" (na hi).
Regarding the phrase "because it belongs to the class of reasoning": is reasoning itself conclusive or not?
In the first case, there is a deviation (vyabhicāra) because the probandum—non-foundation—is absent in that very instance.
Regarding the second case as well, one who intends to show that not all reasonings lack foundation due to the absence of a logical ground says:
"This too... [etadapi].

Furthermore, he states that there is no lack of foundation [for tarka], because it serves as the cause for the worldly activities of engagement and withdrawal, consisting as it does of an inference toward the accomplishment of the desired (iṣṭasādhana), such as: "Whatever has a future ripening is a means to accomplish the desired, because it possesses ripening, like past ripening," and so forth.
Regarding the term *sarvatarka* (all-inclusive reasoning): the "object" (*viṣaya*) refers to things such as cooking and eating, or consuming poison and so forth.

By means of the generality (*sāmānya*) of those—such as "the state of being cooked" (*pākatva*)—one infers that future objects like cooking will be causes of pleasure or pain; it is through this inference that activity (*pravṛtti*) and so forth occur. This is the meaning.

Furthermore, since the determination of the intended meaning of a statement is accomplished through reasoning (*tarka*) alone in both the Pūrva and Uttara Mīmāṃsās, he says "śrutyartha... [to show that] reasoning is well-established.
He also states that Manu considers certain types of reasoning to be established:
"Manu says":
[this refers to] the purification of dharma, which is the determination of its distinction from adharma.
He acknowledges that some forms of reasoning lack a firm foundation:
"This very [reasoning]"—
the sense is that if all reasonings were to lack a foundation, there would be no prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa) at all;
for like the reasoning of the prima facie position, the reasoning of the established conclusion (siddhānta) would likewise be without a foundation.
He mocks the one who says "because there is no difference in being reasoning" with the words "Not so.
Even if reasoning is established in some cases, there is no independence of reasoning regarding the specific cause of the world; thus he explains the remainder of the Sūtra.
By the words "even though" and so forth:
the extreme profundity of Brahman is its being inaccessible to means of knowledge other than the Vedas;
the true nature of the entity that is the cause of the world is its non-duality (*advayatva*).
That which is bound to liberation has liberation as its objective support. He shows that Brahman cannot be reached by anything other than the Vedas with the words "from form" (rūpāt).
He states another point—namely, that "non-liberation" means the absence of liberation—by means of the passage beginning with "Moreover" (*apica*). He asks:
even if the knowledge of an object of a single form is correct knowledge (*samyagjñāna*), why could it not be produced by reasoning (*tarka*)? To this, he replies:

"In that case, such being the situation" means that because cognitions arising from reasoning (tarka) contradict one another, they do not constitute right knowledge (samyagjñāna); for contradiction is incompatible with right knowledge.
The construction is as follows: how could that which arises from *tarka* (speculative reasoning) be right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*), since its object is not established as having a single form?
Anticipating the objection that "surely that knowledge is right because Sāṃkhya is the most excellent," he states the non-establishment of the reason: "And not [from] the *pradhāna*... etc.
Now, one might object: "Surely the intellect arising from reasoning determined by all logicians joined together is the cause of liberation"; to this he says:
"And they cannot [be so].
Therefore, since liberation is impossible through knowledge arising from reasoning, it is not proper to subvert the harmony of the Vedānta texts by means of reasoning.

He concludes the meaning of the portion of the Sūtra—"because, if that were sublated, there would be no attainment of right knowledge, resulting in the consequence of non-liberation"—with the words "therefore, elsewhere.

He then concludes the meaning of the entire section (adhikaraṇa), which is the result of the fact that the harmony [of the Vedas] is not contradicted by reasoning, with the words: "Therefore, elsewhere..."
Therefore, it is based on scripture. //11//
By this, those doctrines not accepted by the learned (*śiṣṭa*) are also explained. (BS 2.1.12)
The subject matter is the Vedāntic harmony which asserts that Brahman is the material cause of the world.

When there arises a doubt as to whether this is contradicted by the logic of the Vaiśeṣikas and others—namely, the principle that "whatever is all-pervading cannot be the material cause of a substance"—the conclusion is that it is indeed contradicted;
for although the elder Sāṃkhyas may lack skill in reasoning, the Vaiśeṣikas and others are renowned for their proficiency in logical thought, and thus their principles remain unrefuted.
Having reached this conclusion by means of the counter-example, he extends the principle with the words "by this [same reasoning]";
the result is as before.

One might object: "Why has the teaching of the Sāṃkhya doctrine been treated as an extension (atideśa) of the Tārkika doctrine, when the reverse could just as well have occurred? Anticipating this doubt, [the author] states the reason for the relationship of teaching and extension between the preceding and succeeding sections: "Of the Vedic...

[The Sāṃkhya system] is proximate to the Vedānta scripture in its aspects such as the reality of the effect (*satkāryatva*), the soul's detachment (*ātmāsaṅgatva*), and self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*).

The doctrine of Pradhāna (Prakṛti) was accepted by the learned, such as Devala and others, insofar as it maintains the "pre-existence of the effect" (*satkāryatva*); thus, because of its strength, it is explicitly taught.
The intention is that the doctrines of atoms (*aṇu*) and so forth are merely extended [by analogy] because they lack a foundation and are weak.
He states that there is no need to ask what the reason for their refutation is: [He says: "There is no need to ask what the cause for the refutation is."
"Because of their equality. He states the reason itself:
"It is equal."

Regarding the statement that Brahman cannot be the material cause of substances because of its omnipresence (*vibhutva*), it should be understood that this is refuted by Scripture (*śruti*), which must be accepted as the means of establishing the subject (*pakṣasādhaka*).

Furthermore, it should be observed that "omnipresence"— defined here as possessing great magnitude (*mahāparimāṇavattva*) consisting in connection with all things— is unestablished in the case of Brahman, which is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*).
Therefore, it is established that there is no contradiction between the doctrine of universal harmony (*samanvaya*) and the logic of the dialecticians. //12//
If it be argued that there is no distinction because of the identity of the enjoyer, [we reply] that this would be as in the world. (BS 2.1.13)

The subject matter is the harmony of the Vedānta texts which teaches that the creation and so forth of the universe proceed from the non-dual Brahman. Regarding the doubt as to whether this is contradicted by perception of difference and other means of knowledge supported by reasoning— such as the argument that whatever is mutually distinct is not non-different from its non-dual cause, like a jar and a cloth produced from clay and thread— the [objection] is raised that reasoning has no firm foundation regarding Brahman.

He raises the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) that [the doctrine of non-duality] is contradicted because it is established upon the distinction of the world— [this being expressed in the sūtra] "Because of the attainment of the state of the enjoyer" (*bhokrāpatti*).
The result of the prima facie argument is that non-duality is not established due to this contradiction.

The distinction is that its establishment occurs in the final conclusion (siddhānta). He raises an objection— beginning with "Even though"— on the grounds that what was stated previously, namely that an objection via reasoning (tarka) is not appropriate because the determination of the meaning of the scriptures is independent [of reasoning], is being challenged here.
There is no sublation [of a scriptural meaning] when that meaning of scripture is not amenable to other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

However, as for the non-difference of earth, water, and so forth from the non-dual Brahman—which is the subject of the scriptural teaching that Brahman is the material cause—that is just like the meaning of the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) "The sacrificial post is the sun"; it is indeed amenable to other means of knowledge and is therefore set aside by the means of knowledge that establish duality.
Thus he provides the resolution.
"Nevertheless" (*tathāpi*):
"having another purpose" (*anyaparatva*) means having a figurative sense (*gauṇārthakatva*).
He states that there is an objection based on reasoning because reasoning is well-established regarding the difference of the world within its own domain: [he says...]

"Reasoning (tarka) also"—this means that even if reasoning and the like possess authority regarding duality, [the opponent] raises the objection: "What follows from this? in response to the question of what contradiction there could be for the harmony (samanvaya) [of the Vedas] on that account.
The proponent (pūrvapakṣin) replies with the words "ataḥ" (therefore):
since reasoning and the like possess validity, it is improper for the Śruti to sublate duality; thus, the meaning is that the sublation of the non-dual harmony (advaita-samanvaya) is logical.
This [verse] clarifies the point by means of a doubt, beginning with "How so? and so forth.
Now, raising the objection—"But by whom was the mutual identity of the enjoyer and the enjoyed stated?"—he replies by means of the presumption based on the meaning of scripture (*śrutārthāpatti*).
Regarding the phrase "of the two":
because it is heard in scripture that those two are non-different from the one Brahman, their identity is postulated;
for if there were a difference between two things that are non-different from one [Brahman], it would follow that even that one [Brahman] would possess difference.
And thus, the meaning is that difference would be sublated;
he precludes the acceptance of this as a desired consequence with the words "na cāsya" (nor of this).
The meaning is that since the scripture (śruti) has scope as a figurative statement, it is not logical for it to sublate non-contingent (niravakāśa) dualistic means of knowledge.
[Objection: But surely, because division is a recent phenomenon, it is sublated by the beginningless scripture of non-duality; to this, he says:
"Just as... (yathā).

The meaning is that the distinction [between the enjoyer and so forth] is beginningless and endless, based on the following inference: "The past and future times are the substrata for the distinctions such as the enjoyer, because they are time, just like the present time."
This being the case, he states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) by means of the analogy of transformation (*pariṇāma*), though it may appear superficially:
"It may be as in the world" (*syāl lokavat*).
Even in the case of the illustration, how is there a mutual distinction among the transformations that are non-different from the single ocean?

Or, having raised the objection as to how these [individuals] can be non-different from the One when they are distinct, he says "nor" (na ca), according to the maxim that "there is no invalidation by what is perceived. Thus,
he states that there is mutual difference between the enjoyer and the enjoyed, yet non-difference from Brahman.
Regarding the phrase "in this way here":
one raises the objection that there is a disparity between the illustration and the case at hand because the individual soul (*jīva*) is not a modification (*vikāra*) of Brahman—
this is expressed by the words "even though" (*yadyapi*).
He states that there is birth conditioned by limiting adjuncts (*aupādhika*), which is analogous to waves and so forth,
with the words "nevertheless" (*tathāpi*). Here,
"birth" (*janma*) means differentiation (*vibhāga*).
Alternatively, the solution has already been stated by the word "even so" (tathāpi).
To the objection—"But how can there be a division of the enjoyer in each body?"—he says:
"of that which has entered into the effect."
He concludes the result of the division based on limiting adjuncts with the words "therefore" (*ityataḥ*).

The meaning is that even though the enjoyer and so forth are non-different from the one Brahman, since their difference is accepted as being like that of waves and the like, there is no contradiction of the monistic synthesis (*advaita-samanvaya*) by the evidence of duality. //13//
The non-difference of that [effect] from [the cause] follows from such terms as "originating" (ārambhaṇa) and others. (BS 2.1.14)
In the very same prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), he states the primary solution by means of the theory of illusory manifestation (*vivartavāda*): "That non-difference...

While stating the connection as having the same subject matter, he declares the difference in meaning between the two solutions based on their respective reliance upon transformation (*pariṇāma*) and illusory manifestation (*vivarta*).
"Having accepted" means:

having admitted the general validity (*utsargika-prāmāṇya*) of perception and the other means of knowledge, difference and non-difference were stated by means of the analogy of transformation for the sake of satisfying those of dull intellect;
now, that admitted validity—
The sense is that [the non-dual scripture] is established as being merely conventional by depriving it of its status as revealing ultimate reality;
thus, there is no sublation of the non-dual scripture by the means of knowledge that apprehend the duality of illusion,
because one perceives a duality such as a staff or a garland in a single rope— this is the primary resolution.

Thus, in order to establish that there is no contradiction with the non-dualistic synthesis (*advaita-samanvaya*), he proves the falsity of duality [with the words] "because of those two" (*yasmāt tayoh*).
[An objection is raised: "If there were identity of essential nature (*svarūpa-ekya*), the relationship of cause and effect would be contradicted"; to this, he says:
"By way of distinction" (vyatirekeṇa) means that the effect's lack of existence apart from the cause is being established, not its identity [with it].
He applies the Śruti passage— meaning that the modification is a mere name beginning with speech, and does not exist apart from the cause— to clarify the sense of the word "only" (eva).
"This has been said" refers to the preceding point. He states another meaning of the word "ārambhaṇa" with the words "furthermore."
The state of fire has departed; the cause alone has vanished.
The three forms of fire, water, and earth consist of the subtle element of form (*rūpa-tanmātra*), which is real.
Since even these consist of pure Being (*san-mātra*), the intention is that only "Being" remains.
He states that "there would be a contradiction of the proposition" (*pratijñābādha*) if the living being (*jīva*) and the body (*gaja*) were different from Brahman—
expressing this with the words "nor otherwise" (*na cānyathā*).
He then provides two examples in sequence to show their non-difference (*ananyatva*):
"Therefore, just as" means by the force of the proposition (*pratijñā*).

The connection is as follows: that which is perceived (*dṛṣṭa*), which is conventional (*prātītika*), destroyed, and impermanent—because its own nature (*svarūpa*) is thus indescribable (*anupākhyatva*) and devoid of existence and manifestation (*sattāsphūrtiśūnyatva*), it is non-different (*ananya*).
Having stated his own view of pure non-duality (*śuddhādvaita*), he raises the doctrine of difference-and-non-difference (*bhedābheda*) with the words "nanu" (now, however).
The meaning is that [Brahman] is endowed with numerous powers (*śakti*), along with their dependent primordial natures (*prakṛti*), and their transformations (*pariṇāma*).

Thinking that in the view of difference-and-non-difference (*bhedābheda*) all systematic arrangements are established, whereas in absolute non-difference there is a sublation of the means of knowledge for duality, [the author] refutes it, saying:
"It could not be so.

The meaning is that because the existence of modifications is denied by the word "only" (*eva*) and the phrase "originating from speech" (*vācārambhaṇa*), the theory of transformation (*pariṇāmavāda*) is outside the scope of the Śruti.

Furthermore, he states "That is the Self" (*sa ātmā*) to show that if saṃsāra were real, there could be no instruction regarding the identity of the individual soul (jīva), who is qualified by it, with Brahman, because of their contradiction.

Anticipating the objection that this unity is to be accomplished through the combination of knowledge and action (*jñāna-karma-samuccaya*) for the sake of instruction, he says "not so," because that would contradict the word "art" (*asi*).
Regarding the word "itself" (*svayam*):
because it is sublated by the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), transmigratory existence (*saṃsāritva*) is false;
thus he says, "And therefore" (*ataśca*).
The meaning is: "because of instruction established by itself.
As for what was said—that plurality is real for the sake of conventional usage—is that [plurality] for the sake of conventional usage subsequent to knowledge, or prior to it?
He says "not today" and so forth, [explaining] "and when sublated":
here, *svabhāva* (intrinsic nature) refers to ignorance; that which is produced by it is "natural" (*svābhāvika*).
The meaning is that since the conventional usage of "subject" (*pramātṛ*) and so forth does not exist after [the attainment of] knowledge, multiplicity (*nānātva*) is not to be postulated.
Nor is the second [alternative] tenable; for if conventional usage is established by means of a multiplicity postulated prior to knowledge, the reality of that multiplicity remains unproven.
As for the claim that the empirical usage of "being a knower" and so forth is indeed real and merely ceases in the state of liberation—that is not so;
thus he says:
"And this is not... (na cāyam).
If saṃsāra were real, the soul’s state of being Brahman would not exist in that condition,
because identity and difference are contradictory in one and the same place at one time.
Therefore, since the non-difference of the transmigrating soul from Brahman is understood to be eternal, the meaning is that saṃsāra itself is merely illusory.
Furthermore, just as in the world a certain person seized by soldiers under the suspicion of being a thief, if he speaks falsely when taking up a heated axe, is burned and bound;

likewise, the proponent of manifoldness (nānātva) is burned. But if he speaks the truth, he is not burned and is released. Similarly, one who perceives unity—realizing "all this has that as its self" (tad ātmakam)—is released. Thus, by means of the scriptural illustration, he declares that unity is real and manifoldness is false.
"Thieves," etc.
This refers to the sphere of conventional discourse, which is the basis for the conventional usage of multiplicity.
By censuring multiplicity, he states that unity alone is the truth:
Regarding the phrase "from death":

furthermore, in this doctrine of both difference and non-difference (*bhedābheda*), liberation is held to result from the cessation of the cognition of difference through the knowledge of the non-difference of the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman; however, that is not tenable, because it is not admitted that the cognition of difference is an error (*bhrama*).
He says, "And not in this [case]," because one valid cognition is not sublated by another valid cognition;
the implication is that the opposite could also be possible.

Now, he reveals the seed of the prima facie argument— that the reality of multiplicity follows from the impossibility of otherwise accounting for the validity of perception and other means of knowledge—
starting with the words "But surely" (nanu) and so forth.
"The absolute oneness" (ekatvaikāntaḥ) refers to its exclusivity (kaivalyam).
The [scriptural] authorities would be sublated and become non-authoritative.

The sense is that it is appropriate for the Vedāntas to have as their purport both difference and non-difference, so as to preserve the authority of perception and other means of knowledge upon which they depend. Now, one might object: "Since the ritual (karma) and knowledge (jñāna) sections proceed by relying on an imagined difference among the factors of action—such as the sacrificers in the former and the disciples in the latter—and since there is no sublation of their own objects of cognition, such as dharma and so forth, their authority remains unimpeded. Anticipating this, he says:
And how [is it] "by means of falsehood"?
The sense is that there would be a sublation of the object of knowledge (*prameya-bādhā*), just as in the case of fire inferred from smoke imagined by dust.

In that regard, he states that for the dualistic sphere, the empirical validity (*vyāvahārika-prāmāṇya*) of perception and the other means of knowledge is established as long as there is no sublation.
It is said in response to this, beginning with "atrocyate":
truthfulness is the absence of sublation;
sublation is the ascertainment of falsity.

In reality, although modifications (*vikāra*) are false, because there is no certainty of that [falsity] regarding them, the empirical functioning of perception and so forth is possible; he explains the aforementioned illustration with the words: "as for an ordinary person while asleep.

Thus, having established that the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding duality possess a transactional validity (*vyāvahārikaprāmāṇya*)—meaning they convey objects free from sublation during the time of empirical usage—[the author proceeds].

In order to establish that the Vedāntas, which are the means of knowledge for duality, possess ultimate validity (*tāttvika-prāmāṇya*) by virtue of making known Brahman—which is free from sublation at all times—the author restates the aforementioned doubt:
"But how [can it be] through the unreal?
Does it mean that the real is not produced from the unreal?
How much less could there be knowledge of the Truth?
As for the first [alternative], that is indeed accepted;
for we do not maintain that the knowledge arising from the sentence is itself the Truth.
Having accepted the illustration, he says:
"This is not a fault.
