The meaning is that there is no fixed rule that the real cannot arise from the unreal, because we observe that even in one who has not been bitten by a snake, there may occur death, fainting, and so forth, which are real, resulting from poison imagined through the delusion of having been bitten.
He states another example with the words "svapne" (in a dream):

the meaning is that there is a deviation [from the rule] because we observe from unreal things such as a snake or its belly the effect of real knowledge, such as the cognition of being bitten or bathing.
Taking up what has been heard, he raises an objection:
"That effect also... He clarifies the point already stated:
Regarding this, [the author] says "tatra brūmaḥ" (to this we reply), and so forth.

"Avagati" (realization) is the mental modification (vṛtti); or, even though it is real like a jar or other objects, the meaning of the word "avagati" is consciousness (caitanya) manifested by the modification, which is the fruit of an object seen in a dream that is merely apparent (prātibhāsika).
He states that, as a consequence, the doctrine of the body being the self is also refuted:
Regarding the phrase "by this":
if the cognition occurring while in a dream were a property of the dream-body, then upon waking, there would be no reconnection of uncontradicted cognition in the form, "I experienced such a dream.
Therefore, since reconnection is observed despite the difference in bodies, the meaning is that the one who reconnects is distinct from the body.
He states that the second rule—that knowledge of the real does not arise from the unreal—is contradicted by scripture, saying:
"And so says the Śruti.
Nor should it be argued that even though women are unreal, the knowledge of a true prosperity arises from the sight of them because it originates from something real.

The point is that since even perception is false by virtue of being qualified by its object, it is possible for ignorance to exist regarding Brahman—which is real in this context—due to consciousness being associated with the false Veda.
Having stated the knowledge of the desired [truth] from the unreal, he states the knowledge of the undesired: "In the same way," etc.
Regarding the cognition of the real from the unreal, he states another illustration:
"In the same way, [from] the letter-forms (*ākāra*)," etc.
The meaning is that it is well known that the real letters *a* and so forth are cognized through the error of [perceiving] line-forms (*rekhā*) as being the letter-forms *a* and so forth.
Thus, by stating that the real arises from the unreal, the rule that "that which performs causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is real" is subverted;

and by stating that the real is known through the unreal, the universal concomitance (*vyāpti*)—namely, "whatever is apprehended through an unreal instrument is sublated, like fire inferred from a counterfeit sign"—is subverted.
Consequently, the meaning is that even though the Vedāntas are imagined (*kalpita*), it is possible for them to convey the real Brahman, and thus they possess ultimate validity (*prāmāṇya*).
As for what was said—that both [identity and difference] are real for the sake of establishing the conventional usage of unity and plurality—that is not so.
For it is impossible to postulate the reality of a difference that is already established by worldly consensus as being in contradiction with a non-difference that possesses an unprecedented result.
Furthermore, if the conventional usage of both were to occur simultaneously, then their reality might indeed be possible.
It is not so;

for by the final cognition of unity, which is independent [of other cognitions], plurality is sublated without remainder, just as silver is [sublated] by the cognition of mother-of-pearl. Thus he says:
Moreover, regarding the phrase "and yet it is the final [truth]":

one might object that the realization of oneness does not arise because it contradicts the non-dual means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) upon which it depends; therefore, he says: "And this [realization]..."

The meaning is that Śvetaketu indeed understood the reality of the Self from the words of his father, because the arising of knowledge is heard [in scripture] and because the causal conditions were present.

Relying upon the conventional distinction between teacher, disciple, and so forth, the comprehension of the meaning of the sentence being known depends upon the conventional validity residing in perception and other means of knowledge;
and that is not contradicted by the realization of ultimate oneness.

However, the sense is that because of its contradiction with that [non-dual knowledge], the real validity of perception and other means of knowledge—which cannot otherwise be subsisted upon—is sublated.
Furthermore, since the cognition of oneness possesses the status of a fruitful valid cognition (*pramā*), the fruitless delusion of duality must be sublated; thus he says: "And this... and so forth.

One might object: "If all duality is false, how can there be worldly conventions such as 'dream is false, waking is true,' and Vedic statements such as 'the true and the untrue became the True'? Anticipating this doubt, [the author] recalls the previously stated analogy of the dream to show that just as in a dream one conducts affairs based on what is sublated or not sublated at that time—thinking "this is true" and "this is untrue"—so too it is in this "long dream" [of worldly existence]. He states:
Regarding the phrase "and previously":
he concludes that the conceptualization of multiplicity as real for the sake of worldly transaction is inconsistent,
stating "therefore."
He raises the objection that this is not something imagined, but rather something heard,
with the words "nanu" (but surely).

He offers this rebuttal: "This illustration pertains to the aspect of the non-difference between cause and effect, not to the quality of being subject to transformation (pariṇāmitva), because that would contradict the scriptural declarations of Brahman's immutability (kūṭasthatva)."
"No," it is said;

[the opponent] objects by means of an illustration that undergoing transformation during creation and being devoid of it during dissolution are not contradictory when taken sequentially: "In the state of persistence... etc.
He says "no," because for that which is immutable (*kūṭastha*), any modification whatsoever is untenable, as it would contradict its immutability.
Anticipating the objection that its immutability might be unestablished, he says:
Regarding the term "of the immutable" (*kūṭasthasya*):

the sense is that because the immutable—which is partless—cannot undergo transformation consisting of a change of state by abandoning its prior form, the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is merely an illusory appearance (*vivarta*), like silver in a mother-of-pearl shell.

Furthermore, he states that the world has no reality because it is a fruitless thing mentioned as a subordinate element to the knowledge of Brahman, which is fruitful and devoid of phenomenal diversity.
And with the words "not as... and so forth, he addresses the following doubt:

since the scripture states, "In whatever way one meditates upon Him, that very thing one becomes," it might be thought that the fruit for the knower is the attainment of Brahman through the realization of its being subject to transformation (*pariṇāmitva*). To this, he says:
"For [Brahman] does not possess the state of being subject to transformation."

The sense is that since the possibility of the fruit of liberation—which is eternally stable and established by the scriptural text "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme"—exists, it is improper to postulate a fruit characterized by suffering, impermanence, and transformation.

Now, an objection is raised: previously, in the sūtra "From which [proceeds] the birth, etc., of this," a proposition was made regarding God as the cause; now, in establishing non-difference through the concluding sūtra "Not different from that," there would be a contradiction because of the absence of the distinction between the ruler and the ruled. Thus he objects:
Regarding the term "immovable" (*kūṭastha*):

he states that there is no contradiction because lordship and so forth depend upon imagined duality, whereas in the ultimate sense there is non-difference, by means of the words beginning with "no" (*na*).

When name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*)—which are of the nature of ignorance—have dissolved into the conscious self (*cidātman*), that [self] is the seed; its manifestation as a gross entity is the creation (*sṛṣṭi*). Since the state of being the Lord (*īśvaratva*) and so forth depend upon that [creation], there is no contradiction; this is the meaning. He explains the summarized point with the words beginning "Therefore" (*tasmāt*).
Regarding the phrase "by way of identity or difference":
it is impossible to assert that name-and-form (nāmarūpa) possess the nature of the Lord (īśvara), because they are insentient;
nor can they be different from the Lord, because that which is imagined lacks both independent existence and independent manifestation. This is the meaning.

He says "māyā" with the intention of expressing the identity of ignorance (*avidyā*) with name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), which consist of the formative forces (*saṃskāra*). If name-and-form were the very self of the Lord (*īśvara*), then the Lord would be insentient; therefore, he says:
"Distinct from those two":
regarding this distinctness and its grammatical derivation, he cites scripture beginning with the words "ether," and so forth.

He states that, through the distinction imagined by limiting adjuncts such as ignorance (*avidyā*), the one occupying the position of the original image (*bimba*) possesses the nature of the Lord (*īśvara*), while those who are like reflections— the individual souls (*jīvas*)— possess the nature of being governed:
"And he [governs] those who are his own self."
One should not be deluded into thinking that multiple individual souls (*nānājīva*) are taught here,
for the mention of difference is made on account of the distinctions within the aggregate of intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth;
rather, it has been stated that the individual soul is but one, being a reflection of ignorance (*avidyā*).
Regarding the absence of duality such as lordship (*īśvaratva*) from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), he cites scripture with the words "And thus" (*tathā ca*).
To the question, "How then [is there] agency and so forth?", he says:
"But its own nature" (svabhāvas tu) means that beginningless ignorance itself functions in the form of agency and so forth.
To the objection that the Lord's true lordship consists in His being the destroyer of the sins and merits of the devotees and non-devotees respectively, he says:
"Does not take" means it does not withdraw [it].
Because of that obscuration of the knowledge of one's own true nature, people wander in delusion, thinking: "I am the doer," "I am the Lord," and "He is my controller."
He states that the meaning already explained is the one approved by the author of the Sūtras, saying:
"The author of the Sūtras also...
He further states that the recourse to the process of transformation (pariṇāma) is not only for the sake of worldly convention, but also for the sake of meditative worship (upāsanā):...
And [he considers] the process of transformation as well.
As it has been said: "The mind of the miserly perceives transformation, but the mind whose impurities have been destroyed perceives manifestation. //14//
And because perception occurs when there is existence. (BS 2.1.15)
Thus, having resolved the contradiction with perception and other means of knowledge regarding their non-difference, he states the inference: "And [because] when there is existence...
The meaning of the Sūtra is that since the effect exists—meaning it is present and perceived—when the cause exists, the two are non-different.
The pot is non-different from the clay, because its existence and perceptibility are necessarily restricted to the existence and perceptibility of the clay, just like the clay itself.
Anticipating the objection that this reason might be irrelevant (*aprayojaka*)— asking why it might not be the case even if there were difference— he refutes it as follows:
And as for the word "not":
the meaning is that if there were a difference between the clay and the jar, there would be a severance of the cause, just as in the case of a cow and a horse.
Since a cow and a horse lack the relationship of cause and effect (nimitta-naimittika), there is an absence of a causal connection.

Therefore, by that reason, the state of being the cause and so forth between the clay and the jar is established, not their non-difference; anticipating the objection that there is a difference in meaning [between the two], he says:
"Nor [is there a difference] because of the relationship between material cause and effect.
Nor is there a difference in meaning by virtue of the relationship between the material cause (upādāna) and the product (upādeya).

The point is that in the example of the clay, even when its presence or absence [is considered], the cause exists; and because it is other [than the effect], its presence is impossible in the same way as [the presence of] a cow or a horse [is impossible in a clay pot].

The literal meaning is that although the potter and the pot stand in a relationship of instrumental cause (*nimitta*) and so forth, they are nonetheless distinct; therefore, the existence of the potter is not necessarily perceived in the pot.
He raises a doubt regarding the deviation (*vyabhicāra*) of the reason found in the sūtra as it was heard:
"But surely" (*nanu*).
He states that the reason consisting of the rule—that the perception of smoke occurs only when fire is present—is not established there:
"No," he says.
He raises the objection that there is a deviation from the rule because there is a necessity [of smoke] in the case of smoke existing as an unbroken, long line—
this is indicated by "Now" (*atha*).

He says, "Not so," because the intended reason is that [the object] is the objective domain of a cognition colored by the cognition of that [other thing], provided that its existence is necessarily contingent upon the existence of that other thing.

The first part of the definition (the *satyanta*) is included to exclude any deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of color-form (*rūpa*), which is grasped by a cognition colored by the cognition of light.
There is no deviation [in the inference], because objects such as jars exist even in the absence of light.
The meaning is that there is no deviation in the case of the aforementioned specific smoke, since it is perceived even without the cognition of fire.
And thus, the meaning of the Bhāṣya is that [the inference] is colored by—that is, accompanied by—the existence (sattā), which is the state of being, of those two, namely the effect and the cause.

Alternatively, we state that the reason is "the state of being that," namely, co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), which consists in being graspable by a cognition whose object is that [co-referentiality].

The meaning is: because we observe a cognition of co-referentiality in the case of "the clay pot" (*mṛd-ghaṭaḥ*), whereas we do not observe such a thing in the case of "fire and smoke" (*agni-dhūmaḥ*).
Having explained the Sūtra as having the purpose of inference (*anumāna*), he now explains it as being directed toward perception (*pratyakṣa*) by means of an alternative reading:
"And because of existence" (*bhāvācca*).
The word "and" (*ca*) serves to conjoin the term "consisting of speech" (*ārambhaṇa*) mentioned in the preceding Sūtra.
Furthermore, the perception that "this is one cloth" is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the cloth's existence as something separate from the threads,
since it is also logically consistent as having as its object a false effect that does not exist separately [from its cause].

Therefore, the meaning is that because of the perceptual apprehension that "the cloth is simply the threads themselves possessing the conjunctions of lengthwise and crosswise extension," there is non-difference [of the effect from the cause].
He extends the logic of the cloth to the thread and so forth by means of the words "In the same way," etc.
The meaning is that through direct perception, in each respective effect, only the cause remains as a residue.

He states that where direct perception is absent, the effect in question must be inferred as non-different from its cause under dispute, because it is an effect, like a cloth: "Where there is no direct perception, [the effect] is to be inferred there as non-different from the cause whose nature is doubted, because it is an effect, like a cloth."
Regarding the phrase "by this":
one might argue that if the cause is to be specified as the remainder, then *pradhāna* and so forth should be the remainder, and not Brahman; therefore, he says: "ta... [and so on].

Regarding the word "among all": since it has been stated that the purport of all Vedānta texts is upon Brahman, that alone remains as non-dual; no other cause remains, because any such cause would lack scriptural authority—this is the intended meaning. //15//
And because of the existence of another [nature], [the Self exists]. (BS 2.1.16)

The author of the Sūtras states "and because of existence" (sattvāt ca), meaning that the scripture, through the use of grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the passage "this world is indeed Being" (*sad eva idam agre āsīt*), teaches that before creation the effect exists in the form of its cause; and since this would otherwise be impossible, he concludes that even the world once it has arisen is non-different from its cause.
He also provides a logical argument for the meaning of the scripture with the words "and that which [exists] as the nature of that":

the pot and so forth exist prior [to their production] as the nature of clay and so on, because they are produced from it; the general meaning is that this is established by the method of difference (vyatireka), just as oil does not arise from sand.

Since the effect possesses existence just as the cause does, and there is no evidence for a difference in their existence, the effect has an existence non-different from that of the cause; thus he states another meaning of the Sūtra with the words "And just as...
Now, since it is impossible for an existing effect to be non-existent at earlier or later times, its existence is invariable.
And that reality is the one, all-pervading pure consciousness alone.
By virtue of its non-difference from that [consciousness], the meaning is that there is non-difference between cause and effect—such as "the clay exists" and "the jar exists"—as they appear. //16//
Nor should it be argued that, in this way, even a jar and a cloth would be non-different from each other due to the non-distinction of their single existence (*sattva*).
In reality, because non-difference is intended by way of the single essence of the sentient being;
if so, what is the distinction between clay and the jar?
We say it is identity (*tādātmya*).
In reality, although existence (*sattā*) is one and the same everywhere, there is no identity (*tādātmya*) between a jar and a cloth because their existences are distinct;

however, since difference does not necessarily entail a difference in existence, the fact that cause and effect possess non-distinct existence constitutes their identity—this is the distinction. //16//

If it be argued that [the Self] is not [non-existent] because of the designation of non-existence, we say no; for [it is designated] by way of another attribute, as is clear from the remainder of the passage. (BS 2.1.17)
Having raised the objection that the prior existence of the effect in the form of its cause is unestablished, he provides the resolution:
"It is non-existent" [is not the case].

Just as in the opening statement, "One should place the pebbles smeared," when there is doubt as to what they are smeared with, the conclusion is reached that they are smeared with ghee based on the supplementary passage, "Ghee is indeed light"; so too here, the certainty that it is existent is reached from the supplementary passage, "That is Being."
This is the meaning.

Since the statement "it was" (āsīt) expresses a connection with past time, he says "of the non-existent [state] and of what precedes and follows," indicating that it was indeed non-existent and unmanifested, but not empty (śūnya).
He extends the aforementioned reasoning to another statement with the words "or non-existent" (asadvā).
The sense is that the qualification "being currently produced" (kriyamāṇatva) is impossible in the case of the void (śūnya). //17//
On account of reasoning and another scriptural word. (Sūtra 18)
The author of the Sūtra states another reason for existence and non-difference:
"by reasoning" (yukteḥ).

The meaning is that the impossibility of otherwise accounting for the activity of those seeking curd and the like toward milk and so forth constitutes the reasoning; by this, the existence of the effect prior [to its production] as non-different from the cause is established.
Anticipating the objection that activity toward a cause might occur due to the notion of causality even though the effect is non-existent, he says, "For [if it were] undifferentiated," etc.

The meaning is that since there is no arising from what is non-existent, or else, if there were such arising, it would follow that everything could arise from everything; consequently, there would be no activity directed toward specific respective material causes (*upādāna*).

This has been stated by the elders of the Sāṃkhya school: "The effect exists [in the cause] because that which is non-existent cannot be produced; because there is the grasping of a material cause; because there is no production of everything from everything; because a potent cause produces only that for which it has the capacity; and because the effect is of the same nature as its cause. Since a potent cause brings about only an effect for which it has the capacity, the effect—which is the object of that capacity—must exist; for what is non-existent cannot be made an object of capacity.
Furthermore, the meaning of the second half of the verse is that the effect is existent because it is non-different from its existent cause.

One might raise the objection: "But even if the effect were non-existent, the restriction of activity could still be established due to some excellence [in the cause]"—this is the sense of the word "atha" (now/if).

Excellence (*atiśaya*) is either a property of the effect or a property of the cause. Regarding the first case, since it would be the locus (*dharmin*) [of that excellence], the existence of the effect in its prior state would be unavoidable; thus he says: "In that case, because it possesses excellence... (*tarhyatiśayavattvāt*).
He says "and power" (śaktiśca) because even in the second case, the existence of the effect would follow.
Power that is distinct from both cause and effect, or which is non-existent like the effect itself, cannot be the regulator of the effect.

Because there would be the undesirable consequence that anything else whatsoever—even a human horn—would be the regulator [of manifestation], since there is no distinction between "otherness" and "non-existence" regarding power (śakti) or elsewhere;
therefore, for this reason, it must be accepted that the effect itself, latent in the form of its cause, is what constitutes power by virtue of being the regulator of manifestation.
Thus, the meaning is that the pre-existence of the effect (satkāryavāda) is established.
Furthermore, if cause and effect were distinct, there would arise the cognition of difference, such as "the clay and the jar are two different things"; thus he says, "Moreover" (apica).
Anticipating the objection that even if they are distinct, such a cognition does not arise because of their inherence (samavāya), he refutes inherence:

Regarding the term "inherence" (*samavāya*): is inherence connected with its inherent relata (*samavāyin*) or not? In the first case, is that connection itself inherence, or is it their own essential nature (*svarūpa*)?
In the first case, there would be an infinite regress of inherence;
in the second, since even the relationship between clay and a jar is established through their own essential nature (*svarūpa-sambandha*), inherence is not proven.
He states the fault in the position that they are unrelated:
"If it is not admitted" means that there would follow the consequence of the absence of qualified cognition (viśiṣṭadhī) regarding substance, quality, and so forth;
the meaning is that what is unconnected cannot serve as the determinant of qualified cognition.
For a relation is that which determines a specific cognition; it does not require another determining factor for itself,
as that would lead to an infinite regress.
Therefore, he raises the objection that inherence (samavāya) is self-establishing by saying "Now" (atha);
[the word] "is connected" (saṃbadhyate) [to this].
The meaning is that it produces a qualified cognition (viśiṣṭadhi) regarding itself and its own relatum.
He refutes this by means of a counter-argument:
"Conjunction also... and so forth.
As for the claim that conjunction requires inherence because it is a quality (guṇa) and not because it is a relation (saṃbandha),
that is not so,
because it is a property (dharma).
Furthermore, because inherence (*samavāya*) would itself entail another relation, and because it is never observed that the property of being a horse belongs to a cow when they are unrelated;

moreover, since "sinlessness and so forth are qualities" (*guṇāḥ*) according to the Śruti, Smṛti, and other texts, and by the technical definition (*paribhāṣā*) that "a quality is a desired attribute in common usage," inherence too must be a quality.
The technical definition that "quality-ness (*guṇatva*) is a specific universal" (*jāti-viśeṣaḥ*), however, is posterior to the establishment of inherence.

Since the cognition that "a universal is eternally inherent in many" depends upon the cognition of inherence (*samavāya*), the quality-ness (*guṇatva*) of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) remains unestablished prior to the establishment of inherence; this is the general direction of the argument. Furthermore, an object must be accepted in accordance with its actual apprehension; otherwise, it would be easy to claim that when a cow is perceived, a horse is its objective basis (*ālambana*).
And thus, because of the cognition of non-difference in the expression "the clay pot," non-difference itself must be accepted;
for it is impossible for *samavāya* (inherence), which is absolutely distinct from those two, to be their regulator. Thus he says:
"tādātmya... (identity).
Thus, it has been stated that by following [the principle of] dependent origination, the effect exists in the form of its cause, but is false in its own nature;
and he states that its falsity is also due to the inability to define its mode of existence (vṛtti):
And how so?

Regarding that, having restated the first [position]—namely, that the whole, such as a cloth, exists either by its own nature in its parts, such as the threads, like the number three and so on, or else part-by-part—he refutes the first alternative with the words beginning "If...
(yadīti).

The meaning is that since the perception of an object existing as a distributed whole (vyāsajyavṛtti) is produced by the perception of all its substrates, it would follow as an absurd consequence that a folded cloth or the like could not be perceived, because none of its constituent parts would be perceptible.
He raises the second objection with "Now [if]... (atha).

He refutes [the opponent's position] with the words "even then," showing that although a sword existing in the hand or the scabbard is perceived even when only the hand is grasped— since the whole can be perceived by the grasping of any of its parts— there would nonetheless be an infinite regress regarding the parts themselves.
Having set forth the first two [alternatives], he refutes them with the words "Now, in each individual part," and so on:
at the time when the cloth exists in one thread, its existence in another thread would not be possible.
The meaning is that [otherwise] there would be the consequence of multiplicity in its occurrence.

He raises the objection— namely, "in the case of cowness"— suggesting that just as there is no fault of multiplicity for a universal (jāti) even when it occurs simultaneously in multiple individuals, so too it should be for the whole (avayavin).
He refutes [the objection] by stating, "No; it is not so," because the subsistence of the whole (*avayavin*) is unestablished, as there is no experience [of it].
He states another defect:
Regarding the term "individually" (*pratyeka*): it follows from the context and the connection [of the words]. Just as Devadatta performs his own task of study either in a village or in a forest.
The meaning is that just as a cow, as a whole, would produce its own effects, such as milk, even from its horns and tail;
thus, by the failure to determine the mode of subsistence (*vṛtti*), the indeterminability (*anirvācyatva*) of the effect has been shown.
Now, he states another fault in the theory of the non-existent effect (*asatkāryavāda*):
Regarding the word "previously" (*prāk*):

just as when it is said "the jar moves," the jar's agency—consisting in its being the substratum of the action of moving—is manifested, so too in the case of "the cloth is born," the agency of the action of being born is experienced.
Therefore, the existence of the agent of birth prior to the birth must be asserted.
The meaning is that if the agent were non-existent, it would follow that the action itself is also non-existent.
Although the fact that origination has an agent is established by experience, he states an inference based on its being an action: "And origination... and so forth.

Anticipating the objection that even though agency is impossible for a non-existent jar during its production, the potter and others possess agency because they are existent, he says: "And of the jar.
He extends this principle by stating that the production of non-existent shards and so forth is like the production of the jar.
Saying "so be it," he restates the doubt and states the fault with the words "if that were so."
The meaning is that this contradicts experience.
Previously, according to his own view, the existence of the effect was established on the grounds that "origination is the first modification of an entity.

Now, he raises the objection based on the view of the logicians (*tārkika*), namely that what is called the origination of an effect is its inherence (*samavāya*) in its own cause, or its inherence in itself as existence (*sattā*).
Regarding the word "atha":
even according to his [the opponent's] view, the existence of the effect is necessary, because that which is non-existent cannot possess relationality; thus he says:
"How so? [The author] states the example: "or of two non-existent things. One might object:

"Unlike a human horn and the like, an effect is not non-existent everywhere and at all times; rather, it is non-existent prior to its production and after its destruction, but existent in the interim. Thus, because of this difference, the status of being related is possible. Anticipating this doubt, he says:
Regarding the phrase "of non-existence" (*abhāvasya*):
here, the words "non-existence" (*abhāva*) are to be explained as synonyms for the word "non-being" (*asat*).
The meaning is that because non-being has no connection with time, it is not logical for it to possess "prior-ness" (*prāktva*).
Now, one might ask: "How can an effect that exists subsequent to the operation of the causal factors (kārakas) be equivalent to the son of a barren woman?
To this he says: "And if...
The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "If the non-existence of the effect—that is, the doctrine of *asatkārya*—had been established, then [the objection] would have been valid."
What, then, is the final determination? To this he says:
"But we...
The intention is that it is because of the Smṛti text: "The existence of the non-existent is not found."
In the theory of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*), he raises the objection that the causal agent would be rendered useless with the words "But surely" (*nanu*).
He further states that because the effect is non-different from the established cause, it must itself be already established.
Regarding the phrase "and because of its non-difference from that":
he says, "this is not a fault," meaning that the activity of the causal factors is for the purpose of manifesting the cause in the form of an effect that is otherwise indeterminable.

For the Sāṃkhyas, who maintain that the effect is real, the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (satkāryavāda) entails the fault of the futility of causal factors, since even manifestation is already existent.

For the proponents of non-duality (advaitavādins), however, everything is logically consistent with how it appears— like a dream— by virtue of the power of Māyā, which is skillful at manifesting the composition of what is inherently uncomposed.
When examined, everything is untenable, for if it were tenable, it would entail the consequence of duality; thus, this is the primary resolution because no other resolution exists.

Anticipating the objection—"Why could the resolution not be that what is different from the cause arises as something non-existent?"—he says, "Remember the refutation of the position of non-existence."

"Even the form of the effect [is unreal]"—the sense is that, for this reason, the view that the manifestation of the indeterminable (anirvācya), which is distinct from both being and non-being and difficult to define in terms of either identity with or difference from its cause, is the result of the operations of indeterminable causal factors, is indeed the best position.
Now, one might object: "But surely, specific states such as broadness and flatness, though not seen in the clay, are observed in the jar."
And thus, [the opponent might argue]: "A pot is different from clay, because it possesses attributes contradictory to it, like a tree"; to this, he says:
And as for the word "na" (not):
in reality, "otherness" (*anyatva*) means true difference (*satyo bhedaḥ*).
He states another instance where the reason is inconclusive (*vyabhicāra*):

"Likewise, day by day" means that although there are changes in the state of the body of the father and others every day, non-difference is logical because there is no birth or destruction [of the underlying substance].

However, in the case of the illustrative example (the clay jar), since the jar and so forth are produced when the clay and so forth are destroyed, one might object that non-difference between cause and effect is not logical due to their possessing contradictory properties in the form of birth and destruction. Thus, he raises this doubt:
Regarding the term "birth":
he refutes [the objection] that the reason is unestablished because there is no destruction of the cause, by saying "no."
The meaning is that because milk, clay, and so forth are perceived as being connected to their effects such as curds and jars, the destruction [of the cause] is not established.

Now, one might object: "In cases where a connection is observed, even if the reason (hetu) is unestablished, there are cases like sprouts where no connection with the banyan seed and so forth is observed; since the reason exists there, there would be a difference between existence and non-existence. To this, he says:
"adṛśya" (unseen).

In that case as well, since the parts of the seed and so forth persist in the sprout and so forth, there is no such thing as birth or destruction; rather, the conventional usage of those terms arises from the accumulation and depletion of other constituent parts—this is the meaning.

Anticipating the objection that one might infer a difference in substance based on the signs of accumulation and depletion, and thus conclude that what was non-existent arises and what was existent perishes, he states the fallacy [of such an inference] with the words "tatredṛg" (in that regard, such...).
Regarding the claim that there is no deviation [from the rule] because difference exists even in the body of the father, he states the subverting argument:
"The father, etc. By this [it is meant]: ...
The meaning is: by stating the concomitance of the cause in all effects.
Having refuted the fault in his own position, he attributes it to the opponent's position with the words:
"But for whom... (yasya punar iti).

Since a non-existent effect cannot be the locus of an excellence produced by the operation of the causal agent, it might be argued that even if it is not an object [of cognition], clay and other such materials could still be its object; thus, the author raises this objection with the words "samavāyi" (the inherent cause).
He then refutes the first alternative of the dilemma—whether the effect is different or non-different from the inherent cause—with the following:
With the words "no," etc.,
he anticipates the second objection and states the acceptance of that consequence: "the inherent cause," etc.
He concludes that effects are non-different from their intermediate causes with the words "Therefore" (tasmāt).
He states the resulting conclusion— that [the world] is non-different from the ultimate cause— with the following:
Likewise, regarding the word "root" (mūla):

he states that in the theory of the non-existence of the effect (*asatkāryavāda*), there would be a contradiction of the initial proposition (*pratijñābādha*), saying: "But if [it were so] prior to production... (18).
And it is like a cloth. (BBs 2.1.19)

"The effect is distinct from its material cause because it is not perceived even when that [cause] is perceived, and because it possesses a larger dimension than it—just as a hare is distinct from a gnat. To show that there is an inconclusive fallacy (*vyabhicāra*) in this argument, the Sūtra states: "And like a cloth" (*paṭavat*). This clarifies the inconclusiveness of the second reason.
And as for "enveloping," *āyāma* means length. //19//
And as with the vital breath and so forth. (BS 2.1.20)

In that very context, having raised the argument that the effect possesses a distinct causal nature because the effect is different from its material cause— just like [the consensus regarding] agreed-upon cases— the author of the Sūtras states the following to show the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*):

And as with the vital breaths and so forth—thus, because the living world is non-different from Brahman, the initial proposition is established; he concludes the meaning of this section with the words: "And therefore, of the whole... (Sūtra 20).
Because of the designation of [Brahman] as something other [than the individual soul], there follows the contingency of defects such as the failure to perform what is beneficial. (BS 2.1.21)

The subject matter is the concordance of the Vedānta texts which asserts that Brahman, non-different from the individual soul (jīva), is the cause of the world. A doubt arises as to whether this [concordance] is contradicted by the reasoning that "if such a Brahman were to produce the world, it would not produce its own undesirable states such as hell, because it is an independent conscious being," or not. In resolving this, relying upon the previously mentioned non-difference of the soul [from Brahman], the defects of the soul [would accrue] to Brahman.
Taking up the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) sūtra, "They would result [in contradictions]," he explains it with the words beginning "Because of the designation as the other," and so forth.
In the prima facie view, since [the Self] is non-different from the individual soul (jīva), the establishment of the concordance (samanvaya) [of the Upaniṣadic texts] is not achieved.

In the established doctrine (siddhānta), the proof of that [fault] is the result. Regarding the phrase "not performing what is beneficial" (ahitākaraṇa), by reversing the negative particle (nañ), it is explained as "performing what is harmful" (ahitakaraṇa) being the fault.
He brings forth the delusion and so forth mentioned by the word "etcetera" (ādi):
And [this is shown] by the passage beginning with "not by itself," etc. (Sūtra 2.1.21).
But it is something additional, because of the designation of a distinction. (BS 2.1.22)

"Since there is no difference between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśa), the defects of the individual soul and the world would belong to Brahman; and the qualities residing in Brahman—such as the power of creation and dissolution, and omniscience—would belong to the individual soul. This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), which cannot be accepted because the individual soul is not observed to possess the capacity for dissolution even within its own body, [the author] explains the aphorism of the established conclusion (*siddhānta*):

The meaning of the concluding section of the Siddhānta (the final established doctrine) is as follows: by the word "tu" (but) and so forth, it is asserted that because a conceptual distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara)—like that between an original object and its reflection—is accepted in the world, there is a systematic arrangement of their respective attributes.
The syntactical connection is: "If we were to say that the individual soul is the creator, then faults would follow; however, we do not say that."
Furthermore, whether these defects are urged after the knowledge of non-difference has arisen, or before it, the first case is not tenable; thus he says: "Moreover" (apica).
Having stated that [the world] is a manifestation of false knowledge, he clarifies this with the word "ignorance" (avidyā).
He provides the superimposition of bodily attributes upon the attributes of the intellect, such as agency, as an illustrative example (dṛṣṭānta).
Regarding the word "birth," he replies to the second [objection] with the words:
"But when it is not sublated."

The meaning is that there is no fault whatsoever: because after [the attainment of] knowledge, attributes such as being the creator are sublated, and prior to that, the establishment [of these attributes] is possible through imagined differentiation. //22//
And like a stone and so forth, that [creation] is untenable. (BsRp_2,1.7.23)
But how can there be the diversity of individual souls (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara), as well as the diversity of their effects, within Brahman, which is of an indivisible and uniform nature?
To resolve this apparent inconsistency through examples, the author of the Sūtras states:
"And like stones, etc. (aśmādivat).
*Kimpāka* is the fruit of the great *tāla* tree.
The meaning is that there is a diversity [of results] due to the distinctions among beginningless potencies (*anādiśakti*) consisting of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of various such actions.
He states the meaning of the word "and" (*ca*) found in the Sūtra:
And because of scripture:
Brahman possesses the defects residing in the individual soul (jīva), because it is non-different from the individual soul.
The inference beginning with "like the individual soul" (*jīvavat*) is sublated by such scriptural texts as those concerning self-evident authority and faultlessness.

Furthermore, since modifications such as agency and enjoyership are illusory, no defect belongs even to the individual soul; how much less could there be the possibility of a defect in the Supreme Lord, who stands in the position of the archetype and perceives all distinctions? As for the claim that Brahman is not the material cause of the diverse effects—
Because they possess a single form,
unlike [the effects] such as clay or thread which exist separately;
that is not so.
The meaning is that there is no deviation [from the rule], because, like the perception of dreams, one perceives a variety of diverse objects within a single form.
Therefore, it is established that there is no contradiction in the concordance [of all scriptural texts] with Brahman, which is non-different from the inner self. //23//
If it be argued that [the soul is not omnipresent] because we see its withdrawal [from the body], we say no; for it is like milk. (BS 2.1.24)
Because we observe the withdrawal [of the world into Brahman].
The subject matter is the systematic connection (*samanvaya*) which asserts that the creation of the universe proceeds from Brahman alone, without any assistant.

Regarding the doubt as to whether this is contradicted by the worldly maxim that "that which is without assistance cannot be a cause," it was previously stated that, due to the distinction of the individual soul (*jīva*) based on limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), the defects of the soul do not attach to Brahman.

Now, by means of a counter-example, he explains a portion of the *pūrvapakṣa* sūtra— beginning with "the conscious," etc.— to show that even through limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), there exists no auxiliary cause such as a prompter for Brahman, because of the absence of plurality among Lords;
the result [of this argument] is as before.
The "conjunction" (upasaṃhāra) of the causal factors is their meeting.
He establishes the final position—that the aforementioned reasoning does not deviate in the case of milk and so forth—by stating:
"This is not a fault."
It is indeed accepted that pure Brahman is not a cause;
however, with the intention that for the Lord (Īśvara) as qualified [by attributes], Māyā alone is the assistant, he says:
"external."

Anticipating the objection that there is no deviation from the reason "lack of assistance" because milk also has assistants such as the act of curdling (*ātañcana*), he states—beginning with "But surely" (*nanu*)—that the deviation remains as it was, since some kind of transformation is observed in milk even in the absence of an assistant. To this, he replies:
"In that case, the assistant would be useless. To that, he says:
"It is being transformed.
[Objection: But surely it is milk that is transformed into the state of curd; why then is it imagined that "quickness is being produced"?
Why could it not be that milk, which is inherently incapable, is rendered capable by means of an auxiliary? To this, he says:
Regarding the phrase "yadi ca" (and if): to the question of what purpose is served by the perfection of auxiliaries for one who already possesses power, he says: "sādhana... (the means...).

In the absence of a specific auxiliary, no modification whatsoever occurs in milk; rather, the meaning is that by means of the addition of the curdling agent (*ātañcana*) and heat, the capacity for the state of excellent curd (*dadhi*) is manifested.
If it is then argued that an auxiliary which manifests the potency must also be mentioned for Brahman, he says in response:
"Complete" means that its power of illusion is independent [of anything else].
He states the proof for such a power:
And there is scriptural authority. //24//
And even as in the world, [the case of] the gods and so forth. (2,1.25)

One might object: "Brahman cannot be the cause because, while being conscious, it lacks assistance, like a potter in the absence of clay and so forth; thus there is no deviation [in the rule] regarding milk and the like. To address this doubt which the Sūtra seeks to dispel, he says: "This may be so... He then states that even that reason suffers from deviation in the case of gods and others: "tasyāpi hetor devādau vyabhicāraḥ" (there is deviation of that reason also in the case of gods and others).
"Like the gods and so forth.
That by which an object is perceived or known is "loka," namely the scriptures such as the mantras and arthavādas, as well as the linguistic usage of elders.
"Abhidhyāna" means volitional resolve (saṃkalpa).
One might object: "In the examples ranging from the gods down to the spider, consciousness is absent in the bodies;
whereas in the cases of the crane and the lotus plant, which possess consciousness, the cloud-sound and the body respectively serve as auxiliary factors for their agency in setting forth the embryo.
Therefore, there is no deviation (vyabhicāra) from the specific reason. Thus he raises the objection.
If he should say [the objection] beginning with "thus," [the author] refutes it by stating "one should say to him" in response to the claim that there is an inconsistency (*vyabhicāra*).
This is the flaw known as "dissimilarity of the example" (*dṛṣṭāntavaiṣamya*).

For in this case, the reason (*hetu*) must be understood as "consciousness" (*cetanatva*) in the sense of being the object of the notion of "I," which is common to the body that has attained identity with the mind; it cannot, however, be the primary nature of the Self (*mukhyātmatva*), because [if it were], your example of the potter would suffer from the fallacy of lacking the probans (*sādhanavaikalya*).
Furthermore, "lack of assistance" for a conscious being means its being devoid of any cause external to itself;
since both of these conditions exist in the case of gods and so forth, there is a deviation [from the rule],
because the body— being included within the self— is not something distinct from it.

And thus, there is a distinction between the potter and the gods and others, because the latter do not depend on anything other than themselves for the production of effects such as jars. There is a distinction between the gods and Brahman, because Brahman does not even require a body. For the commencement of an effect by humans, gods, and others, there is no single uniform set of causal conditions (*sāmagrī*).
For it is heard in the Mahābhārata that by the mere volition of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, a continuous succession of garments arose for Draupadī;
therefore, it is established that Brahman is the cause even when acting without external assistance. //25//
Either the entire [Brahman] would be subject to modification, or else there would be a contradiction with the scriptural texts regarding its partlessness. (BS 2.1.26)
The entire [Brahman] would be involved [in transformation].

Since the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) has been reached—based on the misconception that Brahman undergoes transformation due to the example of milk—the present section (adhikaraṇa) is intended to establish the definitive conclusion that the meaning of the scripture is illusory manifestation (vivarta) and not transformation (pariṇāma). Thus, there is a logical connection between the preceding section and the subsequent section.
He states the connection [of the topic] through its being an effect:
"the conscious" (cetana).
The subject matter is the concordance (samanvaya) which asserts the creation of the world from Brahman, who is partless.

In response to the doubt as to whether this [position] contradicts the logical principle that "whatever is partless cannot undergo transformation," the author explains the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) sūtra—
"kṛtsna..."— by stating:
"By one who asserts that Brahman undergoes transformation, it must be stated whether Brahman is partless or with parts."

Regarding the first [position], it was stated that everything would exist as a transformation (*pariṇāma*) of Brahman; he explains this by means of a negative example (*vyatireka-dṛṣṭānta*) with the words beginning "If Brahman... etc. "Paryaṇaṃsyat" means it would have become transformed (*pariṇata*).

If it were to abide in only one part, it would remain untransformed; for its partlessness is established by the aforementioned scriptural citations. He states the resulting defect with the words "tataśca" (and therefore).

He states another defect—namely, that "the Self is to be seen"—with the words "draṣṭavyatā" (the state of being an object of vision): if the fundamental Self, which is Brahman, does not exist apart from its transformations, then the instruction that "the Self is to be seen" would be devoid of meaning.
Furthermore, he says that if one accepts the birth and destruction of Brahman through its nature as a transformation, there is a contradiction with the scriptural statement, "Unborn, undying."
Regarding the phrase "because of being unborn, etc.":
having raised the objection concerning the position that [the world] possesses parts, he refutes it with the remainder of the Sūtra, beginning with "Now," and so forth. //26//
But on account of scripture, [the world] exists, because [the Veda] is the root of verbal testimony. (BS 2.1.27)
Regarding what was stated— that the position of transformation (*pariṇāma*) is difficult to maintain— he establishes his own conclusion through the doctrine of illusory manifestation (*vivarta*),
citing the word "from scripture" (*śruteḥ*).
By means of the application of the Sūtra, he demonstrates that the two previously mentioned defects do not exist in his own position.

By the words "by the word *tu*," etc., he states that there is no consequence of the entire [Brahman] being transformed, because the scripture declares the existence of the Lord as distinct from the phenomenal world—which is both the object of seeing and the object of transformation—by virtue of His being the Seer and the Transformer, saying:
"That divinity... and so forth.
He says, "To that extent," indicating that separate existence is also heard of through the relation of deficiency and excess;
and for this reason as well, he says that there exists unmodified Brahman.
"So be it.

The meaning is that there exists a Brahman distinct from the visible world, because of the Vedic scripture stating, "This very Self is in the heart," and because of the specific qualification "then," which refers to the time of deep sleep (suṣupti).
He states another mark [of Brahman]: "And likewise by the senses," etc.

Since modifications such as earth and so forth fall within the range of the senses, while the Śruti—"It is not grasped by the eye"—prohibits that [sensory graspability] for Brahman, and because there is Śruti stating that it is beyond the range of speech and mind, the meaning is that Brahman exists as the immutable (kūṭastha).
Having stated that the fault of total pervasion does not exist, he says "and not" (na ca) to show that the second fault also does not exist. [Objection:
But surely Brahman exists even in the form of its effects?
If it exists as separate [parts], then its state of having parts (*sāvayavatva*) is unavoidable, because it is impossible for a single partless entity to exist in two ways;

therefore, the idea that Brahman is partless contradicts the logical principle that "whatever is divided into two is possessed of parts. Anticipating this doubt from one who does not understand the theory of illusory manifestation (*vivarta*), the author, while concealing his true intention, offers the following rebuttal:
And [it is said]: "It has sound as its root.
When the power of even ordinary things perceived through direct perception is inconceivable, what then need be said regarding Brahman, which is accessible through verbal testimony alone?
Therefore, both the partlessness of Brahman and its division into two must be accepted exactly according to the scriptural word.
The meaning is that it is not to be sublated by logical reasoning (*tarka*).

The sense of the traditional teaching (*smṛti*) is that that which is beyond the primary natures—the intrinsic natures of things perceived through direct perception—and which is distinct and accessible only through instruction, has an inconceivable nature (*acintyasvarūpa*).
He raises an objection due to a failure to understand the intended meaning (*āśaya*):
"Is it not so even by means of the word?"—

or rather, this objection "Is it not so? challenges that interpretation of the sūtra as a final conclusion (siddhānta) presented by certain partial theorists (ekadeśins), namely that Brahman is subject to transformation (pariṇāmī).
The meaning is that [the cognition of Brahman] depends upon the knowledge of the word's fitness (yogyatā).
Now, one might object: "If one resorts to the dilemma of whether Brahman has parts or is partless, then all the scriptural texts would be reconciled"; to this, he says:
"Action" (kriyā).
If Brahman were partless, there would be a contradiction with the scriptural texts regarding its being the material cause;
if it were possessed of parts, there would be a contradiction with the term "partless"; and moreover, an alternative between these two is logically untenable in the case of a real entity.
Thus, since no other mode [of operation] is perceived, it follows that the authority of the Śrutis is difficult to establish; to this objection, he reveals his own intention by stating:
"This is not a fault.

Because it is accepted that even a partless, immutable reality may possess transformations of name and form imagined through ignorance (avidyā), the charge of being "difficult to establish" does not apply.
The meaning is that there is no contradiction because the real immutability [of Brahman] possesses the nature of being the substrate for imagined modifications.
Anticipating the objection that if a difference in form were admitted, it would follow that [Brahman] is composed of parts, he explains this by saying "not indeed," and so forth.
Having set aside the objection regarding the consequence of total dissolution, he sets aside another defect with the words "vācārambhaṇa" (beginning with speech).
Now, one might ask: how can the transformation taught by the Śruti be of the nature of falsehood? To this, he says:
And this [creation]—

it has been stated more than once that creation is merely restated as being subordinate to the Lord Brahman, who is beyond all conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*), and is not what is being established;
therefore, he concludes that there is no fault whatsoever in the theory of illusory manifestation (*vivartavāda*).
Therefore, [it is so]. //27//
And likewise in the self, for [the appearances] are indeed manifold. (BBs 2.1.28)
Transformation (*pariṇāma*) is the emergence of another state through the destruction of the previous state,
as in the case of milk becoming curd;
illusory manifestation (*vivarta*) is the emergence of another state without the destruction of the previous form.

Just as the state of silver [appears] in a mother-of-pearl shell, the author of the Sūtras clarifies the doctrine of Māyā by strengthening the fact that Brahman is the material cause through the analogy of the witness of a dream, stating:
"And in the Self... (Brahma-sūtra 2.1.14).
The horses are those yoked to the chariot. //28//
And because of the faults in one's own position. (BsRp_2,1.9.29)
Furthermore, since defects such as the consequence of total pervasion (kṛtsnaprasakti) apply to the positions of the Sāṃkhyas and others as well, they should not be raised against us;
for according to the maxim, "The defect which is equal for both [parties]," the author of the Sūtras says: "In one's own position... [svapakṣadoṣa].

Regarding the objection that if *pradhāna* is partless, there would be the consequence of its being entirely transformed, whereas if it has parts, it contradicts the accepted doctrine of its partlessness— the author raises this doubt with the words "But surely" (*nanu*).
Is the state of equilibrium a modification of the *guṇas*?
Or [it may be] a composite.
In the first case, it cannot be the primal nature (mūlaprakṛti),
because it is a modification (vikāra).
In the second case, there is an absence of manifoldness (*prapañca*), because the aggregate lacks substantial reality and thus has no root.
Now, if it is argued that the partless qualities (*guṇa*) themselves are the primordial nature (*prakṛti*) of the various transformations:

In that case, intending to show that the total destruction of the root would be unavoidable due to the consequence of universal application, he refutes [the objection] with the words "not so," and so forth.
The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "Therefore, because [the reasoning] is equal, we are not to be questioned."

If each individual entity—such as *sattva* and the other two qualities (*rajas* and *tamas*)—is the material cause (*upādāna*), accompanied by the other two qualities and being partless (*niravayava*), then the entire material cause would necessarily result in the form of the effect; since this would imply the destruction of the root cause, the argument for partlessness is fallacious. Therefore, because the qualities possess parts due to their capacity for transformation (*pariṇāmitva*), like clay and so forth, there is no consequence of the whole [cause] becoming the effect, as transformation can occur in only one part. Thus, he raises the following objection:
He raises an objection: "One might think... He refutes this by stating, "Even so," [meaning] that even in the absence of this fault, another fault would arise.

Now, one might object: "The parts of the qualities (*guṇa*) are not the initiators [of the world] like threads; rather, it is the potencies residing within them that are inferred from the diversity of effects. Anticipating this doubt, [the author] states with the words "But... (*atha ca...*) that even Brahman would possess parts due to its illusory potencies (*māyika-śakti*). Furthermore, he points out that the same defect applies even in the theory of atoms (*aṇuvāda*): [text continues].
"So be it";
the connection is that the fault is the same as in the Sāṃkhya system.
Regarding two partless atoms, their conjunction must be either all-pervasive (*vyāpyavṛtti*) or non-all-pervasive (*avyāpyavṛtti*).
In the first case, there would be the consequence that its effect, which possesses double the dimension, would be no more than a single atom, because a larger magnitude (prathiman) is impossible.

For when one atom is pervaded by another atom from above, below, and on all sides, a substance greater than that cannot possibly exist. In the second case, the consequence is that atoms would possess parts (sāvayavatva).
To the objection that it is improper to state an equality of faults—just as when someone says "You are a thief," the reply "You too are a thief" is inappropriate—he says:
"But it has been avoided.

For it has been stated in the doctrine of Māyā that everything is consistent, as in the case of a dream; therefore, it is established that there is no contradiction to the concordance [of the Vedānta texts] with respect to the partless Brahman. //29//
And [the Self] is endowed with all [powers], because that is seen from scripture. (2.1.30)

"Sarvopetā" [is the sūtra]. There is a doubt as to whether there is a contradiction—according to the principle that "the power of illusion belongs to one who possesses a body"—between the *samanvaya* (harmonization) which asserts the creation of the world by Brahman who possesses the power of *māyā*, and the [scriptural] statement that Brahman is bodiless; or whether there is no such contradiction. In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), it is argued that there is indeed a contradiction because the reasoning [of the opponent] is not fallacious. [The sūtra provides the answer: because the previously mentioned possession of power has been established, there is a single subject matter [for both statements].
Stating the connection (*saṅgati*), he explains the aphorism on the established conclusion (*siddhānta-sūtra*) with the words beginning "of one," etc.

It should be understood that from this point until the end of the chapter, the result— the contradiction or non-contradiction between the prima facie (*pūrva-pakṣa*) and the final position (*uttara-pakṣa*)— is exactly as previously stated.
Abhyātta means pervaded on all sides;
avākī means devoid of the organ of speech;
anādara means free from desire. //30//
If it is argued that [the Self] is not [the agent] because of its being devoid of instruments (*vikaraṇatvāt*), that has already been answered. (BS 2.1.31)
Having restated the logic of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), he refutes it with the words "because of being devoid of instruments" (vikaraṇatvāt).
Even though gods and other sentient beings possess powers, their agency is observed only when there is identification with a body; in its absence, as in deep sleep, that agency is not observed.
Therefore, the meaning of the objection is this: even though Brahman possesses power, it cannot be an agent because it is bodiless;
nor is power possible for that which is bodiless.
[The reply is: although agency is impossible for the individual soul (jīva) which is devoid of organs, it is possible for the Lord (īśvara).
This was stated in the sūtra: "And as in the case of gods and others in the world.

The purpose of that [sūtra] is to provide the following resolution: since it is impossible for a body—which is itself a mental construction—to be the locus of *māyā*, it is logical that only the undifferentiated pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) is the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of *māyā*. //31//
Not so, because [the world] possesses a purpose. (BS 2.1.32)
It is not so, because [the world] possesses a purpose.
The subject of the discussion is the systematic harmony (*samanvaya*) which asserts that the world originates from the all-pervading Brahman.
Does this [assertion] contradict the principle that "a conscious being who is not deluded does not create a fruitless object"? It does not.

In the face of this doubt, he explains the sūtra of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*)— beginning with the words "otherwise" (*anyathā*)— by way of an objection to what was previously stated: that agency belongs even to one who is bodiless, on the strength of scriptural testimony (*śruti*), which declares his capacity [to act].
Anticipating the objection that the Lord might engage in creation for the sake of others even in the absence of a fruit for Himself, he cites scripture: "And it comes to pass...
It is a worldly axiom that whatever activity is undertaken by a discerning being is for the sake of its own fruit.

Nor is there any deviation [from the rule] in the case of the activity of a compassionate person, because even that [activity] is motivated by the desire to remove one's own mental agitation caused by the inability to endure the suffering of others; this is the sense.
Furthermore, he states that the fruit of such great exertion must be declared:
Regarding the phrase "gurutara" (more significant):
if it is argued that the activity of the Lord (*īśvara*) is likewise for his own sake, he says:
"yadīyamapi" (if this [activity] of his too...).
The meaning is that, if [the world] were not for the sake of the self, the absence of activity previously mentioned would follow.
Anticipating the objection that God is not a rational being, he states the contradiction with scripture,
beginning with "Now" (atha).
The fault of the intellect is the absence of discrimination. //32//
But as in the world, [the Lord's activity] is mere sport (līlā). (2.1.33)
He explains the *siddhāntasūtra*— that there is an exception (*vyabhicāra*) to the stated rule in the case of the play (*līlā*) of kings— with the word "but" (*tu*).
[The word "but" indicates that] it is distinct.
"Beyond play" (līlātiriktam) means: in those beautiful regions where there are pastimes (vihāra) consisting of sport; the sense is that in such places.
While it might be conceivable that even the play of kings and others occasionally yields some fruit, such as the exhilaration of pleasure, nevertheless, in the case of [mere] sighing and so forth—
He states another instance of deviation— where there is activity by a discerning person, yet no result intended for oneself exists therein—
with the words "And as...
The nature of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is mobility, or rather, its *prārabdha* karma is the cause of inhalation and so forth.
The nature of the Lord is Māyā accompanied by time and karma.
Now, why is it said that the Lord's creation of the world is merely for the sake of sport (līlā),
rather than being some kind of fruit?
Let it be so imagined; to this he replies:
"No," meaning that it would contradict [the Lord's] state of having all desires fulfilled.
Now, one might ask: why does the Lord not remain silent?
Why does He create a world that is fruitless for Himself and brings suffering to others? To this, he says:
"And it is not His nature."
The meaning is that since creation is unavoidable when the collection of conditions such as time and other factors is present.
Regarding the statement that a result must be asserted because of the great effort involved,
he states there the non-establishment of the reason:
With the words "Even though...

and so forth, he states the sublation of the reasoning—namely, that even for a small undertaking a fruit must be declared because it is observed to be so in the world—by saying "Even if... and so forth.
There is no lack of authority for the scripture concerning creation, nor is there madness on account of the scripture concerning omniscience; such is the distinction.
He states that because this creation is merely an illusion (māyāmātra), like a dream-creation, it has no expectation of a fruit:
And this [is not so].

Nor should it be forgotten that the scriptural passages concerning creation, though seemingly fruitless, are not purposeless; for they possess meaning as being subordinate to the knowledge of Brahman, which does have a fruit—this is the sense of the statement. //33//
Inequality and cruelty [cannot be attributed to the Lord] because He has regard [for merit and demerit]; for thus Scripture shows. (2.1.34)

"Neither partiality nor cruelty [can be attributed to Brahman]. The subject of this section is the systematic harmony (*samanvaya*) which asserts that the creation of the world proceeds from a faultless Brahman. A doubt arises as to whether this is contradicted by the logical principle that "one who acts with partiality is possessed of defects," or not. Regarding this, the author of the *pūrva-pakṣa* argues that the creative agency previously described as being for the sake of sport (*līlā*) is untenable if it depends upon factors such as the karma of beings, because that would result in the loss of its status as the Supreme Lord (*anīśvaratva*).

He presents the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) by means of an objection— starting with the words "Furthermore" (*punar ca*)— on the grounds that if [Brahman] were indifferent, it would follow that defects such as passion (*rāga*) and so forth would arise.
The point asserted in the *Janmādi-sūtra* is that Brahman alone is the cause of the world.
The ordinary person is a fool;
"blameless and stainless" is the Śruti;
"there is none hateful to me, nor any dear" is the Smṛti.
In the compound "svacchatvādi," the word "ādi" (and so forth) includes immutability (*kūṭasthatva*);
the analysis of the compound is: that which consists of clarity and the like, and which is the very nature of the Lord (*īśvara-svabhāva*).
If [the Lord] were to act unequally without depending on a cause, there would be defects such as partiality (*vaiṣamya*) and the like.
He establishes the final conclusion— that God is not independent—
starting with the words "evam prāpte" (this being the case).
Nor does dependence imply a lack of sovereignty.
Because the status of being a king or a lord does not cease as long as one depends upon service for the bestowing of results.

[Objection: "In that case, let the diverse creation proceed from merit (dharma) and demerit (adharma) alone; what is the use of a Lord (Īśvara)? To this, he says: "But the Lord is like the rain-cloud."

The meaning is that because the uncommon cause (asādhāraṇahetu) produces its effect only when accompanied by the common cause (sādhāraṇahetu), God is not rendered redundant; otherwise, it would follow that the rain-cloud (parjanya) is likewise useless.
The syntactical connection is as follows: "This Lord causes that person whom He desires to lead upward—that is, to elevate—to perform good deeds."
Nor should it be argued that partiality remains inevitable for one who causes some people to perform good deeds and others to perform evil deeds;
for when individuals engage in various actions through their own nature—consisting of the tendencies toward virtue and vice acquired from beginningless time—the Lord is merely the common cause.
Thus, the sense is that the Lord is beyond reproach. //34//
If it be argued that [the distinction between the soul and the body] does not exist because there is no division of action, we say: no, because [the cycle] is beginningless. (BS 2.1.35)

The author of the Sūtras raises an objection— that because there would be no karma caused by inequality in the first creation, it would be uniform, and consequently, the subsequent kalpas would likewise be so— and then provides the resolution:
"Not due to karma."
Anticipating the objection that the inequality [in the world] is caused by karma performed subsequent to the first creation, he states the circularity [of the argument]:
"sṛṣṭyuttareti" (after the creation).
The phrase "the first creation" is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*).

It should be understood that if there were a single uniform nature at the beginning, then since causes would be absent when unequal karmas arise in the middle, it would be impossible to avoid the consequence that subsequent creations would also be identical.
The refutation is easy to understand. //35//
And it is both logically consistent and empirically observed. (BBs 2.1.36)
He asks for the proof that there is no such thing as a "first creation" with the words,
"But how?
He shows that the proof consists of scripture and other means supported by logical reasoning through his commentary on the Sūtra.
"Upapadyate" (it follows/logically follows):
the meaning is that if one accepts creation even without a cause, the sections on knowledge (*jñāna-kāṇḍa*) and ritual action (*karman-kāṇḍa*) would become purposeless.
Now, having raised the objection that God or ignorance might be the cause for the diversity of pleasure and so forth, he refutes it step by step:
By the words "there is no Lord," etc., [the author] asks:
"What, then, is the cause? To that, he says:
"attachment and so forth."

Attachment, aversion, and delusion are the afflictions (*kleśa*); by their latent impressions (*vāsanā*), actions (*karman*)—which consist of a mixture of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*)—are projected.
Ignorance (*avidyā*), however, depending upon those [actions], is the cause for the diversity of creation, such as pleasure and so forth.
Therefore, the meaning is that one must accept an beginningless stream of afflictions and actions, characterized by their association with ignorance as a cooperative condition (*sahakārin*).
Furthermore, if creation were to have a beginning, the production of the first body would be impossible due to the absence of a cause;
nor can karma be the cause.

Because action is impossible prior to the body, all disputants must therefore accept the beginninglessness of saṃsāra in order to avoid the fallacy of mutual dependence between action and the body; thus he says: "And not...
(na ca).

Regarding the point that the inner self (pratyagātman), though not yet possessing vital breath at the very beginning of creation, might be designated by the term "jīva" on account of its future function of sustaining [the body], he says:
"And it will not sustain [it].
The sense is that in cases such as "A householder should marry a suitable wife," one must resort to a future state only out of necessity.
The true nature of this tree of saṃsāra— whether it is real or false— is not apprehended without instruction;
nor is there an end without knowledge,
nor is a beginning apprehended.
Precisely because it is non-existent;
nor is there a firm foundation, which is to say a middle state of persistence,
because its nature is seen and then lost— such is the meaning of the verse from the Gītā.
Even though saṃsāra is beginningless, the restriction "one only, without a second" is justified because it is false.
Therefore, it is established that there is no contradiction with the concordance (samanvaya) regarding the faultless Brahman. //36//
And because all dharmas are possible. (BBs 2.1.37)
And because all things arise [from it].

Regarding the subject matter—the Vedāntic synthesis which asserts that Brahman, though devoid of attributes (*nirguṇa*), is the material cause (*upādāna*) of the universe—there arises a doubt as to whether this is contradicted by the logical principle that "whatever is devoid of attributes cannot be a material cause, just as color [is not the cause of taste]. In response: let the Lord be the instrumental cause (*nimitta*) of the unequal creation, since there exists karma which acts as its motivator (*prayojaka*).

To this objection— namely, that [Brahman] cannot be the material cause because its pervader, the possession of qualities (*saguṇatva*), is absent— the author states the intent of the sūtra setting forth the established conclusion (*siddhānta-sūtra*) with the words "conscious" (*cetana*).
The status of being the illusory material cause (*vivartopādānatva*) is not contradictory even for that which is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*).

The point is this: since "being unknown" (ajñātatva), which serves as the condition for being the substratum of an error, exists [in Brahman], whereas "possessing qualities" (saguṇatva) is non-pervasive because errors regarding eternality and so forth are observed in respect to qualities such as sound;

for although omniscience and omnipotence are not well-known in the world as attributes of a cause, it is nonetheless well-established that whoever is the agent of something must be the knower and capable of producing all of it.

Since it is heard in scripture that the Lord is the creator of all, his unsurpassed omniscience and omnipotence are established by implication in accordance with what is well-known; intending this, he says: "omniscient and omnipotent.
[He is] "possessed of great illusion" (mahāmāya).
This was stated in order to wash away the mud of all doubts regarding the [Brahman's] status as both agent and material cause;
therefore, it is established that there is no fault whatsoever in the established doctrine of the Upaniṣads. //37//

Thus ends the first quarter of the second chapter in the *Bhāṣyaratnaprabhā*, a commentary on the *Śārīrakamīmāṃsā* composed by the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya Śrī Govindānanda Bhagavatpāda. //1//

Thus ends the first quarter (pāda) of the second chapter, titled "The Removal of Contradictions Regarding the Consistency of Vedānta with the Smṛtis of Sāṃkhya, Yoga, Kaṇāda, and Others, and with the Reasoning Employed by Sāṃkhya and Others.
Second Quarter of the Second Chapter:
The Sāṃkhyas, Tārkikas, Buddhists, Jains, Pāśupatas, and others...
I bow to that preeminent scion of Raghu, whose true nature they do not know. //1//

START BsRp_2,2.1.1ḥ racanānupapatteś ca nānumānam / BBs_2,2.1 / Having raised the objection that, just as all properties are possible in Brahman, they might likewise be possible in Pradhāna, [the author] refutes this: "And because of the impossibility of design, there is no inference [of Pradhāna]."
"And because the construction [of the world] is untenable, there is no inference [for the existence of a creator].
