Now, it may be argued: this treatise was commenced in order to ascertain the purport of the Vedāntas so as to remove obstacles to the determination of the meaning of those texts for those seeking liberation; and since that [purport] has been ascertained as being free from defects, this present section, which consists of the refutation of opposing views, is therefore not relevant to this treatise."
He raises an objection, saying "Even though," because the refutation of that [other view] is not required for those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*).
He replies that it must nevertheless be performed, because without the refutation of the opponent's position, the stability of one's own position is impossible.
"Even so" (tathāpi):
if that is the case, then the refutation of the opponent's position should be performed even before establishing one's own position; to this he replies:
"Regarding the meaning of the Vedānta."
The determination of the purport of the Vedānta is of primary importance because it is included within the means of producing that fruitful knowledge.
One might object: "But surely, since it functions through passion and aversion, the refutation of other systems should not be undertaken.
Thus he raises this doubt with the word "nanu" (but).
Indeed, this discussion has been commenced with the primary aim of determining the truth;
and the determination of the truth is not accomplished without a lack of faith in the doctrines of others,
and that lack of faith is not accomplished without the certainty that those doctrines are rooted in error.

And since that [opponent] cannot proceed without this verse— because its purpose is to preserve his own established doctrine and to establish the existence of Pradhāna— this verse is relevant to this treatise.
With the intention that "since it is relevant, it must be accepted even by one who is free from passion," he provides a reply by accepting it,
beginning with the words "Certainly" (bāḍham), and so forth.
"By way of pretext" means by means of a pretense;
the meaning is that since there are many grounds for the faith of those of dull intellect in those [other systems], an effort is made to refute them.
However, one's own faith in one's own doctrine and hatred toward other doctrines are accepted because they serve the purpose of establishing the primary goal.
Nor is this [rejection] hatred;

for it should be understood that rejection brings about hatred only when it is done through the thought that [the other position] is an opposing side, and not when it is done with the desire to determine the truth.
He raises the objection of tautology:
Regarding the phrase "nanvīkṣateḥ":
previously, it was stated that the Sāṃkhya and other systems are non-Vedic because their proponents' reasoning, which purports to support the meaning of the Śruti, has been refuted;

now, however, their independent arguments—which do not depend on the Śruti—are being refuted. Thus, because there is a difference in subject matter, this is not a redundant repetition. This is what he says.
Regarding the phrase "that is said":

the subject here is the Sāṃkhya tenet that the non-intelligent *pradhāna* is the material cause (*upādāna*) of the world. Since there is a doubt as to whether this is based on valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) or on error, the connection [of the sūtra] is established by way of an objection: because the attributes mentioned in the sūtra "and because all qualities are possible" are compatible with the *pradhāna*, it alone must be the material cause.
Demonstrating that [the system] is rooted in valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), he states the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) with the words "In this regard, the Sāṅkhyas...

The connection between the two sections is established because the knowledge of one's own established doctrine (*svasiddhāntajñāna*) serves as a prerequisite for the refutation of the views of others (*paramatanirāsa*).
Since this [section] consists of the refutation of the views of others, it is connected to all the topical discussions (*adhikaraṇa*) within this chapter.

It should be understood that throughout this chapter, the result of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is the failure to establish the systematic coherence (*samanvaya*) of the meaning of the stated scriptures due to contradiction with doctrines rooted in authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), whereas the result of the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is the establishment of that coherence.
The distinction is that the connection with the Śruti (scriptural authority) belongs to this section because its purpose is to establish the firmness of the concordance with the primary Śruti.
"Bheda" means differences or modifications;
he states the pervasion (vyāpti): those modifications which are endowed with [the nature of] something are of that as their material cause (tatprakṛtika).
The word "yathā" (just as) [means]:
every effect has for its material cause a substance consisting of pleasure, pain, and delusion, because it is permeated by them.
He states the inference "like a jar and so forth" with the word "tathā" (likewise).
To the question, "For what purpose does the Pradhāna undergo transformation?", he replies:
Regarding the phrase "of the sentient being" (cetanasya):
the "object" (artha) consists of enjoyment and liberation;
it means that [Prakṛti] proceeds for that purpose by its very nature, and is not impelled by any sentient being.
As it has been said: "The purpose of the Puruṣa alone is the cause; the instrument is not set in motion by anyone. He recalls the other inferences stated by them with the words "tathā" (likewise).

For it has been said: "Because of the finite measure of diverse objects, because of their commonality, because of their activity proceeding from a potentiality, because of the distinction between cause and effect, and because of the non-distinction of the manifold universe [at its origin]."
Thus,
in this verse, the logical mark (*liṅga*) "because of the presence" (*samanvayāt*) has been explained.
The remaining [marks] are now being explained.
For instance: the unmanifest is the cause of the diverse entities such as earth and the rest, because they are finite, like a jar.
Nor is there a deficiency of the probandum (sādhyavaikalya) in the example.
Because even clay is unmanifest prior to the production of a jar, by virtue of being characterized by the effect— the jar and so forth— which is as yet unmanifest; and likewise,
since jars and other such things proceed from the power of their cause, it must be stated that the effects beginning with the Great Principle (mahat) also proceed from the power of their cause,
and that cause possessing such power is the Unmanifest (avyakta).
Furthermore, the differentiation of an effect from its cause is observed as its birth; for instance, clay is born from earth, and from that [clay] comes the jar.
Likewise, non-differentiation is observed as dissolution in the reverse order: the jar dissolves into clay, that [clay] into earth, the earth into water, and the water into fire.

These two—differentiation and non-differentiation—which are observed in the diverse multitude of entities (*vaiśvarūpya*) and are treated as distinct positions, must both find their rest in some single cause, because they are respectively characterized by differentiation and non-differentiation, just as [the states of] clay...
The meaning is "like the separation and non-separation of a jar.
He states the established conclusion: "To this we say."
Is it being proved by means of inferences that the world has an insentient nature as its material cause, or rather that it has an independent insentient nature as its material cause?
In the first case, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*).

Because we accept that māyā, which consists of the three guṇas, is beginningless; regarding the second [point], he says "yadi" (if), meaning that in the example of the pot and so forth, there is the fallacy of the unestablished nature of the probandum (*sādhyāprasiddhi*).
That "prakṛti" is independent and insentient would be established by the force of an example only if such an example existed somewhere;
for surely, an example is observed somewhere—this is the logical connection (*anvaya*).
He states the meaning of the word "independent":
"Unpresided over by an intelligent being" (cetanānadhiṣṭhitam):

Having stated the non-establishment of the probandum belonging to the opponent, he states the counter-reasoning (satpratipakṣa) and expresses the pervasion (vyāpti)— that whatever effect consists of a variegated arrangement has for its material cause an insentient entity presided over by an intelligent being— by means of the example "the house," etc.
This world has a conscious being as its presiding cause over an unconscious material nature,
because it is an effect, like a house; such is the formal argument.

To state the subverting argument (bādhakatarka) mentioned in the Sūtra— namely, that the manifold arrangement [of the world] would be impossible in the opposing view— he describes the variety of the universe with the word "tathā" (thus):
the external world, such as earth and so forth, is the object of enjoyment.
The internal [world] consists of the body and so forth, which is the substratum for experience; this is the distinction.
The meaning is: that whose arrangement—the specific, non-common configuration of its parts—is such [as described].
How could such a diverse world be fashioned by insentient primordial matter (*jaḍaprakṛti*) without being presided over by consciousness?
The meaning is: "not in any way whatsoever.

He states the pervasion (*vyāpti*)—that whatever is insentient and not presided over by consciousness does not perform an action—which is rooted in reasoning, with the words: "a clod of earth," etc. (*loṣṭa*...).
The meaning is that in objects such as clods of earth, which are impelled by volition, the performance of an effect is not observed.
Furthermore, the primordial nature (prakṛti), though beginningless and insentient, is presided over by a conscious being,
because it is subject to transformation.
He says "like clay, etc. (mṛdādivat).
Now, one might object: in the examples of clay and so forth, both [properties] exist—namely, insentience and being presided over by a sentient agent.

In that case, for the reason of being subject to transformation (*pariṇāmitva*), only insentience (*acetanatva*) is the pervader (*vyāpaka*), because it is internal (*antaraṅga*) as the very nature of clay and so forth;
however, being presided over by a conscious agent (*cetanādhiṣṭhitatva*) is not the pervader,
because it is external (*bahiraṅga*) due to its dependence on external factors such as a potter for the clay and so forth.

And likewise, having raised the objection that even though it undergoes transformation (*pariṇāmitva*), the primordial nature (*mūlaprakṛti*) is associated only with the property of insentience (*acetanatva*) and not with being presided over by a conscious agent (*cetanādhiṣṭhitatva*), [the author] refutes this with the words "nor" (*na ca*).

In the example of the kitchen, the essential nature of the kitchen (*mahānasasvarūpa*), though internal, does not possess the pervasion (*vyāpakatva*) of smoke; whereas fire, though external and distinct from it, does possess it. Thus, being internal is not a factor for pervasion.
The sense is that [the Pradhāna] is not the instigator.

Furthermore, since there is no sublation to the acceptance that whatever is insentient transforms only when presided over by a sentient being—and indeed, because this is supported by scripture—one must accept it as such;
thus he says: "And this being so... [na caivaṃ sati...].
He states that the word "ca" (and) is used in the Sūtra for the purpose of indicating the non-establishment of the reason, namely, "because of the concomitance with pleasure, pain, and delusion":
"And because [concomitance] and so forth are not possible.
The meaning is that inference is not tenable.
The word "ādi" (and so forth) is intended to include [qualities] such as dimension (*parimāṇa*).
Since sound and the other objects are experienced as being external, it is unestablished that they consist of internal pleasure and the like; furthermore, this is because they are their causes.
For there can be no connection between a cause and its effect by way of identity.
The meaning is that [the two] are not perceived together, like a staff and a jar.

Furthermore, if pleasure and so forth were inherent in the jar—just as clay is in a jar—and were conjoined with sound and other qualities, then pleasure and so forth would be perceived by everyone without distinction, just as the clay in a jar is.
Since such perception does not occur, he states that the absence of the reason is certain through non-perception of what is otherwise perceptible (*yogyānupalabdhi*).

Regarding the phrase "sound and so forth": even though the object is one and the same, due to the diversity of human latent impressions (*vāsanā*), it is observed that for some there arises a cognition of pleasure, for some a cognition of pain, and for others a cognition of delusion. Therefore, the meaning is that objects do not possess the nature of pleasure and the like [in themselves].
Having thus refuted the reason "because of homogeneity" (*samanvaya*), he refutes the reasons such as "because of limited magnitude" (*parimāṇa*) and so forth with the word "likewise" (*tathā*).

When it is established that intellect (*buddhi*) and the rest are preceded by a combination because they are limited in magnitude, it follows that multiple entities— sattva, rajas, and tamas— in a combined state are established.
The Sāṃkhya’s position is that Brahman cannot be established because of the impossibility of association within a single entity.
What is this "limitedness"? It is certainly not limitation by space.
Because it does not exist within the space contained within its own side, its existence as a real entity is unestablished;
nor is there delimitation by time,
since the Sāṃkhyas do not accept the existence of time.
Furthermore, because [the reason] is established by the mere association with the qualities of ignorance (*avidyā*), it results in proving what is already proven (*siddhasādhana*).

Nor is there a real delimitation (*pariccheda*) [of the object], for even though *sattva* and the other qualities are mutually distinct, there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) due to the absence of the probandum [in those cases]; thus he says:
Regarding the term "sattva":
as for what was stated— that the Pradhāna is that wherein the distinction between cause and effect reaches its culmination—
that is not correct.
Because completion [of the world] is possible either in Brahman or in Māyā;

and there is no pervasion (vyāpti) such that whatever division belongs to an effect must be completed in something insentient that is not presided over by a conscious being, since one observes the presiding of a conscious being in all insentient things— thus he says:
The word "kārya" (effect) [is used here].
By this, non-differentiation (*avibhāga*) is also explained.
As for the other pervasion (*vyāpti*), namely: "whatever is finite is preceded by the unmanifested primordial nature (*avyakta-prakṛti*)," [it is also established].
Furthermore, there is a deviation [from the rule] regarding its qualities, which are beginningless yet limited.

By this, the claim that "the material cause of insentient modifications must itself be insentient, because the relationship of material cause and modification occurs only between similar things" is refuted;
for similarity is established even when the insentient material cause is presided over by a sentient being.

Furthermore, because the rule of similarity has been refuted in the [sūtra] "Not so, on account of the difference in nature" (na vilakṣaṇatvāt), the meaning is that the mark of "activity from power" (śaktitaḥ pravṛtti) is otherwise established, since the activity of an effect is possible through the power of a cause dependent upon a conscious being. //1//
And because of the activity [of the world]. (BBs 2.2)
An independent, insentient entity should not be inferred as the cause,
because its engagement for the purpose of creation is untenable; thus, the sūtra should be construed by connecting the word "untenability" (anupapatti) with the particle "ca" (and).
Anticipating the question, "What is the difference between creation (racanā) and activity (pravṛtti)?", he states the nature of activity [in the verse beginning with] "sāmya":
the state of equilibrium of the guṇas is indeed the dissolution of the principles (tattvas).
In that case, no effect whatsoever would arise, because it would follow that there is no dissolution [of the equilibrium].
Rather, first there occurs an inequality characterized by the departure from equilibrium;

thereafter, there arises a relationship of primary and subordinate factors (*aṅga-aṅgibhāva*), wherein one quality becomes the primary factor through its manifestation and another becomes the subordinate factor as a residual element.

When that [Prakṛti] exists, there is activity (pravṛtti) consisting of the production of effects such as the Great Principle (mahat) and so forth; "arrangement" (racanā) refers to the distinction [of these effects], meaning the deployment of various effects by that activity.
The activity of the Guṇas is preceded by the superintendence of a conscious being.
Because it is an activity, like the activity of a chariot and so forth; thus he says: "That too... (sāpi).
The meaning is that it is impossible for [the world] to proceed independently in the absence of a cause.

However, some explain the logical mark "activity from capacity" (*śaktitaḥ pravṛttiḥ*) as follows: because differentiated entities possess the power of activity, they must have an insentient nature that is not presided over by a conscious being.
This [reason] also suffers from the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to the *guṇas*.
Furthermore, if "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) is used as a qualification, there is a contradiction (*viruddhatā*);

for in the case of jars and the like, which possess the capacity for activity while being effects, one observes a pervasion (*vyāpti*) with the opposite of the stated probandum—namely, having a conscious being as their presiding cause. This was made known by the Sūtra: "And because of activity" (*pravṛtteśca*).
Now, even if activity is not observed in the world among independent insentient things, let that activity be established in the *pradhāna*; to this, he says:
"And because it is based on what is observed" (dṛṣṭācca).
The meaning is that for you, who rely upon inference, it is impossible to establish supersensuous objects without an example.
Now, the Sāṃkhya raises an objection: "If the activity of the Pradhāna is refuted, then the activity of a conscious being in creation must be asserted; but that [activity] is not tenable."
Regarding the word "nanu":
he accepts the impossibility of activity for a pure consciousness,
saying "True."
In that case, the activity of a purely insentient entity would be established, since otherwise creation would be impossible;
to this, he replies: "Even so" (tathāpi).
The sense is that even though the pure conscious principle (cetanā) does not act by itself, the activity of creation proceeds from the mutual relationship between the conscious and the unconscious.
The Sāṃkhya criticizes this Vedānta doctrine with the words:
"But not [so]," etc.
Every activity is observed to have its basis solely in the non-conscious;
however, nowhere is the activity of a conscious being ever observed to be connected with the non-conscious.
Therefore, the meaning is that creation does not proceed from a conscious being.
Having heard both views, the neutral person asks:
"What then?"

The meaning of the question is this: Is the Sāṃkhya view correct—that the activity observed in insentient things such as chariots belongs to those very objects themselves and that consciousness is not the cause therein—or is the Vedāntin view correct—that the activity is prompted by a conscious agent, such as a horse or other driver?
The Sāṃkhya replies:
Regarding the word "nanu":
"of both" means of both the activity and its substratum.

The point is that since the occurrence [of activity] is established by means of a perceived substratum alone, one should not postulate the activity of an unperceived conscious being. As to how the self is established if it is not perceptible, he says:
"by activity" (*pravṛtti*).

The logical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: since the presence of breath and so forth is observed as a mark (*liṅga*) that distinguishes a living body from things such as chariots, the existence of a conscious being is established.

The meaning is that the self is proven by the following inference: "The living body possesses a self because it possesses breath and so forth; by contrast (*vyatireka*), [it is] like a chariot and so forth."

The phrase "the substratum of activity" (*pravṛttyāśraya*) is stated to indicate another inference: "The activity of the body is accompanied by one who possesses knowledge other than its own substratum, because it is an activity, like the activity of a chariot."
The meaning of the particle *eva* is that it is the very establishment of existence (*sadbhāvasiddhi*) that [constitutes the cause], not the state of being an instigator (*pravartakatva*).
The point is that if something inferred were a cause for activity merely by its existence, then even space (*ākāśa*) would follow as a cause in all instances.
Furthermore, he states that even the error of the Cārvākas—who hold that the self (*ātman*) is imperceptible—is itself a logical mark (*liṅga*).
"From this very reason" means "precisely because of its imperceptibility.
The underlying sense is that if the self were perceptible as distinct from the body, error would be impossible.

"From observation"—the words "of activity and consciousness" are to be supplied as the remainder. Having accepted the opponent's claim that insentience alone is the substratum of activity, the proponent establishes that sentience is the motivator: The opponent argues: If it is held that the self is the agent of action because it is the substratum of desire (*icchā*), then the body would also have to be considered the agent, since it too is the substratum of desire. For we observe that when a person desires to eat, the body indeed performs the act of eating. Furthermore, the body is not the substratum of the cognition "I am," which is the cause of desire; rather, the self is the substratum of that cognition. Therefore, the self alone is the agent. To this, the proponent replies: This is not so. It is observed that even in the absence of the cognition "I am," the body acts toward its own benefit. For instance, when a person is bitten by a snake, the hand—which is the substratum of the cognition "I am"—is withdrawn from the vicinity of the mouth, while the foot, which is not the substratum of that cognition, moves away from the snake. Moreover, in the case of a person who has fallen into a deep sleep and lacks the cognition "I am," the body still performs actions such as coughing or sneezing. Therefore, the body alone is the agent. To this, the opponent replies: No, for the body is insentient (*acetana*). Since the body is composed of earth and other material elements, it is insentient like a clod of earth or a stone. And it is impossible for an insentient thing to be an agent. Therefore, the self alone is the agent. To this, the proponent replies: Even if the self were the agent, it would be an agent only through the body, just as a potter is an agent only through the clay. For it is never seen that an agent acts without an instrument. Furthermore, the self is not the agent of the body's activity in the same way that a potter is the agent of the pot's production; rather, the self is the motivator (*prayojaka*) of the body's activity. How so? Because the body is observed to act only when impelled by the self. Just as a charioteer is the motivator of the chariot's movement, so too is the self the motivator of the body's activity. Thus, the self is established as the agent through its role as the motivator. The opponent objects: If the self is the motivator of the body's activity, then why does it not motivate the body to act toward what is undesirable? For example, why does the self not motivate the body to take poison or fall from a mountain peak? To this, the proponent replies: The self does not motivate the body to act toward what is undesirable because it is itself subject to suffering. For one who desires happiness and fears suffering will not motivate the body to engage in activities that lead to suffering. Therefore, the self is the motivator of the body's activity only toward what is desirable. Thus, the self is established as the agent through its role as the motivator. The opponent objects: If the self is the motivator of the body's activity, then why does it not motivate the body to act toward what is desirable at all times? For example, why does the self not motivate the body to eat whenever it desires food? To this, the proponent replies: The self does not motivate the body to act toward what is desirable at all times because it is dependent on other factors. For the self requires the presence of external means (*sādhana*) such as food and drink. Just as a farmer, though he desires a harvest, cannot produce grain without seeds, water, and manure, so too the self cannot motivate the body to act toward what is desirable without the necessary external means. Therefore, the self is the motivator of the body's activity only when the appropriate conditions are met. Thus, the self is established as the agent through its role as the motivator. The opponent objects: If the self is the motivator of the body's activity, then why does it not motivate the body to act toward what is desirable immediately after waking from deep sleep? For the self is present there as well. To this, the proponent replies: The self does not motivate the body to act toward what is desirable immediately after waking from deep sleep because the memory of the previous desire is absent. For the self motivates the body to act toward what is desirable only when it remembers its previous desire for that object. In the state of deep sleep, however, the mind (*manas*) is withdrawn within and the memory of the previous desire is lost. Therefore, the self does not motivate the body to act at that time. Thus, the self is established as the agent through its role as the motivator. The opponent objects: If the self is the motivator of the body's activity, then why does it not motivate the body to act toward what is desirable when it is in a state of distraction (*vikṣepa*)? For the self is present there as well. To this, the proponent replies: The self does not motivate the body to act toward what is desirable when it is in a state of distraction because it is overcome by another desire. For the self motivates the body to act toward what is desirable only when it is free from the influence of a contrary desire. In a state of distraction, however, the self is overwhelmed by a different desire and thus fails to motivate the body toward its original object. Therefore, the self is established as the agent through its role as the motivator. The opponent objects: If the self is the motivator of the body's activity, then why does it not motivate the body to act toward what is desirable when it is in a state of delusion (*moha*)? For the self is present there as well. To this, the proponent replies: The self does not motivate the body to act toward what is desirable when it is in a state of delusion because it is confused about the nature of the object. For the self motivates the body to act toward what is desirable only when it correctly perceives the object as beneficial. In a state of delusion, however, the self misperceives the object and thus fails to motivate the body toward its true purpose. Therefore, the self is established as the agent through its role as the motivator. The opponent objects: If the self is the motivator of the body's activity, then why does it not motivate the body to act toward what is desirable when it is in a state of fear (*bhaya*)? For the self is present there as well. To this, the proponent replies: The self does not motivate the body to act toward what is desirable when it is in a state of fear because it is preoccupied with avoiding the source of fear. For the self motivates the body to act toward what is desirable only when it is free from the impulse to flee danger. In a state of fear, however, the self is intent on self-preservation and thus fails to motivate the body toward other goals. Therefore, the self is established as the agent through its role as the motivator. The opponent objects: If the self is the motivator of the body's activity, then why does it not motivate the body to act toward what is desirable when it is in a state of exhaustion (*śrama*)? For the self is present there as well. To this, the proponent replies: The self does not motivate the body to act toward what is desirable when it is in a state of exhaustion because it is incapable of exertion. For the self motivates the body to act toward what is desirable only when it possesses the capacity for effort. In a state of exhaustion, however, the self is devoid of energy and thus fails to motivate the body. Therefore, the self is established as the agent through its role as the motivator. The opponent objects: If the self is the motivator of the body's activity, then why does it not motivate the body to act toward what is desirable when it is in a state of intoxication (*mada*)? For the self is present there as well. To this, the proponent replies: The self does not motivate the body to act toward what is desirable when it is in a state of intoxication because it is under the influence of a substance that impairs its judgment. For the self motivates the body to act toward what is desirable only when it is in its natural state. In a state of intoxication, however, the self's faculties are deranged and it fails to motivate the body appropriately. Therefore, the self is established as the agent through its role as the motivator. The opponent objects: If the self is the motivator of the body's activity, then why does it not motivate the body to act toward what is desirable when it is in a state of old age (*jarā*)? For the self is present there as well. To this, the proponent replies: The self does not motivate the body to act toward what is desirable when it is in a state of old age because the body's capacity for action is impaired. For the self motivates the body to act toward what is desirable only when the body is capable of responding. In a state of old age, however, the body's organs are weakened and it fails to carry out the self's intentions. Therefore, the self is established as the agent through its role as the motivator. The opponent objects: If the self is the motivator of the body's activity, then why does it not motivate the body
"That is being stated":

the positive and negative concomitances (*anvaya-vyatireka*) between the consciousness of horses and other animals and the operation of chariots and so forth are clear; by means of these two, the fact that consciousness is the instigator [of action] is agreed upon even by outsiders.
Thus he says: "even for the Lokāyatikas."

Someone raises an objection: "Since that which is an initiator must itself possess activity, like a horse or the like, there can be no status as an initiator in the Self because of the absence of the pervading property (vyāpaka) [activity] within it"—this is expressed by the words "nanu" (but surely).
He refutes this by stating that there is no such universal pervasion (vyāpti) due to its deviation (vyabhicāra) in the case of gems and the like.
"No.
Even though there is unity in reality, he says "no" because there exists a superimposed duality that must be set in motion.

Regarding the term *avidyā*: the meaning is that there is no occasion for objection, because it has been stated that the Lord’s status as the inner ruler (*antaryāmitva*) and so forth arises through the power (*vaśa*)—that is, the capacity—of that very connection with the conscious self (*cidātman*) which is imagined by that same illusion (*māyā*) in the form of ignorance (*avidyā*), namely, the entry [of the Self] into the manifold expansion of name and form (*nāmarūpa-prapañca*) imagined by that ignorance itself. //2//
If it is argued that [the soul] is like milk or water, then in that case as well: BBs 2.2.3.

It is established that the activity of that which is beginninglessly insentient proceeds by means of a sentient being and so forth, because it is an activity, just like the activity of a chariot and the like.

In this regard, having raised the objection that there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of milk and so forth, he explains the Sūtra— stating that even in that case, since it is equivalent to the subject (*pakṣa*), the establishment of the probandum (*sādhya*) occurs through inference and scripture, and thus there is no deviation— with the words beginning "It might be argued as follows" (*syādetat*).
[He says] "the subject of the probandum" (*sādhyapakṣa*).
The meaning is: because it is similar to the subject (*pakṣa*) which possesses the property to be proven (*sādhyavat*).
"Non-presentation" means, in other words, that it is not a ground for deviation (*vyabhicāra*).
He states that there is no deviation [from the rule] because the cow and so forth exist as the instigators of the milk;
this is shown by the words "of the conscious being" (cetanāyāśca). This has been demonstrated.
The ellipsis is "by means of inference and scripture.

Having raised the objection that there is a contradiction between what precedes and what follows in the author of the Sūtras—namely, the statements "for [the soul is] like milk" and "even there"—he declares that there is no contradiction by means of these two Sūtras, based on both worldly perspective and scriptural perspective: "Upasaṃhāra... (III.1.3).
And because [the self] does not persist through separation [from the body], and because it is independent. (BBs 2.2.4)

Anticipating the objection that even for the Pradhāna, merit (dharma) and so forth, or the Puruṣa, might be the instigator of activity, the Sūtra has been set forth; he explains it with the words beginning "Of the Sāṃkhyas," and so on.
The meaning is that since action cannot exist apart from Pradhāna, and since Puruṣa is indifferent, it is illogical to claim that creation occurs at one time and dissolution at another.
The point is that even action, being of the nature of Pradhāna, is insentient and eternally present; therefore, it cannot be the regulator of occasional activity. //4//
And because it does not exist elsewhere, [the self] is not like grass and so forth. (BBs 2.2.5)
Furthermore, suspecting that the Pradhāna might act spontaneously and occasionally due to the force of examples, the author of the Sūtras refutes this with the words beginning "anyatra" (elsewhere).
He asks:
"How so? The answer is:
"By means of another cause."
He establishes the final position— that there exists another cause, such as a cow and so forth— by stating:
"To this it is replied."
"Abandoned" means destroyed.
Regarding the statement that milk possesses a natural state because it cannot be produced at will, he says:
"And not according to one's desire. //5//

The first point is that the primordial matter (*pradhāna*) does not act of its own accord, because if one were to admit that it acts spontaneously, it would follow that there is no dependence upon the purpose of the Spirit (*puruṣārtha*).
He refutes the objection that this consequence is acceptable:
"Therefore, [it must be] Pradhāna.
This means that if the aforementioned consequence were accepted, there would be a loss of the original thesis.
He states another point—namely, that there is no spontaneous activity due to the impossibility of its purpose—by first raising an objection:
He says "sa yadi" and so forth; and he says "tathāpi" [nevertheless], meaning that if a purpose is required, it must be stated.
In the immutable *puruṣa*, experience (*bhoga*) is not tenable, because it is impossible to produce an excellence such as inherent happiness, and because superimposition (*adhyāsa*) is not admitted.

Furthermore, if the activity of *pradhāna* were for the sake of experience, there would be the consequence of no liberation, due to the absence of discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*), which is the cause of liberation.
If, on the other hand, its purpose were liberation, then since liberation—consisting in abiding in one's own nature—is self-evident, the activity of *pradhāna* would be rendered useless.
The meaning is that there would be the undesirable consequence of the absence of enjoyment.
He refutes the third [position] with the words:
"as serving both purposes."

They are called *mātrās* because they are measured (*mīyante*) or experienced (*bhujyante*), meaning they are objects of enjoyment. He refutes the statement in the *Kārikā*—"the unmanifest (*avyakta*) acts for the sake of the liberation of the *puruṣa*, just as the world engages in activities for the sake of satisfying its desires"—with the words "And not... (*na ca*).
The meaning is that eagerness, which is a specific kind of desire, is not appropriate for either a purely insentient self or for [the self] alone.

For the Person (puruṣa) possesses the power of vision because his nature is consciousness, and the primordial matter (pradhāna) possesses the power of creation because it consists of the three qualities (guṇas).
If it is argued that the primary cause (pradhāna) engages in creation because its two powers cannot be purposeful without the creation of the visible world, we say: no.
Since the two powers are eternal, it would follow that creation is also eternal. Thus he says:
"The power of seeing... (verse 6).
Having refuted the agency of the Puruṣa, the author raises it again by means of an analogy and then negates it: "If it be argued that it is like a man and a stone, even so [the objection remains].
To the Sāṃkhya who says, "In doing so, you abandon the independence of the Pradhāna and the neutrality of the Puruṣa which you have accepted," he replies:
And how so?
There are two reasons for stating that the Puruṣa possesses neither physical motion nor the quality of effort (prayatna):
because both Pradhāna and Puruṣa are eternal and all-pervading, their proximity is eternal.
The argument that there is an activity—namely, the polishing of the stone, its stabilization through rectitude, and its occasional proximity—is not a valid presentation;
the meaning is that this does not constitute a proper parallel example.
[Objection: But surely there exists a fitness for the relationship of seer and seen between the conscious and the insentient.
To the objection that their relationship consists in that very state [of fitness], he says:
"fitness" (yogyatā).
The meaning is that since fitness, consisting in the nature of consciousness and insentience, is eternal, it would follow that the relationship is also eternal.

Just as the position that the Pradhāna acts independently was refuted by considering the alternatives—that its fruit is enjoyment, liberation, or both—so too must the position that the Pradhāna acts under the control of the Puruṣa be refuted on account of the absence of a fruit; thus he says:
"as before."
Raising the objection as to how the Supreme Self, being indifferent (*udāsīna*), can be the instigator [of activity] according to the final doctrine (*siddhānta*), he says:
"The Supreme Self... In the Sāṃkhya system, both [attributes] are contradictory because they are [both considered] real.
In our view, there is no contradiction between the imagined and the unimagined; this is the excellence [of our position]. //7//
And because the status of being the principal [member] is untenable. (BBs 2.2.8)
Is the state of the Pradhāna eternal like that of the immutable (kūṭastha), or is it subject to modification?
Regarding the first case, he states the flaw:
Regarding the phrase "in that [case]": if there were a relationship of part and whole (aṅgāṅgibhāva), there would be a destruction of the very nature of their equality;

consequently, because of the fear that the immutability (kauṭasthya) [of Prakṛti] would be violated, a relationship of part and whole is untenable, and thus the meaning is that creation itself becomes untenable.
He refutes the second [position] with the words "of the external" (bāhyasya).
The meaning is that a cause for the cessation of the equilibrium that has persisted for a long time must be stated, yet such a cause does not exist. //8//
And because, in the case of an inference otherwise, there would be a lack of the capacity for knowledge. (BBs 2.2.9)
It has been stated that there is no inherent inequality among the *guṇas* because their natures are mutually independent;
anticipating the objection that the reason for this is unestablished (*hetvasiddhi*), the author of the Sūtras provides the following rebuttal:
"Otherwise... (*anyathā*).
Because the nature [of the qualities] is not independent, but rather inferred as being dependent, the fault mentioned in the preceding sūtra does not apply.
Nor is this a deviation from established tenets (apasiddhānta), because the nature of the qualities is accepted in accordance with their effects; thus he says:
"The functioning of the qualities is mobile" (calaṃ guṇavṛttam).
He offers a rebuttal by accepting that there is no defect regarding the impossibility of the relationship between the subordinate and the principal mentioned in the preceding sūtra:
"Even so... (evamapi).

The meaning is that if one were to postulate a power of knowledge for the sake of accomplishing an effect, it would result in the doctrine of Brahman (brahmavāda). He abandons this admission with the words "vaiṣamya" (inequality) //9//
And because of contradiction, [the Sāṃkhya system] is inconsistent. (2.2.10)
He explains the Sūtra with the words "paraspara" (mutually):
the sense organ of cognition is merely the skin alone; it is a single [organ] that serves as the cause for the cognition of multiple objects such as sound and so forth.
The five organs of action and the mind make seven organs;
the five organs of cognition, the five organs of action, and the mind make eleven;
and intellect, ego, and mind make three.
"One" is simply the intellect (*buddhi*).

Having thus explained [the objection] as being due to internal contradiction between earlier and later [statements], he states another point— namely, "and because of the conflict between Śruti and Smṛti"—
with the words "it is well-known."
Therefore, since the Sāṃkhya system is rooted in error, it is established that there is no contradiction between it and the faultless harmony of the Vedānta.
Unable to endure the inconsistencies within its own doctrine, the Sāṃkhyaist objects: "To this, he says... [atrāha].

The meaning is that the soul (*jīva*) is the sufferer (*tapyo*) and transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) is the causer of suffering (*tāpaka*); since their distinction is not admitted [by the opponent], the relationship of sufferer and causer of suffering well-known in the world would be sublated. He explains this with the words:
"For [if they were] one... (*ekaṃ hi*).

And thus, the meaning is that the loss of the conventional usage of difference would follow, which is inconsistent. Now, one might object: "Even though their material cause is one, there is indeed mutual difference between them, just as there is between heat and light, both of which have fire as their single essence; therefore, there is no loss of conventional usage. Anticipating this, he states that, unlike fire, there would be no liberation for the Self from those two: The meaning is that the loss of the conventional usage of difference would follow, which is inconsistent. Now, one might object: "Even though their material cause is one, there is indeed mutual difference between them, just as there is between heat and light, both of which have fire as their single essence; therefore, there is no loss of conventional usage. Anticipating this, he states that, unlike fire, there would be no liberation for the Self from those two:
With the words "And if... and so forth, [the author] addresses the following objection:

"Even though the substratum (dharmin) exists, liberation is possible as the destruction of its own nature (svabhāva), because we observe the destruction of waves and the like while the water itself remains. Anticipating this doubt, he states that the illustrative example (dṛṣṭānta) is unestablished:
The phrase "yo 'pi" (even that which... [is used].

Furthermore, he states that if difference is admitted, there is a deviation from established doctrine (*apasiddhānta*), whereas if it is not admitted, there is a contradiction with what is well-known in the world (*lokaprasiddhibādha*): [He says: "Even that... etc. Moreover, if one accepts difference, there is a departure from established tenets; if one does not accept it, there is a contradiction with worldly consensus. Thus he says:
And it is well-known [that they are distinct].
For an object (artha) is a "tormentor" (tāpaka) because it causes suffering to one who desires it through its acquisition, loss, and so forth; the seeker is the one who suffers (tapyas).
He states the sublation [of the identity] of these two if they were non-different:
Regarding the word "yadi":
since there is no object for one who is not a seeker, it follows by implication that there is an absence of being an object because there is an absence of a seeker;
thus he says, "likewise, of the object as well."
He refutes the acceptability of the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) with the words "And this is not the case.
For "being an object" (arthatva) consists in being the object of desire.
Furthermore, that [result] could not belong to anyone other than the one who desires it,
because there is no such thing as a self being for its own sake, since it is impossible for the object of desire itself to be the desirer.
Therefore, the meaning is that a distinction [between the two] must be admitted.
For this reason as well, he states that there is a difference:
"the related," etc. The grammatical connection is that likewise the object and the seeker of the object are also distinct.
Having first stated the essential natures of the beneficial (*artha*) and the harmful (*anartha*), he clarifies their nature as causes of affliction with the words:
"favorable to the seeker.
Having stated the impossibility of liberation according to the Advaita view, he states its possibility according to his own view:

Regarding the phrase "in another birth" (*jātyantareti*): the meaning is that the conjunction of the *puruṣa* with that suffering intellect (*buddhi*)—which is the relationship of owner and owned—is caused by beginningless non-discrimination (*aviveka*). The remedy for this is discrimination (*viveka*). Therefore, although the *puruṣa* is eternally liberated, liberation is established for it in some sense through figurative attribution (*upacāra*).

Just as victory and defeat residing in the warriors are attributed to the king, so too bondage and liberation residing in the intellect—which is absolutely distinct from the *puruṣa*—are attributed to the *puruṣa*.
As it has been said: "She alone is bound and she alone is liberated.
He establishes the final conclusion regarding this point:
"In this regard..."

Is it said that the impossibility of the state of the afflicted and the afflictor is from the perspective of ultimate reality (paramārtha-dṛṣṭi), or from the perspective of conventional practice (vyavahāra-dṛṣṭi)?
It is not the first; thus he says:
"No; because of oneness alone.
The word "faultiness" is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
He explains its faultlessness with the words beginning "bhavet" (it might be):
the meaning is that this subject-object relationship is not real, but rather it does not exist [in an ultimate sense].

Taking the standpoint of conventional usage— that the relationship between the sufferer and the causer of suffering is observed precisely where [the body exists]— the proponent of the final doctrine says:
"Do you not see?"
He raises the objection that if the body were subject to suffering, it would follow the doctrine that the body is the self—
beginning with "But surely" (nanu). The Sāṃkhya,
who asserts that suffering does not belong to the insentient body alone, must state whether suffering belongs to the conscious [self] in its isolated state, or...
Is it of the body as a composite, or of heat, or rather of the *sattva*?
He says "not today" and so forth;
he states "it is said.
He says that it is not the second or the third [alternative].
With the words "nor even," etc.,
he raises the fourth objection: "existence."

He offers a rebuttal to the objection that, because the sevenfold qualities (sattva and the rest) are both the heated and the heater, the Puruṣa would lack bondage and thus the commencement of the treatise would be futile:
"No; by means of those two."
He raises the objection that even though the *puruṣa* is unattached, there is suffering because it is reflected in the *sattva* which undergoes suffering—this is expressed by the word "sattva.
He then replies: "In that case, our own position is reached, namely that suffering is merely illusory, like the movement of the moon in water."
Regarding the phrase "from the perspective of ultimate reality" (*paramārthataḥ*):

if it is asked how suffering is understood to be false merely by means of the word "as if" (*iva*), that is explained as follows—the word "as if" expresses a similarity between the intellect (*buddhi*) and the state of being the sufferer (*tapyatva*).
And if that similarity in the person (*puruṣa*) takes the form of being the sufferer, it is merely imagined, because in reality there is an absence of suffering; thus he establishes this.
Regarding the phrase "na cet" (if not):
if the person (*puruṣa*) is in fact devoid of suffering, then the word "as it were" (*iva*) does not constitute a fault, because its purpose is to indicate false suffering.
If it is argued that a false similarity itself is a fault, he says "no":
"No" [is the reply].
The meaning of the word "even" (eva) is that both having an object and being without an object are merely imagined.

The sense is: since for the Sāṃkhya the states of being the sufferer and the causer of suffering are products of ignorance (avidyaka), nothing at all is faulty even for me; rather, it simply results in what is already observed [in experience].

If, out of fear that admitting the capacity for suffering would constitute an abandonment of one's own tenets (*apasiddhānta*), it is asserted that the person (*puruṣa*) truly possesses the capacity for suffering, even so there would still be an abandonment of one's tenets, because its immutability (*kauṭasthya*) would be lost;
furthermore, there would be no liberation.
He says, beginning with "Now," that because truth (satya) is like the self (ātman), its cessation is impossible;
furthermore, he states that because of the permanence of passion (rajas), there is a continuity of suffering.
Regarding the term "nityatve" (in the case of eternality),
the Sāṃkhya here raises an objection with the word "tapyatva" (the state of being subject to suffering).
The *sattva* or the *puruṣa* is the power that undergoes affliction (*tapyā-śakti*), while *rajas* is the power that causes affliction (*tāpaka-śakti*).

Ignorance (*aviveka*) is the instrumental cause (*nimitta*), and *tamas* is the vision characterized by non-discrimination; being accompanied by this, the conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is "with its cause" (*sanimitta*). The meaning is that it consists in the *puruṣa*'s state of being the master of the *guṇas*, because it depends upon that [instrumental cause].
Liberation is the absence of burning [suffering].
The proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntin) refutes [the opponent's view] that "there is no liberation because of the non-cessation of the causal sign" by saying: "No."
One might argue that liberation occurs through cessation by means of discrimination even in the absence of the disappearance of *tamas*; therefore, he says,
"And of the *guṇas*," the sense being that this is because it is accepted that "the functioning of the *guṇas* is restless."
Having stated the impossibility of bondage and liberation according to the opposing view, he concludes his own position with the words:
"But for the follower of the Upaniṣads...
Since, in reality, there is no bondage due to oneness, there is no occasion for the suspicion that liberation might be non-existent.

The meaning is that, since conventional discourse accepts difference, the relationship between the sufferer and the cause of suffering constitutes bondage; and because its cessation through the knowledge of reality is logically established, there is no occasion for objection. //10//
Or rather, [the production of] the large and the long occurs from the short and the spherical, as in the case of the large and the long. (BBs 2.2.11)

By way of restating the subject matter (*vṛttānuvāda*), he states the connection of this section (*adhikaraṇa*), which consists in establishing his own position through the aphorism "as in the case of the large and the long" (*mahaddīrghavat*), with the words: "pradhāna...

etc. Although the doctrine of atoms (*paramāṇuvāda*) ought to have been refuted immediately after the refutation of the Sāṃkhya position, [it is treated here] for the purpose of establishing his own view in the *Smṛtipāda*.

The meaning is as follows: although this is so because of the connection [of the example], it was previously stated that the *pradhāna* cannot be the material cause (*upādāna*) because its qualities—pleasure and the like—are not present in the world; likewise, it might be argued that Brahman also cannot be the material cause because its quality, consciousness (*caitanya*), is not present [in the world]. This objection is resolved here by means of the application of the illustrative example. The subject matter is the Vedāntic synthesis (*samanvaya*) which maintains that the creation of the world proceeds from the conscious Brahman.

In response to the doubt— namely, whether this [position] contradicts the logical principle that "whatever quality belongs to the inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa) produces a quality of its own same class in the effect-substance, as in the case of the whiteness of a thread"— it is argued that because the principle is unerring, there is indeed a contradiction. To this,
the author explains the sūtra of the established conclusion (*siddhāntasūtra*), which states that there is no such contradiction because the principle is subject to exceptions (*vyabhicāra*).

By the words "this," etc., [the author states: although it was established in the sūtra "Not so, because of the difference in nature" (*na vilakṣaṇatvāt*) that the creation from the non-conscious proceeds from the conscious, nevertheless, this sūtra does not have its purpose already exhausted, because it is intended to state an instance of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) by means of the Vaiśeṣika system's own methodology.
At the time of dissolution, atoms remain motionless and uncombined; at the time of creation, action arises in them due to their conjunction with selves possessing unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*).

From that conjunction, the production of other substances occurs, according to the general principle that the qualities of the cause produce corresponding qualities in the effect. Having stated this process in general terms, he explains it specifically:
Regarding the phrase "when two":
an atom is spherical; the dimension residing in it is called sphericity (*pārimāṇḍalya*).
The meaning is that this constitutes an exception to the previously stated principle, namely, that [a quality] does not originate a quality of its own same class.
He states another instance of such an exception:
"Even when two... and so forth.
The word "two" (dve) should be read twice;
for this being so, the production of a tetrad (caturaṇuka) from four dyads (dvyaṇuka) is logically established.
However, according to the literal reading [of the text as it stands], the production of a large tetrad from two dyads would not be tenable.
It should be understood that without magnitude or plurality residing in the cause, magnitude cannot belong to the effect.

However, the authors of the *Prakaṭārtha* state that in the commentary composed by Rāvaṇa, it is observed that the cause of the magnitude seen in an effect produced from two dyads is what is called "accumulation" (*pracaya*), which is a loose conjunction of parts; thus, they maintain that this commentary represents the view of the ancient Vaiśeṣikas.
In every case, there is a deviation [from the rule] because the dimensions of shortness and minuteness residing in a dyad do not originate [other dimensions].

Even though logicians postulate that a dyad arises from two atoms alone, and a triad from three dyads, nevertheless, considering that reasoning is unstable and thus no such fixed rule exists, [the author says] "even when many [atoms are involved]."

The meaning is that the process is the same: qualities such as white and so forth, which are the agents (*kāraka*), produce qualities of their own kind; however, the dimension (*parimāṇa*) of the effect-substance is not produced by the dimensions of the causes, but rather is produced by the number residing in the causes.
Having thus demonstrated the process, he states the deviation (*vyabhicāra*) while applying the aphorism (*sūtra*).
"Thus, in this way":
this was stated by relying on an indefinite process, namely that both the large and the long arise from atoms alone. Relying instead on a definite process, he states the inconsistency:
The phrase "or as" (yathā vā) means that there is a deviation (vyabhicāra) in the sense that from minute and short dyads (dvyaṇuka), neither a minute substance nor even a short one is produced.
In the sūtra, the word "or" (vā) has the sense of "and" (ca), serving to include the unmentioned minute atoms (aṇu).

And thus, the application of the sūtra is that from the short and the spherical—namely, the dyad and the atom—there arises the large, the long, and the minute, just as the non-conscious arises from the conscious.

In this regard, the distinction is that from the short [the dyad] arises the large and long triad (tryaṇuka), and from the spherical [the atom] arises the minute dyad (dvyaṇuka). He raises an objection regarding the disparity between the illustration and the case at hand:
Now, if you think that the contradictory quality is indeed insentient, he says:
"For [it is] not insentient," etc.
Having accepted that the effect-substance is pervaded by another dimension, he states the equality of the intended portion:
"Not so.
He then abandons that acceptance:
Regarding the word "na ca" (nor):
for it is only when another dimension has arisen that it becomes an obstructer;
since there is no such obstructer prior to its arising, the meaning is: why should the spherical dimension (*pārimāṇḍalya*) not originate in the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*)?
Now, one might object that a substance is produced simultaneously with its contradictory dimension; to this he says:
"even though it has begun.
[If there were] simultaneous production, it would be a departure from established tenets (*apasiddhānta*).
The intention is that, therefore, the absence of contradiction is established.

Having raised the objection that because [the atoms] are occupied with initiating qualities such as minuteness (*aṇutva*), spherical dimension (*pārimāṇḍalya*) and so forth cannot initiate their own corresponding qualities, he refutes it with "And not... (*na ca*).
The state of being distracted is established otherwise;
the reason for this is:
"because of another dimension."
He cites the Sūtras regarding the existence of other causes: "kāraṇa... [Sūtra 4.2.10].
Because the causes—the dyads—are numerous, there is magnitude in the triad; because of the magnitude of the clay, there is magnitude in the jar.
The meaning is that in a very large mass of cotton produced from two cotton-piles, "largeness" arises due to accumulation, which is a specific kind of conjunction of parts.
He states that "atomicity," which is the opposite of largeness, occurs in a dyad (dvyaṇuka) through the number "two" residing in the atoms—
this is expressed by the word "that" (tad).

By the phrase "by this," he extends the principle: that which is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) of largeness (*mahattva*) is itself the non-inherent cause of length (*dīrghatva*), which coexists in the same substratum as largeness; and that which is the non-inherent cause of minuteness (*aṇutva*) is itself the non-inherent cause of shortness (*hrasvatva*), which is invariably concomitant with minuteness.
The meaning is that, because of their magnitude and so forth, and because they lack a cause, the non-concurrent nature of spherical dimension (*pārimāṇḍalya*) and the rest is established.
Furthermore, one should not say that these do not produce similar qualities because they lack a specific proximity; thus he says:
"Nor... (*na ca*).
The meaning is that, like plurality and so forth, even spherical dimension (*pārimāṇḍalya*) and the rest are no different insofar as they reside in the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*).

He states the result of the argument—that their non-productivity [of further qualities] is not due to the effect-substance being overcome by a contrary quality, nor due to distraction, nor due to non-proximity—by saying:
"Therefore... (*tasmāt*).

As for the argument that— despite the deviation (vyabhicāra) in the case of general qualities such as atomicity (pārimāṇḍalya) regarding the pervasion (vyāpti) that "the quality of a cause produces a quality of its own kind"— there is another pervasion, namely, "that which is a specific quality (viśeṣaguṇa) residing in the inherent cause of a substance produces a quality of its own homogeneous class," and since consciousness (caitanya) is a specific quality, its status as a producer is unavoidable.
That is weak;

for it must be understood that there is a deviation (vyabhicāra) in the case of the blue and other colors residing in the threads that cause a variegated cloth—since those are causes of a variegated color of a different genus—and because consciousness lacks the status of a quality by virtue of being the Self.
Therefore, it is established that the production of something of a different genus from consciousness is logical.
In this regard, he states another example:
"And from conjunction" (saṃyogāt ca).
Now, Brahman, being conscious, is a substance because it is the material cause of the effect.
Therefore, since that which is dissimilar cannot be the material cause (*upādāna*), one must cite some substance (*dravya*) itself as the example of something that produces a dissimilar effect;
it is not the quality (*guṇa*) of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) that should be cited. Thus he raises an objection with the words:
"Substance" (*dravye*).

He provides a rebuttal, stating that this is an example regarding the aspect of producing something of a different nature— namely, that from a conscious quality (guṇa), like a substance (dravya), there arises the unconscious— by saying "No.
He then states that the lack of restriction (aniyama) is what is accepted by Kaṇāda.
"The author of the Sūtras also..."— to the question of how there is no fixed rule by this much alone, he says:
"This has been stated."

He raises the objection that, although there is no tautology by the logic of "non-difference in characteristics" (*navilakṣaṇatva*), there is nevertheless a tautology due to the section on extension (*atideśādhikaraṇa*)—
namely, "But [this is] an extension" (*nanvatideśaḥ*).

He states that this [section] is commenced for the purpose of refuting the rule that the production of similar qualities [occurs] by means of the examples of sphericality (*pārimāṇḍalya*) and so forth.
"It is true" means that this applies by extension to that very [case]. //11//
In either case, there is no action; therefore, that [agent] does not exist. (2.2.12)
He begins the examination of the Vaiśeṣika doctrine:
"In either case, there is no action; therefore, that [world] does not exist.
Thinking that no connection with the preceding incidental section is required, he proceeds to show that the Pradhāna, when not presided over by a Lord, cannot be the cause.

He states the purport by saying "now," while explaining that this [section] follows immediately after the Sāṃkhya section due to the connection of a counter-example: "let there be causality even for atoms presided over by Him."
The subject here is the Vaiśeṣika tenet that the world is originated by atoms through the sequence beginning with dyads (dvyaṇuka).
Regarding the doubt as to whether this is based on valid means of knowledge (māna) or on error (bhrānti), the author states the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa): "And that... and so forth.
The meaning is: by means of those [entities] such as cloth, earth and so forth share a commonality, namely, being an effect-substance (*kāryadravyatva*).

The subject under dispute—earth and so forth—is possessed of parts and is composed of multiple substances accompanied by conjunctions of their own smaller dimensions, because they are effect-substances (*kāryadravyatvāt*).
The formal argument (prayoga) is: "like a cloth and so forth.
The qualifying attributes of the probandum (sādhyaviśeṣaṇa) are intended for the purpose of establishing the atoms as they are desired by [the proponent] themselves.
Now, one might ask: "How is the establishment of atoms achieved by this much alone? To that, he says:

"And this [is as follows]: "The term *sa cāyam* means that the atom (*paramāṇu*) is understood as the ultimate limit—the final ground of cessation—of the process of reduction of size, from which the state of being composed of parts (*sāvayavatva*), which serves as the delimiting condition of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*) in the disputed case, ceases.
The sense is that since inference proceeds only so long as there are parts, it is established that the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) is partless (*niravayava*) when reduced beyond that."
To one who argues that the reason—being an effect-substance—is unestablished because of the doctrine of the eternity of the world, he says:
"And all...
[The object of dispute] possesses a beginning and an end.
The meaning is: "because it possesses parts, like a cloth.
Having refuted the non-establishment of the reason (*hetu*), he now refutes its lack of probative force (*aprayojakatva*).
Regarding the word "not" (na ca):
in response to the inquiry as to how many kinds those [impurities] are, he says—
“those” (tāni).
Anticipating the objection that these [atoms] cannot be the cause of the world because they too are destroyed at the time of dissolution (pralaya), he says: "And of them...
[The meaning is: there is no destruction of the whole (avayavin) due to the separation or destruction of its parts.

The meaning is that because atoms are partless, there is no destruction, since causes of destruction such as the division of parts are impossible. He states the sequence of creation resulting from their permanence with the words "tataḥ" (from that).

Thus, the result of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that because the doctrine of Kaṇāda is rooted in valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), there is a contradiction with the systematic harmony (*samanvaya*) of the Vedānta, and therefore it is not established.
The author establishes the final conclusion (*siddhānta*)—that there is no contradiction because that [doctrine] is rooted in error—with the words:
"In this regard, this... (*tatredam*).
At the time of dissolution, the conjunction of divided atoms must be explained as resulting either from the action of one or from the action of both;
and for such action, a cause such as effort (prayatna) is observed,
as for instance, bodily movement arises from the conjunction of the self with that which possesses effort.

Just as the movement of trees and the like results from the impact of wind and so forth, and the upward motion of [objects] results from the pushing of the hand and so forth, is such a visible cause for the action of the atom admitted or not?

Regarding the second [alternative], there is no production of action; as for the first, it is not possible because effort and so forth occur only after creation. Thus, in both cases, action is impossible.
Therefore, due to the impossibility of action, there is an absence of that creation of dyads and so forth preceded by conjunction; such is the meaning of the Sūtra.

The distinction is that impact (*abhighāta*) is a specific kind of conjunction with a moving substance for a stationary object, whereas that same [conjunction] is called pushing (*nodana*) when the object is already moving. One might raise the objection— “Now, as for the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*)”— that even in the absence of a visible cause, motion arises in atoms due to their conjunction with a self that possesses the unseen force (*adṛṣṭavat*).
He refutes [the opponent's position] by means of a dilemma preceded by conceptual construction (vikalpa): "But that again...
It should be understood that this dilemma was formulated with the thought: "Why should the atom not be the substratum, just as the insentient self (jaḍātman) is?"
He applies the Sūtra here as well: "In both ways.
To the objection that the unseen merit or demerit (adṛṣṭa) presided over by the individual soul (jīva) may be the cause, he says:
"And of the self" means that, due to its insentience, it lacks the capacity to be a controller; this is the remainder of the sense.
The fact that a separate Lord could be the controller will be refuted later on.
The lack of consciousness in the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) has been stated as the reason for its not being caused by karma;
he states another reason:
"because it would be inherent in the self" (*ātmasamavāyitve*).
He raises the objection that, like gravity, the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) is also a cause of motion in whatever it is conjoined with as its substrate—
this is expressed by the phrase "like the unseen force" (*adṛṣṭavadā*).

He refutes this by stating that since the conjunction with an omnipresent entity (*vibhu*) exists at all times within atoms, there would be a continuous succession of motions, which would result in the impossibility of cosmic dissolution (*pralaya*).
Regarding the term "saṃbandha" (connection):
since occasional activity cannot be regulated by *adṛṣṭa* (unseen merit/demerit), one might suppose that regulation comes from God;
therefore, he says: "niyāmakāntara... (by another regulator).

The meaning is that since eternal knowledge is not established—due to the contradiction with the pervasion (vyāpti) that "whatever knowledge exists is produced by a body"—God does not exist as its possessor; even if He did exist, He could not be the controller because He would be eternally present [and thus incapable of initiating action].
He concludes the meaning of the Sūtra:
"Thus, in this way":
having refuted that conjunction is the cause, he refutes its very nature— stating,
"And conjunction [of] the atom..."

The meaning is this: if conjunction were all-pervasive (*vyāpyavṛtti*), then because one [atom] would be contained within the other, it would be impossible for the effect to have magnitude; consequently, every effect would be merely the size of an atom.

Furthermore, he states that conjunction is observed to reside in only one part of a composite substance (*sāṃśadravya*); therefore, due to the contradiction with that observation, its all-pervasiveness should not be postulated—this is expressed by the words "dṛṣṭa" (observed).
The connection is with the phrase "if the conjunction of the atom were by way of a single part.
Since even a conjunction residing in a spatially conceived location—due to the differentiation of directions—is itself merely conceptual, no effect could arise from it;
or if an effect were produced, it would be false. Thus, the meaning is that this would constitute a departure from established tenets (apasiddhānta).
Having applied the Sūtra to the refutation of the creation theory of the followers of Kaṇāda, he now applies the Sūtra to the refutation of dissolution as well— namely, "And so too...
Creation arises from the conjunction of atoms through their action.
The theory that dissolution occurs due to the separation [of atoms] is not tenable;
for the simultaneous separation of infinite atoms lacks any observed efficient cause (nimitta), such as a specific impact.

Furthermore, since merit and demerit (adṛṣṭa) exist for the sake of pleasure and pain, they cannot serve as the motive for a dissolution devoid of pleasure and pain; thus, dissolution does not occur through action motivated by adṛṣṭa.
A division [of causes] is possible.
Thus, since the visible and invisible causes do not exist, action does not exist in either way—neither as having conjunction as its purpose nor as having disjunction as its purpose.
Therefore, due to the absence of action, there is an absence of creation and dissolution, which are preceded by conjunction and disjunction; such is the application of the sūtra. //12//
And because of the admission of inherence, there would be an infinite regress due to its being equal [to the entities it connects]. (BS 2.2.13)

"And because of the admission of inherence, there is the non-existence [of atoms]; the impossibility of the atomic theory follows by implication. This means that since dyads and inherence are equally distinct from atoms, just as a dyad would require another inherence, so too would inherence require another inherence, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthiti*).
Now, one might object: "Inherence, which is the regulator of specific cognitions such as 'the cloth is here in these threads,' does not require any further relation."
He raises an objection, saying "But here," on the grounds that [the relation] is eternally connected by its very nature.
He refutes this, stating that since conjunction (saṃyoga) also admits of a connection by way of its own nature (svarūpa-sambandha), there would be no need for inherence (samavāya).
"No," [it is argued].
If it is because of the difference between related entities that dependence is required, then that applies equally to inherence (*samavāya*) as well.
And this is also true regarding the technical definition of a quality (*guṇa*).

Even though action, generality, and so forth lack the property of being a quality (*guṇatva*), since inherence (*samavāya*) is admitted for them, "being a quality" is not a pervader (*vyāpaka*) of "being an inherent substratum.

Nor is it a pervaded (*vyāpya*), because even for a quality, a relation of its own nature (*svarūpa-sambandha*) is possible— just as in the case of inherence— and thus there is no supporting reason (*tarka*) for a necessary concomitance.

Therefore, the very fact that [an entity] is distinct from its relata is the cause for the requirement of another relation; since this [distinction] is equally present in the case of inherence (*samavāya*) as well, an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) is unavoidable.
And that [regress] causes the destruction of the root.
The meaning is that, since inherence is not established by her [the opponent], the dyad (dvyaṇuka) which is inherent in it is likewise not established. //13//
And because it exists eternally. (BBs 2.2.14)
He explains the Sūtra with the words "Moreover" (apica):
if [cognition] has experience as its intrinsic nature, then its activity must be said to be contingent upon a cause.
Furthermore, since the cause—consisting of time, unseen destiny (adṛṣṭa), and so forth—is eternally present, there would be the consequence of activity occurring at all times;
the meaning is that if it were not the cause, there would be an absence of activity. //14//
And because it possesses form and other qualities, the opposite [of the argument] follows from observation. (BBs 2.2.15)

Furthermore, he states the system of the opponent in order to apply the aphorism: "Moreover, atoms possess inherent causes (samavāyikāraṇa), they are gross relative to their causes, and they are non-eternal, because they possess color, because they possess taste, because they possess smell, and because they possess touch, like a jar.
He begins with the words "of those possessing parts," and so forth.

If it is objected: "But here, 'atom-ness' (paramāṇutva) is the delimiting condition of the subject (pakṣatāvacchedaka); how then can 'grossness' (sthūlatva), which is contradictory to it, be established as the probandum? We reply: No, because air-ness, fire-ness, and so forth serve as distinct delimiting conditions. Nor is there a lack of logical necessity (aprayojakatā).

Because, [if it were] devoid of causes and eternal, it would be impossible for it to possess form and so forth, just like the self (*ātman*). Nor should it be argued that, in the separate proof that "air has causes," there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*), even though the reasons such as "possessing form" do not suffer from partial unestablishedness (*bhāgāsiddhi*);
for wherever there is touch, that must have a cause.

The point is that at the time of apprehending the pervasion (vyāpti)—namely, "wherever there is form, it has a cause"—there is no establishment of the probandum (sādhya) with respect to the delimitation of air-ness (vāyutva) and so forth. [The argument is:
"Atoms are eternal, because, while existing, they lack a cause."

Having raised the counter-argument (*satpratipakṣa*) that "it is like the self," he refutes it by showing the non-establishment of the qualificand (*viśeṣyāsiddhi*): "And as for [the claim] 'eternality'... Here, *sattva* means "being" (*bhāvatva*), intended to exclude prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*).
The negation of eternality is relative to a counter-correlative,

because it is a non-existence (abhāva), like the non-existence of a jar; thus, if eternality were established anywhere, then by the specific negation of eternality in the effect— on the grounds that "the effect is non-eternal"— eternality would be established in the atoms which constitute the cause.

Otherwise, since a negation is impossible in the absence of a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), [the author] refutes what was stated by Kaṇāda by restating it and showing its alternative establishment: "As for that which...
Having accepted the conventional usage of the negation of eternality with respect to an effect, he has stated the well-known existence of the counter-correlate in the case of Brahman.

In reality, however, the very usage of "particularity" is unestablished; for without the knowledge of the eternity of the cause through another means of valid cognition, it is impossible to employ the usage that "the effect is non-eternal. Thus he says: "Nor [is it established] by the word... and so forth.
The point is this: if there were another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the permanence of the cause, then this conventional usage would have its root;
