however, prior to that knowledge of the root, no real entity is established by mere conventional usage alone, because it would follow that even the conventional usage regarding a spirit (*yakṣa*) in a banyan tree would establish its existence. But once the root is known, everything is established by that very knowledge, and thus the presentation of conventional usage is redundant.
Having thus refuted two *Kāṇāda* sūtras regarding the eternity of atoms, he refutes the third with the words "yadapi" (as for that which...).
If the meaning of the sūtra is that the knowledge of the cause of existing atoms— which are the gross effects observed— is ignorance (*avidyā*), [then it is untenable].
In that case, the state of having imperceptible causes would be the reason for eternality;
however, that is not so, because it is subject to deviation in the case of the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*). This is the meaning.
If "being devoid of constituent substances" were the qualification of the reason, then the qualificand would become redundant.
And he states that this would result in redundancy with the words beginning "Now" (atha). Atoms are eternal.
He raises an objection regarding the meaning of the Sūtra— "because its destruction is not perceived, as in the case of the self"—
with the words "athāpi" (even so).
The destruction of cloth and other such objects is observed to result from either the disjunction or the destruction of their constituent parts, such as threads;
since neither of these two [causes] exists for partless atoms, they are eternal—this is the meaning.
He offers a rebuttal by resorting to the theory of transformation (*pariṇāmavāda*), suggesting that something capable of destroying the atoms might nonetheless exist:
"No.
If it were thought that "origination" (ārambha) is the production of a distinct substance through the conjunction of parts,
then there would be a rule that the destruction of a substance occurs only by means of two [factors].
There is no proof for the existence [of the cloth] at the commencement [of its production], because a cloth distinct from the conjoined threads is not perceived.
Therefore, by the force of experience, one must accept that the cause itself, which is inherently without distinction, becomes the effect in the form of a state possessing distinctions.

Thus, even for atoms—which are of the nature of transformations of ignorance—their destruction is logically established as their attainment of the state of being a cause through the concealment of their individual, solid form by time and other factors acting as the occasion for dissolution.
Just as the solidity of clarified butter melts through contact with fire without the destruction of the conjunction of its parts or the parts themselves, so it is here.

Nor should it be suspected that this is not a valid illustration because solidity, being a qualification of a conjunction, is a quality (*guṇa*), and thus its case would not apply when a substance (*dravya*) is destroyed;
for the illustration is given on the basis of the principle that even a substance possessing qualities can be destroyed by some cause.
Furthermore, the definition of a quality (*guṇa*) is not a restrictive criterion.

In reality, solidity is simply a substance (*dravya*), being a specific transformation of ghee that persists even when it is liquid; for instance, ghee is solid [in one state] and liquid [in another].
Nor should it be argued that, despite its being a substance, its destruction occurs solely through the disjunction of its parts.

The point is that because clarified butter (*ghṛta*) is a composite whole (*pariṇāmin*), its division is impossible; furthermore, such division is impossible when the hardness of the atoms (*paramāṇu*) is destroyed.
Moreover, the destruction of atoms is established by the [scriptural] statement regarding the dissolution: "There was no dust, nor anything else whatsoever."
Therefore, he concludes that they do not possess the status of being the ultimate cause with the words:
"tasmāt" (therefore). //15//
And because there are faults in both cases. (2.2.16)
Having stated the pervasion— that whatever possesses a greater number of qualities is grosser than that— the author offers an alternative analysis with the words "tadvat" (in the same way):
is it postulated that the earth atom possesses more qualities, and therefore the atoms of water and the other elements possess one quality fewer respectively, or not?
He states the fault in the first case with the words "kalpyamāne" (if it were being postulated):
the meaning is that [the atom would become gross] due to the accumulation of form, that is, due to its bulkiness.
The argument should be formulated as follows: "An atom of earth is grosser than one of water, because it possesses a greater number of qualities, just like a jar."
He refutes the argument that [the cause] would be purposeless with the words "na cāntareṇa" (nor without).
The sense is that there would be a contradiction with what is observed.
Regarding the position that this is not so, [the author] states the fault in either case— whether all atoms possess one quality each or four qualities each—
with the words beginning "But if it were not postulated," and so forth. //16//
And because of non-possessiveness, there is absolute lack of dependence. (2.2.17)

Not only is there indifference toward the doctrine of atoms because it is illogical, but it is also unacceptable both in its textual form and its meaning because it is rejected by the learned; thus he says:
"And because it is not accepted" (aparigrahācca).
He begins to elaborate on the meaning of the word "and" (ca):
Moreover,
he states the indicator of absolute difference: "having distinct characteristics."
The definitions of substance, quality, and action are, respectively, the universals of substanceness, qualitiness, and actionness,
or else the limiting conditions (upādhis) such as being the substratum of qualities;
and the definition of a quality is that which possesses a universal while being devoid of qualities and being non-productive of action.
Action is the independent cause of conjunction and disjunction;
generality is eternal, one, and inherent in many;
particularities reside in eternal substances.
The definitions are distinct: "eternal relation" is *samavāya*.
The meaning is that by these [definitions], their absolute mutual difference is established.
"Being such" (*tathātva*) means absolute difference.
That which is contradictory by virtue of that [reason] is the relationship between property and property-possessor:
qualities and so forth would not be properties of substance, because they would be absolutely distinct from it.
The meaning is "like a hare's horn" and so forth.
Having presented the fact that difference does not sublate [non-difference], he states non-difference: "Now, it becomes... and so on.
The dependence of qualities and so forth upon substance is established by positive and negative concomitance;
thus, qualities and the like are non-different from substance,
because they are dependent upon substance.
The meaning is: whatever is different from something else is not dependent upon it, just as *kuśa* grass is different from a rabbit.
[Objection: If there is non-difference, how can there be a difference in words and cognitions such as "substance" and "quality"? To this, he says:
"Substance" (dravya) [is used here].
The intention is that even a conceptual distinction exists;
otherwise, just as with absolute difference, absolute non-difference would also preclude the relationship of attribute and substrate (dharmadharmibhāva)—this is how it should be understood.
Addressing another logician who asserts that qualities and so forth possess identity with the substance, he says: "If that were the case.
Here, the Sāṃkhya should be understood as the Vedāntin.
Alternatively, the mention of Sāṃkhya is because even for the follower of Kapila, there is the doctrine of identity (tādātmya).
Although dependence on that [the cause] constitutes being a property of that [cause],
and this is not present in smoke, [it is nevertheless relevant].
Even though [the smoke] exists even without fire,
nevertheless, considering its being an effect of that [fire] to mean its dependence upon it, he raises the objection of deviation with the words "But surely... (nanu).
He accepts both its being an effect and its being something else with the words "True.
Nevertheless, the intention is that there is no deviation (vyabhicāra), because what is intended as the reason is the state of being perceived as identical [with the cause].
He raises the objection that this reason is otherwise established (*anyathāsiddhi*) with the words "of qualities and so forth" (*guṇādīnām*).

The meaning is that even though there is no non-difference between qualities and so forth and the substance, the cognition of identity is established by virtue of their being inseparably connected (*ayutasiddhatva*).
He refutes [the opponent's position] by means of an alternative analysis:
"But that...

Since whiteness resides in the cloth and the cloth resides in the threads, there is no identity of location between the cloth and its whiteness; therefore, the first [objection] is that the cognition of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)—namely, "the white cloth"—would not occur.
Regarding the phrase "not being in a separate location," he explains two sūtras of Kaṇāda:
Regarding the phrase "for they are like threads":
since intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is the very form (*svarūpa*), he states that "if there is non-separateness" (*apṛthaktvabhāvatve*), then the non-difference desired by us is established.
Thus he says: "because of the state of being non-separate."
He states the reasoning for non-difference:
"of that" (tasya) means "of the quality" (guṇasya).
Thus, the established doctrine that the six categories are absolutely distinct has been refuted on the grounds of its contradiction with experience.
He refutes another doctrine with the words "yuta" (joined): Is inseparability (*ayutasiddhatva*) a property of both [relata] or of only one of them?
He says "not today" and so forth—
meaning "previously. Having raised the second objection, he refutes it.
With the words beginning with "atha" [the author] introduces the following:

having accepted the statement that while the cause is established separately, the effect is not established separately, he raises a dilemma as to whether the relation belongs to that which is unestablished or to that which is already established; he first entertains the second alternative by stating, "having become established."

The meaning is that since conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is accepted as the attainment of two things previously unattained, it would follow that even the threads and the cloth are in conjunction; thus, it would constitute a departure from established tenets (*apasiddhānta*).
To the objection—how can there be conjunction in the case of a newly produced cloth, given the absence of action therein—he says: "Just as... (*yathā*).

Furthermore, since there would be an infinite regress if the relation itself were related [to its relata], and since that which is unrelated cannot be a regulator, the relation is also difficult to define; thus he says: "Nor also...
The relation is distinct from the relata.
He raises the objection— “The relation,” etc.— on the grounds that it is cognizable by a verbal cognition distinct from that [relation], just like any other entity.

He provides the resolution: "No; for even in the case of oneness [there is no fault]. [The opponent argues that] if one seeks to prove a conceptual difference, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*); however, if one seeks to prove a real ontological difference, there is the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*vyabhicāra*).
[The author replies: No; for even in the case of oneness...

The meaning is that even while remaining its own essential nature (svarūpa), such as being denoted by words like "human" and so forth, it becomes cognizable through distinct words and cognitions—such as "father" in relation to a son—and yet it does not thereby become divided; thus, there is no deviation (vyabhicāra) from the rule.
He states the conclusion:

"Thus, by perception" means that because [the absence] is cognizable through a word and a cognition of a different character, the non-existence of another entity— such as conjunction— which is reached through a mark consisting of a definition structured by perception, is determined due to its non-perception apart from the related relata.
This is the meaning.

For conjunction is not perceived as anything other than the immediate proximity of two fingers; the point is that inherence (*samavāya*), however, never ascends to the level of experience for anyone anywhere. He refutes the objection that if the relation were non-different from the related entities, then because the related entities would always exist, there would follow the consequence of a cognition of the relation at all times: The meaning is this: one does not perceive a conjunction (*saṃyoga*) over and above the immediate proximity (*nairantarya*) of two fingers. As for inherence (*samavāya*), it does not ascend to the level of anyone's experience whatsoever. He thus refutes the doubt that if the relation were non-different from the related entities, then since the related entities would always exist, there would necessarily follow the cognition of the relation at all times.
"Nor indeed" (nāpi):

the meaning is that it has been stated that the cognition of a relation between two fingers, or between two material objects (*rūpin*), existing in a state of contiguity, occurs in dependence on another [cognition] and not by itself.
Previously, the creation of dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth was refuted by the rejection of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) between atoms (*paramāṇu*).

Now, the conjunction of the soul—which is otherwise unperceived—with atoms is rejected as the cause of motion in those atoms, and the conjunction of the soul with the mind is rejected as the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) of cognition and other mental states—thus [it is said]: "likewise, the atom and the soul.
Although the position of imagined parts (*kalpitapradeśapakṣa*) has already been refuted, he brings it up again to state another fault called "over-extension" (*atiprasaṅga*).
"Imagined" (*kalpita*) means "inference" (*ūha*). These are things whose objects have been inferred, whether they be existent or non-existent.
In the second case, the establishment of conjunction is not possible, because there is no locus-limiting factor for the coexistence of two things and their respective absences in one place.
In the first case, however, there is the undesirable consequence that all objects could be established by mere conjecture (*ūha*), since conjecture is under one's own control.
The meaning is that [the power of meditation] consists in abundance and boundlessness because it arises from that [meditation].

He says "And not... and so forth, [anticipating the objection]: "If all success were achieved through mere reasoning (ūha), then the fixed rules regarding the bondage and liberation of entities would be lost."
Having refuted conjunction (*saṃyoga*), he refutes inherence (*samavāya*) with the words "Moreover" (*kiñcānyat*).
The meaning is that another objection against his [the Vaiśeṣika's] position is now being stated.
Adhesion means cohesion;
the meaning is that it is impossible for there to be the pulling of one [part] by the pulling of another. A dyad is not inherent in anything partless.
The meaning is: "because it possesses parts, like the earth which is not inherent in space.
[Objection: But if the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) were not inherent [in its cause], it could not be dependent upon it.
Because that [dependence] is impossible without a relation;

and one might object that the effect-substance does not have dependence [on its cause] through conjunction, since it does not conjoin with its material cause—thus he raises the doubt: "The effect... etc.

He offers a rebuttal— saying "no"— on the grounds that because the primordial nature (prakṛti) and its transformation (vikāra) are non-different, the relationship of substrate and superstrate (āśrayāśrayibhāva) is untenable.
To one who argues that this relationship exists because of their difference, he replies:
"Because of mutual dependence.
Then how is the conventional usage of an effect being dependent on a cause explained? He says: "Of the cause itself," [meaning] it is due to an imagined distinction.
He states that even the partlessness of atoms is untenable, beginning with "furthermore":
atoms possess parts.
Because of their smallness, like a jar.
The meaning is that, in the case of the opposite [position], they would not possess the status of being limits for the various directions, just like the self (*ātman*).
Now, as for this conventional usage of the distinction between directions such as "east" and "south" in relation to an atom, those [atoms] which serve as its limits...

He raises the following objection: "Those very parts (*avayava*) that are spoken of by you as my atoms (*paramāṇu*), if they too possess parts, then those [latter] must be their parts; in this way, that beyond which no further division exists is itself the partless atom.
This is what is meant by the words "those which you... and so forth.
He refutes this, saying:
"No; it is gross."
The meaning is this: if it were said that an atom is a substance incapable of being divided even with its own self, then the name "atom" would have been applied to Brahman alone;
for anything other than that, being small, must necessarily possess divisions of parts due to its susceptibility to spatial division (*digvibhāga*).

If, on the other hand, it were said that an atom is that which belongs to the class of earth and so forth and is the ultimate limit of small dimension, then it could not be the fundamental cause (*mūlakāraṇa*).
Because they are perishable, like a jar;
nor is the reason unestablished, for atoms are perishable.
"Because it belongs to the same class as earth and so forth, like a jar"— this is the proof [adduced].
Now, having raised the objection that "since a partless substance lacks a cause for its destruction, it must be indestructible like the self," he recalls the previously stated refutation:
By the words "perishing" and so forth,
[it is shown that] because everything other than Brahman is of the nature of ignorance (ajñānika), the partlessness of substance is unestablished;
for destruction at the time of cosmic dissolution (pralaya) is possible through the destruction of efficient causes such as unseen merit/demerit (adṛṣṭa).

The sense is that upon liberation, when ignorance is destroyed through knowledge, the destruction of its effects— the atoms— becomes possible. Regarding what was stated— that whatever is an effect-substance is composed of multiple substances aided by conjunction—
he says "no" to that:
The same applies to the commencement of an effect.
*Kaivalya* means predominance.

Even when the substance of the effect exists, because the conjunction [of the constituents] is the cause, the conjunction that initiates curd is not a different conjunction from the conjunction that initiated the milk.
And thus, because there is deviation (vyabhicāra) in the case of curd and the like, there is no pervasion (vyāpti); this is the meaning.

Furthermore, let the pervasion be simply that "whatever is an effect-substance (kāryadravya) originates from a substance," for the sake of parsimony (lāghava), rather than "it originates from a single substance which is conjoined with another and possesses a dimension not smaller [than its cause]."
Because of [the objection of] respect,
and because there is a deviation [from the rule] in the case of a rope composed of long and wide silk cloths that has a smaller dimension;
nor should it be said that the rope is not a distinct substance.
Because this would result in the collapse of the very notion of a whole (*avayavin*).
Furthermore, since the property of being a partless substance (*niravayava-dravyatva*) resides in a single self (*ātman*), simplicity (*lāghava*) precludes the proof of multiple partless atoms.
As for the argument that their existence is established by the fact that they constitute the ultimate limit of the gradation of minuteness (*aṇutva-tāratamya-viśrānti-bhūmi*): [this is not tenable].
That is not so;
for [the process] comes to rest in the *truṭis* described as being composed of three atoms (*tryaṇuka*). Nor should it be said that those very things called *truṭis* constitute the world itself.
This is because the possession of parts and non-eternality are inferred from the property of being earth (*pṛthivītva*) and so forth.

Nor should it be argued that if the possession of parts must eventually rest somewhere, then atoms are established; whereas if it does not rest, there is an infinite regress—because the resting point for the possession of parts can be found in *māyā* or in Brahman.
Therefore, there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the existence of atoms.

Objections have already been stated, such as that because conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and inherence (*samavāya*) are impossible for partless entities, it is illogical for them to originate dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth through inherence.
Now, completing the remainder of the aphorism with the words "and because of non-acceptance" (*aparigrahācca*), he concludes the meaning of the section:
"Thus it is so. Therefore, it is established that there is no contradiction between the Vedānta intent and the Vaiśeṣika doctrine, which is rooted in error. //17//
Even if the whole were caused by both [parts], it would not attain that [status]. (BBs 2.2.18)
Having refuted the Vaiśeṣika, he refutes the Nihilist (Vaināśika) with the words "the aggregate" (*samudāya*).

Since the Vaiśeṣika is a partial nihilist (*ardhavaināśika*) because he accepts the extremely rapid destruction of the body and so forth due to differences in dimension, the author states the contextual connection (*prasaṅga-saṃgati*) by saying that immediately after his refutation, the proponent of universal momentariness (*sarvakṣaṇikavādī*), who is present in the mind [of the opponent], is now being refuted.
Regarding the term "Vaiśeṣika":

in order to state the distinction between the doctrine to be refuted here and the doctrine already refuted [in the Sūtra] by the statement "Non-existence is not [the case], because of perception" (NS 4.1.34), he analyzes that doctrine with the words "And that...
(sa ca).
[Objection: Since the scripture spoken by the Sugata is one, how can there be a multiplicity of forms? To this, he says: "Because of the difference in understanding," etc.
This is because there is a difference in the intellects of even a single disciple who explains the scripture, due to the differences in their respective states.
The meaning is that it is of many kinds due to the distinction between disciples of dull, middling, and superior intelligence.
He states those very types [of practice] with the words "therein" (tatra).
There are four disciples: the Sautrāntika, the Vaibhāṣika, the Yogācāra, and the Mādhyamika.

Among them, although there is a dispute between the first two regarding whether external objects are imperceptible or perceptible, they agree on their existence; therefore, having unified their tenets, [the author] refutes them, saying:
"In that regard, those who [assert] the existence of all..."

The distinction is as follows: the primary elements (*bhūta*) and their derivatives (*bhautika*) are external, while the mind (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitta*) are internal, pertaining to the realm of desire and so forth.
Regarding this, a doubt arises: is this established doctrine based on valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) or is it based on error (*bhrānti*)?

In this context, while raising the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) that [the world] is rooted in valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa-mūla*), he demonstrates the opponent's established conclusion (*siddhānta*) with the words:
"In that regard, it is real" (*tatra bhūtam*).

In the prima facie view, the result is the non-establishment of the Vedāntic conclusion—that the stable phenomenal world has Brahman as its cause—due to its contradiction with the momentary doctrine based on valid means of knowledge.
It should be understood that there is no contradiction with the established doctrine (siddhānta) in this regard.

Considering that the four elements beginning with earth—consisting of objects and sense organs—are merely material aggregates of atoms and do not constitute any further composite whole (avayavin), he analyzes the atoms [as follows]:
"And in the fourfold [elements]... and so on.
The meaning is that they are of four kinds:
earth atoms have the nature of being hard and solid,
while water atoms are viscous.
The fiery [elements] are hot;
the nature of the aerial [elements] is movement or motion.
Having thus described the external aggregate, he speaks of the internal aggregate:
"So be it.

The aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) consists of the sense-faculties together with their objects; although objects are external, they are considered internal because they are perceivable by the sense-faculties located within the body.
The aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) is the stream of storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) characterized by the thought "I, I."

The aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) is the experience of pleasure and so forth; the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) is conceptual cognition characterized by names such as "cow" or "horse"; and the aggregate of mental formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) consists of attachment, aversion, delusion, merit, and demerit.
In this context, the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) is designated as "mind" (*citta*) and "self" (*ātman*);
the other four aggregates are mental factors (*caitta*), and their collection constitutes the internal [person],
meaning that which carries out the entire course of worldly existence.

Since no whole (avayavin) is perceived apart from its parts (avayava), the parts alone remain; and since "whatever exists is momentary, like a flash of lightning," their momentariness is established. Having thus reached the position that this doctrine is rooted in valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa), he applies the aphorism concerning the final conclusion (siddhāntasūtra): [The opponent argues: Since a composite whole distinct from its constituent parts is not perceived, the parts alone remain; and because of the principle that "whatever exists is momentary, just as a flash of lightning," these [parts] possess momentariness. Thus, it is argued that this established tenet (siddhānta) is based on valid cognition. To this, he applies the sūtra of the final conclusion:
Regarding the phrase "this which":
at the beginning of creation, the spontaneous aggregation of atoms and aggregates is not possible,
because they are insentient.
Nor is consciousness, called "mind" (*citta*), which is a blazing [flame], the cause of the aggregate;
for there would be a mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*) such that the aggregate arises when the body-form has arisen, and consciousness arises when the aggregate has arisen.
Furthermore, you do not admit any soul (*jīva*) or Lord (*īśvara*) other than momentary consciousness who could be the creator of the aggregate.
Nor can it be said that atoms and aggregates proceed toward aggregation by themselves, independent of an agent,
for that would entail the consequence of no liberation.
To the objection that the continuum of the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) might be the aggregator, he says:
Regarding the term "of the substratum" (āśayasya):
that in which passion and the like reside is the substratum (āśaya), namely the continuum (saṃtāna).
Is this [continuum] different from the members of the continuum (saṃtānin), or different from the cognitions (vijñānin), or non-different?

Even in the first case, is it permanent or momentary? Not the first, because it would entail the doctrine of a permanent self (nityātman) which we [Buddhists] do not accept. Regarding the second, he states the fault:
Regarding the term "momentariness" (*kṣaṇikatva*):
for that which is momentary, there is no activity distinct from its birth; therefore, its engagement for the purpose of combining with atoms and so forth is untenable.
The meaning is that this would contradict [the doctrine of] momentariness.
By this, the position that the continuum is non-different [from its moments] is refuted,
because it is logically impossible for that which is momentary to possess the quality of being a unifier.
Therefore, because there is no agent of conjunction, the formation of a composite body is not possible; this is the meaning. //18//
If it is argued that [the elements] arise because they are mutually dependent, we say no, because they are merely the cause for the arising [of the next]. (BS 2.2.19)
Anticipating the objection that a composite might still be possible even in the absence of a unifier, he refutes it with the words "itara... etc.
A *pratyaya* is that which proceeds toward (*pratyeti*) or goes toward (*gacchati*) the effect; thus, it is the cause.
The meaning is that once the formation of the aggregate is established through ignorance and the other factors alone, the occurrence of worldly transaction follows as a matter of course.
He states these [factors], beginning with ignorance, by saying:
"And those..."
Ignorance (*avidyā*) is the perception of stability in things that are momentary;
from that arise the formative forces (*saṃskāra*), namely passion, hatred, and delusion;
and from those, the first consciousness (*vijñāna*) of the one dwelling in the womb arises.
From that storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna), the four elements beginning with earth arise; because they serve as the support for "name" (nāman), they are called "name.
From that, form (rūpa) consisting of white and black—that is, semen and blood—is produced.
The stages of the embryo known as the *kalala*, *arbuda*, and *peśī* constitute the meaning of the term "name-and-form" (nāmarūpa); this is the essential point.
Consciousness, the four elements beginning with earth, and form—these constitute the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) for that which is born from the faculties;
the mutual conjunction of name-and-form and the faculties is contact (*sparśa*); and from that arises feeling (*vedanā*), such as pleasure and so forth.
From that, moreover, comes craving for sense objects; from that, the grasping that takes the form of active engagement;
and from that, because birth arises from it, there is "becoming" (bhava), consisting of the factors [of existence] and so forth.
From that, birth (*jāti*) is the arising of the body, meaning the manifestation of the collection of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*).
The maturation of those arisen aggregates is the aggregate of aging (*jarā*), and death (*maraṇa*) is their destruction.
For one who is dying, the internal burning caused by affection for sons and others is sorrow (*śoka*); the lamentation such as "Alas, my son! caused by that is wailing (*paridevana*);
and the experience of the undesirable is suffering (*duḥkha*).
By that, "dejection" refers to mental anguish; the word "iti" is intended to include afflictions such as honor and dishonor.
It is not only for the Sugatas that ignorance and the other [afflictions] are accepted.
But he says "of all [proponents]"— that is, *sarveṣām*— to address the view that this applies even to all theorists.

He concludes the objection that the formation of a composite is established by implication, because there is a mutual relationship of cause and effect such that birth and so forth have ignorance and so forth as their cause, and ignorance and so forth have birth and so forth as their cause.
"Thus it is so":
he explains the portion concerning the established conclusion (siddhānta) with the words "that is not so."

Having accepted that ignorance and the other factors serve as successive causes, [the opponent] objects that "since there would be no cause for the aggregate, the aggregate could not exist," and [the author] recalls what was stated previously with the words "nanu" (now then).
Having raised the alternative— whether ignorance and the rest are merely indicators of the aggregate or its producers— if it is the first case, then some producer of the aggregate must be stated.
To the objection that "that does not exist," he says: "In this regard it is said: 'If...
The phrase "in those things which stand in the relation of substratum and superstratum" is a qualification of the enjoyer.

The meaning is "when their substrata are unperceived. When stable atoms—which are capable of aggregation and act as agents—exist accompanied by the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), it has been stated that because they cannot function as agents of aggregation through the mere absence of cognition, there is no cause for the occurrence of aggregation. This [cause] does not exist in the case of the doctrine of momentariness (*kṣaṇika-pakṣa*).
He asks, "What need is there to say more?"—
that is, "Why?"—
meaning that [the argument applies] even to those things devoid of a substratum, a superstratum, or an agent of aggregation.
In the reading "āśrayāśrayiśūnyeṣu," the meaning is "in those things devoid of the relationship between the benefactor and the beneficiary.
He raises a second objection: "Now, this [might be so]... (athāyam).
He refutes [the opponent's view] by stating that there would be a mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*) regarding the arising of the aggregate and of ignorance and the other factors—
asking, "How so?
Indeed, this natural flow of aggregates in the relationship of cause and effect does not depend upon an assembler.

He raises the following objection: "Now, you might think... [that] since ignorance and the other factors, based on a preceding aggregate, bring about a succeeding aggregate, there is no fault of mutual dependence.
The purpose of the rebuttal is that if the nature [of these factors] were either determinate or indeterminate, it would result in the fallacy of contradicting one's own tenets (apasiddhānta).
The term *pudgala* refers to the body (*deha*), because it is filled (*pūryate*) and it wastes away (*galati*).

Furthermore, he says "moreover" (*api ca*) to show that on the view that the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*) is momentary (*kṣaṇika*), even the conventional usage of enjoyment (*bhoga*) and liberation (*apavarga*) would be difficult to establish.
The meaning is this: if that which someone desires does not exist at that time, then the desire is futile; if it does exist, then momentariness is destroyed.
He concludes the refutation of the composite (saṃghāta) under discussion:
Therefore, [it is so]. //19//
And because the preceding ceases when the succeeding arises. (BBs 2.20)
For the arising of effects is considered by the Sugata to be of two kinds: dependent upon causes and dependent upon the collection of conditions.

Among these, the first is of the nature: "from ignorance comes volitional formations, from those comes consciousness," and so forth; the second is: "from the collection of earth and the other elements comes the body," and so forth.
Having accepted the first [position] therein, the second was refuted by means of the absence of an agent of aggregation;
now the author of the Sūtras refutes the first with the words "uttara" (the subsequent).
An object that is momentary is called "momentary.
Being in the process of ceasing is the proximity of a destroyer;
having ceased is the state of being past.

One might object: "Even though [the entity] is pervaded by destruction at the time of its effect, its causality remains intact because it exists in the preceding moment. This is the doubt raised by the words "This entity" (*ayaṃ bhāva*).
The meaning is: "having the nature of existence" (*sadrūpa*).
Is the operation called "producing the effect" distinct from its arising, or non-distinct? Having stated that it is not the first case, he raises the second alternative:
Regarding the word "atha":
*bhāva* means origination (*utpatti*).
For it has been said: "That which is the coming-into-being (*bhūti*) of things is itself the action (*kriyā*), and that very same thing is called the causal factor (*kāraka*)."
The meaning is that for those momentary entities (*kṣaṇika-bhāva*), their very coming-into-being (*bhūti*) is both the action (*kriyā*) and the agent (*kāraka*).
Even a thing that has perished could serve as either the efficient cause (*nimitta*) or the material cause (*upādāna*);
however, if that were so, there would be no production of a jar or the like when the clay or other materials do not exist at the time of the jar's emergence.
He refutes [the objection] that "if there were existence, the momentariness would be lost" with the words beginning "even so" (*tathāpi*),
and he confirms the fault mentioned in the first position.
"Even without [these]" means that since the arising and destruction of a real entity cannot be established, it is not momentary; thus he says,
"Moreover."
Since those two, being of the nature of the essence [of reality], are included within the real entity (vastu), it should also be understood that the real entity is beginningless and endless.
He raises the second objection: "Now, suppose it exists..."
He states the specific distinction: "produces," etc. He refutes [the objection]:
"Even so" means that through their conjunction, the momentariness of the entity would be destroyed. Having raised the third alternative— that there is no conjunction at all— he refutes it:
Now, [the sūtra begins with] "But absolutely... (athātyanta). //20//
If [the effect] does not exist [at the time of the cause], there is a contradiction with the thesis; otherwise, there would be simultaneity. (2.2.21)
In order to explain the Sūtra, he recalls the context with the words "momentary destruction" (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*):
Is the production of an effect causeless or does it have a cause?
Regarding the first point, he states that there would be an abandonment of the thesis with the words "Now, if [the object] were non-existent," and so forth.

The meaning of the thesis is this: depending upon—that is, having reached—the fourfold causes consisting of the object, the sense organ, the auxiliary conditions, and the mental impression (*saṃskāra*), the mind arises as the cognition of form and so on, as well as the mental factors (*caitta*) such as pleasure and the like, which are of the nature of the mind.
Just as for the cognition of blue, the blue object is the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*),
the eye is the instrumental condition (*karaṇa-adhipati-pratyaya*),
and light is the cooperative condition (*sahakāri-pratyaya*).
The distinction is that the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapūrvapratyaya*) is a formative force (*saṃskāra*).
Having stated the fault of the person regarding the abandonment of the thesis, he also states the fault of the thing itself:
"And if it were without a cause."

Regarding the position that [phenomena] possess causes, [the author] explains the remainder of the Sūtra— beginning with "Now, in the subsequent moment," etc.— to show that the thesis of momentariness would be abandoned because the causal material such as clay would have to coexist with its effect.
They are called *saṃskāras* because they are thoroughly conditioned (*samyak kriyante*).
The meaning is that all entities have a beginning and an end. //21//
The non-attainment of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) [is established] because there is no interruption. (BBs 2.2.22)
By the first two sūtras, the [theory of] aggregate has been refuted;
by the subsequent two sūtras, the causal relationship and momentariness have been refuted. Now, he refutes the two kinds of destruction favored by that [opponent]:

"Discernment" (pratisaṃkhyā) means that which is conditioned, produced, cognizable by the intellect, and merely an object of knowledge; it is other than the three [categories] whose nature is insubstantiality. This is the meaning.
What is that? He says:
"That too," meaning it is *nirupākhya*, i.e., devoid of any essential nature (*niḥsvarūpa*).
*Pratisaṃkhyā* is a cognition that is contrary and adverse, characterized by the thought, "I shall make an existing entity non-existent.
Cessation (*nirodha*) of some entity occurs through this [cognition].
However, he says that for pillars and the like, which are fragile by their own nature, there is cessation even without being preceded by such a cognition.
"Contrary to that" (tadviparītaḥ).
Having stated the activity of others, he explains the Sūtra with the words "of these" (teṣām).
Entities are those that possess a continuum.
A continuum is defined as the flow of entities in the form of cause and effect;
within that continuum, does the final moment produce another moment or not?
In the first case, there is a contradiction with its being the last,
because the continuum remains uninterrupted;
in the second case, it follows that the final [moment] would be non-existent.
According to our own established tenet that existence consists in the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*),
if the final [moment] were non-existent, it would follow that the preceding moments are also non-existent,
because they would be devoid of causal efficiency.
Therefore, because the interruption of the continuum is impossible, there is no attainment of cessation; thus he says:
"Not, first of all...
He says: "Not the second..."

Nor [is there absolute destruction], because of the recognition that "this is the same clay" even in states such as the jar, the potsherd, or the powder; thus, the meaning is that there is no absolute destruction of the persisting substance, such as the clay.

Since recognition is not observed in the case of a seed [persisting] through its sprout and subsequent stages, [the opponent might argue] that the persisting entity is interrupted; therefore, he says:
"Unclear" (aspaṣṭā):
the meaning is that sprouts and so forth exist within a continuous underlying substance, because they are effects, like a cloth; thus, the non-interruption of the underlying substance is established.
The conclusion is that because entities possess stability, momentary cessation is impossible. //22//
And because there would be faults in either case. (2.2.23)
He refutes their preferred view— that it is the analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*) of ignorance and the other [links]—
with the words "in both ways.
Restraints (*yama*), observances (*niyama*), and so forth are the preparatory requisites (*parikara*).
The instruction on the meditation that "all suffering is momentary" is the instruction on the path. //23//
And [the soul] is in space as well, because there is no distinction. (BS 2.2.24)

"Because of the authority of scripture (āgama-prāmāṇya). The meaning is that by stating that space (ākāśa) is an effect, its status as a real entity (vastutva) is established, just like a jar or similar objects. Now, one might ask: "How can the reality of space be established for the Buddhists, who disagree with the authority of scripture? To this, he says:
Regarding those who hold erroneous views:
the reality of space is established by the inference that "sound is grounded in a real entity because it is a quality, like smell and so forth."
The meaning is that it is impossible for the eight substances, beginning with earth, to be the substrata of qualities perceivable by the sense of hearing.
Having established that space is a positive entity (bhāva), he refutes its being a non-entity (abhāva) with the words "Moreover" (api ca).

The meaning is as follows: just as there is no absence of the universal "pot" even when a single pot exists, so too there is no space—which consists in the absence of the universal "material substance"—even when a single bird exists; thus, the movement of another bird would be impossible.

Anticipating the objection that there is an absence of obstruction delimited by a particular location, [the author] states "where... and so forth, asserting that space is precisely that particular location delimited by the absence, and not the absence itself.
"It will fall" means that the bird will move through [it].
Furthermore, he states that the non-substantiality of space contradicts his own treatise:
Furthermore, [the word] "api ca" [introduces the following]:
what is its correct basis (*samyan-niśraya*) or support (*āśraya*), such that it is called "having what as its basis" (*kiṃsaṃniśrayā*)?
For it is never observed that a non-entity, such as a hare's horn, can serve as a basis.
He states another contradiction with the words "Moreover" (apica):
the property called eternality, defined as being non-counterpositive to destruction, is not possible in the case of a non-existent thing.
The meaning is that this is because it would contradict the existence of the subject (dharmin). //24//
And because of mindfulness. (BBs 2.2.25)
He refutes the momentariness of the self with the words "because of recollection" (anusmṛteḥ).
Recollection is memory produced by a prior experience; since it has the same substratum as that experience, the self, which is the substratum of both, must be enduring—this is the meaning.
He says— "For how could I..."— to show that if [the self] were momentary, there would be no connection between two cognitions.
Furthermore, he says that the self is permanent because of the recognition of identity between the agent of the prior perception and the agent of the recollection "I saw."
Moreover, the form of recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) should be understood as: "I, who previously saw that, am the very same person who today remembers it.
The statement "I see this" is a description of the connection with another cognition.
The phrase "I who saw [it] am the same I who see [it]" is for the purpose of illustrating another form of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*).
He states the subverting argument (*bādhaka*) regarding the opposite case: "If indeed... and so forth.

Regarding the point that if there were a difference between the seer and the rememberer, the cognition would be "I remember" and "another saw," he provides an example with the words "yatraivam" (where it is thus).
He states the supporting argument:
"I remember.
The meaning is that there is no dispute regarding the fact that wherever there is the cognition "I remember" and the cognition "another saw," people understand the agent to be distinct.
Since no such subverting cognition of difference is observed in the case of the present recognition under discussion, the permanence of the self is unavoidable; thus he says:
Regarding the phrase "but here, [the notion] 'I am not'":

just as no one subverts the heat and other qualities of fire, so too the prior perception expressed as "I did not see" is not denied; by this, it is stated that recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) is a valid means of knowledge (*pramā*) because there is no sublation.
Thus, he says that when the identity of the seer and the rememberer is established, their permanence (*sthāyitva*) is demonstrated as a consequence.
"In that case, such being the situation" (tatraivaṃ sati):
To one who says, "Even if the self is connected with two moments, let there be its destruction in the third moment," he replies: "In that way" (tathā).

The construction is as follows: beginning from the present state up until the final breath before death, one recognizes one's own successive cognitions as being performed by oneself alone; and by connecting those past cognitions, performed by oneself, from birth back to the limit of the present state, [one realizes the self].
He raises the objection that "it is like the recognition of a self in the flames of a lamp due to the fault of similarity" (the word *sa iti*).

Since the cognition of similarity depends upon the cognition of the subject (*dharmin*) and the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), and since a permanent cognizer does not exist, the cognition of similarity is impossible.
He offers a rebuttal with the words beginning "that" (*tam*), [arguing] that otherwise there would be a contradiction of one's own tenets regarding the existence of a sentient being (*sattva*).
This might be so.
The cognition of similarity is not produced by the cognitions of the arising of preceding and succeeding entities and does not apprehend the similarity between those two;
rather, it is a certain conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) which, taking its own internal form as its object by treating it as external, does not touch upon other moments.
Therefore, it does not depend on a permanent observer—thus he objects:
Regarding this "this is like that":
it must be stated here whether, in the cognition of similarity, three entities appear—namely, "that," "this," and "this is similar to that"—or not.
For one who says they do not appear, there is a contradiction with one's own experience.
Furthermore, because there would be no difference in meaning, the employment of three words would not occur.

Therefore, he provides the rebuttal— “not by that”— to show that non-appearance is unestablished, since through the three words there is the manifestation of distinct meanings that are mutually connected.
If it is argued that the three objects which appear are not external but are indeed non-different from the cognition itself, we say: no.
For if the three were non-different from a single cognition, they would necessarily follow as being non-different from one another as well.
To the Vijñānavādin who asserts that this is an acceptable consequence (iṣṭāpatti), he replies:
Regarding the phrase "For when... (yadā hi):

If the three entities known through the cognition of similarity—which are distinct [from one another] and well-known to all the world—are not accepted for fear of the consequence of a permanent observer, then, because momentary cognitions possessing those respective forms are mutually unaware of one another, it would be impossible for there to be a conflict (*vipratipatti*) consisting in the manifestation of multiple contradictory positions regarding a single substratum (*dharmin*); consequently, the practical activity (*vyavahāra*) of proving one's own position and so forth would be impossible.
Therefore, the distinction between cognition and the object of cognition must be accepted in accordance with experience.
And thus, for one who cognizes the similarity between two external objects—thinking "this is similar to that"—the permanence of the self (*ātman*) is unavoidable.
[Objection: But surely external objects do exist as momentary particularities (*svalakṣaṇa*) which are grasped by non-conceptual perception (*nirvikalpaka*).

Anticipating the objection that external objects such as permanence and similarity— which are determined through conceptual construction— appear as imagined externalities, and that consequently there is the conventional usage of disagreement and so forth, [the author] refutes this by stating,
"In this very way."
Only that which is established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) should be asserted.
Indeed, there is no valid cognition whatsoever for momentariness.

It should not be argued that the perception "the jar exists now" is the proof for momentariness—in the sense of its existence as a mere present moment—by taking as its object the non-existence of the jar at a time other than the present.
Because that [cognition] has as its object merely the state of being present, the non-existence of [the object] at other times is not established.

Furthermore, there is no pervasion (vyāpti) such that "whatever exists is momentary," because even lightning and the like are seen to persist for two or three moments, and thus no corroborative instance (dṛṣṭānta) exists.
Furthermore, inference is not possible without an enduring inferential subject (*anumātṛ*).
Therefore, the meaning is that the Tathāgata, who speaks of matters established by non-perception, is one whose word is not to be trusted.
Moreover, in the case of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), is similarity the cause [of error] by way of being a defect, or by way of being the object?
Even in the first case, [the cause] must be either existent in its own nature (*svarūpasat*) or known (*jñāta*).
Not the first, because if one perceives only the mother-of-pearl in dim darkness while not knowing its whiteness, there would result the error of non-difference from silver.
Nor the second, because...
This is because it has already been stated that such knowledge is impossible without a permanent knower;
nor is it a cause by way of being an object, as he says: "And not... (na ca).

The meaning is that because there is the mental imprint "that is I," and because there is no such imprint as "I am similar to that," [the author] refutes the status of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) as an error; he then refutes its status as doubt by stating "it might be."
The meaning is that even when an insentient object is recognized, doubt might occasionally arise due to the possibility of sublation; however, this is not the case with the Self.
He concludes—stating "therefore"—that the doctrine of the momentariness of the Self is utterly inconsistent, because it contradicts recognition that is both non-doubtful and non-erroneous. //25//
Not from the non-existent, because it has never been observed. (2.2.26)

The Sugatas (Buddhists) assert that non-existence, like the horn of a hare, is absolutely non-existent and eternal, and that from the destruction of clay and other materials, an unreal jar or similar object is produced;
he refutes this with the words: "Not from the non-existent."

It is not only that [the world] comes into being by force, but they themselves also demonstrate it. Two negatives convey the original meaning; thus, he states this point: because [entities] such as a jar manifest after having destroyed [their material cause], such as clay.
Regarding the phrase "from the destroyed":
he states the reasoning for the claim that the effect arises from the destruction of the cause with the words "from the immutable."
"From that which is devoid of destruction" means from that which is eternal.
If an eternal and unsurpassable entity were capable of producing effects, then all its effects would occur in a single moment.
Furthermore, because there would be no effect in the subsequent moment, it would follow that [the cause] is non-existent.

Nor is it tenable to argue that the sequence of effects arises from a sequence of enhancements produced by auxiliary causes; for if those enhancements themselves required further enhancements, it would lead to an infinite regress.
If there were no dependence [on conditions], the effect would likewise not depend on any excellence [produced by them], and thus auxiliary causes (sahakārin) would be rendered useless.
Therefore, the meaning is that the production of an effect does not arise from a permanent entity.
The causal efficacy of a momentary entity has already been refuted in the section beginning with "And because of the arising of the subsequent" (*uttarotpāde ca*).
He explains the Sūtra— "In this regard, this..."— for the purpose of refuting the status of non-existence as a cause:
if there were a distinction between the non-existence of a seed and other forms of non-existence, [then it could serve as a cause].
In that case, the admission of the Lokāyatikas—that "the sprout arises from the seed alone" by way of the absence of anything else possessing specific qualities—would be meaningful;
however, he says "by which... to show that such [an admission] does not exist.
He applies the Sūtra:
"Of that which is without distinction.
The meaning is that since things such as a hare's horn are never observed to perform a causal function, a non-entity (*asat*) cannot be a cause.
To the objection that "let there be a distinction even for non-existence," he says: "If...
Having stated the reductio ad absurdum (*tarka*) that there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) if non-existence were a cause, he states an inference (*anumāna*):
Nor is it [the case] that "non-existence is not a cause because of its non-existence," meaning it is like [anything] commonly accepted [as such].
Non-existence is not the material cause, because it lacks connection with the effect;
just as a thread that is not connected with a bowl and so forth is not the material cause of that bowl and so forth— thus he says, preceded by this reasoning:
And because of non-existence [of anything else]. Therefore, since it is that which is associated [with all effects], clay and so forth are indeed the existent material cause; thus he says: "clay."
Having restated the argument that it is impossible for a permanent entity to be a cause, he refutes it with the words "As for what was said," and so forth:
on the strength of experience, one must admit that only those things whose nature is stable can be the causes of a sequence of effects through the gradual proximity of auxiliary conditions.
Nor should it be said that it is illogical for a potent [cause] to depend on auxiliary factors; for if even the impotent did not depend [on them], the entire universe would be non-auxiliary.

Therefore, in the case of gold and the like—which are inherently devoid of excellence—the sequence of effects such as earrings arises from the sequence of excellences produced by auxiliary factors such as heating with fire.
Nor should it be argued that if a particular excellence (*atiśaya*) does not depend on another excellence, then the effect (*kārya*) likewise need not depend [on its causes];

for if a cloth did not depend on clay, then—since there is no difference in their being effects—it would follow that a pot also need not depend on clay. Thus, dependence is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) even in the case of auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*). As for what was said—that in the state where the effect is absent, the cause would result in non-existence—that is incorrect.
That is not so;
for existence is established even for that which lacks a cause, since there is no contradiction [in its being existent].
Indeed, existence does not consist solely in the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*).
Because that [causality] is impossible for what is non-existent, existence is distinct from it;
for the capacity for causal efficiency belongs to what exists, not to what does not exist.
Therefore, existence—which consists of an uncontradicted nature and serves as the delimiting factor of causality—is indeed distinct from causality itself.
Therefore, the sense is that it is logically consistent for things that are continuous and stable to function as causes.
He also points out a contradiction with what was stated previously, saying: "Moreover" (api ca). //26//
And thus there would be the accomplishment [of effects] even for those who are indifferent. (2,2.27)
It has already been stated that if production occurred from non-existence, then even a rabbit's horn would be produced;
now he states another over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) with the words, "of those who are indifferent."
"Of those not exerting effort" means of those devoid of exertion; "an empty vessel" refers to a pot or similar container;
"of one who expands" means of one who is occupied with activity.

Therefore, it is established that there is no contradiction between the doctrine of momentary external objects—which is rooted in error—and the systematic unity of the eternally immutable Brahman. //27//
It is not non-existence, because [the world] is perceived. (BBs 2.2.28)
"Not non-existence, because of perception.

Does this [sūtra] contradict the doctrine of the Yogācāras—who assert that the Vedāntas teach an undivided, attributeless Brahman-consciousness as the material cause of external objects, yet maintain that there is no object other than that [consciousness], which is distinct, possessed of form, and momentary—or does it not? Such is the inquiry regarding their doctrine.

Based on the fact that doubt is rooted in both pride and error, he states the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) by relying on the previously mentioned refutation of the doctrine of external objects (*bāhyārthavāda*),
beginning with the words "In this way" (*evam*).
The result of the preceding and subsequent positions is their respective contradiction or lack of contradiction.

Now, one might object: "How can a single scripture of the Sugata have the intention (*tātparya*) regarding both the existence and non-existence of external objects, given their contradiction? Anticipating this, the author states that there is no contradiction because of the difference in the capacities of the disciples (*adhikāribheda*).

By asserting that the Vijñānavādin knows the Sugata’s true intention, he declares his superiority over those who advocate for external objects (*bāhyārthavādin*), who are of inferior capacity, with the words:
"Of some... (*keṣāñcit*).

And it has been said by Dharmakīrti: "The teachings of the Lords of the World follow the dispositions of sentient beings. This means that the instructions of the Sugatas conform to the intellects of their disciples. Now, [one might ask]: "If external objects do not exist, how can there be the conventional usage of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and the objects of knowledge (*prameya*)? To this, he says:
Regarding the phrase "in that":

consciousness itself is the object of cognition (*prameya*) by virtue of having the imagined forms of blue and so forth; it is the fruit of the means of cognition (*mānaphala*) by virtue of being the nature of its manifestation.

The meaning is that the conventional usage [of such terms] proceeds through the conceptual construction of a distinction, wherein there is "measurement" (māna) by way of the nature of power (śakti), and the "measurer" (pramātṛ) by way of the aspect of being the substratum of that power.
To the question, "Why should this not be a primary (mukhya) distinction?", he says:
"Even though [it exists]" means that there is no conventional usage of the term "object of cognition" (prameya) for blue and so forth that have not ascended into the intellect (*buddhi*).
Therefore, the meaning is that only the form ascended into the intellect is the object of cognition, not the external [object].
He sets forth arguments preceded by a question regarding the non-existence of external objects, beginning with "How so? and so forth:
the object of knowledge does not exist apart from cognition.
Because it is impossible for anything to exist apart from that, like a human horn; thus he says:
"because of its impossibility."
He explains the impossibility [of the opponent's position] with the words "for that" (sa hi).
If [the world were merely] atoms, there would be no such cognition as "this is one gross pillar."
The meaning is that the aggregate (*samūha*) is non-existent.
[An objection: Even in the absence of a whole (*avayavin*), universals (*jāti*) and so forth might still be external objects; to this, he replies with the words "In this way" (*evam*).

The meaning is that if there were either non-difference or absolute difference between the universal (*jāti*), qualities (*guṇa*), and actions (*karman*) on the one hand and their substratum (*dharmin*) on the other, then—just as in the case of the substratum itself or another distinct substratum—the relationship of property and property-possessor (*dharmadharmibhāva*) would not exist.
Furthermore, since difference and non-difference are contradictory, universals and the like do not exist as real entities.

Moreover, if cognition lacked a specific relation consisting of similarity to the object of knowledge (*jñeya-sārūpya*), it would follow that it could have everything as its object; therefore, such a specific [similarity] must be admitted.

And thus, since it is only the specific feature residing in the cognition that is made an object by the cognition, there is no establishment of an external object due to the absence of proof and because of [the fault of] complexity; so he says:
"Moreover" (apica). "Partisanship" (pakṣapāta) refers to the conventional usage of the qualification of a particular object.

Furthermore, he states that the object of knowledge is non-different from knowledge, because it is apprehended at the very moment knowledge is apprehended and is thus necessarily grasped simultaneously with it, just like knowledge itself:
Moreover, the object of knowledge is non-different from knowledge, because it is necessarily apprehended at the same moment that knowledge is apprehended, just as knowledge is. Thus he says:
Furthermore:

even if there were a real difference between cognition and its object, their simultaneous apprehension (*sahopalambhana*) could still occur due to the relationship of the grasped and the grasper; therefore, he says:
"And this is not so" means that because there is no cause for a connection between momentary cognition and an object, there is no relationship of grasped and grasper.
Furthermore, waking consciousness does not have an external object as its support.
He says "in dreams, etc. to show that [the object] is not real because it is a cognition, like the cognition of dreams and so forth.
He raises the objection that the inference is sublated by the impossibility of the diversity of cognitions— asking "How so?"—
and answers by showing that it can be explained otherwise.
Regarding the term *vāsanā*:
*vāsanā* is simply prior cognition included within the beginningless continuum;
by its power, the variety of cognitions having forms such as blue arises, even when there is an interval of many moments.
The meaning is that it is just as the redness of cotton is due to the latent impression (vāsanā) of the seed;

and because this is agreed upon by both disputants, he says "Moreover" (apica) to show that it is indeed the latent impressions, and not external objects, that are the cause of the diversity of cognitions.

Since the doctrine of momentary consciousness-only (kṣaṇika-vijñāna-mātra-vāda) is rooted in valid cognition, it follows that it contradicts the doctrine of eternal consciousness; to this objection, he explains the sūtra of the established conclusion (siddhānta-sūtra) with the words beginning "Not non-existence" (nābhāva).
Is the non-existence of external objects due to their non-apprehension, or is it due to their non-apprehension as distinct from cognition?
"It is not so today," because [the world] is perceived; thus it has been stated.
He raises the second objection:
[Objection: "But surely, [it is not so] that I am not [the Self].

Since the distinction between knowledge and the object of knowledge—by virtue of their relationship as subject and object—is established through the perception of the witness (*sākṣipratyakṣa*), the statement of non-difference contradicts direct perception.
To this, he replies with the words beginning "Certainly" (*bāḍham*).
He says "And for this reason" (*ataśca*) to show that even according to your own statement, people perceive external objects as distinct from cognition;
for if external objects were absolutely non-existent, their perception through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) would be impossible.
He says "otherwise" because, due to its being an illustration and because of its possibility, the word [for the self] would not be like that of external objects.
He states that the particle *eva* (only) is appropriate— rather than the particle *vat* (like)— precisely because of the uncontradicted experience of difference.
"Therefore" (tasmāt):

[The opponent] raises an objection with "But surely" (nanu), suggesting that the statement "the object of knowledge does not exist apart from the cognition because it is impossible for it to exist otherwise" is merely a restatement of a previously mentioned refutation.
What is this "impossibility" (asaṃbhava)?

Is it non-existence, or the certainty of non-existence, or irrationality, or the absence of possibility consisting of a doubt with a predominant alternative? It cannot be the first, because it would be indistinguishable from the probandum (sādhya).
The second [alternative] is not tenable;

for in the case of a collective cognition (samūhālambana) such as "the jar and the pillar are large," there is a determination of the existence of difference between two objects possessing contradictory properties—namely largeness, duality, jar-ness, and pillar-ness—from a single non-large cognition that apprehends them.
Therefore, this [argument] is not sound.
"Occurrence" (saṃbhava) is the ascertainment of existence, which depends upon valid cognition (pramāṇa);

"non-occurrence" (asaṃbhava) is the ascertainment of non-existence, which depends upon the absence of valid cognition, and not the reverse— thus he clarifies this very established rule with the words "yaddhi" (for that which...).

Stating that the result of the aforementioned established position is the possibility of external objects through perception and other means, he refutes the third [position] with the word "here" (iha):

It is not proper to determine the non-existence of external objects such as pillars— which are ascertained by valid means of knowledge— merely on the grounds that they cannot withstand the conceptual alternatives of being either different from or identical to their constituent atoms.
For the same lack of logical consistency applies to your position as well;

for it is not tenable that a single, non-material consciousness should have as its object a collection of many material things, because that would entail the consequence of [the consciousness itself] being both material and manifold.
This is not an acceptable consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*),

because if the apprehension of a composite whole (*samūhālambana*) were abolished, the conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) regarding the duality of objects and so forth would be lost, since cognitions are mutually unaware of one another's content.
Therefore, even if it is logically untenable, an object must be accepted as being fit for conventional usage according to how it is experienced.
Nor is it the fourth [alternative], because such a possibility is useless once [the object] has been ascertained;
the point is that its function is to serve as a prerequisite for the operation of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in some instances.

Regarding the claim that there is no external object because it is logically possible for the very similarity between the object and the cognition to be the objective support (*ālambana*) of that cognition, he says:
"And not...
As for the objection regarding complexity (*gaurava*) that was raised:
That is not a refutation, because it is based on valid authority; thus he says:
"externally."

Precisely because the difference between cognition and its object is established by the direct experience of all people in the world, for that very reason even the rule of simultaneous perception (*sahopalambhaniyama*) does not prove non-difference; thus he says:
"For this very reason."
Just as the color-form of a visible object, although its perception is necessarily contingent upon the perception of light, is not non-different from light,
so too the object is not non-different from the cognition;
for even though they are distinct, the restriction [of their relation] is established through the relationship of the apprehended and the apprehender.
Nor is there an impossibility of cognition being related to an object distinct from itself due to its momentariness;
the point is that it possesses stability.
Cognition is distinct from multiple objects.
He states a counter-argument (*satpratipakṣa*)— namely, "because of being one, like 'cowness'"—
with the words "Moreover" (*api ca*).
Nor is the reason unestablished,
because the unity of cognition is ascertained from the uniform cognition "cognition,
cognition," and that [cognition] does not have a genus as its object.
He states, "because there is no certainty regarding the distinction between individuals," namely, "not of the qualified object" (*na viśeṣyasya*).
Having stated the difference of the jar and so forth from consciousness (*caitanya*), he now states its difference from the knowledge consisting of a mental modification (*vṛttijñāna*).
"So be it. The meaning is: "A jar is distinct from two [entities] because it is a single entity, like milk."
He states the subverting argument—that the abandonment of the conventional usage of one's own school would follow—if one does not admit that objects are distinct from cognition:
"Moreover" (api ca).
It is both illogical and unaccepted [by you] that two successive, self-luminous, momentary cognitions could stand in a mutual relationship of the grasped and the grasper.
And thus, the proposition of their difference is not tenable,
because the apprehension of difference is impossible without the other's apprehension of the locus and the counter-correlate (dharmin and pratiyogin) in relation to one another.
Consequently, the enduring self that apprehends their difference must itself be admitted to be distinct from them.

Thus, in the absence of a distinction between the subject (*pakṣa*), the probandum (*sādhya*), the reason (*hetu*), and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), the thesis (*pratijñā*) "this is momentary and non-existent" is not tenable. Furthermore, the thesis that "the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is mere individuality excluded from everything else," while "the universal (*sāmānya*) is that which follows many [individuals] and consists in the exclusion of what is not that (*atadvyāvṛtti*)"— is also not tenable.

If all diverse objects were merely cognition, it would be difficult for one cognition to be known by another or by something else; consequently, the proposition that the subsequent cognition of blue is the "perfumable" (*vāsya*) and the preceding cognition of blue is the "perfumer" (*vāsaka*) would be untenable, because there would be no cognizer distinct from those two.
Furthermore, the "affliction of ignorance" (*avidyopaplava*) is the association with ignorance.
Therefore, "blue" is a real phenomenon (saddharma);
"a human horn" is a non-real phenomenon (asaddharma);
and "formless" is both a real and non-real phenomenon (sadasaddharma).
A proposition such as "consciousness exists" or "a human horn does not exist" is difficult to establish on the grounds of its formlessness and so forth,
because it must be accomplished through knowledge of multiple objects.
Furthermore, the propositions that "this [self] is bound by ignorance" and "this is liberated by knowledge" are also established only through knowledge of many things.

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the instruction for the benefit of disciples—that what is generally desired is to be grasped and what is undesired is to be abandoned—is understood as being accomplished through manifold cognitions.

Therefore, the meaning is that the distinction between the apprehended object (*grāhya*) and the apprehending subject (*grāhaka*) must be accepted for the sake of conventional discourse such as the thesis (*pratijñā*).
He states another argument for the distinction between cognition and its object:
"Furthermore" (kiñcānyat):
the meaning is that since there is no difference in the experience of the object (*artha*) as there is of the cognition (*jñāna*), it is logical to accept [the reality] of the object as well.

One might object: "Cognition is accepted because it has itself as its own object (*svaviṣayatvāt*), whereas the object is not, because it is apprehended by another (*paragrāhyatvāt*). To this, he replies:
Now, regarding the term "consciousness" (*vijñāna*):
he states that the Buddhist disciple has displayed sheer folly by accepting what is contradictory and abandoning what is not contradictory—this is expressed in the words "absolutely," etc.
(*atyanta-*).
Having accepted that knowledge is self-cognizable, [the opponent] has fallen into folly; [the author] states "and not" (na ca) to show that, in reality, self-cognizability is untenable.

The meaning is that when [the self] is the agent (kartṛ) subordinate to an action, it cannot possess the status of an object (karman) termed "primacy"; therefore, its being the object of a cognition whose agent is itself is non-existent.
Nor should it be said that "self-cognizability" consists merely in having oneself as one's own object;
for the point is that where there is non-difference, even the relationship of object and subject is impossible.
He raises the objection that if knowledge were not self-cognizable, two defects would arise—
beginning with "But surely" (nanu)—
and he then dispels these two defects, namely infinite regress (anavasthā) and parity (sāmya).
Regarding the phrase "both of those as well":

since non-eternal cognition possesses birth and other such characteristics, it is insentient like a jar; therefore, because it cannot apprehend its own birth and so forth by itself, it has a requirement for a grasper (grāhaka).
However, since the Witness (sākṣin) is independent with respect to both its existence and its manifestation, there is no infinite regress (anavasthā).
Nor is there equality [between them], because of the disparity between consciousness and insentience; this is the meaning.
To the question "Where is the witness? he says:
Regarding the phrase "of that which is self-established" (*svayaṃsiddhasya*):
the meaning is that since the distinctions between momentary cognitions cannot be established in the absence of an independent witness (*sākṣin*), such a witness must be accepted.
Furthermore, he states that the witness must be admitted because he is the establisher of the nature of non-eternal cognition.
Furthermore:
by asserting that consciousness depends upon another cognition, one would be stating its lack of epistemic validity;
and by asserting that it manifests by itself, one would be stating its voidness of a knower.

And thus, because it would not be an object for either a knower or a cognition—like a lamp placed within a stone—the consciousness (*vijñāna*) would be non-existent; therefore, its witness must be accepted. This is the meaning. You have merely established what is already accepted by me: that consciousness is devoid of any other knower distinct from itself. Nor should you say that this leads to its non-existence due to the absence of a knower.

The Śākya raises the objection that [the self] is indeed the knower itself— [responding with] "Certainly. He refutes this by stating that since the relationship between knower and known is impossible if there is non-difference, another knower is necessarily required.
No;
the consciousness under dispute is knowable by something other than itself,
because it is an object of knowledge.
The meaning is "possessing a body.
Is the transcendent witness known by another or self-known? In the first case, there would be an infinite regress.
He raises the objection that in the second [verse], the Vijñānavāda itself might be stated in a different manner:
"Of the witness" (sākṣiṇaḥ).
By you, consciousness is said to be endowed with birth and destruction.
Therefore, because it is a rule that an effect is insentient, we have established that it must be cognizable by something other than itself;
