it is observed that a single agent may be connected with multiple purposes;
however, it is not observed that a single sentence possesses multiple meanings.

But in the case of employing multiple meanings, as in "bring the milk" (*paya ānaya*) and so forth, there is indeed a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*) due to repetition (*āvṛtti*), because the act of bringing would have to be connected separately with both water and milk; this is the meaning.
He states the resulting conclusion:
Regarding the phrase "it is one":

if a single word cannot have multiple meanings without repetition, then there would be the fault of having to repeat the word "asṛjata" (he created) in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad for the sake of connecting it with the ether and other elements previously mentioned; therefore, he says "and not... (na ca).

The meaning is that the birth of fire mentioned in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad is preceded by the birth of ether and so forth, because it is the birth of fire, just like the birth of fire mentioned in the Taittirīya Upaniṣad; thus, when the birth from ether and so forth is combined, there is no fault of repetition, since one simply infers another scriptural statement such as "It created that ether."
He provides an illustration for the principle that a sequence found in one Vedic text (śruti) may be adopted in another Vedic text with the words "And as...
He raises an objection regarding the disparity between the illustrative scriptural passages on the grounds of whether they have the primary purport (tātparya) of describing creation or not:

With the words "nanu" and so forth, [the author] states this, considering that if one accepts the priority of fire (*tejas*), two things—the substratum (the creation of space) and its property (priority)—are both heard in scripture and must be sublated, which constitutes complexity (*gaurava*);
whereas if space has priority, there is only the sublation of the implied priority of the creation of fire, which constitutes simplicity (*lāghava*). Thus he says:
"It is not so," he says.

Furthermore, he states "for it is not" [in the text], meaning that it is better to abandon the quality of being first for fire— which is a subordinate attribute— than to abandon the nature of being primary.

Furthermore, is the priority of fire accepted because it is established by scriptural texts concerning creation, or because its priority is manifested through implication by the scriptural text regarding creation due to its position at the beginning?
It is not the first case; thus he says: "Moreover... (apica).
Having restated the second [position], he refutes it with the words "But from the sense... (arthāt tu).

As for what was said—that because conceptual alternatives are impossible regarding a real entity (*vastu*), the primacy of both [names] cannot be established as fixed according to the different recensions (*śākhā*)—[that is now addressed].

Nor can there be primacy for both [air and fire] through simultaneous production, like a two-part sprout, because that would result in the subversion of the sequence "from air, fire arises"; therefore,
he says "vikalpa" (option), meaning that this [sequential order] is indeed accepted.
He says "Moreover" (api ca) to show that there is not only no contradiction between the two scriptural passages, but also a friendly harmony between them;
the grammatical connection is that "ether" (viyat) is to be included [in the list].

Having restated what was said by the proponent of the non-origination of space (*viyat-anutpatti-vādin*), [the author] refutes it with the words "And as for what was said," etc., on the grounds that since the primary sense and intended meaning of the proposition and the scriptural text concerning non-duality (*advaita-śruti*) are understood, they cannot have a figurative meaning.
The principle of the identity of cause and effect is the principle of their non-difference (*tadananyatva-nyāya*).
The sense is that even water situated within milk is not perceived as milk because of their difference; [this is the point].

Anticipating the objection that "let there be no correct knowledge, since it is possible for the Veda to be based on error," he says, "And not of the Veda," [meaning] it is not so, because of its non-personal origin (apauruṣeyatva).

*Māyā* is delusion; by that [delusion], there is falsehood, which is false speech, and through that, deception, which is the communication of what is not as it is. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the desire to deceive, negligence, and lack of proficiency are included.
Having stated the primacy of the *pratijñā* (the initial proposition), he states the primacy of the scriptural text concerning the non-dual (*advaita*).
The term "sāvadhāraṇā" (definitive) means that it is intent upon the negation of all duality.

He states another defect: if both [the cause and the effect] were secondary (figurative), there would be no presentation of the subject as something marvelous, nor would there be the establishment of that [non-duality] through examples such as clay and so forth.
"Not so," etc. //6//
But wherever there is modification, there is division, as in the world. (BS 2.3.7)

Regarding the argument that "space is not produced because it is a single part of the substance *vastu* due to the absence of causal totality (*sāmagrī*)," he states a counter-argument (*satpratipakṣa*) with the words "But as for that which... and so forth.

Having stated the positive concomitance (*anvaya*)—"whatever is differentiated is a modification (*vikāra*), like a jar and so on"—he states the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)—"but that which is not a modification is not differentiated, like the Self."
"But it is not unmodified.

Anticipating the objection that there is a deviation [from the rule] in the case of space and so forth, he says "by this" (etena), meaning: "it is not so, because they are equal to the subject of the proposition (pakṣasamatvāt)."
The meaning is "by way of being differentiated.
He raises an objection regarding the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to the self (*ātman*) by saying:
"Now, [it may be objected]... (*nanu*).

He says "no," because there is no deviation [in the reason], since a distinction that has the same ontological status as its substratum (*dharmi*) is the cause [of the cognition], whereas in the case of the ultimate self (*paramārthātman*), the distinction is merely imagined and thus possesses a different ontological status.
And here, the qualification is "being a substance other than ignorance" (*ajñānānyadravyatvam*).
Therefore, there is no deviation [of the reason] with respect to ignorance, its relation, and so forth.
But is it not the case that the self is an effect,
because it is distinct?

Anticipating the objection that this inference is similar to a fallacious one—such as "because it is a real entity (vastu), like a jar"—he states that it is not similar to a fallacy because there is a subverting argument (bādhaka): if the Self, which is heard in scripture as the supreme cause, were itself an effect, it would follow that it is non-existent (śūnyatā). Thus, the Self is not a non-entity. On the contrary, if space were not an effect, there would be subverting arguments such as the postulation of multiple eternal substances and the abandonment of scriptural propositions; therefore, [the opponent's inference] is not equivalent to a fallacy. He says:
Regarding the term "of the self," he says "because it is the self" in response to the one who claims that this leads to an undesirable consequence (iṣṭaprasaṅga).
Is the non-existence of the self known by someone or not?

In the first case, that which is the knower remains, and thus there is no emptiness. In the second case as well, there is no emptiness because of the absence of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa); such is the meaning.
Furthermore, whatever effect depends upon something else for its existence or manifestation must be sublated;
however, the Self is not an effect because, being independent, it is not subject to sublation—
this he states with the words beginning "nahyātmā" (for the Self is not...).

The literal meaning is: "Indeed, no effect can be adventitious to any cause, because existence (*sattā*) and manifestation (*sphūrti*), when established, do not depend on anything else. In this regard, he explains the non-dependence of manifestation:
"No," [they say].

As it was stated by Sureśvarācārya: "The knower, the means of knowledge, the object of knowledge, and likewise the resulting cognition—all these are established through whose grace; when that [grace] is established, what else is required?"
Thus,
as the Śruti says: "The person is self-luminous," and "By his light all this shines."
[Objection: But if the self were established by itself, the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) would be useless; to this he says:
"Of that" (tasya). [Objection:
Why should the object of cognition (prameya) not also be self-luminous? To this he says:
"No," [he says].

The implication is that, therefore, there is no futility of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). To the objection—"Why should even the self (*ātman*) not have its establishment dependent upon a means of valid cognition?"—he replies:
"But the self," [he says].

This is the meaning: for knowledge whose own existence is ascertained is what ascertains the existence of the object of cognition; because when there is doubt regarding the knowledge—such as "was a jar seen in the house or not?"—or when there is the ascertainment of its absence—"it was not seen"—there is no ascertainment of the nature of the object.
Furthermore, the ascertainment of the existence of a cognition does not arise from itself,
because it is impossible for an effect to be self-luminous;
nor does it arise from another cognition, because that would lead to an infinite regress.
Therefore, the determination of the existence of cognition must be stated by the witness alone;
if, in that case, the determination of the witness's own existence were dependent upon cognition, there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence (anyonyāśraya).
Therefore, because it establishes everything, the self is established by itself.
To the objection that even for that which is self-luminous, why should there not be sublation, he says: "And not... (na ca).
For that which is insentient (jaḍa) is adventitious because its manifestation depends on something else, and it is subject to sublation; it does not have the nature of light (prakāśa).
This is because that which has the nature of being the witness of all sublation cannot be negated by another, and because it is impossible for a thing to negate itself.
The meaning is that even by one who is most skillful, its inherent nature cannot be perceived.

Having thus stated that the Self is not subject to sublation because it is self-luminous, he says "likewise, I myself" to show that it is also not subject to sublation because it possesses intrinsic existence.

The meaning is that although there is a deviation from existence in the case of knowledge and the object of knowledge, there is no such deviation in the case of the knower, because he is always of one and the same nature.
[An objection is raised: "Let it be granted that the living knower does not have a different nature; however, it might be so for one who is dead. To this, he says:
"So be it.
Annihilation means destruction;
otherwise, it is impossible even to conceive of [the object] having a different intrinsic nature or being false.
The meaning is that there is no sublation of the real nature of the self, which is established by the experience "I am.

Thus, by refuting the voidness of the self, it has been stated that the consequence of universal emptiness is undesirable; consequently, he states that the inference of the self's being an effect is fallacious:
Thus:

since the non-product nature [of space] is established, and because its material cause (upādāna) accompanied by ignorance (avidyā), as well as its instrumental causes such as the unseen force (adṛṣṭa), exist, the reason for the non-arising of space—the absence of a causal complex (sāmagrī)—is unestablished in its own form (svarūpāsiddhi); furthermore, due to the sublation by the aforementioned counter-argument (satpratipakṣa), the fact that space is an effect is beyond reproach. Thus he says:
And as for the point regarding "being an effect":

having restated the argument that space cannot be the originator [of the self] because the self and ignorance are of different classes (*vijātīya*), he refutes it with the words beginning "As for that which... and so forth.
Is the restriction of homogeneity (sājātya-niyama) based on the cause alone, or on that which inheres [in it] (samavāyin)?
Having rejected the first, he raises the second alternative with the words:
"It might be thus."
Is the homogeneity [of the cause] determined by the property that delimits its status as an inherent cause (*samavāyitāvacchedakadharma*), or by existence (*sattva*) and so forth?
It is not the first; thus he says:
"That too... (*tadapi*).
Nor should it be said that the rope and so forth are not a distinct substance, for that would lead to the absurd conclusion that cloth and other such things are likewise not distinct substances.
The second [position] is what we accept.
He says "sattva... because the self and ignorance are of the same genus (*sājātya*) by virtue of being real entities (*vastu*).

Having set aside the rule that the material cause must be of the same genus, he now sets aside the rule that [the cause] must be multiple and conjoined, in order to establish that the Self—though non-dual and unattached—is the material cause.
[The author] says "nor indeed," etc., [to address this]:
Is this rule applicable to any cause of origination in general, or only to that which originates a substance?
It is not the first case; thus he says:
Regarding the term *aṇu*:
the first motion is that which produces the conjunction serving as the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) for both the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) and cognition (*jñāna*).

Although the atom and the mind, conjoined with the self possessing unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭavat*), are the initiators of the first motion, nevertheless, because the substratum of the motion is a single entity, the rule regarding multiplicity [of motions] is violated; thus he says:
"Each one indeed" means with other substances that are inherent causes (samavāyin).
Having raised the second [objection], he refutes it by not accepting the doctrine of origination (*ārambhavāda*), beginning with the words "dravya" and so forth.

As for the claim that when a different taste arises in the milk-atoms, curd is commenced by those very same atoms—
that is not so,

furthermore, a convention regarding substances and qualities being of human origin cannot serve as a basis for determining the meaning of the Veda.
Regarding the objection that since a creator is seen in the world to have assistants, how can there be creation from Brahman who is without assistance, he says:
And so it has been said.
He states that the reason [consisting in] the emptiness of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva-śūnyatva*) is also unestablished,
beginning with the words "And as for what was said," and so forth.
The distinction is that [ether] is the substratum of sound.
Ether, which possesses sound and other qualities, does not exist during the dissolution (pralaya), according to the Vedic revelation: "There was neither dust nor the sky."
If it is argued that "in the absence of space, there would be solidity," this son of a Naiyāyika is well-trained indeed!
For solidity is neither the absence of space nor a property thereof; rather, solidity is a particularity of a material substance or a particularity of its conjunction.
The sense is that this [space] does not exist during the dissolution (pralaya).

To the objection—based on the scriptural text "Brahman has space as its body" (ākāśaśarīraṃ brahma)—that since space is the very nature of Brahman, just as heat is the nature of fire, how could there be an absence of space while Brahman exists?—the author replies with the words "And just as... (yathā ca).
The meaning of the scripture is that Brahman is equal to space because of its all-pervasiveness (*vibhutva*).

With the words "Even though... and so forth, [the author] states that the scriptural authority is not sublated by the marks of touch, being a substance, and being a partless substance, together with the marks such as being divided, due to [Brahman's] all-pervasiveness.
The term "impermanent" is used for the sake of the following reasoning: if there were no modification of the substratum (dharmin), there would be no destruction of its qualities (guṇa).
The reason (hetu) is simply the state of being a locus of qualities;
and that consists in possessing qualities that have the same ontological status (samasattāka) as itself.
Therefore, there is no deviation in the case of the self which is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇātman*).
The meaning of the word "element" (*bhūta*) and so forth is [the nature of being an element].
He also states the unestablished nature of the essential character (*svarūpāsiddhi*):
Regarding "and [the case] of omnipresence (*vibhutva*) and so forth":
omnipresence is either conjunction with all corporeal substances or a specific dimension; neither exists in the example of the qualityless Self (*nirguṇātman*).
Furthermore, since conjunction is necessarily restricted to that which possesses parts (*sāvayavatva*), it is contradictory to the probandum of being unproduced (*ajatva*).

However, the omnipresence (*vibhutva*) consisting in the increase of its own nature (*svarūpopacaya*) is not equal for the Self and space, because of the scriptural text: "He is greater than space" (*jyāyān ākāśāt*).
Any occasional attribution of equality with space to Brahman is merely figurative, based on some partial connection with attributes.
Or [it may be argued] by way of non-attachment.

However, due to the fivefold compounding (*pañcīkaraṇa*), its lack of tangibility is unestablished; and because it is an effect-substance (*kāryadravya*), its partlessness (*niravayavatva*) is also unestablished.
The meaning is that the genus *dravyatva* (substantiality) is unestablished in the self (*ātman*).
The similarity intended by the portion "eternal" (*nitya*) is not meant here.
[Objection: But surely the scripture, stating, "As this space is infinite, so the self is infinite," expresses similarity precisely through eternity.
He says "no" with the words "by this," meaning that space is impermanent because it is an effect.
The meaning is that the Śruti, by means of relative infinity, makes known the primary (mukhya) infinity.
Furthermore, because space is limited, it cannot serve as a primary point of comparison; thus he says, "greater" (jyāyān).
The scriptural authority for the absence of a primary object of comparison is the passage beginning with "Not of that" (*na tasya*).

He concludes that there is a coherent unity (*samanvaya*) regarding the creator, the self that is Brahman, by harmonizing the Chāndogya Śruti with the more powerful Taittirīya Śruti through their constituting a single syntactical whole (*ekavākyatā*).
Therefore, [it is so]. //7//

By this, Mātariśvan (the Wind) is explained.
Because this is an extension (*atideśa*), there is no need for a separate introduction or connection;

Regarding the doubt as to whether there is a contradiction with the scriptural statement "From space, air [arises]," based on the presence or absence of syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*), he extends the discussion of the secondary view (*gauṇapakṣa*), the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), and the established conclusion (*siddhāntapakṣa*) by saying "In that case also," and so forth.
For in the preceding section, the immediate succession of fire (*tejas*) after space was established.

Regarding this, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) states the intention of the one who maintains the figurative interpretation (*gauṇavādī*), beginning with "And therefore": since air and fire are mentioned in immediate succession, the scriptural statement of the sequence "from air, fire" would be contradicted; and since the priority of fire [as the first element] would be destroyed if there were a temporal sequence, the two passages do not form a single syntactical unit.
Thus, the prohibition of setting (or merging) is an indicative mark (*liṅga*) for the impossibility of a literal origination.
The repetition of that very same indicative mark is found in the passage, "Vāyu and the intermediate space—this is the immortal.
The meaning of the word "and so forth" (ādi) is another indicative mark of being the self of all, namely, "Vāyu alone is the individual totality and the universal totality.
Likewise, in the Saṃvarga-vidyā, another indicative mark to be understood is the hearing of lordship through the mere mention of the word: "For Vāyu indeed withdraws all these, beginning with fire."

When it is argued that there is no contradiction between the two scriptural passages because the production of air is figurative— based on the understanding from these marks that air is beginningless and endless— the reply is that the production of air is indeed primary.

This is because the scriptural declaration (pratijñā) intended to be explained is more powerful, because there are numerous statements regarding the production of air found here and there which establish that very point, and because this is supported by the aforementioned marks such as being differentiated.
Thus, through the syntactic unity of the two scriptural passages—“Having created space and air, he created fire”—there is a coherent integration (*samanvaya*) within Brahman.

As for the indicative marks (*liṅga*), they must be interpreted as being relative, since they serve to praise the air that is the object of meditation. He states the primary established conclusion (*mukhya-siddhānta*) with the words beginning “pratijñā” (the promise).
That for which a counter-measure has been provided— a resolution based on relativity— is "thus" (tathā).
Having raised an objection against the commencement of the discussion, he states the further doubt with the words beginning with "nanu" (but surely), etc.
The word "mātra" (mere) is used to indicate that the mere words of the passage beginning with "Vāyu indeed gathers all these together" are the source of the doubt, not the actual meaning.
He states that very doubt with the word "saṃvarga" (the gatherer).

The meaning of the word "and so forth" (ādi) refers to the meditation on the individual and the collective, as well as the meditation [on Vāyu] expressed in the passage, "He knows Vāyu as the calf of the quarters. //8//
But the non-existence of that which exists is impossible, because it cannot logically occur. (BS 2.3.9)

"But non-existence [of Brahman] is impossible because it is not logically established. This is because the scriptural texts declaring the beginninglessness of Brahman—such as "Without beginning or end, greater than the great, eternal," and "And there is no progenitor of this"—are contradicted by the scriptural text concerning its origin: "Thou art born, O thou whose face is everywhere."

When there is doubt as to whether a contradiction exists or not based on the presence or absence of syntactical unity (*ekavākyatva*), the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) holds that a contradiction does exist.

By means of the connection through an illustrative example (*dṛṣṭāntasaṃgati*)— just as the immortality of air and so forth is relative by virtue of the power of the scriptural texts concerning its origin, so too the beginninglessness of Brahman is relative— it brings forward the position of the partialist (*ekadeśin*).
"Space":
Brahman is born from something,

He states "so it is" (*tathā*) to show that the scripture concerning birth is more powerful because it is supported by the inference that [the soul] is like space.
Nor does an infinite regress follow from the absence of an initial cause, since beginninglessness is established through the analogy of the seed and the sprout.

And thus, just as one lamp is produced from another lamp, one Brahman is produced from another Brahman; and since the scripture speaks of "origination," the scripture concerning its "beginninglessness" must be interpreted accordingly. Consequently, the established concordance (*samanvaya*) of Brahman—which is both beginningless and endless—is not proven. To this objection, the author states the primary conclusion with the words "tām" (that [scripture]).
Brahman is not born,
because it is devoid of a cause,

The conclusion of the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) is as follows: because the scriptural texts regarding the beginninglessness of Brahman are more powerful—supported by the inference that "it must be like a jar [in its dependence on a cause] through the method of difference" (*vyatireka*), and because the opposite view would entail the absurdity of an effect being produced without a cause—the indicative mark of causality (*kāraṇatvaliṅga*) sublates the literal meaning of the texts concerning birth; thus, the scripture on birth must be interpreted as referring to the non-difference between cause and effect. Consequently, the concordance (*samanvaya*) of Brahman as being without beginning or end is established.
Furthermore, there is no lack of proof for the reason (*hetu*).
Because the cause cannot be determined.
To explain: Is the cause of Brahman, which is pure existence (*sanmātra*), pure existence itself as a universal (*sāmānya*), or as a particular (*sadviśeṣa*), or is it non-existence (*asat*)?
He says that it is none of these three.
By the words "for it is pure being" (*sanmātram hi*) and so forth [it is shown that the example is inappropriate].
As for the lamp being the cause of another lamp, that is not a valid illustration.
Furthermore, there is a disparity between the ether, the wind, and Brahman, due to their being either divided or undivided, and due to their respective natures as causes or effects.
The reason consisting of the nature of being a cause would lead to an ungrounded infinite regress.
He states the sublation [of that view] even by means of reasoning with the words beginning "And not from the modifications," and so forth.
If no cause is admitted, there is the consequence of the doctrine of chance;
if a beginningless cause is not admitted, there is the consequence of infinite regress; if such a cause is admitted, there is the consequence of the doctrine of Brahman.
The meaning is that this is because other causes, such as *pradhāna* and so forth, have been refuted. //9//
Light [is the source] from that, for thus it says: "BBs_2,3.10" [tejo 'tastathā hy āha].

Regarding the statement "It created fire" and the scriptural text "From air, fire [arose]," there arises a doubt as to whether or not there is a contradiction between these two scriptures. In this state of doubt, although it is impossible for a general cause to produce a specific effect, since Brahman and air both possess the general quality of being the material cause of the specific form of fire, they are of equal strength; thus, a contradiction exists.
Thus ends the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) by way of a counter-example.
The seed of doubt consists in the possibility or impossibility of syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) throughout the remainder of the chapter.
In the prima facie view, the result is the lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*) due to the contradiction among the scriptural texts (*śruti*).
It must not be forgotten that it has been stated in the Siddhānta (the final conclusion) that [the Vedic texts] possess authority (*prāmāṇya*).

Thus, in the Pūrvapakṣa (the prima facie view), since only that which is to be produced (*kārya*) is an illusory manifestation (*vivarta*), and because imagined air cannot serve as the substratum for the imagination of fire, Brahman alone is the material cause (*upādāna*) of fire; and since there is an abundance of scriptural passages to the effect that Brahman alone is the material cause of all effects, [the word "air"] must be understood in accordance with those [passages].
He brings forward the established conclusion of a certain school—that there is no contradiction because the fifth case-ending has the sense of "succession"—with the words:
"First, it follows that fire has Brahman as its source," and so on.
The prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) consists merely in setting forth the contradictions among the scriptural texts.
It should be understood that both [the *apasiddhānta* and the *virodha*] constitute the position of a partial proponent (*ekadeśin*) due to contradiction with the tenet;
both of these are treated as the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) in relation to the primary tenet (*mukhyasiddhānta*). He establishes the tenet:
"Thus it follows" means:
rendered useless;
that is to say, its meaning is sublated.
The fact that air has fire as its material cause (prakṛti) is determined by the fifth [scriptural] statement;

nor is it impossible for that which is imagined (kalpita) to be a material cause, because even if it cannot be the substratum (adhiṣṭhāna), it can still be a subject of transformation (pariṇāmin), just like clay and so forth.

In the *Chāndogya*, however, only Brahman’s status as the creator (*sraṣṭṛtva*) is heard, not its status as the material cause (*upādānatva*). Nor can its status as the material cause be established from the indicative mark (*liṅga*)—namely, the desire "May I be many"—which pertains to the non-difference of the effect [from the cause]; for a direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) is stronger than an indicative mark, and thus the mark must be interpreted so as not to contradict the scriptural statement. The intention of the Siddhānta text is that this interpretation is as follows: since air is non-different from Brahman, it is not contradictory that fire, which is born from air, also has Brahman as its material cause.
"Because of the context here" means because of the connection in the sentence "From wind, fire was produced.
"In that context" means in the context of production.

Furthermore, he states "Moreover" (*api ca*) because a case-ending expressing an independent agent (*nirapekṣa-kāraka-vibhakti*) is stronger than a case-ending dependent on a governing word (*upapada-sāpekṣa-vibhakti*); thus, the ablative case (*pañcamī*) does not signify sequence.

Without a governing word such as "above" (*ūrdhvam*) or "immediately after" (*anantaram*), sequence is not conveyed by the ablative alone; therefore, a connection with the meaning of a governing word must be postulated.
The *apādāna* case-factor, known as *prakṛti*, indeed appears through the independent ablative (*pañcamī*).

Specifically, in this context, the meaning of *apādāna* for the ablative is established by the subject matter of the treatise; and the principle is that when there is a conflict between what is already established (*klpta*) and what is to be inferred (*kalpya*), the latter is sublated. This is the established rule.
He states that [the effect] is produced through a succession:
Regarding the phrase "even when":
the meaning is that the boiled, heated milk of that cow is the direct effect, whereas curds and so forth are produced through a succession [of intermediate stages].
Curdled milk mixed with curds is *āmikṣā*.
Regarding the proof that Brahman exists in the form of air, [the author] says:
"And it shows."
Regarding the designation of that which is born from a lineage as being "born from him," he states the traditional authority (*smṛti*): "And so it is.

Having raised the doubt—how can there be such an emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*) that the intellect and other faculties arising from the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and so forth proceed from Me alone—he says:
By the words "even though" (*yadyapi*) and so forth, the remainder [of the argument] is as follows:

since [the world] is descended from the lineage of God through a succession—that is, by way of a continuous tradition—it is logical to employ an emphatic restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) for the purpose of excluding any other ultimate cause.
He states the meaning of this term:

"Of these" means that the purpose [of the scriptural statements] such as "From Him [come] these, into Him [they go], and by Him [they are sustained]" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.1) is fulfilled simply by their being born from Brahman, whether directly or indirectly.

It is established that the non-sequential scriptural texts are to be understood as forming a single coherent statement (ekavākyatva) in accordance with the more powerful sequential scriptural texts, [thereby showing that fire originates] from Brahman, the cause of fire, through the intermediaries of ether and air. //10//
The Waters. BBs_2,3.11. Start BsRp_2,3.5.11. End BsRp_2,3.4.10.
"Water. This is an extended application (atideśa).
For it is said in the *Muṇḍaka* text of the *Atharvaveda*: "From this [Brahman] are born breath, mind, and all the sense organs."
In the mantra, "Space, wind, fire, water, and earth—the supporter of the universe," it is heard that water is born from Brahman.

Regarding the doubt as to whether this contradicts the scriptural statement, "From fire, water [arose]," the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) holds that since both texts are of equal authority, there is indeed a contradiction.
However, because water is combustible by fire, its birth from fire is impossible; therefore, the ablative case in the latter text is intended to signify sequence, and thus there is no contradiction.
Having raised this further doubt, he explains by extending the aforementioned principle [to this case] with the words "Therefore" (*ataḥ*).
To the question, "How can there be a determination that water is born from fire when there is a contradiction with perception? he replies:

Regarding the phrase "because of the statement": the meaning is that even though there is a contradiction between water and fire when they have been made tripartite (*trivṛtkṛta*), it is determined by the statement "fire [consists of] water" that there is no contradiction between those two when they are beyond the senses (*atīndriya*). He says that this extension (*atideśa*) is not only for the sake of knowing the absence of contradiction with scripture, but also for the sake of determining the order of the origin of the five elements: He said: "But the mention of fire first is because of its preeminence. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.4.1) "The mention of fire first," that is, before water, occurs because of its preeminence. Fire is preeminent because it is useful for all beings; for all beings depend upon fire for their maintenance. Furthermore, fire is preeminent because it manifests itself clearly in the form of light, whereas water does not manifest itself as clearly as fire. Therefore, although water was produced first, fire is mentioned first because of its preeminence. This is the meaning. And so on. The word "and so on" implies that the order of the origin of the elements should be understood according to the sequence of their manifestation. For example, among the organs of action, the hands are mentioned first because they are preeminent due to their utility for all beings. Similarly, among the organs of perception, the eyes are mentioned first because they are preeminent due to their utility for all beings. Likewise, among the objects of the senses, sound is mentioned first because it is preeminent due to its utility for all beings. Thus, the order of the origin of the elements should be understood according to the sequence of their manifestation. However, the order of the origin of the elements is not fixed solely by the sequence of their manifestation. Why? Because it is seen in another scriptural passage. As it is said in the Taittirīya Upaniṣad: "From the Self, space was born; from space, air; from air, fire; from fire, water; from water, earth. (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1). Here, space is mentioned first, and then air, fire, water, and earth. Therefore, the order of the origin of the elements is not fixed solely by the sequence of their manifestation. What then? It is fixed by the sequence of the creation of the world. As it is said in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa: "In the beginning, this [world] was non-existent. From that, existence arose. That made itself a self. That turned into an egg. It lay for a year. Then it broke open. One of the two shells became silver, and the other gold. That which was silver is this earth; that which was gold is this heaven; and what was the membrane between them is the atmosphere; what were the veins are the rivers; and what was the fluid within is this ocean. (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 11.1.6.1–3). Here, space is mentioned first, and then air, fire, water, and earth. Therefore, the order of the origin of the elements is fixed by the sequence of the creation of the world. And so on. The word "and so on" implies that the order of the origin of the elements should be understood according to the sequence of the creation of the world. For example, among the worlds, the earth is mentioned first because it is preeminent due to its utility for all beings. Similarly, among the Vedas, the Ṛgveda is mentioned first because it is preeminent due to its utility for all beings. Likewise, among the gods, Agni is mentioned first because he is preeminent due to his utility for all beings. Thus, the order of the origin of the elements should be understood according to the sequence of the creation of the world. But why is the order of the origin of the elements not fixed solely by the sequence of the creation of the world? Because it is seen in another scriptural passage. As it is said in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad: "From this, verily, the ether was produced; from the ether, air; from air, fire; from fire, water; from water, earth. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.3.3). Here, the ether is mentioned first, and then air, fire, water, and earth. Therefore, the order of the origin of the elements is not fixed solely by the sequence of the creation of the world. What then? It is fixed by the sequence of the dissolution of the world. As it is said in the Garbhopaniṣad: "Earth dissolves into water; water dissolves into fire; fire dissolves into air; air dissolves into the ether; the ether dissolves into the Unmanifest; the Unmanifest dissolves into the Imperishable; and the Imperishable dissolves into the Peaceful. (Garbhopaniṣad 5). Here, earth is mentioned first, and then water, fire, air, the ether, the Unmanifest, and the Imperishable. Therefore, the order of the origin of the elements is fixed by the sequence of the dissolution of the world. And so on. The word "and so on" implies that the order of the origin of the elements should be understood according to the sequence of the dissolution of the world. For example, among the worlds, the earth is mentioned first because it is preeminent due to its utility for all beings. Similarly, among the Vedas, the Ṛgveda is mentioned first because it is preeminent due to its utility for all beings. Likewise, among the gods, Agni is mentioned first because he is preeminent due to his utility for all beings. Thus, the order of the origin of the elements should be understood according to the sequence of the dissolution of the world. But why is the order of the origin of the elements not fixed solely by the sequence of the dissolution of the world? Because it is seen in another scriptural passage. As it is said in the Praśna Upaniṣad: "When a person departs from here, he goes to the air; the air makes way for him like the hole of a chariot wheel. When he has passed through the air, he goes to the sun; the sun makes way for him like the hole of a door. When he has passed through the sun, he goes to the moon; the moon makes way for him like the hole of a palace. When he has passed through the moon, he goes to lightning; the lightning makes way for him like the hole of a house. When he has passed through lightning, he goes to a man; that man is a carrier of food. (Praśna Upaniṣad 1.10). Here, the air is mentioned first, and then the sun, the moon, the lightning, and the man. Therefore, the order of the origin of the elements is not fixed solely by the sequence of the dissolution of the world. What then? It is fixed by the sequence of the meditation. As it is said in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad: "Now, the instruction regarding the five fires: 'O Gautama, at the time of the new moon, the gods offer the oblation to the moon as the sacrificial fire. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.4.1). Here, the moon is mentioned first, and then the lightning, the rain, the earth, and the man. Therefore, the order of the origin of the elements is fixed by the sequence of the meditation. And so on. The word "and so on" implies that the order of the origin of the elements should be understood according to the sequence of the meditation. For example, among the worlds, the earth is mentioned first because it is preeminent due to its utility for all beings. Similarly, among the Vedas, the Ṛgveda is mentioned first because it is preeminent due to its utility for all beings. Likewise, among the gods, Agni is mentioned first because he is preeminent due to his utility for all beings. Thus, the order of the origin of the elements should be understood according to the sequence of the meditation. But why is the order of the origin of the elements not fixed solely by the sequence of the meditation? Because it is seen in another scriptural passage. As it is said in the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad: "From Him, verily, the ether was produced; from the ether, air; from air, fire; from fire, water; from water, earth. (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.1.3). Here, the ether is mentioned first, and then air, fire, water, and earth. Therefore, the order of the origin of the elements is not fixed solely by the sequence of the meditation. What then? It is fixed by the sequence of the creation of the body. As it is said in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa: "From the Self, the ether was produced; from the ether, air; from air, fire; from fire, water; from water, earth; from earth

The topical connection (*adhikaraṇasaṃgati*) arises from the cause-and-effect relationship between water and the earth.
The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is established by two grounds: the scriptural mention of "food" (*anna*) and the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of "becoming rain.
The meaning of the scriptural statement "that very [water] becomes that very [earth]" is as follows.

And thus, since there is a contradiction—food [being produced] from water in one place, and earth from that [water], and then food from that [earth] in another—it follows that they do not form a single coherent statement; this being the prima facie view, the author establishes the final conclusion with the words "evam prāpte" (this being the case).
"Adhikāra" means context or subject matter.
Form is the characteristic mark;
milk is *payaḥ*, which is as white as that,
while blood is red like glowing coals (*aṅgāra*).
He explains the place denoted by another scriptural term with the words, "another scriptural passage also" (śrutyantaram api).
The meaning is that the fact that earth is the place immediately following water is established by another scriptural passage; therefore, food is also of the nature of earth.

The meaning of the Śruti is as follows: at that time of creation, that which was the "scum" (śara) of the waters—that thickened state like the scum of boiled milk—was itself condensed; it became a solid mass, and that hard transformation of the waters became the earth.
With the intention of explaining in what location the creation of rice and other foodstuffs took place, he says:

Regarding the phrase "pṛthivyāstu" (of the earth), this is the ablative case. Having raised the objection— how can there be a sublation by context, indicative mark, and position of the scriptural statement regarding food, which is accompanied by the indicative mark of the occurrence of rain— he says:

"Also because of the remainder of the sentence": when there is a conflict between a strong and a weak means of knowledge, it is better to somehow interpret the strong means of knowledge with minimal sublation than to completely sublate many weak ones; according to this principle, the fact that the *śruti* and *liṅga* refer solely to food is set aside, and they are interpreted as referring to the earth, which consists of both food and non-food.
The sense is that if food alone were grasped by those two [passages], there would result an absolute contradiction of the context and other factors which concern the earth alone.
By stating that food is born from rain, it is indicated that the earth is produced from water; thus, the earth is born from water (*abjā*).
The literal meaning is that [the earth] is [produced from water] because it possesses the nature of earth (pṛthivītva), just like food (anna).

Thus, by interpreting the Chāndogya Śruti in accordance with the Taittirīya Śruti, it is established that there is no contradiction in the concordance (samanvaya) of the scriptural texts concerning the creation of the elements within Brahman. //12//
But he [the individual soul] [arises] from that very meditation on Him, because of His characteristic marks. (BS 2.3.13)

Now, having raised the objection that those elements possess independence by virtue of the relationship between the substratum and the dependent based on their reliance upon those [elements], he refutes it:
"But from the meditation on Him alone, for that is His mark.
Having relied upon the aforementioned elements, he presents the doubt and the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa).

By the words "What are these? and so forth, it should be understood that since the seeds of doubt have not been explicitly stated, the arguments for the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) and the final (uttarapakṣa) positions constitute those seeds.
Now, is it here being questioned whether the elements possess the status of material cause (upādānatva) through their own independence, or rather the status of agent (kartṛtva)?
Not the first, because it would contradict such logical principles as "because the arrangement is impossible" (Brahma Sūtra 2.2.1); thus he raises the objection with "nanu" (but).
Nor the second.
The intended meaning is that [the elements] are insentient.

Just as by words such as "human" living beings who identify with their respective bodies are denoted, so too in scriptural passages such as "from space, air," the deities who identify with those respective elements are denoted by the words "space" and so forth;
since it is possible for them to act as agents toward their own effects, such as air, the meaning of the ablative case is their status as independent causes.

Thus, because of the qualification "itself" in the scriptural text, "It made itself its own self," it is established that Brahman possesses the capacity for universal agency independent of anything else; therefore, the scripture teaches that Brahman is the independent instrumental cause. Consequently, since there is a contradiction between the two scriptural declarations—one of the Lord as the agent and the other of the elements as the agent—both being independent of each other, there can be no harmonious reconciliation (*samanvaya*) regarding Brahman. To this, he states the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) with its full implications:
"This is not a fault."
The meaning is "of the beings," that is, of the deities presiding over them.

Just as Brahman, having assumed the state of ether and so forth, is the material cause (*upādāna*) of all, so too Brahman, having assumed the state of the individual soul (*jīva*) as the deity presiding over those [elements], is the agent (*kartṛ*). Thus, there is no contradiction with the scriptural texts concerning the Lord's status as the agent through this indirect succession (*paramparayā*).

The qualification "by himself" (*svayam*) should be understood, according to the view of the *ekadeśin* (partial proponent), as being for the purpose of excluding another Lord, and not for the purpose of excluding dependence on the state of being an individual soul; this is how the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) of that school is to be inferred.
He states the primary conclusion:
"Thus, this being the case.

By words such as "ether" (*ākāśa*), there is no indication by secondary metaphor (*lakṣaṇā*) for a deity, because there is no sublation of the primary meaning; furthermore, the ablative endings signify the sense of "source-material" (*prakṛti*), as that is their more established conventional usage in that context.
Likewise, insentient elements possess no agency at all; how then could they have agency independent of God?
Even if agency were possible for deities, nevertheless, because it is heard that even sentient beings are governed by God, they too lack independence.
What more need be said? Thinking that insentient elements (*bhūta*) lack independence, it was stated:
"Because of its mark" (*talliṅgāt*).

The meaning is this: although Brahman exists as the material cause (*upādāna*) even in the form of those various insentient things, its direct agency over all is solely through its aspect as the Lord (*Īśvara*), which is distinct from the individual soul (*jīva*), because there is the mark (*liṅga*) of its being the controller of all.
And because of the context, he says "likewise" (tathā) to show that [the Self] is directly the agent of everything;
having restated what was previously mentioned, he refutes it.
As for the phrase "yattu" (but as for that):

the meaning is that the Supreme Lord's entry into beings by way of being their inner controller (*antaryāmin*) constitutes a connection; it is by virtue of this that the hearing of "seeing" (*īkṣaṇa*) occurs in relation to those elements, but this does not imply that they possess consciousness or independence.
By this, the term "tadabhidhyānāt" (from his meditation upon that) has been explained.

Thus is the application of the Sūtra: That Lord, although abiding as each respective self, is the direct agent of all, because of the mark (liṅga) of His being the inner controller (antaryāmin). If agency were mediated through the state of being a *jīva*, then agency would belong to the *jīva* alone; consequently, the agency of the inner controller would not be established, and His status as an inner controller would be untenable. Furthermore, since the "seeing" heard in the texts regarding the elements—such as in the passage "That fire saw"—is logically possible only through the meditation upon Him, that is, the vision of the Lord, the one who saw is indeed the Supreme Self. On this point, he cites another scriptural passage and the context:
"Not another" [means]:

therefore, since there is an absence of independence in anything other than Īśvara due to the consequence that the category of the entity "Īśvara" would be lost, it is established that there is no contradiction between the scriptural statement regarding the agency of Īśvara and the scriptural statement regarding the elements. //13//
But the sequence [of the elements] is established from this [preceding order] by way of reversal; and it is logical. (2.3.14)
But by way of contrast:

although here the contradiction with scripture is not resolved—thus there is an apparent lack of connection—nevertheless, once the order of origination has been determined, the order of dissolution, which resides in the mind, is now investigated. Considering that these two intermediate connections (antarasaṃgatī) are merely incidental (prāsaṅgikī), he says:
Regarding the phrase "of the elements" (*bhūtānām*):

here, because the order is determined to be the reverse of the order of origination, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) holds that the fruit is the concentration of the mind upon the inner Brahman (*pratyagbrahma*), preceded by meditative absorption on the dissolution of the elements in reverse order.

In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), however, since the destruction of the effect follows the destruction of the cause, the Brahman that serves as the substratum for the dissolution of all things is not established; thus, the aforementioned concentration cannot be achieved—this is the distinction.
Regarding those who say that when there is a dissolution of the great elements (*mahābhūtas*), there is no consideration of a sequence because such a thing does not exist at all, he replies to them:
"All three [stages] as well.

The statement "there is no fixed rule" was made out of disregard; however, when there is an expectation for a sequence regarding the dissolution mentioned in scripture (*śrauta*), the very sequence of origination mentioned in scripture must be adopted.
The prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) position is that [the order of dissolution follows the order of origination] because it is scriptural (śrauta) and therefore internal (antaraṅga).

However, it is observed in the world that when the cause ceases, the effect perishes. Thus, even though the order of origination is scriptural, it is not adopted in dissolution; rather, only the worldly order is adopted. This is because the Vedic scripture depends on the understanding of objects as perceived in the world, and because the worldly order is more internal and appropriate than even the scriptural one.
For it has been established by the principle of non-difference (*tadananyatva*) that the cause itself is the very nature (*svarūpa*) of the effect;

indeed, it is not logical for an effect to persist even for a moment once its own nature is destroyed. Therefore, the sequence of emergence is unfit to be applied to dissolution. He establishes this as the final conclusion with the words "Therefore we say," etc., on the grounds that [the sequence of emergence] is rendered redundant by the constraints of the worldly sequence.
Why is it accepted that Brahman is the substratum in which all effects dissolve through a gradual succession, rather than being so directly? To this, he says:
"For [it does not happen] by transgressing its own cause."
The meaning is that if the pot were destroyed [without leaving a trace], there would follow the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of not perceiving the clay.
The remainder of the Smṛti text, "And the air dissolves into space, and that [space] dissolves into the unmanifest," is the meaning of the word "etc.
(ādi). By the principle that "a relation depends upon suitability" (yogyatā), it is established that there is a sublation of what is unsuitable. //14//
If it is argued that consciousness and the mind [are distinct] because their respective marks appear in succession, we say no, because there is no distinction [in the nature of their manifestation].
Because there is no distinction in the interval [between the two].

Having relied upon the previously stated sequence of the origin and dissolution of the elements (*bhūta*), a doubt arises as to whether that [sequence] is contradicted by the sequence of the origin of the organs (*karaṇa*) or not, based on whether the organs are non-material (*abhautika*) or material (*bhautika*).
Therefore, preceded by a restatement of what has occurred, [the author begins] with the words "of the elements" (*bhūtānām*) and so forth.
To one who claims that the instruments of action do not exist at all, he says: "Of the sense-faculties... [and so on].
Furthermore: "The intellect is higher than the mind; but He who is beyond the intellect..."
The Smṛti statement, "Others [say] the sense organs are the ears and so forth," is to be understood here.
Words that have other referents are called "indicative marks" (liṅga).
He states the requirement for the sequence of the instruments:
Regarding the phrase "of those two":
since there is an expectancy [for a sequence], he says "moreover" (apica) to indicate that the order established by direct scriptural statement (śruti) is to be accepted.
"Consciousness" (*vijñāna*) is that by which one cognizes; it is the intellect (*buddhi*) together with the sense organs.

Between the Self and the elements, consciousness and the mind (*manas*) are mentioned in sequence based on their indicative mark—the scriptural passage concerning creation beginning with "From this [Self] are born breath, mind," and so forth.
Thus, the meaning of the portion of the Sūtra is the objection that the previously stated order is broken by the order of the instruments (the senses).

Nor should it be argued that because the organs are composed of the elements (bhautika), they must follow immediately after the elements; for there is no evidence for their being composed of the elements.
Thus, according to the stated sequence—where space arises first from the Self and subsequently air—the organs [arise] from the Self.

Consequently, there is a contradiction in the sequence beginning with "the elements" (bhūtāni); thus, due to the contradiction between the *Taittirīya* and *Atharvaṇa* Śrutis, there is no coherent convergence (*samanvaya*) upon Brahman—this is the result of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).
He establishes the final position (*siddhānta*):
No.

In the Taittirīya Śruti, "From the Self, space [arose]," etc., the sequence appears by implication through the ablative case (*pañcamī*) as one of cause and effect. There is no sublation of that by the textual order (*pāṭhakrama*) of the Atharvaṇa, because no specific sequence contrary to the sequence of meaning is heard; for the textual order is subordinate to the cognition of the sequence of meaning.

The meaning is that, because it is impossible for [the order of] the principal [elements] to be sublated, the sequence of the text must be interpreted so as not to contradict the sequence of the meaning of the Vedic revelation; thus, the sequence of the organs follows the sequence of the elements.
Furthermore, he states that their sequence follows that [of the elements] because they are composed of those elements:
He says: "Furthermore, because they are composed of the elements, their sequence follows that [of the elements]."
Regarding the word "yadi":

it should not be argued that because the vital breath (prāṇa) cannot be a modification of water, the suffix *mayaṭ* in "consisting of food" (*annamaya*) and so forth does not have the sense of "modification.

For, since the organs are distinct and thus products, they require a cause; and when the Vedic texts such as "consisting of food" provide what is required by that expectancy, it is logical—provided there is no subverting evidence—that the suffix *mayaṭ* carries the sense of "modification."

If, however, the suffix *mayaṭ* were taken in the sense of "abundance," it would result in stating something that was not even expected; for by the scripture itself, through the consumption of fire, water, and food, the growth of speech, breath, and mind, as well as their destruction in the absence of those elements, has already been shown, thus leaving no room for dispute.

Alternatively, the meaning of *mayaṭ*—namely, that their growth is dependent upon the gross elements—is heard as a mark (*liṅga*) of their material nature: the vital breaths, the senses, and the mind are material, because they possess growth dependent on the elements, just like the body.

[The opponent says: "But if they are material (bhautika), how can their origin be mentioned separately in the Atharva Veda, since their origin is already established by the mention of the origin of the elements? To this, he replies:
"The designation also... [etc.]
Even while accepting their non-material nature through a bold argument (*prauḍhavāda*), he states that there is no contradiction with the Śruti:
"But if...
Since there is no evidence for a temporal sequence between the organs and the elements, the aforementioned order of the elements is not violated.
And the meaning is that the statement of the Atharva Veda is not an authoritative means of knowledge because it is merely a recitation.
If so, how is the determination of the sequence established? To this he says: "In that manner."

"This [universe] was in its gross state prior to its emergence; it was Prajāpati, the Sūtrātman"—the sense here is that the sequence appears to be first the creation of Prajāpati consisting of subtle elements, and then the creation of the mind and so forth.

Thus, concluding the result of the final position—that there is no contradiction between the scriptural accounts of the origin of the elements and the origin of the instruments (organs), and therefore the concordance with Brahman is established—he says:
"Therefore... //15//
But the designation [of the Self] as "moving and non-moving" must be figurative, based on its dependence upon those [bodies], because it exists only when they exist. (BS 2.3.16)
Because it is the cause of all things moving and non-moving.

Thus far, the contradiction among the scriptural texts concerning the elements has been refuted in order to determine the cause denoted by the word *tat* (That). Now, up to the conclusion of this section, the contradiction among the scriptural texts concerning the individual soul (*jīva*) is refuted for the sake of purifying the meaning of the word *tvam* (Thou).

Here, the question arises: is there a contradiction between the scriptural texts stating that "the individual soul is neither born nor dies" and the scriptural injunctions regarding the *Jāteṣṭi* sacrifice and the *Śrāddha* rites?

When it is argued that there is a contradiction because of this doubt, the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin) maintains that the scriptural texts concerning the soul's birth and so forth are sublated by the injunctions for rites such as the *jāteṣṭi*, aided by the conventional designations of "birth" and other such terms; thus he says: "They exist."

And thus, although there is no sublation of the order of the elements by the order of the origin of the organs, there would be sublation by the order of the origin of the individual soul (jīva); this constitutes the connection as a counter-example.
The distinction is that in the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) the identity of the individual soul and Brahman is not established, whereas in the final conclusion (siddhānta) it is established.

With reference to the birth and so forth of that conscious being, the purificatory rites (saṃskāra) such as the *jātakarma* are prescribed as the means for achieving results in a future life for that very consciousness.

Thus, when there is a mutual contradiction between the subject of reference (*uddeśya*) and the predicate (*vidheya*), according to the maxim "the subject must be interpreted in a way that does not contradict the predicate," he establishes the final conclusion— that birth and so forth are conditioned by the body and not inherent [to the self]— with the words beginning with "tām" (her).
This body is "devoid of life," meaning it has been abandoned by the living self (jīva).
The primary application of designations such as "birth" and so forth refers to the bodies of moving and non-moving beings;

however, with respect to the living self, they would be secondary, figurative, and based on limiting adjuncts (upādhi), since they exist when the adjuncts exist and do not exist when they are absent—this is the meaning of the sūtra.
He also cites scripture regarding the birth and death of the individual soul (jīva) as being due to limiting adjuncts (upādhi), beginning with the words "sa vā" (That indeed).
He states the meaning of the term "being born":
Regarding the term "body," he explains its state of being subject to death with the words:
"departing."
One might object: "Is it not the case that the birth and other states of the individual soul (jīva) are refuted later on?
If they are refuted here as well, would this not be a redundancy? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Of the individual soul."

Thus, it is established that since scriptures such as those concerning the *jāteṣṭi* sacrifice refer to births and so forth that are merely conditional (*aupādhika*), there is no contradiction with the scriptural statements regarding the unborn nature of the individual soul (*jīva*). //16//
The self [is not produced], because of the Veda and because of its eternity, according to those [scriptures]. (BS 2.3.17)

"There is no self [produced from Brahman], because of the scriptural statement and because of its eternity; for that reason. Since there is a mutual contradiction between the scriptural texts concerning the origination of the individual soul (jīvātman)—such as "From this Supreme Self all individual souls issue forth like sparks from a fire"—and the scriptural texts concerning its non-origination—such as "He has entered here even to the tips of the fingernails" and "The Self is unborn"—there arises a doubt.

Let there not be birth and death of the individual soul (jīva) coinciding with the birth and destruction of the body, because [otherwise] injunctions and the like—which are causes for attaining heaven and so forth to be experienced in another body—would be impossible.

To this, the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) offers a counter-example, asking: "Why should those two [birth and death] not belong to the soul at the beginning and end of a kalpa, just as they do to space, since that is possible? He states this as follows:
In this context, "first attained" means as before;
"obstruction" (uparodha) means sublation (bādha).

[Objection: But surely, since it is the unmodified Brahman itself that has entered here as the individual soul (jīva), and not some other reality, the initial proposition is established; to this, he replies: "And not...
[The individual soul is different from the Supreme].

The collective meaning is as follows: because of the possession of contradictory attributes, there is a contradiction of one's own thesis if that which is distinct remains unchanging; therefore, since the scripture concerning origination—supported by the logical mark of "being divided" and accompanied by reasoning—is more powerful, the scripture concerning "entering" must be explained to mean that the Lord has entered in the form of a modification consisting of the individual soul (*jīva*).
[This refers to the phrase] "having a similar form."
It is determined that living beings (jīvas) exist because they are heard of as examples [in scripture].
An objection is raised: "But since in passages such as 'From the Self, space was produced,' the production of the individual soul (jīva) is not mentioned, its existence is untenable.
To this, he replies: "And not... (na ca).

Thus, the meaning is that since [the Self] exists as a modification (*vikāra*), its "entry" occurs by way of the individual soul (*jīva*), which is itself a modification—just as it is said that [the clay] made itself into the form of the manifold of modifications.
Scriptural texts concerning non-birth and so forth refer to the non-origination and so on of the individual soul during the interval between cosmic cycles (*kalpa*);
and the scriptural text "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*) refers to the clay [as the underlying reality].
When it is argued that this should be explained like the sentence "the pot" (which expresses non-difference), the author establishes the final position with the word "evam" (thus):
"The cause [of the appearance of difference] is either the division itself as real, like the substratum, or it is adventitious."
Not the first, because it is unproven; thus he says:
"In this regard, it is said: 'not of this'.
In the second case, the soul's status as a modification is not established by itself.
He states that [the argument] is not a valid reason,
beginning with "buddhyādi.
He then states the proof for the distinction based on limiting adjuncts (aupādhika-bheda):
And likewise:
having raised the objection that the suffix *mayaṭ* signifies "modification," he says,
"and being composed of that."
A *jālma* is one who is dull-witted due to passion and dependent on women.

The meaning is that the suffix *mayaṭ* is used in the sense of "abundance" (*prācurya*), because the individual soul (*jīva*), through ignorance of its own true nature, becomes dependent on the intellect (*buddhi*) and other faculties, thereby partaking in distinctions such as being an agent.
Having set aside the *liṅga* [scripture], he states the interpretation of the *śruti* supported by it:
Regarding the phrase "yadapi" (even that):
he cites scripture concerning the birth and destruction of the individual soul (*jīva*) as being merely due to its limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), by saying "tathā" (so it is).
Having arisen—that is, having been born—equally from these elements that have evolved into the body and the self, one perishes after them as they dissolve;
the meaning is that after death, following the dissolution of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), there is no consciousness.
But [it was said] that he is a mass of pure intelligence (*prajñānaghana*).
Since the claim that "there is no perception" is contradictory, he says "tathā" (so).

The syntactical connection is as follows: the Śruti establishes the answer that the absence of perception is merely the absence of specific cognition due to the dissolution of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), not the absence of the cognition of the Self's own nature.

The meaning of Maitreyī’s question is this: "By stating that 'in this very self, which is a mass of consciousness, there is no consciousness after death,' you have led me into a state of delusion—into the midst of delusion, into confusion. I do not understand this matter; tell me the meaning of what you have said. To this, the Sage replied:
Or rather, [the meaning is as follows]:

"moha" refers to a delusive statement; "uccheda" is the destruction of its prior state; that which has this as its property is "ucchedadharman," meaning subject to transformation. That which is not so is "anucchedadharmā," meaning non-transforming;
therefore, the sense is that it is indestructible.
If that is so, why was it said that "there is no perception after death"? To this he replies:
"merely" (mātra).
The meaning is that it was stated thus because of the lack of contact with objects (*viṣaya*) by means of the subtle elements (*mātrā*).
He states the reason for the claim that a distinction between contradictory attributes is superimposed, as in the case of an object and its reflection—
namely, "thereafter" (*ata ūrdhvam*).

Furthermore, since liberation would be impossible if the individual soul (*jīva*) were subject to modification, it must be stated that the statement "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*) has the purpose of establishing an indivisible unity.

And thus, since the scriptural texts concerning the necessity of living— which are required by the principal sentence that possesses a fruit— are more powerful, the texts concerning the origination and so forth merely restate what is already established by those [necessity-of-living texts]; therefore, it is proven that there is no contradiction.
"Because of this very reason, [the Self] is the knower.
(BBs 2.3.18) "Because of this very reason, [the Self] is the knower.

Here, the contradiction between the scriptural texts concerning the self-luminosity of the Self—such as "The Self alone is its light"—and the scriptural texts concerning the possession of non-eternal knowledge—such as "seeing with the eye, hearing with the ear"—is resolved.
The meaning is that He is the eye, the seer, and the ear, the hearer of this world.

The logical connection (*saṃgati*) consists in the relationship between the reason and the probandum (*hetu-sādhyabhāva*), because by taking up the previously stated reason for the non-origination of the individual soul (*jīva*), one establishes its self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*).
For if there is no origination, it is established that the self-luminous Brahman itself, when conditioned (*upahita*), is the individual soul; thus, the self-luminosity of the soul is proven.
Nor is the purpose already established;

for even if the individual soul (*jīva*) were self-luminous while unarisen, the means of knowledge would be rendered useless. Thus, by the force of scriptural texts on non-eternal knowledge supported by reasoning, the scriptural texts on self-luminosity are sublated, leading to the doubt that the soul might be different from Brahman. It is precisely to establish its fitness for identity with Brahman that self-luminosity is proven here.

Thus, it should be understood that from the beginning of the section up to its conclusion, the result is that the individual soul's lack of fitness for identity with Brahman is established in the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), whereas its fitness for such identity is established in the final conclusion (siddhānta).
He rejects the objection that this is merely an unintended consequence (iṣṭāpatti) by stating: "They were questioned."
He states that the individual soul (*jīva*) is not self-luminous because its knowledge is dependent upon a means of realization, unlike the Lord (*īśvara*); thus he says:
"Therefore, because it is occasional...
One should understand that, according to the literal reading of the commentary (*bhāṣya*), the reason (*hetu*) is non-different from the probandum (*sādhya*).

Thus, when it is argued that the scriptural statement regarding the self-luminosity of the individual soul (jīva) is contradicted, the author establishes the final conclusion with the word "evam" (thus).
The particle "cet" (if) here signifies certainty.
The self-luminosity of the individual soul (jīva) arises not only from its non-difference from the self-luminous Brahman, but also from scripture; thus he says:
"consisting of consciousness" (*vijñānamaya*).
The meaning is that this refers to the context [of the Upanishadic passage] beginning with "He who consists of consciousness."

The Self, being itself awake and self-luminous, looks on at the seven [organs], speech and the rest, whose functions have been withdrawn; that is to say, it perceives the objects experienced during sleep. In this regard, the meaning is that for the knower—the witness of the intellect-substance (buddhisattva)—there is no destruction of consciousness during this dream state.

To establish the synthesis of cognitions of smell and so forth produced by the nose and other senses, it must be stated that the Self is of the nature of knowledge; thus he says with another scriptural passage, "Now...

Even though the Self is of the nature of eternal consciousness, because it is inherently unattached (*asaṅga*), there is no connection with smell and the like. Therefore, the means of knowledge are for the purpose of the mental modification (*vṛtti*) that effects such a connection; hence, they are not useless. Thus he says:
"Smells" means delimitation; "for smelling" (gandhāya) means for the sake of the internal organ's function directed toward that object-domain. This is the meaning.

He refutes the argument that "the Self is not of the nature of consciousness because consciousness is absent even when the Self exists in states such as deep sleep"—beginning with the words *yat tu*—as follows:

regarding the claim that "one does not see during those various states including deep sleep," the reason for saying that one does not see while actually seeing, being one whose knowledge is unimpaired, is this: [text continues].
"No," [he says];
the meaning is "because it is incapable of perishing.
To the question "Why does it not see?", he replies:
"But not [so]"—

by stating that the function (vṛtti) is dependent upon a means, it is said that the reason— that the knowledge of the essential nature (svarūpa-jñāna) is not dependent on a means— is unestablished (asiddha). Furthermore, the argument regarding the futility of the means has also been refuted.
By the passage beginning with "hearing," it has been explained that the cognitions of impermanent things, such as hearing, have mental modifications (*vṛtti*) as their objects.
The self is not knowledge,
because it is a substance (*dravya*).

Such arguments as these are contradicted by scripture (*āgama*), because the scriptural testimony regarding self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*)—which is required by the principal statements that possess fruit—is more powerful.

Furthermore, for a partless self, there can be no quality of non-eternal cognition arising from conjunction with the mind; nor can there be knowability through a cognition inherent in itself due to the absence of inherence (*samavāya*); and finally, there is the contradiction between the status of being an object and that of being an agent.

Furthermore, since the property of being knowledge (jñānatva) resides in only one [entity], it is simpler (lāghava) to hold that the self alone is knowledge; and because the Vedic scripture stating "Desire, resolve... and so forth declares that mental modification (vṛtti) is a transformation of the mind, it is insentient. Thus, for us, there is no burden of having to accept a duality of knowledge.
Therefore, it is established that the self's self-luminosity (svaprakāśatva) is beyond reproach. //18//
[The soul is atomic] because of its departure, movement, and return. (2.3.19)

Because it is self-luminous, [the author] examines size (*parimāṇa*)—which is only slightly external to the nature of the Self—as being either the locus and the located, or as having an internal and external relationship; he then demonstrates the subject matter and the doubt regarding "passing out, going, and returning":
*utkrāntigatyāgatīnām* // [2.3.19] He shows the subject matter and the doubt: [text continues...]
Regarding the word "now":

having raised the objection that the meaning of this [present] section has already been covered by the passage beginning with "Not so, because of the scriptural statement that the Self is not [of limited size]," he states "But surely... and so forth, in order to explain the lack of contradiction between the scriptural texts concerning the atomicity of the Self and those concerning its magnitude.

Not only is the atomicity of the self established through the logical inconsistency of [scriptural] statements regarding its departure and so forth, but it is also established by the scriptural text, "This self is atomic";
thus he says, "by its own word.
In the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), because the individual soul (jīva) is atomic, its identity with Brahman cannot be established.
Considering that its establishment occurs in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), he states the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) while explaining the aphorism,
beginning with "In that regard, it is obtained," and so forth.
The phrase "the atom [is established] from scripture" (*śruter aṇuḥ*) has been supplied by drawing it forward from the subsequent aphorism.
The word "departure" (utkrānti) is to be understood as the remainder of the sentence.

The meaning is that the soul (jīva), being on the verge of death, returns from that world such as the world of the moon to this world along with these [factors] beginning with the intellect (buddhi) in order to perform karma. //19//
And by means of its own self, it [is the cause] of the two subsequent ones. (BBs 2.3.20)
Some maintain that the "departure" (utkrānti) of the self from the body does not mean its actual exit, which would imply atomicity, but rather the cessation of its lordship over it;
yet, even while accepting that [interpretation], he states that atomicity is nonetheless necessary:
"by its own self," etc.
