The construction of the sūtra is as follows: because of the connection with the agent as its own self in the subsequent [processes] of departure, going, and returning, [the soul] is atomic.

To the objection—"Why should there not be a statement of 'going' even for that which is not the substratum of going, just as there is a statement of 'cooking' for that which is not the substratum of cooking?"—he says:
"Of going... (gamer).
The meaning is that it is established by common experience that motion resides in its agent, because the agent is the cause of the excellence consisting of conjunction and disjunction.
He states— “not of intermediate size”— that the individual soul (jīva) is atomic, because, while not being of intermediate size, it possesses motion, like an atom.
He abandons his own position with the words "and of two real [entities]";
the meaning is that departure is not merely the cessation of ownership.
Regarding the point that "departure" (utkrānti) is indeed the exit from the body, he states another indicative mark:
"of the parts of the body. Here, "apādānatva" means the state of being a limit or point of departure.

Or rather, the ellipsis is that this self departs through other openings such as the mouth; furthermore, he states that the self is atomic because of the scriptural teaching regarding the movement and return of the living being even within the body—beginning with "He... [referring to the passage *sa etasmāj jīvaghanāt*].

The meaning is that at the time of sleep and so forth, that living self (jīva), taking the sense organs, goes to the heart; then, taking the luminous semen (śukra) and the entire collection of sense organs, it returns again to the state of waking. //20//
"If it be argued that [the soul] is not atomic because of scriptural testimony, we say no, because of the context of the other. (BS 2.3.21)

Because of the context of the other [deities] and because of the section concerning Brahman. Now, one might ask: "Given the scriptural mention of greatness, how can this belong to the section concerning the Supreme (Brahman)? To this, he says:

Regarding the phrase "of another": since it is a general rule that whatever Vedic scripture (vedānta-śruti) exists is situated within a section concerning another [subject], he states— by the words "viraja" (dustless)— that this [scripture] is situated therein because it is taught beginning with Brahman.
The meaning is "instruction.
He raises an objection— beginning with "But surely"— that the context [of the Upanishad] is set aside by the scriptural statement consisting of the word "consisting of consciousness" (*vijñānamaya*).

He states that there is no contradiction—by saying "śāstra... (scriptural)—because, while the difference between the minute individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman is admitted, its greatness is spoken of from the perspective of the scriptural vision of non-difference; just as Vāmadeva’s statement "I am Manu" expresses his identity with the Self of all.
And [the soul is not of atomic size] because of its own word and because of its measurement. (BS 2.3.22)
Thus, the atomicity [of the soul] has been inferred from such scriptural passages as those concerning its departure [from the body];
in this regard, he also cites scripture itself with the words "by its own word" (*svaśabda*).

"The individual soul (jīva) is a hundredth part of a hair-tip extracted [from its whole], and from that, again, a hundredth part is extracted"— the meaning is that "extracted measure" (uddhṛtya-māna) refers to extreme minuteness. "Bāla" means a hair.
The tip of an iron pin fixed upon a wooden stick is like the tip of an awl; that living being whose measure is extracted from that [measure] is likewise [measured]. //22//
There is no contradiction, as in the case of sandalwood. (BBs 2.3.23)

However, because of the greatness of the skin—which is conjoined with the self and serves as the instrument for perceiving touch pervading the entire body—it is not contradictory that the self performs its pervasive function.
Regarding the phrase "of the skin and the self":

since the connection resides in the composite whole (the body) and the composite whole is a single entity, the meaning is that the conjunction with the self resides in the entirety of the skin. //23//
If it is argued that [the soul's size] varies according to its state of residence, we say no, because this is accepted; for [the soul resides] in the heart. (BBs 2.3.24)

Regarding the phrase "siddhe hi": the meaning is that there is no parity [between the two cases], because it is already established (*siddha*). *Vaiśeṣya* (the state of being specific) is simply *viśeṣa* (specificity).
Since the smallness of a drop of sandalwood paste is perceived through direct perception, it is reasonable to postulate that it performs a pervasive effect by pervading the skin;
however, since there is doubt regarding the atomicity of the individual soul (jīva), it is more reasonable to postulate its pervasiveness based on the observation of its pervasive effects.

This is because of the general rule (utsarga) that "that which is the substratum of pervasive effects is itself pervasive"—this is the meaning of the portion of the Sūtra representing the prima facie argument (pūrva-pakṣa).

The inference that "the self is minute because it performs pervasive actions, like a drop of sandalwood paste," is incorrect, as it is subject to deviation (vyabhicāra) in the case of the skin and so forth; thus he says:
"And there is no inference here.

To provide the portion of the refutation—meaning that because the atomicity of the individual soul (*jīva*) has been ascertained by the previously cited scriptural texts, and its location in the heart has been ascertained by the texts concerning its abiding in the heart, there is no disparity with the illustrative example—he says: "To this it is replied. (24)
Or rather, [the designation is] due to a quality, as in the world. (BS 2.3.25)

Having stated that, like the self, the knowledge of its attributes is also inherently atomic, whereas its occasional possession of the dimensions of the body is due to external factors, he states another view— that it is inherently all-pervasive—
with the words "or from its qualities" (guṇāt vā).
By the word "or" (vā), the non-inclusion of the sandalwood example is indicated; he states that [example] as follows: "It may be... (syāt) //25//
The distinction [of the self from the body] is like that of fragrance; this is the twenty-sixth [aphorism].
He raises an objection regarding what is to be excluded by the subsequent sūtra, asking: "How so?
Knowledge does not pervade a location distinct from that of its possessor.

"Because it is a quality (*guṇa*), like color (*rūpa*); and there is no deviation [from the rule] in the case of light (*prabhā*), since that too is a substance (*dravya*). To this, he states the deviation in the case of odor (*gandha*):
"Beyond this" means that the separation of a quality from the substance is its dissociation from its substratum.
Now, one might object that because the separated parts are so minute, the destruction of the substance does not appear; therefore, he says:
"Even though it is not being diminished":
the word "even" (api) is used for emphasis; the meaning is that by means of the mark of its previous state, that substance is inferred to be indeed not diminishing.
[The subject] under dispute is that whose parts are not disjoined.
The meaning is that it is like a commonly accepted [object], because it lacks the diminution of weight and so forth from its previous state.
He raises an objection:
Regarding the phrase "it might be so": the statement "because the separated parts are small" is an illustration; it should also be understood as referring to the entry of other constituent parts.

The meaning of the objection is that although the specific modification of the parts—consisting of their separation and entry—is present, it is not perceived; thus, because there is no decrease in weight, the reason [for the absence of increase] is otherwise established (*anyathāsiddhi*).
The parts that arrive are either atoms (*paramāṇu*) or triads (*trasareṇu*).
Not the first [alternative],
because it would follow that the odor residing in that [substance] would likewise not be perceived; thus he refutes it with "No."
He states the second [objection]:
"clearly" (*sphuṭa*).
The meaning is that if the fragrance of the motes of light (*trasareṇu*) were not clear, [the following would hold].
Therefore, the intention is that one must state the separation of the quality from the odor itself as it exists in flowers and so forth.
He raises an objection: "Odor is not separated from its substratum (the possessor of qualities), because it is a quality, just like color."
He says "no" [to the objection] that there is a sublation [of the inference] because the separation [of the soul from the body] is perceptible. //26//
And thus it shows: BBs_2,3.27.
Regarding the fact that the pervasion of the body by the Self occurs precisely through its quality of consciousness, the author of the Sūtras cites scripture:
"And thus it shows.
He explains this as follows:
"Regarding the heart," [it is said]. //27//
Because they are taught separately. (BS 2.3.28)
Regarding that very point, there is a sūtra intended to explain another scriptural passage:
"separately" (pṛthak).
The meaning is that [the self] sleeps having taken up the power of cognition—the capacity for knowledge—of the senses by means of consciousness, which is the attribute of sentience.
And this refers to the intention whose scope is the pervasion of the quality of consciousness. //28//
But that designation [of the Self] is due to its having those qualities as its essence, just as in the case of the Wise One (the individual soul). 2,3.29.

In this context, since the scriptural texts regarding the atomicity and omnipresence of the self appear contradictory and thus face the prospect of invalidity, the position of certain partial scholars (ekadeśins)— namely, that there is no contradiction because the individual soul (jīva) is atomic while the Lord (īśvara) is omnipresent— is presented. Refuting that, he explains the sūtra of the established conclusion (siddhānta-sūtra) with the words beginning "the word 'but' (tu)," and so forth.

Therefore, because it is non-different from Brahman, the individual soul (jīva) is all-pervading like Brahman; this is stated in Śruti and Smṛti supported by the inference: "And so, he indeed is this...
and such Smārta declarations as "He is eternal, all-pervading, and stable."

By this, the objection that there is a circular argument—namely, that the knowledge of the non-atomicity of the individual soul (jīva) depends on the knowledge of its non-difference from Brahman, while that knowledge of non-difference depends on the knowledge of its non-atomicity—is refuted.

The point is as follows: once the non-atomicity [of the soul] has been ascertained through Śruti and Smṛti passages consistent with the primary Great Sentences (mahāvākya), the knowledge of non-difference arises; thus, when there is a conflict with the primary sentences, the subordinate Śruti passages concerning atomicity are interpreted as referring to an atomicity conditioned by limiting adjuncts (aupādhika-aṇutva), in accordance with the maxim: "But when there is a conflict with the principal, an improper assumption must be made regarding the subordinate."

Furthermore, since the experience of coolness pervading the entire body cannot otherwise be accounted for, the scriptural texts concerning atomicity must somehow be interpreted as mere explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) referring to a superimposed atomicity;
for even by worldly logic, those [scriptures] are weaker. With this in mind, he says:
"Nor [is there an experience of coolness] for one who is atomic."
He raises an objection with the word "skin" (*tvak*).

He refutes it by pointing out the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*): if sensation were to pervade the entire body through the skin because of its connection with the atomic self (*aṇvātman*), then this would lead to an absurd consequence.
"No," he says,
rejecting the notion that this undesirable consequence is acceptable:
"only on the sole of the foot."
Therefore, the conjunction of the small and the large does not pervade the large [object],
because we do not observe the conjunction with a thorn to pervade the entire body;
likewise, since the conjunction of the atomic self resides only in one part of the skin, the experience of sensation pervading the entire body would be impossible.

Nor should it be argued that, according to our established doctrine (*siddhānta*), because the connection between the skin and the self (*ātman*) is all-pervasive, there would follow the consequence of pain pervading the entire body upon contact with a thorn; for there is a restrictive rule (*niyama*) that the connection of the self extends only as far as the portion of the skin connected to the object, and that this much-extending connection is the cause of the pain. Nor should it be argued that, in such a case, the mere connection between the object and the skin should be the cause of that pain, rendering the pervasion of the self unnecessary.
For feeling consists of pleasure, pain, and their experience;
and it is not possible for these pervasive effects to have a limited substrate, because it is logically untenable for an effect to be separated from its substrate.
Nor is their pervasiveness unestablished.
Because it is impossible to deny that one who is heated by the sun and immersed in the Gaṅgā simultaneously experiences a pleasure and a pain pervading all their limbs;
as for what was said— that even a quality can be separated from its possessor, like fragrance— that is not so, he says:
And [it is] not [the case that] "of the atom":
odor is not separated from its substrate,
because it is a quality (*guṇatvāt*).
Regarding the phrase "like form," he cites scripture, saying:
"And so it has been said.
Nor is there any sublation by perception.

The point is this: although the odor is perceptible, its lack of a substrate is not; therefore, the clear perception of the odor occurs due to the arrival of large *trasareṇu* particles whose touch is unmanifest (*anudbhūta*) but whose odor is manifest (*udbhūta*).
Because other constituent parts enter [the substance], there is no sudden depletion of the original substance.
Previously, having accepted that consciousness is a quality (*guṇa*), the atomicity of the self—the possessor of that quality (*guṇin*)—was refuted by means of its pervasiveness.
He states that its quality-status is currently unestablished: "And if consciousness...

Having established all-pervasiveness (*vibhutva*) independently of the Sūtra, he explains the Sūtra in order to demonstrate the movement [of the soul] despite the arguments for its atomicity (*aṇutva*).
By the words "How so? and so forth:

in the statement "For consciousness and the mind are within the heart," it is the intellect (*buddhi*) under discussion that is referred to by the pronoun "that" (*tat*), because it is the appropriate referent.
The description of [the self] as atomic and so forth is due to the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of the qualities of the intellect upon the self, not by its own nature.
He states "and likewise" because [the doctrine of atomicity] contradicts the scriptural teaching of infinity (*ānantya*).

The meaning is that, since the sentence "That thou art" has as its object an indivisible non-difference— just like the sentence "This is that"— by virtue of its grammatical coreferentiality with a substance that is neither effect nor cause, infinity is real while atomicity is merely superimposed.

And this has been stated in the *Aṅguṣṭhādhikaraṇa*: "A qualification pertaining to the subject (uddeśya) that is contradictory to what is to be established (pratipādya) is not intended to be significant. Two measures have been mentioned: the measure by the tip of a hair and the measure by the tip of a tawny insect. Having rejected the first, he rejects the second:
The same applies to the other case as well.

By means of the quality of the intellect (*buddhi*) acting as a cause, a quality is superimposed upon the Self; it is by means of that very superimposed quality of the Self that the individual soul (*jīva*) is perceived as having the size of the tip of an awl and as being limited. However, in its own nature, it is indeed infinite.
Thus [it is said]: "It is not grasped by the eye, nor by speech, nor by the other senses, nor by austerity, nor by ritual action."

Having stated, "Then, with his being purified by the clarity of knowledge, he, meditating, beholds Him who is partless," and having said, "This subtle Self," [the author] explains that even if [this] refers to the individual soul (jīva), the meaning of the word "subtle" is merely the superimposed state of subtlety; thus he says:
"Of the individual soul as well..."

Regarding what was stated— that the self pervades the body solely by means of the quality of consciousness (caitanya) due to its being taught separately— he replies with the words "so too by means of prajñā.
Here, *prajñā* means the intellect (*buddhi*).
If consciousness (caitanya) is wisdom (prajñā), then the distinction between them is merely figurative; thus he says:
"or it is a mere designation.
Now, one might argue that since consciousness is a quality (guṇa), the distinction should be primary; to this he replies: "No."
"For it is not here" means because of the scriptural teaching that [the Self] is devoid of qualities (nirguṇa).
He further states that other things previously mentioned, such as the intellect (buddhi) and so forth, are merely limiting adjuncts (upādhi):
With the words "hṛdaya" and so forth,
he explains the example from the Sūtra,
beginning with "yathā" (just as).
"Non-existence" is stated from a superficial perspective;
"the state of not being subject to saṃsāra" is what is to be established.
The remainder is easily understood. //29//
And because it is co-existent with the self, there is no fault in perceiving it. (BBs 2.3.30)
Now, one might object: "Let transmigratory existence (saṃsāritva) belong to [the Self] by itself; what is the use of the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of the intellect (buddhi)?
To this he says: "And as long as this...
Being identical with the intellect (buddhi-tādātmyāpanna), it is "cognition" (vijñāna); that is to say, it is a modification (vikāra) consisting of Brahman, [appearing as] an atom (aṇu).
To the question "Why might this not be so?", he says: "In another place.
This means that [the self] consists of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*), that is, it abounds in intellect (*buddhi*).
The phrase "with what [is it equal]? is the required supplement to the question.
Based on the authority of the scripture (*śruti*), it has been stated that the intellect (*buddhi*) persists as long as the transmigrating self exists;
and he states this also by means of reasoning (*yukti*), because as long as the root exists, the separation of the effect is impossible.
Furthermore, regarding the word "falsely" (*mithyā*):
in order to show that the destruction of the bondage of the intellect and so forth occurs through right knowledge alone, he cites scripture with the words "it shows."
The grammatical connection is that [the wise person] transcends death. "Having the color of the sun" means self-luminous;
"beyond darkness" means untouched by ignorance—this is the meaning. //30//
But [the self] exists even before [manifestation], because its manifestation occurs like that of masculinity and so forth. (BBs 2.3.31)
He raises the objection regarding the non-establishment of [the self] being "constantly present" with the words "nanu" (but surely):
in deep sleep, there would be no merging with Brahman if the intellect (*buddhisattva*) were still present.
The meaning is that if it [the intellect] were to exist during the dissolution (pralaya), there would be a contradiction of the dissolution itself.
He states "puṃstva... [and so on], indicating that the intellect exists as long as the self does, in both its gross and subtle forms.
Masculinity refers to semen;
by the word "etcetera," the beard and so forth are included.
The meaning is: of this connection with the intellect.
Regarding the point that during deep sleep the intellect and other faculties exist in the form of seeds and are manifested upon awakening, he cites scripture,
saying "it shows.
The phrase "they do not know" indicates the existence of the seed whose nature is ignorance (*avidyā*).
The statement regarding manifestation is that those tigers and other animals appear once again. //31//
Otherwise, there would follow the consequence of either eternal perception or eternal non-perception, or else the necessity of one or the other being restricted.
The author of the Sūtras states the proof for the existence of the intellect (buddhi) with the word "eternal" (*nitya*):
"For it is by the mind alone that one sees."
"And the intellect does not act," "Consciousness performs the sacrifice," and "He is to be known by the mind."

The meaning is that in various scriptural passages, such as "the mind and the object of volition," the substance of the intellect (buddhi) is well known to be denoted by terms such as "mind" (manas) and so forth.
To the question of how one thing can be spoken of in multiple ways, he says: "In some places... and so on.

Egoism (*ahaṅkāra*) is characterized by pride; consciousness (*vijñāna*) should also be understood as *citta*, which is primarily characterized by thought or primarily characterized by memory. Although the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is established through the perception of a witness and is also mentioned in scripture, nevertheless, for one who disputes both perception and scripture, he establishes it through the impossibility of simultaneous attention (*vyāsaṅga*), beginning with the words "And that... (*tac ca*).
He applies the Sūtra with the words "otherwise":
if there were a connection between the five sense-faculties and the five objects, there would necessarily be simultaneous perceptions of all five at once.
This is because the causal complex (sāmagrī) is present even when the mind is absent.
The meaning is that if there were no perception despite the presence of the causal complex, then it would follow that there is never any perception at all.
Therefore, the implication is that one must accept the mind as the factor that determines the occasional nature of perception.

One might object: "Even when there is contact with fire, just as burning occurs only occasionally, let the occasional nature of perception also be so; what need is there for the mind? Anticipating this, he explains the phrase "or else there would be a restriction to one of the two" with the words "Or rather" (*athavā*). When the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is present, either constant perception must be admitted, or else a restriction—consisting in the obstruction of the power of one of the causes by something—must be admitted.

The meaning of the word "yathā" (just as) is that the power of fire is obstructed by a gem; [the opponent] might say, "Let there be such an obstruction," to which [the author] replies, "And not... (na ca).
Nor should it be argued that the obstruction of power belongs to the sense organ itself,

because there is no obstructing factor present. Furthermore, it is not logical to claim that the unseen (adṛṣṭa) acts as an obstructer when the visible causal complex is complete, for that would lead to an over-extension of the principle.
Nor can there be distraction (*vyāsaṅga*), because such distraction is impossible in the absence of a mental obstruction (*pratibandhaka-manas*).

For instance, when the simultaneous perception of taste and other qualities would otherwise occur, one must posit that distraction in the form of a desire to perceive taste (*rasa-bubhutsā*) is what obstructs the perception of color and so forth.
And since it is a quality, like color, it must have a substratum that possesses qualities (guṇin).

In this regard, because the Self—which is unattached, devoid of qualities, and immutable—cannot logically be the possessor of qualities, the mind alone must be accepted as the possessor of qualities; thus, the existence of the mind is established through the impossibility of [the Self] being distracted.
Having this in mind, he concludes:
Regarding the phrase "therefore":
"attention" (avadhāna) means the desire to know (bubhutsā).
Nor should it be argued that the desire to know is not the determining factor for perception, because one perceives foul odors and the like even without desiring to do so.
This is because it is accepted that, despite the presence of many objects, the mind acts as a restrictive factor for [the arising of cognition] in only one instance.

Furthermore, according to their view, desire and the like are attributes of the self; thus, it should be understood that for them, the mind is difficult to obtain [as a separate entity], since distraction is possible through the self itself, which possesses desire and other such qualities.
Now, he cites scripture to show that distraction is mental in nature—
namely, "And so it is.
Not only is the existence of the mind established through the fact of distraction, [but also by scripture].
But he says "and desire, etc. to show that [the self] is also the substratum of desire and so forth.
He states the result of declaring the intellect to be authoritative:
Therefore, [it is not so]. //32//
The Self is an agent, because the scriptures would otherwise be purposeless. (BS 2.3.33)

Thus, by stating the superimposition of atomicity upon the Self, its natural greatness has been established. Now, he proves agency, which resides outside of that [atomicity]: "The Self is an agent, because the scriptures would otherwise be purposeless."

Regarding the doubt arising from the conflict between the scriptural texts on non-attachment—which state that the Great Self is eternally of the nature of consciousness and not an agent—and the scriptural texts on injunctions and the like, which imply agency;

and regarding the attainment of the Sāṃkhya position that the Self is a non-agent because the injunctions and other scriptures are justified by the agency of the intellect alone—the author sets forth the final conclusion (*siddhānta*).

Fearing the charge of tautology—since the superimposition of agency upon the Self is already established by the statement that the Self has the quality of intelligence as its essence—he proceeds as follows:
He says "tadguṇa... [and so forth] to show that there is no tautology, because this is an elaboration of the superimposition of agency upon the Self for the purpose of refuting the Sāṃkhya position;
"adhikāra" here means the context or occasion.
In reality, [the Self] is unattached;

since it has been stated that there is no contradiction between the scriptural texts concerning non-attachment and agency—on the grounds that agency arises from ignorance—the three sections consisting of the inquiry into agency are connected to this chapter (pāda).
The mutual contradiction or non-contradiction of these scriptural texts constitutes the result of the prima facie (pūrva-pakṣa) and the final (uttara-pakṣa) positions.

Alternatively, the distinction here is that in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the fruit [of the argument] is the futility of the scripture due to the absence of bondage, whereas in the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), the scripture is purposeful because of the existence of the connection with agency and so forth.
To the objection—"Let the purposefulness of the scripture be established through the agency of the intellect (*buddhi*); what is the use of the agency of the individual soul (*jīva*)?"—he says:

"For that [action] belongs to one who exists as an agent" means that agency must be predicated of a conscious being alone—one capable of the cognition "this is to be done by me"—and not of the unconscious intellect (buddhi).
Furthermore, the sense is that agency must be predicated of the Self alone, who is the enjoyer, according to the maxim: "The fruit of the scripture belongs to the performer. //33//
Because of the instruction regarding the distribution [of the fires]. (BS 2.3.34)
Dream is an intermediate state.
That Self is immortal because it is taught that it moves or goes according to its desire; thus, the Self is the agent. //34//
Because of appropriation. (BBs 2.3.35)

Among the vital breaths (*prāṇas*), having taken up the collection of sense organs capable of cognition by means of consciousness (*vijñāna*) and the intellect (*buddhi*), it lies down; thus, "having grasped the vital breaths, it turns about. The meaning is that the self possesses the agency of appropriation (*upādāna-kartṛtva*), because appropriation would be impossible in the absence of agency. //35//
And because of the designation [of the agent] in the action, [the self exists], provided there is no reversal of the grammatical indication. (BBs 2.3.36)
If the word *vijñāna* were not a designation for the living self (*jīva*), then there would be a contradiction with its designation in the nominative case;
[otherwise], it would have been designated with the instrumental case, which indicates an instrument.

Therefore, since in this scriptural passage the word *vijñāna* is used in grammatical apposition with the verb *tanute* (he extends), which denotes the agent, the meaning of the Sūtra and the Bhāṣya is that the agency of the Self in the action is indicated.
As in the case of perception, there is no fixed rule. (BBs 2.3.37)
He introduces another sutra with the words, "Regarding this, it is said":
"If the living being (jīva) were independent, he would do only what is desired; if he were not independent, he would not be an agent."
The meaning is that this follows from the maxim "the agent is independent" (*svatantraḥ kartā*).
Even though independence exists, activity is not restricted due to the diversity of causal factors (*kāraka*); he refutes this with the sūtra beginning with "just as" (*yathā*).
He raises an objection due to a lack of agreement regarding the illustrative example: "Even in the case of perception...

[The author] states that the illustrative example is established because the eyes and other sense organs exist for the purpose of connecting with objects through consciousness, whereas the Self, being of the nature of consciousness, possesses independence in the perception of its own connection.
"No.
[The author] says "Moreover" (apica) to address the doubt: "If the self indeed requires the instruments for the sake of connection with objects, how can it be independent?"

Independence (*svātantrya*) does not mean being independent of anything other than itself, for that would entail the consequence that even God lacks independence since He depends upon the karma of living beings.

Rather, independence is the state of not being impelled by other causal factors (*kāraka*), while simultaneously being the instigator of those other causal factors; by this [definition], He is independent.

The meaning is that even though the soul performs what is not a means to the desired [end] due to the error that it is a means to the desired, its activity remains non-determined and its autonomy is not contradicted. //37//
Because of the reversal of capacity. (BBs 2.3.38)
To provide another reason for the soul's status as an agent, the Sūtra states:
"Because of power" (śakti).
The meaning is that the soul must possess an agentive power that is the opposite of the instrumental power belonging to the intellect.
What follows from that? To this he says:
"And when there is the cognition...
[referring to] that which is apprehended by the notion of "I."

He alone is the agent, and he alone is the individual soul (jīva); that which is required as an instrument for him is the mind (manas). Thus, the meaning is that the agency of the individual soul is established. //38//
And because of the absence of meditative absorption (samādhi). (BBs 2.3.39)
He states that the self's agency must also be asserted because otherwise the injunction for the means of knowledge would be inexplicable—
namely, "samādhau" etc.
It is logical that only one who is the enjoyer of the fruit of liberation should be the agent of the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) which is its means.

Otherwise, if the Self were not the agent, then since the intellect—which is not the enjoyer—could not be the agent either, it would follow that meditative absorption (samādhi) is impossible; this is the meaning. //39//
And just as a carpenter acts in both ways. (BBs 2.3.40)
And just as in the case of the carpenter, who acts in both ways;
having relied upon the previously stated agency of the self, he states the doubt and the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) with the words beginning "In this way, for now," and so forth.

Once the agency of the self has been established by refuting the Sāṃkhya position, the view of the Mīmāṃsakas and others—that this [agency] is real because there is no sublation—is reached. Nor can there be sublation by the scripture concerning non-attachment (*asaṅgatva*), because that scripture serves as a mere praise (*stāvaka*) due to the force of the scriptural statement on agency accompanied by the experience "I am the agent. Having thus reached this preliminary conclusion, he establishes the final Siddhānta, even though it deviates from the literal wording of the Sūtra:

Regarding the statement "it is not intrinsic," he says "anirmokṣa" (there would be no liberation) to show that the previously mentioned argument— "because there is no subverting proof"— is unestablished.

One might object: "Surely, agency is indeed the power of action, and this exists even in liberation; nevertheless, because the effect of that power—the capacity in the form of action—is absent, the status of liberation as the supreme human goal (puruṣārtha) is established. To this, he raises the objection with the words: "nanu sthitāyām" ("Surely, while [the power] remains..."). He then answers the question of how there can be an avoidance of the effect when the power exists: "satyāṃ śaktau kathaṃ kāryaparihāraḥ" ("While the power exists, how can there be an avoidance of the effect?"). To that, he says:
And this is the refutation of that [objection]:
if power (śakti) exists in liberation, then the effect would also exist, because power is impossible in the absence of the capable object (śakya).
For even during the dissolution (pralaya), there exists a subtle effect capable of re-emerging;

thus, he offers a rebuttal— stating "not even of the instrumental causes"— by arguing that because the effect is projected together with its instrumental causes such as merit (dharma) and so forth, liberation would be impossible.
Since an effect possessing a cause is possible, it should be understood that the causes themselves are also connected to power (śakti) through a mediated succession;
the meaning is "by means of that which is connected [to the effect] via its connection.

Alternatively, the third case is used with different grammatical referents (*vyadhikaraṇa*): "by that effect for which power is the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) or the implied factor (*ākṣepaka*), and by means of the connection with that effect."

One might object: "Is it not the case that, by the power of the scriptures, just as a human attains divinity through action, the non-agency of the agent is established? Thus he raises the doubt with the word 'nanu'.

[The reply is: From knowledge comes liberation, which is called non-agency; therefore, one should understand that agency is merely due to ignorance (avidyā), since knowledge is the remover of ignorance alone.
If liberation were [attained] through action, he says "no" to that; for it has been stated that there would be no liberation if one were to accept the agency of the Self as being innate.
Now, [the author] states "Moreover" (*apica*) to show that [the nature of Brahman as being] free from attachment and change is not inherent, because it contradicts numerous scriptural passages.
Nor is it reasonable to assume that numerous well-established scriptural passages are merely commendatory (*stāvaka*).
Nor is the experience "I am not the agent" contradicted;
the meaning is that this [experience] is accounted for as an *adhyāsa* (superimposition), since it apprehends an agency that is indifferent to both the real and the false.
He cites scripture regarding the superimposed nature of agency:
And likewise:
he states that agency is sublated by the experience of the wise, saying "for not... etc.

He raises an objection: "If there were no conscious being distinct from the aggregate of intellect and so forth and different from the Supreme, then the Supreme itself would result in being the transmigrating soul; and that is undesirable, because it would contradict the eternally liberated nature of the Supreme."
"Only the Supreme.
We do not say that there is bondage for the Supreme, the pure element of consciousness;

rather, we say that bondage and liberation belong to that very same [consciousness] when it has attained the state of a *jīva*—having become differentiated by ignorance (*avidyā*) through being reflected in the intellect (*buddhi*) and other faculties due to ignorance.
He offers a rebuttal, noting that even in the world, a conceptual distinction is seen to establish the properties between an object and its reflection—
this is expressed by the words "not [due to] ignorance" (nāvidyā).
He cites scripture regarding the point that bondage, conditioned by ignorance, does not belong to the pure Self:
And likewise:

since agency conforms to the presence and absence of the limiting adjunct (upādhi) that is the intellect (buddhi), and because of scriptural testimony, it is not inherent; thus he says, "Similarly in dream... and so forth.
The Self alone is desired because it is bliss; thus its essential nature is "one whose desire is the Self. Because there is no object of desire other than itself, it is "desireless" (akāma).
Because its desire is the Self and because it is desireless, it is "one whose desires are fulfilled" (āptakāma) and "free from sorrow" (viśoka); thus he says: "from sorrow... [and so forth].
The meaning is that it is beyond sorrow and untouched by suffering.
He states that this very nature of the self in deep sleep constitutes the supreme human goal:
"This... [is that].

The meaning is that there exists nowhere else than this the goal (gati), that which is to be attained (prāpya), the perfection of sovereignty (saṃpad-aiśvarya), the world (loka), the object of experience (bhogya), or happiness (sukha).

It has been stated that the Self is non-agent by its own nature, but is an agent through the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as the intellect (buddhi); thus, it exists in both ways. He applies the Sūtra to that point, beginning with the words "He says this" and so forth.
"Samprasāda" refers to deep sleep.

Just as the redness of a crystal is caused by an external adjunct such as a flower, so too the agency of the Self is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) to be caused by adjuncts such as the intellect (*buddhi*).

Nor is it reasonable to claim that those two [concomitances] refer to the intellect's status as an instrument (*karaṇa*) rather than its status as the material cause (*upādāna*) for the Self's agency.

The point is this: because the status of being an instrument (*karaṇatva*) is subordinate to the status of being the material cause (*upādānatva*) which is connected to the effect, it is established that the intellect (*buddhi*), when conjoined with consciousness (*cit*), is indeed the material cause in both respects. Likewise, there is the agreement of the Great Sayings (*mahāvākya*) regarding the agency and material causality of the ego (*ahaṅkāra*), which is called the intellect and is superimposed non-differently from consciousness. Now, one might object that there is a disparity between the illustration and the subject: a carpenter is an agent by himself because he possesses the power to manipulate tools such as axes with his own hands and so forth; however, the Self (*ātman*) is incapable of such action because it is partless. Anticipating this objection, [the author] addresses it through the aspect of agency conditioned by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).
And there is the example of the carpenter.
To the objection—“Why should agency, as restated by the scripture, not be inherent?”—he says:
“Nor is it inherent.”
He raises the objection that agency is indeed intrinsic during the state when there is no [external] instrument, saying:
"But [it exists] in the intermediate state" (*nanu saṃdhye*).

Furthermore, if agency belongs to that which is qualified by instruments, then since those instruments would be included within the agent, the case-ending for the agent (*kartṛvibhakti*) would have to apply to them as well.
And this is not the case; therefore, he says "likewise" (tathā) to show that agency does not belong to the isolated self alone.
First, regarding the state of sporting in a dream, he says that the absence of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) is unestablished.
"It is not, first of all, a junction" means that because the dwelling (*vihāra*) is false, its agency as well is false;
thus he says: "The dwelling, too."
"Jakṣat" means "as if eating.

It has been stated that if the ear were the agent characterized by the act of hearing, then the agentive case-ending (*kartṛvibhakti*) would apply to the sense organs rather than the instrumental case-ending (*karaṇavibhakti*); to this, he replies:
And since the world exists,
the use of the instrumental case for the agents is not contradictory, as it is observed [in usage];
furthermore, there is indeed the application of the term "agency" [to them].
The intention is as expressed in such passages as "Consciousness performs the sacrifice.
Having accepted that the material cause possesses an agent, the agency of the isolated Self alone was refuted.
Now, he states that because that [Self] is inactive, it has no need for an agent:
Moreover:
previously, having accepted that consciousness (*vijñāna*) is the living self (*jīva*), the scriptural statement "he stretches out" was cited regarding the agency of the self;

now, since it might be concluded from that scripture that the unconditioned Self possesses agency, [the author] states that consciousness is indeed the intellect (*buddhi*), and it is of that [intellect] alone that agency is here predicated.
Intending to establish the agency of the self as conditioned by that [intellect], he says:
"But he who...

Since the word *vijñāna* is well-known in Vedic texts such as "this one consisting of consciousness" (*vijñānamaya*) to refer to the intellect (*buddhi*), and because it is mentioned here immediately after the sheath consisting of mind (*manomaya-kośa*) and is characterized by faith and other qualities, it is indeed the intellect.
The meaning is "consciousness.
Regarding that very point, he states another indicative mark: "Consciousness, the gods... etc.

In the Śruti passage beginning with "The great Yakṣa, the first-born," it is stated that the intellect (buddhi), whose essence is Brahmā Hiraṇyagarbha, is the eldest; therefore, the meaning here is that the "eldest" Brahman being worshipped by the gods—that is, the senses—is indeed the intellect (vijñāna). "Yakṣa" means that which is worthy of worship.

Furthermore, since another Vedic scripture states that sacrifice is an effect of the intellect (*buddhi*), he says "This very [sacrifice]" to show that here too, the knowledge of the performer of the sacrifice is the intellect.

Having meditated with the mind (*citta*) and uttered the mantras with speech (*vāk*), the sacrifice is born; therefore, the meaning is that the sacrifice is the prior and subsequent sequence of the mind and speech.
As for what was said— that if the intellect were the agent, it would follow that its capacities are reversed— that is not so;
for rice grains do not soften by themselves, nor do pieces of wood burn by themselves.
He says "nor" (na ca) because all the factors of action (kārakas), such as the pot, assume the status of being the agent (kartṛtva) in their respective functions.
To the objection that if the intellect and so forth were the agents, there could be no talk of them being instruments (karaṇa), he says:
Regarding the term "perception" (*upalabdhi*):

just as wood, although it is the agent (*kartṛ*) in its own operation, serves as the instrument (*karaṇa*) with respect to the act of cooking, so too the intellect (*buddhi*) and the rest, although they are the agents of actions such as determination (*adhyavasāya*) and volition (*saṃkalpa*), serve as instruments with respect to perception—this is the meaning.
Now, one might ask: "To whom then does the operation of perception belong? To this he says:
And as for the phrase "that [soul]":
in that case, the soul alone would be the agent in that [state], because of the established principle that "he who possesses an activity is the agent of that. To this, he says:
Regarding the word "not" (*na ca*):

if it is asked how the instruments such as the intellect (*buddhi*) can be said to possess instrumentality if perception (*upalabdhi*) is eternal, the answer is as follows: the indivisible witness-consciousness (*sākṣicaitanya*), becoming differentiated by the modifications of the intellect (*buddhivṛtti*), arises as delimited by objects.

Thus, the intellect and other factors possess instrumentality with respect to perception—which is called consciousness delimited by objects—while agency belongs to the Self as conditioned by the intellect and so forth, not to the Self alone.
The point is that agency cannot belong to the intellect alone, because consciousness cannot logically engage in an insentient operation.

Furthermore, regarding the claim that if the intellect were the agent, it would follow that the individual soul (*jīva*)—which is the object of the notion "I"—must have some other instrument, and thus the dispute is merely over a name: he dispels the misconception that agency was attributed to the isolated Self alone by stating:

Regarding the term *ahaṅkāra*: in order to refute the Sāṃkhya view, it was stated that agency—which is superimposed through non-difference from the intellect (*buddhi*)—resides in the *ahaṅkāra*, whose nature is consciousness (*cit*). However, that [agency] belongs only to the Self as qualified by the intellect, which is accessible to the notion of "I" (*aham-dhī*), and not to the pure Witness (*sākṣin*), because it is impossible for the Witness, whose nature is the seer, to possess the attributes of the seen.

Thus, since the insentient intellect (*buddhi*), which serves as the qualification of the qualified Self (*viśiṣṭātman*) when it acts, is itself logically established as the instrument (*karaṇa*), there is no consequence of having to postulate another instrument.

The meaning is that for one who maintains that the intellect alone acts—without superimposition (*adhyāsa*)—the consequence of requiring another instrument is unavoidable. Therefore, although reasons such as "the meaningfulness of the scriptures" (*śāstrārthavattva*) establish only the agency of the Self in general, they lack the capacity to prove innate agency; thus, it is only superimposed agency that is relied upon by the scriptural injunctions regarding agency.
Therefore, it is established that there is no contradiction between the scriptural passages concerning non-attachment and those concerning agency in rites such as the injunctions. //40//
But [the soul is] from the Supreme, because of the scriptural statement to that effect. (BS 2.3.41)
"But that [superimposition] is from another, because of scriptural testimony.
Just as in the case of the superimposition of redness upon a crystal, a red substance is the instrument— since there is the experience "this crystal is red"—
so too has it been stated that the intellect, which undergoes transformation through desire and so forth, is the instrument for the superimposition of agency and other attributes upon the Self.

Relying upon the agency superimposed on the individual soul (jīva) and based on the scriptural statements regarding the Lord’s status as the "causer" (kārayitṛ), the author states the doubt with the words "yadidam" (as for this...).

Here, the connection to the chapter (pāda) arises from the resolution of the contradiction between the scriptural passages such as "eṣa hyeva" (for he indeed...)— which indicate the independence of the agent— and those scriptural passages concerning injunctions and the like that indicate [the Lord's] causality.
He sets forth the prima facie argument according to the view of the Mīmāṃsakas,
beginning with the words "In that regard" (tatra):
Since no absence of agency is observed in the presence of the collection of causal factors such as the intellect, even in the absence of God, God is not the instigator [of action].
Furthermore, he states that if [the Lord] were the prompter, there would be the undesirable consequence of cruelty and so forth—
namely, "And by means of that which consists of afflictions.
He then raises an objection, suggesting that this challenge has already been answered:
Regarding the word "nanu":

previously, it was stated that assuming the individual soul (*jīva*) already possesses merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*), its agency in creating a diverse world is not contradictory because it depends upon those factors; however, now that the soul's agency is established as being dependent on the Lord (*īśvara*), the possession of merit and demerit is itself established.

He says "True" to explain that dependence on karma is not possible, because it would lead to a circular argument: the establishment of [the Lord's] being the cause depends upon the establishment of His possessing those [karmas]; the establishment of the Lord’s causality depends upon the establishment of the individual soul's agency; and the establishment of the individual soul's agency depends upon the establishment of the Lord's causality. Thus, the dependence on karma cannot be maintained.
Let it be that [the Lord] acts independently of karma; to this he replies with the words "akṛta" (unearned).
If He were to act independently, He would join men who possess merit (*dharma*) with suffering and those who possess demerit (*adharma*) with happiness.

Alternatively, if [the Lord] were compassionate, all beings would be of one and the same form through happiness; consequently, the diversity of the world and the scriptural injunctions regarding ritual acts (*vidhi*) and so forth would not exist.

Therefore, for the sake of making the meaning of the scriptures on injunctions and the like purposeful, the agency of the individual soul (*jīva*) must be stated as being dependent upon passion and hatred by its very nature;
and in that case, there is a contradiction with the scriptural texts concerning the Lord’s status as the causal agent (*kārayitṛtva*).
When it is argued that this scripture is merely a praise of the Lord (Īśvara), the author establishes the final conclusion with the words "etām" (this).

Just as when the collection of causes such as sandalwood is present, although there is no perception of pleasure apart from merit (dharma), the existence of dharma is established solely on the authority of scriptures such as, "One indeed becomes virtuous through virtuous action."
The sense is that, in this way, the Lord's status as an enforcer by means of the authority of scripture is also established. //41//
But [the Lord] takes account of the effort made [by the individual soul], because otherwise the injunctions and prohibitions would be rendered meaningless, and so forth. (BS 2.3.42)

Anticipating the objection that "since the diversity of results is established by merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) alone, there is no need for a Lord (*īśvara*)," [the author] replies: "If the diversity of sprouts were established by seeds alone, then the rain-cloud would be rendered useless.
If it is argued that the rain-cloud is not useless because specific causes depend upon general causes, then the Lord is also not useless, as He too serves as a general cause.
Thus he says: "Like the rain-cloud."
He explains the illustration with the word "yathā" (just as):
*gucchāḥ* refers either to the knots of very long creepers or to clusters of flowers (*puṣpastabaka*).
The distinction is that *gulmas* are short creepers.

Is it being argued that if God is the causal agent (*kārayitṛ*), the individual soul (*jīva*) would lack agency (*kartṛtva*), or is it an objection regarding a circular argument (*cakraka*)? It is not the first case; thus he says:
"This is not a fault," he says;
the sense is that we observe the primary status of the student—who is dependent on the teacher—as the agent of study.
He thus refutes the circular argument (*cakraka*).
"Moreover" (api ca): the remainder [of the sense] is that the agency of the individual soul (jīva) and the causative agency of the Lord (īśvara) are both irreproachable.
He provides the proof for the Lord's dependence on other factors by means of the fact that the authority of the scriptures concerning injunctions and so forth would otherwise be untenable:
With the words "How so? and so forth, [the author] explains that when there is such dependence, there is no pointlessness;
otherwise, if there were independence, he elaborates upon the resulting pointlessness:
Regarding the term "Lord" (īśvara):
he alone would be appointed to their position, consecrated [therein];
that is to say, he alone would perform the duties of those two.

And thus, because the individual soul (jīva) is entirely dependent on the independent Lord, the scripture concerning injunctions and so forth would be ineffective and useless; this is the connection [of the argument].
"Human effort" (puruṣakāra) means exertion.
He states the meaning of the word "and so forth" (ādi):
"So be it.
The aforementioned defect, such as the "attainment of what was not done" (akṛtābhyāgama) and so forth, [does not apply].

Therefore, since the Lord acts as the impeller while being dependent upon karma, it is established that there is no contradiction between the scriptural passage beginning with "For He alone... and the scriptural passages concerning injunctions and the like. //42//

The individual soul is a part [of Brahman], because of the designation of difference and also because of the contrary; moreover, some record that it possesses the nature of a servant, a kitava, and so forth. (BS 2.3.43)

Some hold that the individual soul (*jīva*) is a part [of Brahman], eternal, self-luminous, non-atomic, and a non-agent. Here, by establishing the identity of the purified referent of the term *tvaṃ* with Brahman, the contradiction between the scriptural texts concerning difference and non-difference is resolved; thus, there is a connection to the present section (*pāda*).
In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the non-difference of the inner self from Brahman is not established.
The distinction is that in the final conclusion (siddhānta), that [relationship] is established.

Having taken as the object the relationship between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara), which is implied by the previously mentioned relation of the beneficiary and the benefactor, he states the doubt arising from the observation of two kinds of examples—
beginning with the words "tataśca" (and therefore).

Because a relationship of well-known ownership is possible, the lack of restriction—namely, that "it is some kind of relationship"—is not tenable; expressing dissatisfaction with this, he says, "Or rather" (*athavā*).
By this, the category of difference established by such scriptural passages as "He who dwells within the self" (*ya ātmani tiṣṭhan*) is shown.
Thus, the category of difference established by such scriptural texts as "That thou art" (tattvamasi) is to be regarded.

Consequently, since the scriptures concerning difference and non-difference possess equal force, there arises a conflict; and because no definitive relation can be determined in that conflict, the previously mentioned relationship of beneficiary and benefactor—which depends upon a specific relation—remains unestablished. This constitutes the transition [of the objection]. Since the scriptures on difference merely restate a difference consisting of distinct entities as it is commonly perceived in the world, they are weaker than the scriptures on non-difference, which have an unknown fruit as their object. Therefore, following the scriptures on non-difference, the relationship of part and whole is postulated, based upon a difference that has been conceptually constructed.
Thus he establishes his conclusion with the words "Therefore," and so forth.
To the objection— namely, that while fire possesses parts, how can the partless Lord possess parts— he replies:
Regarding the phrase "like a part":
the word "jīva" is to be supplied as the subject.
An objection is raised: if there is only a distinction [between them], then the relationship of owner and owned is appropriate, not the relationship of part and whole.
Regarding the phrase "nanu ca" (but surely):
since non-difference also exists, he says "ataḥ" (therefore) to explain that there is a relationship of part and whole.
The meaning of the Śruti is that one becomes immortal by knowing Him who, having fashioned name and form, enters them and exists engaged in worldly activity—He whom you deceive when He goes or stays.
To provide a logical argument for the non-difference established by Śruti, he says:
"And consciousness... [caitanyaṃ ca].
The meaning is that the individual soul (jīva) is indeed Brahman because it possesses consciousness, just like Brahman. //43//
And because of the wording of the mantra (BBs 2.3.44).
The expansion, greatness, and manifestation of this thousand-headed Puruṣa is equal to that [extent]; yet the Puruṣa is greater, more vast, than that expansion.
Regarding the term "beings" (bhūtāni) as meaning embodied living souls (jīvas), he provides the restrictive qualification:
"not harming" (ahiṃsan).
The meaning is that by not committing violence against any living beings other than those [acts] which are "tīrthas"— that is, actions prescribed in the scriptures— one attains the world of Brahmā.
Here, since the word *bhūta* is used in the sense of "living beings," the intention is that it is likewise so in the mantra mentioned in the Sūtra.
Even though they are the feet of the beings, from what [source] is their status as parts? To this he says:
"A part is a foot. //44//
Moreover, it is also recorded in the Smṛti: BBs_2,3.45: "And furthermore, it is remembered."

The author of the Sūtras cites the Bhagavad Gītā to show that the individual soul (jīva) is a portion of the Lord as described in the Puruṣasūkta mantra, stating "Moreover" (api ca). Anticipating the objection— given the well-known state of absolute difference between the ruler (īśitṛ) and the ruled (īśitavya), how can the soul, who is the ruled, be a portion of the Lord?— he shows that its status as the ruled is possible even through an imagined (kalpita) distinction.

He states that [the Lord] possesses the nature of being a part (*aṃśatva*) on the strength of the scriptures which teach non-difference established as nothing else—beginning with the words "As for that which... etc.
Regarding the objection that if the Lord's status as a controller is merely adventitious (*aupādhika*), why should the individual soul (*jīva*) not be that controller instead—he replies:
Regarding the term "niratiśaya":

the limiting adjuncts such as the body are utterly inferior; and due to the gradations among the limiting adjuncts consisting of ignorance, there exists the distinction between the Lord and those subject to His lordship.
Not in reality.
As it was said by Sureśvarācārya: "The relationship between the Lord and the one to be ruled arises from ignorance regarding the inner self;
when that darkness is destroyed by perfect knowledge, he is the Lord even of the lords."
Thus //45//
The Supreme is not like that, as in the case of light and so forth. (BsRp_2,3.17.46)
He introduces the subsequent sūtra with the words, "Regarding this, it is said":
"The Lord (Īśvara) is made miserable by the sufferings of His own parts."
The meaning is: "because it possesses parts, like Devadatta.
To the question "What follows from that?", he says:
Regarding the phrase "tataśca" (and therefore):

the meaning is that, in comparison with the attainment of the totality of all aspects of suffering [resulting] from knowledge, worldly existence (*saṃsāra*) is better, because there one experiences only one's own suffering. He analyzes the thesis "it is not for this purpose": The meaning is that, in comparison with the attainment of the totality of all aspects of suffering resulting from knowledge, worldly existence (*saṃsāra*) is better, because there one experiences only one's own suffering.
He analyzes the thesis "it is not for this purpose": [as follows].

The meaning of the resolution is as follows: since agency and other such qualities are established only for that which is conditioned by the intellect (*buddhi*), and since the intellect has no connection with another body, the individual soul (*jīva*) conditioned by it likewise has no connection with another body; thus, because there is a distinction between experiencers due to the distinction between their respective intellects, there is no confusion (*sāṃkarya*) regarding karma and so forth.

He states this with the words beginning "And therefore" (*ataśca*), and so forth.

As for this prattle of Bhāskara— that the reflection is not imagined through its association with an adjunct (*upādhi*), but rather by its very nature (*svarūpeṇa*), and therefore the reflected image, being imagined, cannot persist in liberation and thus lacks the status of a *jīva*— this must be disregarded as arising from ignorance of the secret of our established doctrine (*siddhānta*).

For if the face in a mirror were imagined like silver in mother-of-pearl, then just as there is a sublation of the nature [of the silver] in the form "This is not silver," there would likewise be a sublation of the face in the form "This is not a face."

Therefore, because there is no sublation of the mere conjunction—expressed by "there is no face in the mirror"—and because there is an uncontradicted experience of non-difference from one's own face expressed as "this is indeed my own face," it is only as a conjunct [entity] that the reflection is imagined.

Furthermore, since the sentences concerning entry speak of the entry known as the state of being a reflection belonging to Brahman itself without modification, there is no imagination of its essential nature (*svarūpa*).
The teachers have already exerted great effort on this point in the *Darpaṇa-ṭīkā*, so we shall desist here.
Thus, it has been stated that even though the essential nature is one according to our own view, there is no confusion due to the difference between the conditioned individual souls (*jīva*);
now, he begins to explain the confusion of others, which is indicated by the word "and" (*ca*) in the Sūtra:
By the words "of those" (*yeṣām*) and so forth:

intelligence (*buddhi*), pleasure (*sukha*), pain (*duḥkha*), desire (*icchā*), aversion (*dveṣa*), effort (*prayatna*), merit (*dharma*), demerit (*adharma*), and mental impression (*bhāvanā*)—these nine are the specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) of the self (*ātman*).
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "proximity and so forth" (*saṃnidhānādi*), indifference (*audāsīnya*) is expressed.
The Sāṃkhya raises his own objection:

Even though there is no distinction among all persons regarding their proximity to *prakṛti*, it is *prakṛti* itself that proceeds toward each individual person specifically for the sake of experience and liberation.
Thus, because the activity of the *pradhāna* is restricted by the human purpose that is its objective, there is an orderly arrangement (*vyavasthā*) such as experience (*bhoga*) and so forth;
otherwise, if one does not accept this restricted activity, the activity of the *pradhāna* would be for the sake of manifesting its own majesty, which would result in a failure of its objective.

Since the insentient *pradhāna* lacks discrimination regarding the objective, and since the human purpose—which is yet to come—is itself insentient and thus lacks the power to regulate it, no such orderly arrangement would exist.
He says "this is not so" because it is devoid of logical consistency (*mānayukti*).
The sense is that when someone brings about the subversion of a thesis by means of a restrictive factor (*niyāmaka*), it is intended that the very same [subversion] applies to that person.
He states that even in the view of the logicians (tārkika), there is a confusion regarding experience and so forth, beginning with the words "of the followers of Kaṇāda" (kāṇādānām).
The cause is the conjunction of the mind (manas-saṃyoga).
The result is pleasure and so forth;

he raises the objection regarding the established position— that the conjunction of the mind with the self, which is produced by the self's unseen merit (adṛṣṭa), is the cause of that very self’s pleasure and so forth—

Because there is no restriction regarding what has not been seen. (BS 2.3.51)

He refutes the second [position] with the words:

The meaning is "because it possesses the nature of a regulator.
Even while accepting the conceptualization of spatial location, he says: "it is to be postulated."

He states another defect regarding the position that [the self] occupies a specific location (pradeśapakṣa):
Regarding the term "region" (*pradeśa*):
Is that region of the self in which the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) arises mobile or stationary?

Not the first [option], because it is impossible for a part to have motion or division if the whole is immobile, and because this would result in the fallacy of the doctrine of atomic selves (*aṇvātmavāda*).

In the second case, since the experience of another is also seen in that very same location, it follows that unseen merit or demerit (*adṛṣṭa*) exists there as well; thus, there arises the undesirable consequence of two selves experiencing [the results] through a single body.

Even if one were to argue that the locations are distinct due to the difference between the selves, the confusion of experiences would remain as it was because those two [selves] are still contained within a single body; furthermore, this leads to the proliferation of the doctrine of a self with parts (*sāvayavātma-vāda*).
Moreover, in whichever part of the self the unseen merit or demerit has arisen due to contact with the body and so forth, it remains in that very same immobile location.

If [the self] were considered to be "stationed" [in one place], then because there would be an absence of unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) in the self as delimited by a body in heaven and so forth, there could be no experience [there]; therefore, a difference in location is not the determining factor.

The sense is that there is no proof for the existence of unseen merit or demerit (*adṛṣṭa*) in something remote from the body and its enjoyments.

As for what some have said—that even though the mind is one, because the individual selves are distinct, the specific instances of conjunction (*saṃyogavyakti*) differ; thus, through a particular instance of conjunction, the unseen merit and so forth belong to a particular self alone, and there is no confusion (*asāṃkarya*)—that is not correct.

Because there is no difference in the nature of the conjunctions with individual bodies, it would follow that all such conjunctions serve as the cause for perceiving [objects] within every single soul residing inside one body;
and thus, the status of being an enjoyer for all souls within a single body would be unavoidable. Furthermore, you have asserted this confusion by accepting the omnipresence of many souls.

He states that the omnipresence of agents is unestablished at present, because of the experience of their limited nature—such as "I am right here"—and because there is a lack of evidence; thus he says:
"And the impossibility of omnipresence. Furthermore, if many [agents] were omnipresent, they would have to occupy the same location.
And that is incorrect because it has not been observed;
thus he says, "he speaks.
If it is argued: "But surely the coexistence of color, taste, and so forth within a single jar is observed," [the response follows].
This example is not accepted by us;

for since form consists of light alone, taste of water alone, and smell of earth alone, there is no non-difference between each respective quality and its own substratum, and because there is no jar existing apart from the substrata such as light and so forth.
Furthermore, the plurality of selves is also unestablished.
Because the defining characteristic of being a self (ātmatva) is non-different;
thus, Devadatta’s self is not different from Yajñadatta’s self, because it is a self,
like Yajñadatta’s self.
Here the Vaiśeṣika raises an objection: "By the ultimate particulars (*antyaviśeṣa*).

Particulars (*viśeṣas*) reside only in eternal substances; they are themselves the differentiators of their own substrates and do not require a further differentiator for themselves, and thus they are called "ultimate" (*antya*).
The meaning is that, in this way, a distinction between selves arises due to the difference in the defining characteristic of being of the nature of a particular.
First of all, the postulation of specific qualities is not for the sake of knowing the distinction of the self from what is non-self,
because the distinction from the non-self is already established by the very fact of being a self.
Nor is that postulation for the sake of knowing the mutual distinction among selves.

The meaning of the rebuttal is as follows: since the difference between selves (*ātmabheda*) remains unestablished even now, it is not logical to postulate a difference between selves merely on the basis of postulating a difference between their specific qualities (*viśeṣabheda*).

This is because there would be a circular dependency (*anyonyāśraya*): the establishment of a difference between selves depends upon the establishment of a difference between their specific qualities within those selves, while the establishment of that [difference in qualities] depends upon the cognition of the difference between the selves.
As for the claim that space, direction, and time serve as examples of the omnipresence (*vibhutva*) of many [entities], that too is untenable; thus he says:
"Of space and the rest.
Since omnipresence resides in a single [entity] due to parsimony (*lāghava*), there is no plurality of omnipresent entities.

Just as in a single space there is a distinction between loud and soft sounds due to the difference in instruments such as the drum and the lute, so too, even though the Self is one, the distinction between pleasure and other states is possible due to the difference in limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as the intellect (buddhi). Since it has already been stated that such a distinction is untenable even if there were a plurality of selves, he concludes that the postulation of plurality is futile:
[He concludes: "The postulation of plurality is in vain."
Therefore:

thus, since there is no contradiction between the scriptural texts concerning the elements and those concerning the enjoyer, it is established that the non-dual Brahman is the consistent substratum (samanvaya). //53//

Thus ends the third quarter of the second chapter in the *Bhāṣyaratnaprabhā*, a commentary on the *Śārīrakamīmāṃsā* composed by the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya Śrī Govindānanda Bhagavatpāda. //3//

In this context, the "vital breaths" (prāṇas) are the objects [of dispute].

Since there is a doubt as to whether they are produced or not due to conflicting scriptural statements (śruti), and since there is no definitive conclusion because those statements are of equal force, the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa) results in the conclusion that [the texts] lack authority.

The word "or" (*athavā*) means that there is no contradiction because the scriptural statement regarding the existence of the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) at the time of dissolution is stronger due to its lack of any other possible application; therefore, the scriptural statement regarding their origination is figurative, just like the scriptural statement regarding the origination of the individual soul (*jīva*).

The phrase "or" is used to indicate that the figurative position, like the non-authoritative position, is merely a prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) for one who maintains the primary established conclusion (*mukhya-siddhāntin*).
The principal proponent says,
"Therefore" (*ataḥ*). He anticipates the objection regarding the word "thus" (*tathā*):

Alternatively:
there is a section in the third chapter concerning the "Sacrifice upon Receiving a Horse" (*aśvapratigraheṣṭyadhikaraṇa*); this is its subject-text (*viṣayavākya*).

Regarding the statement, "As many horses as one might accept, so many four-potherd offerings to Varuṇa should he perform," there arises a doubt in the subsequent section as to whether this offering to Varuṇa belongs to the giver or the receiver. Having raised the objection that it must belong to the receiver because of the scriptural expression "one might accept" (*pratigṛhṇīyāt*), it will be established that it belongs only to the giver of the horse, based on the indicative mark (*liṅga*) found in the opening passage: "Prajāpati led a horse to Varuṇa."

Therefore, the meaning of the word *pratigṛhṇīyāt* ("one should accept") is "one should cause [another] to accept horses," which amounts to saying "one should give. Once the sense of the sentence—"He who gives horses shall perform the Vāruṇī sacrifice"—is established, the following inquiry arises: Is this sacrifice occasioned by the giving of horses in a worldly (secular) context or in a Vedic context?
In this regard, there is the rule: "One does not give [horses] with manes."

Thus, since a fault arises from giving a horse according to worldly custom—which is prohibited—this sacrifice (iṣṭi) is intended for its removal. This being the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) established by the sūtra, "But because of the fault, the sacrifice should apply to the worldly [gift]," the final conclusion (siddhānta) is as follows: "For here, Varuṇa seizes him who accepts a horse";
thus, having proclaimed the fault of the giver, the sacrifice is enjoined.
The word *varuṇa* is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) as referring to the disease known as dropsy (*jalodara*).
Furthermore, it is not well-known in common worldly usage that this disease occurs as a result of giving away a horse;
nor is such a conventional meaning established by this very sentence itself.

For those who argue that there is a fault in giving and that the ritual action is intended to remove that fault, this is incorrect because it results in a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) due to a difference in meaning.

Furthermore, it is not tenable to claim that the word *varuṇa*— derived from the etymology "he conceals" (*vṛṇoti*)— is a restatement of the fault caused by transgressing a prohibition, for that would entail abandoning its conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*).

And since, even in the case of a Vedic gift, one is able to refer to the suffering produced by the loss of the horse through the aforementioned understanding, this [passage] is therefore an *arthavāda* (explanatory praise) that restates what is already established; thus, having deliberated that "this sacrifice belongs to the giving of a horse connected with the sacrifice," it was stated:
"And the mishap involving the drink is like that."
It is heard in scripture: "If, while the drinking of Soma is being performed, there should be a complication such as vomiting, then one should offer this Śyāmāka rice-oblation to Soma-Indra.

In this regard, the logic of the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) position from the section on the "Sacrifice for Receiving Horses" (*aśvapratigraheṣṭi*), which is separated by many sūtras, is referred to here by the word "tadvat" (in the same manner). Accordingly, in the case of ordinary (non-Vedic) vomiting of Soma drunk for the purpose of balancing the bodily humors (*dhātusāmya*), this oblation should be offered because of the defect known as the drying up of the sense-faculties (*indriyaśoṣa*) caused by the vomiting.

The meaning of the *pūrvapakṣa* (prima facie) sūtra is that the statement, "He who vomits Soma is deprived of his senses through his virility," is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of what is already observed.
The *siddhānta* (conclusion), however, is that since the disposal of the remnant occurs during Vedic Soma-drinking, there is no fault even in vomiting;
