In the Veda, however, from the indicative mark of the mantra—"May my speech not go beyond the navel"—which is intended for proper digestion, it follows that in the case of vomiting, there is a deficiency in the ritual action; therefore, that constitutes a fault.
Thus, it is established that in the case of vomiting the Vedic Soma, there is an oblation to Soma-Indra (saumendra caru); such is the meaning of these and other sūtras. //1//
Because figurative application is impossible. (BS 2.4.2)
[Objection: But would not even the initial proposition (pratijñā) be figurative? To this he says: "And thus, with regard to the meaning of the proposition.

The sense is that, in accordance with the proposition intended to be taught through the introduction and conclusion—that [Brahman] is non-dual—the origin of the vital breaths (prāṇas) must be taken in its primary sense.
He states "likewise" because this same proposition is seen in another Śruti text, such as the Muṇḍaka;
the meaning is that this proposition is to be regarded as the reason for the primacy of the origin of the vital breaths.
Now, he explains the meaning of the scriptural mention of the existence of *prāṇa* during dissolution by means of a question, beginning with "How?

This sentence does not intend to convey that the Supreme Cause, Brahman, possesses *prāṇa* at the time of the Great Dissolution (*mahāpralaya*); rather, its meaning is that it refers to the existence of *prāṇa* in the form of the intermediate primordial nature (*avāntaraprakṛti*) known as Hiraṇyagarbha during the intermediate dissolution (*avāntarapralaya*).

[Objection: But if the modification in the form of Hiraṇyagarbha exists, how can it be said that at that time there is no modification? To this he says: "svavikāra... (its own modification). The meaning is: the production of that which is the gross effect of itself, namely, the causal Brahman (kāryabrahman).

If it is asked: "But why is the indicative mark (*liṅga*) consisting in the existence of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) during the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*), as stated in scripture, interpreted as referring to the intermediate dissolution (*avāntarapralaya*) rather than being used to prove that the vital breaths are unproduced?
We reply: it is on the strength of the powerful scriptural texts concerning birth, such as "From this [Self] the vital breath is born" (*etasmāj jāyate prāṇaḥ*).
If it is further asked: "How can Brahman, which is a modification (*vikāra*), be the material cause (*prakṛti*)?", he says:

Regarding the term "designated" (*vyākṛta*): in such Vedic texts as "In the beginning, he [Hiraṇyagarbha] was born together with Being" (*hiraṇyagarbhaḥ samavartatāgre*), and in Smṛti passages such as "He is the first creator of beings" (*ādikartā sa bhūtānām*), there is a well-known status of Brahmā, Virāṭ, and others— though they are of the nature of modifications— as being in the state of the fundamental cause through the relationship of material cause and modification (*prakṛti-vikāra-bhāva*).

The meaning is that, in relation to what precedes it, even a modification (vikāra) may serve as the material cause (prakṛti) in relation to what follows. Some explain this sūtra in accordance with the section concerning ether (viyad-adhikaraṇa); he refutes them as follows:
"Ether," [so it is said]. //2//
And because it is heard [in scripture] prior to that. (BBs 2.4.3)

The construction of the Sūtra is as follows: "Because of its being primary" (*tatsāmānyāt*) means that, in view of the reading of the word "is born" (*jāyate*) as being primary with respect to ether and the rest, the birth [of the vital breaths] is primary according to the Vedic revelation (*śruti*) among the preceding vital breaths;
the meaning is that there is a commonality (*sāmānya*) with that birth of ether and so forth, namely, the fact of being denoted by the same word.

The principle that it is not proper for a single word in a single sentence to have a primary sense in one instance and a secondary sense in another—resulting in a lack of uniformity—is extended to other cases as well:
"Wherever [the word] is heard later... (Sūtra 3).
Because speech is preceded by that [mind]. (BBs 2.4.4)
Regarding the claim that even in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad the origin of the vital breaths (prāṇas) is not heard, he says in response:
"Because speech is preceded by that" (tatpūrvakatvād vācaḥ).
In this sūtra, the word "speech" (vāk) is an elliptical expression (upalakṣaṇa) for both the vital breath and the mind.

The construction is as follows: since it is stated that speech, breath, and mind are preceded by fire, water, and earth respectively, the claim that their origin is not heard [in the scripture] is unestablished.
By "on account of that similarity" (tatsāmānyāt) is meant the commonality of being instruments (karaṇatva) shared by the eyes and so forth with speech and the rest.

In this context, according to the view where the suffix *mayaṭ* primarily denotes a modification (*vikāra*), the fact that the vital breaths are effects of Brahman remains established, because fire, water, and earth are modifications of Brahman.

Even if it is argued that the suffix *mayaṭ* is used figuratively because the vital air (*prāṇa*), being wind, cannot be a modification of water but merely exists dependent upon it, nevertheless, if the vital airs were modifications [of water], their dependence on the elements would serve as a logical mark (*liṅga*) for their being effects of Brahman;
this is established both by the explicit statement of their being effects of Brahman in other scriptural passages such as "He created the vital air" (*sa prāṇamasṛjata*), and so forth.

Therefore, it is established that because there is no contradiction between the scriptural texts concerning the origin of the vital breaths and the scriptural texts concerning their existence, there is a coherent connection (*samanvaya*) with Brahman as the cause.

It should be understood that the fruit of the sections (*adhikaraṇas*) consisting of the investigation into the subtle body (*liṅga-śarīra*) is the cognition of the distinction between the "sign" (*liṅga*) and the meaning of the term "thou" (*tvaṃ-pada*). //4//
And because the seven [stages] are specified as distinct states of progression. (BBs 2.4.5)

Thus, since there is doubt arising from the contradiction among the scriptural texts regarding the determination of the number of the vital breaths (*prāṇas*)—which have acquired their existence through birth—due to the relationship between the supported and the supporter, the author states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*):
"On account of the mention of seven and because of being specified. Here, *viśaya* means doubt.
In this context, the sense-faculties are the objects.
The seven vital breaths (*prāṇas*) consist of the five faculties of cognition, speech, and the mind; these same [seven], together with the hand, make eight.
"Seizing" (*graha*) means the state of being a binder.

They are called *grahas* (seizers) because they seize and bind; their state of being binders is dependent upon their objects, and thus they are *atigrahas* (over-seizers), meaning the objects that transcend the *grahas*.
There are two ears, two eyes, two nostrils, and speech—these seven vital breaths (*prāṇas*) located in the head; and two directed downwards, namely the anus and the generative organ—making nine.

These ten, together with the organs of knowledge and action, are the *prāṇas* in the person's body; the established conclusion (*siddhāntakoṭi*) states that the self (*ātman*) and the mind (*manas*) constitute the eleventh *prāṇa*.
These same [ten] together with that which is called the heart (*hṛdaya*), namely the intellect (*buddhi*), make twelve;
together with the ego (*ahaṅkāra*), they make thirteen.

Alternatively, because seven are understood from scripture as "the breaths that are in the head," or because they are qualified as "breaths" by reference to their location in the head, the term "breath" is applied to those located in the head.
The application of the Sūtra is that there are exactly seven vital breaths (*prāṇas*) by way of an exhaustive enumeration of the sense-faculties (*indriya*).
He raises an objection— that the number seven is contradicted by the distributive repetition (*vīpsā*)— with the words "But surely" (*nanu*).
They are called "dwelling in the cave" (guhāśaya) because they lie within the cave of the heart;
the meaning is that they are placed or deposited in their own respective locations.
One should understand their number to be fourteen by means of the mind.
The proponent (pūrvapakṣin) offers a rebuttal:
"This is not a fault. //5//
But since [the self] is established as having hands and so forth, it is not thus; therefore, it is not so. (BBs 2.4.6)
Even by the proponent of the final doctrine (siddhāntin), among the eleven distinctions of mental modifications, intellect (buddhi) consisting of determination,
ego (ahaṅkāra) consisting of pride,
and mind (citta) consisting of memory must be included within the count of twelve and so forth.

In response to the objection that it would be simpler to include [the intermediate state] within the first seven [stages of existence], the author establishes the final position with the words "herein":
it is "seized" or connected by the act of grasping (*ādāna*).
He states the very connection [between the two views] with the words "by the two hands.

Therefore, the syntactical connection is as follows: one should not think that, because it is impossible for a higher number to be included within a lower one, there must be exactly seven vital breaths (prāṇas) out of deference to parsimony.
Then, in response to the inquiry as to how many sense organs there are, he says: "The latter," etc.

According to the principle that "when there is a mutual contradiction among scriptural texts, the scripture supported by other means of valid cognition is stronger," the other scriptural passages should be interpreted in accordance with the eleven-fold prāṇa-texts, which are themselves supported by the inference based on the mark of functional activity (kāryaliṅgānumāna).
"It is true.
He states the eleven effects as marks [of the ego-sense]: "Sound," etc.
The three times constitute "traikālya"; that whose function has those as its object is "traikālyavṛtti.
The meaning is that since the other sense organs grasp only the present, the mind must be admitted for the sake of knowing the past and so forth.
He refutes what was stated [by the opponent] regarding "because it is specified":
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "and seven," and "not by that many":
the meaning is that grasping and the other [mental factors] are of an entirely different genus from the ear and the other [sense organs].
The point is that if those [organs] were their functions, then the taking up [of objects] and so forth would not occur for the deaf and others.

Having raised the objection, "In that case, how is the word 'prāṇa' used for the apertures?", he says, "But as for the primary [meaning]," indicating that it is by way of metaphorical indication (lakṣaṇā).
The statement "seven vital breaths arise" is for the purpose of meditation (*upāsanā*).
However, the scriptural passage "eight graspers" (*aṣṭau grahāḥ*) is intended as an illustrative indication (*upalakṣaṇārthā*);
this should be understood because the anus, the generative organ, and the feet are likewise equally binding (*bandhakatva*).

Now, one might object that this explanation of the Sūtra is inconsistent, because the understanding of the sevenfold nature of the five sense organs, speech, and mind lacks a common substratum (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) with the specification of the four head-located [organs], and because of the fault of restrictive enumeration (*parisaṃkhyā*) already mentioned. Out of dissatisfaction with this, he says: "This other... He applies the *pūrvapakṣa* Sūtra to the doubt as to how many sense organs there are: [The Sūtra: "Some say there are seven. (NS 3.1.67) [Commentary: When the doubt arises as to how many sense organs there are, he presents the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).
Regarding the word "seven":
the meaning is that those vital breaths (*prāṇa*) which accompany that individual self (*jīvātman*) are themselves designated as "senses" (*indriya*) because they are the cause of its experience.

Furthermore, in the state of death, the person who resides in the eye as the visual organ—existing in the form of a ray of the Sun who is the benefactor—turns away and returns from the external region to his own master, the Sun.
Then, at that time, this one who is about to die becomes one who no longer perceives forms.
When the divine portion has entered into the deity, the subtle body (liṅga) merges with the mind in the eye and the heart; it is in this sense that those standing nearby say, "He does not see.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the following is included: "he does not smell, he does not speak, he does not enjoy, he does not hear, he does not think, he does not touch, he does not cognize."
The claim that "only seven [limbs] move along with the living being" is unproven,
because the movement of the hands and other limbs is also perceived through the scriptural mention of their being "graspers" (graha).
He establishes this conclusion with the words beginning "evam" (thus), and so forth.
He states the memory [of the self] as being accompanied by the *puryaṣṭaka* prior to the release from the bonds of the hands and so forth: "by the *puryaṣṭaka*.

This consists of the five vital breaths (*prāṇa*, etc.), the five subtle elements (*bhūta-sūkṣma*), the five organs of knowledge, the five organs of action, the fourfold internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), and ignorance (*avidyā*).

Desire and action constitute the "eightfold city" (puryaṣṭaka) which serves as the mark (liṅga) for making the Self known; since this is possible, it is not proper to restrict all the scriptural texts [to a lower number].
Thus he says: "The word 'all' also...
Therefore, because there is no contradiction among the scriptural passages concerning number, it is established that Brahman is the cause of the eleven organs. //6//
And they are atomic. (BBs 2.4.7)
"And [the organs] are atomic.

This is the Sāṃkhya objection: since the organs are all-pervasive (vibhu) according to the Śruti text, "All vital breaths (prāṇas) are infinite," their departure (utkrānti) is unestablished; rather, they possess localized functions (vṛtti) consisting of manifestations within their respective bodies, and it is not these that undergo departure and so forth.

In response to the doubt as to what the magnitude of the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) is due to their association with that [Self], the author establishes the final conclusion (siddhānta) with the words beginning "now" (*adhunā*).
The meaning is that after the determination of their origin and number, their magnitude is now being investigated.
Subtlety (*sūkṣmatva*) is the state of having unmanifest color and touch;
limitation (*pariccheda*) is smallness (*alpatva*).

He states the contradiction with the previously mentioned reasoning—that if the intellect and so forth were all-pervasive (*vibhu*), then the atom-like nature (*aṇutva*) of the self conditioned by them could not be established:
Regarding the phrase "having that as its essence" (*tadguṇasāratvam*):
having restated the objection previously mentioned, he refutes it with the words "of those that are all-pervading" (*sarvagatānām*).

It is established that because the scriptural teaching of infinity is intended for the purpose of meditation, there is no contradiction between it and the scriptural passages concerning the departure [of the soul] and so forth. //7//
And he is the most excellent. (BBs 2.4.8)
And it is the most excellent;
because it is an extension (*atideśa*), it does not depend on [logical] connection and so forth.
The principle stated in the passage "In the same way, the vital breaths" is extended here.

He raises an objection, asking "For what purpose?", on the grounds that an extended application (atideśa) is not appropriate because there is no doubt as to whether the vital breath (prāṇa) is born or not.
He then states a further doubt based on the scriptural testimony regarding the existence of the vital breath during the certain great dissolution (mahāpralaya).
"In the *Nāsadāsīya* indeed" means that it is studied beginning with the words "Non-being was not.
In that case, at the time of dissolution (*pralaya*), there was neither death— the destroyer— nor anything subject to death, namely, the effect.
The nectar (amṛta) to be enjoyed by the gods did not exist;
neither the moon, which is the sign (praketa) of the night in the form of a mark, nor the sun, which is the sign of the day, existed—
this is the grammatical connection with "together with self-power" (svadhayā saha).
The word *svadhā* refers to the food to be offered to the ancestors;
alternatively, it means the power (*māyā*) sustained by itself, and the ultimate truth is that with that [power], that one Brahman alone existed.
Here, the meaning of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that the term *anīt* signifies that it performed activity (*ceṣṭā*).

Therefore, the meaning is that there was nothing else whatsoever superior to or more excellent than that Brahman. The rebuttal is easy to understand. Now, one might object: "Since the word 'best' (śreṣṭha) is not commonly known to refer to the vital breath (prāṇa), how can it be the Sūtra? To this, he says:
"And [the word] 'best'... and so forth.
He explains the scriptural passage beginning with "And the Prāṇa is the eldest" as follows:
"pūyeta" means it would become pus.
The meaning is that its embryo would not come into being; it would not exist.

Being the cause of the life of speech and so forth is a quality of the vital breath (prāṇa). Thus, since there is no contradiction with the scriptural texts concerning the bringing [of the elements], it is established that the scriptural texts regarding the origin of the vital breaths have their harmonious application (samanvaya) in Brahman. //8//
The vital breath (*prāṇa*) is neither the wind nor a mere physiological function, because it is taught separately [from them]. (BS 2.4.9)
Having examined the sense organs, their origin was extended [to the vital breath] in order to distinguish the prāṇa from their activity.
Now, he distinguishes the nature of the prāṇa as it has arisen:
"It is neither air nor a function, because of its separate instruction."

Is the principal vital breath (*mukhya prāṇa*) merely air, or is it the common function of the organs, or is it a distinct principle? Since there are scriptural texts regarding the difference and non-difference between air and the vital breath that contradict one another, a doubt arises; therein, he states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). He states the second prima facie view, that of the Sāṃkhya: ... [The text continues with the Sāṃkhya argument] ... Therefore, the *prāṇas* are the five subtle elements (*tanmātras*), which are the causes of the gross elements. Thus ends the second section. Now, the third section begins. Here, the doubt is as follows: Is the *prāṇa* taught in the Upanishads something different from the self (*ātman*), or is it the self itself? On this point, the prima facie view is stated: "In this world, the *prāṇa* is different from the self. Why? Because of its distinctness. For the *prāṇa* is mentioned as distinct from the self in such passages as, "From him, the *prāṇa* arose" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 3.3). Furthermore, because of its being an object of meditation. For the *prāṇa* is presented as an object of meditation for the sake of attaining greatness, as in, "He who meditates on *prāṇa* as Brahman becomes great" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.1.1). Also, because of its being subject to increase and decrease. For the *prāṇa* is said to increase and decrease, as in, "When a man sleeps, his *prāṇa* goes out" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.12). Moreover, because of its being a means of departure. For the *prāṇa* is described as the means of departure for the soul, as in, "By the *prāṇa* alone, departing from this world, he goes upwards" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.2). And because of its being an instrument. For the *prāṇa* is mentioned as an instrument for the self, as in, "With the *prāṇa* as his companion, he attains all worlds" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.1.2). Therefore, the *prāṇa* is different from the self. To this, the following is said: "But it is the self. The word "but" sets aside the prima facie view. The *prāṇa* is not different from the self; rather, it is the self itself. Why? Because of the designation of its nature. For the nature of the *prāṇa* is designated as belonging to the self in such passages as, "I am the *prāṇa" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.22). Also, because of the teaching of its entering. For the self is taught as entering the body through the *prāṇa*, as in, "Having entered by means of the *prāṇa*" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.21). Furthermore, because of the mention of its being the self. For the *prāṇa* is mentioned as being the very self, as in, "This is the *prāṇa*, this is the self" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.23). Also, because of the teaching of its immortality. For the *prāṇa* is taught to be immortal, as in, "The *prāṇa* is indeed the immortal" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.22). And because of the teaching of its being the lord. For the *prāṇa* is taught to be the lord of the organs, as in, "The *prāṇa* is the lord of all these" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.21). Therefore, the *prāṇa* is the self. But how is it that the *prāṇa* is designated as different from the self in the aforementioned passages? To this, the following is said: "It is a mere distinction of functions, like in the case of the priests. Just as in the world, the same person, when acting as a priest, is designated differently according to his specific functions—such as being called a "Hotṛ," "Adhvaryu," "Udgātṛ," or "Brahman"—so too the self, while remaining one, is designated as the *prāṇa*, the mind, and so forth, according to its various functions. How is this known? From the context. For in the context of the self, the *prāṇa* and other organs are mentioned as its powers, as in, "From him, the *prāṇa* arose" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 3.3). Also, because of the teaching of its identity. For the identity of the *prāṇa* with the self is taught in such passages as, "I am the *prāṇa" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.22). Therefore, the *prāṇa* is the self. But if the *prāṇa* is the self, then how is it that it is taught as having a beginning and an end, and as subject to increase and decrease? To this, the following is said: "It is a metaphorical designation based on its connection with the body, as in the case of the light. Just as the sun, though eternal, is metaphorically designated as rising and setting due to its connection with the movement of the earth, so too the *prāṇa*, though eternal, is metaphorically designated as having a beginning and an end, and as increasing and decreasing, due to its connection with the body. Therefore, the *prāṇa* is the self. But if the *prāṇa* is the self, then why is it taught as an object of meditation for the sake of greatness? To this, the following is said: "It is for the purpose of meditation on the qualities of the self, as in the case of the 'All-pervading'. Just as the quality of being "all-pervading" is taught for the sake of meditating on the self, so too the *prāṇa* is taught for the sake of meditating on the qualities of the self. Therefore, the *prāṇa* is the self. But if the *prāṇa* is the self, then how is it that it is mentioned as an instrument? To this, the following is said: "It is an instrument by way of its being a power, as in the case of the intellect. Just as the intellect, though being the self, is an instrument by way of its being a power, so too the *prāṇa* is an instrument by way of its being a power of the self. Therefore, the *prāṇa* is the self. But if the *prāṇa* is the self, then how is it that it is mentioned as departing? To this, the following is said: "Its departure is due to the departure of the limiting adjuncts, as in the case of the ether. Just as the ether does not depart but appears to do so due to the departure of jars and other objects, so too the *prāṇa* does not depart but appears to do so due to the departure of the body and other limiting adjuncts. Therefore, the *prāṇa* is the self. But if the *prāṇa* is the self, then how is it that it is mentioned as having a plurality of forms? To this, the following is said: "The plurality is due to the plurality of its powers, as in the case of the fire. Just as fire, though one, is mentioned as having many forms due to the plurality of its powers, so too the *prāṇa*, though one, is mentioned as having many forms due to the plurality of its powers. Therefore, the *prāṇa* is the self. But if the *prāṇa* is the self
Alternatively:
he introduces the aphorism as the established conclusion (siddhānta) with the words,
"To this it is replied."
In the Śruti, it is stated that the Brahman in the form of the mind (manas) possesses four feet by way of speech, breath, sight, and hearing; among these,
the breath (prāṇa) shines— that is, is manifested— by the wind as its presiding deity (adhidaivika), and once manifested,
it "heats," meaning it becomes capable of performing its function.

He states with the word "tathā" (so it is) that, through the evidence of the mutual dialogue found here and there in the Śrutis between Prāṇa and Vāk and the others, as well as the evidence of their separate origin, Prāṇa is distinct even from the sense organs and their non-differentiated functions.
Having refuted the view that Prāṇa is a function of the senses by means of Śruti, he now refutes it by means of reasoning as well:
And it is not the case that [the function] belongs to all [senses] collectively;
for the function accomplished by the eye is not the same as that accomplished by the ear and so forth,
because the sense organs are each individually the cause only for specific functions such as the perception of a single form.
The meaning is that the functioning of a collective whole is not possible because such a whole does not exist.

Regarding the phrase "due to the absence of vital breath" (prāṇābhāvāt): it means there is no evidence for a movement conducive to a single function called "vitalizing" (prāṇana) among the ears and other sense organs.

The meaning is that because hearing and the other [senses] are non-vibratory and thus heterogeneous, they are not conducive to the vitalizing function (*prāṇana*) which consists of vibration; therefore, due to the absence of such an intermediate operation (*avāntaravyāpāra*), the activity of all the organs collectively is not "prāṇa.
Furthermore, if prāṇa were merely a function, then speech and the other organs would have to be considered primary.
To show that this is not so, he says:
"In the same way, of the vital breath (prāṇa).
Just as a jar is neither a different entity from clay nor merely clay itself, because it is a modification (vikāra) of it; [so it is with the vital breath].
Thus, he states the interpretation of the scriptural passage concerning non-difference—that "prāṇa is a modification of air"—with the words:
"It is said. The meaning is that *prāṇa* is simply air that has entered the body and exists in five states through its modified form. //9//
But [the self is] like the eye and so forth, because of its being taught together with them and other reasons. (BS 2.4.10)
He raises the objection that if the vital breath (*prāṇa*) lacks the function of an instrument, it would follow that it is an enjoyer like the individual soul (*jīva*):
"It might be so," etc. [The answer is:
the vital breath is not an enjoyer.
He states the meaning of the sūtra— "because [the body] is an instrument for experience, like the eye and so forth"—
with the words beginning "the word 'tu' (but)," and so on.

The meaning is that, just as the *bṛhat* and *rathantara* [sāmans] are recited together because they are identical in being always employed together or in being *sāman*s, so too is the breath (*prāṇa*) recited together with the instruments because of its identity in being an accessory (*upakaraṇa*); thus, there is no "unestablished reason" (*hetvasiddhi*).
Furthermore, the breath is not the enjoyer.
Because it possesses parts, because it is insentient, and because it is material, it is like the body. //10//
And because it is not something to be produced, there is no fault; for thus the scripture shows. (BBs 2.4.11)
Now, one might raise the following objection: "Indeed, whatever serves as an instrument of experience is seen to have an object, such as the eye and so forth;
however, since the vital breath (prāṇa) is without an object and lacks any specific function, it cannot be an instrument. This is expressed by the words:
"It might be so."

He offers a rebuttal: because the previously stated pervasion is subject to deviation in the case of the body, and because there exist unique functions such as maintaining the body and the senses, and departing from it, the status of the breath (*prāṇa*) as an instrument of experience—just like the body—is unimpaired even though it lacks an object; however, unlike the eyes and other senses, it does not function as an instrument for cognition or action, by virtue of which it would possess an object. Thus he refutes [the objection].
By the words "not yet," etc., [it is meant]:
regarding their own excellence (*ahaṃśreyasi*), that is, on account of their own superiority,
they *vyūdire*, meaning they engaged in dispute.
"Devoid of its mere functions" means it remains in a state like that of a mute person and so forth; "inferior" (avara) means low.
The meaning is that the living being (jīva), protecting with its vital breath (prāṇa) the nest called the body— the house— sleeps;
"then" means at that very time.
By that vital breath (prāṇa), whatever the living being eats is done by that very prāṇa; this is the meaning.
Thus, it is stated that there exists a function of the prāṇa which is not common [to the other vital breaths]. //11//
The fivefold activity is designated as being like that of the mind. (BBs 2.4.12)
In that very context, he explains another reason for [the existence of the Self] with the words "And for this reason," etc.;
"vṛtti" means state.
The act of churning fire and so forth is a heroic deed (*vīryavat-karma*).

Anticipating the objection that—just as with the functions of desire and the rest—there is no fixed rule of five even regarding knowledge, he himself raises this lack of conviction and adopts an alternative position, beginning with the words "But here too... and so forth.
Valid cognition is *pramāṇa*; erroneous cognition is *viparyaya* or delusion;
the cognition of a hare's horn and the like is *vikalpa*;
and *tāmasī* mental modification is sleep (*nidrā*).

Memory is well known [as a mental function]. Since error and the senses are functions of ignorance (avidyā), they do not have the nature of mental functions; expressing his own view with dissatisfaction at this [conclusion], he says: "many... [etc.].
He states another meaning of the Sūtra with the words "jīva" (the living self).
Thus, it is established that there is no contradiction between the scriptural texts concerning the difference and non-difference of the vital air (prāṇa) [and the self]. //12//
And it is subtle. (BBs 2.4.13)

Having thus explained the origin and nature of the chief vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa), he teaches its atomicity (aṇutva) regarding a doubt concerning its dimension, stating: "And it is atomic. He then states a further objection:
"Is it not the case that even omnipresence [is denied]?
A creature smaller than a mosquito is called a *pluṣi*, while a *puttikā* is an even more minute being; a *nāga* is an elephant.

The objection that there is a contradiction—since the scripture stating "the prāṇa departs" suggests the prāṇa is limited in size, whereas the scripture stating "it is equal to all this" suggests its omnipresence—is resolved by the fact that the two scriptural statements do not conflict due to a difference in their respective subjects: the internal (ādhyātmika) prāṇa is limited, while the cosmic (ādhidaivika) prāṇa is omnipresent. Thus he replies:
"That is being stated":

furthermore, since at the beginning it was said that the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is small, being equal to a louse and so forth, its equality with the body of Virāj is expressed by "equal to these three worlds," and its nature as the *sūtra*-self is expressed by "equal to this [universe]"; thus he says that the systematic arrangement of the subject matter is well-established.
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "and also," in the passage "and the atoms," it was established that "all are infinite" refers to the infinity of the sense organs for the purpose of meditation;
however, here, because a different resolution is stated— namely, that the omnipresence of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) pertains to the divine realm (*ādhidaivika*)— there is no tautology.
Others, however, say that there is no tautology because in the former case the objection of the Sāṃkhya was refuted incidentally, whereas here the contradiction with scripture is refuted. //13//
But the presiding [deities] over light and so forth [are the individual souls], because of the scriptural teaching concerning them. (BS 2.4.14)

Previously, the distinction between the atomicity and omnipresence of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) was stated through its internal (*ādhyātmika*) and divine (*adhidaivika*) divisions. In connection with that, [the author] states the dependence of the internal vital breaths upon the divine ones: "But there is the presiding over by light and so forth, because of the scriptural teaching thereof.

This is established by the instrumental case-ending in the scriptural passage, "For one expresses names with speech, one sees forms with the eye," which possesses both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).

Because this would contradict the statement that speech and the other organs are independent means [of perception], the Śruti passage beginning with "Fire, having become speech... intends to show that they have non-conscious fire and so forth as their material causes (*upādāna*), and not that they have presiding deities (*adhiṣṭhātṛ-devatā*) as their cause.
Nor should it be argued that although speech and the others are capable of their own functions, there is no contradiction in their requiring a presiding agent due to their being non-conscious; for...
This is because the individual soul (jīva) is the presiding agent.
Furthermore, if the deities were the presiding agents, they would, like the soul, be enjoyers in this body;
and thus, due to the contradiction of having multiple enjoyers in a single location, the weak soul could not be the enjoyer. This is the meaning of the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa).
He establishes the conclusion with the words "Thus [the prima facie view] having been reached," and so forth.
In the passages "Fire, having become speech" and "The sun, having become the eye," their becoming [those things] consists precisely in their being presided over by the deities of fire and the others.

He states that the relationship is not of the nature of being derived from that [as its material cause], because it is impossible for the sun’s orb situated at a distance and so forth to have the eyes and other organs situated in the face as their material cause;
thus he says: "And this [is] of fire.
It should be explained that the wind, having become the presiding deity of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), entered the nostrils; thus he says: [the following].
"So be it.
It shines, it blazes; the meaning is that it performs its own function.
Regarding this matter of the nature of the controller and the controlled, he states another indicative mark:
"He, indeed, [carried] speech.

The meaning is that this Prāṇa, having caused Speech—the first among the functions in the Udgītha rite—to transcend Death in the form of evils such as falsehood, and having thereby liberated it from Death, brought it to the state of being the essence of the deity Agni.

Furthermore, he states that the scriptural passage beginning with "Moreover, when one has died, speech merges into fire, breath into wind, sight into the sun," etc., also illuminates the relationship of controller and controlled;
thus he says, "In all cases.
[Objection: But it is observed that the movement of carts and the like is impelled by oxen and such.
However, the production of curd and so forth is observed even in the case of milk and other substances that are not presided over [by a conscious agent];
thus, since both possibilities exist, how can there be certainty? To this, he says: "And when it is possible in both ways... etc.
He introduces the aphorism in order to refute other objections that have been stated:
"As for what was said... (yadapi). //14//
[The soul] possesses vital breath, because of the scriptural statement. (BS 2.4.15)
"By the corporeal [body] alone"—
the word "enjoyer" is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence].
The "connection" is the relationship between the enjoyer and the enjoyed.

Now, after the entry of the vital breath (prāṇa) into the body, that Self who presides over the eye—the sense organ which has entered this cavity in the orb of the eye—is the ocular self (cākṣuṣa); the eye is for his seeing of forms. Although the Self depends upon the instruments [of perception], yet he who knows that which is to be known, the knowledge, and the egoism which is their substrate, is the Self, whose very nature is consciousness (cidrūpa).
The meaning of the scripture is that the sense organs are required for the manifestation of smell and so forth, but not for consciousness itself.

Furthermore, because of the recognition—"I who saw the form, I am the very same one who hears"—it follows that there is only one embodied experiencer, and not many deities; thus he says, "Moreover" (api ca). //15//
And because that [nature] is eternal. (BBs 2.4.16)

Anticipating the objection that there might be no fixed rule—such that at one time the gods are the enjoyers and at another time the individual soul (jīva)—the author of the Sūtras states, "And of that," [sūtra 3.1.7], to show that this is not so, because the rule is that the soul alone is the enjoyer within a body acquired through its own karma.
This is because, during departure from the body and other such states, the vital breaths (prāṇas) never deviate from the soul; therefore, the soul alone is the master of the vital breaths.
He states another interpretation— that for the deities, there is merely the status of presiding overseers, like the owner of a chariot and its driver— by saying,
"And [the self] is eternal through the embodied [self] alone.

The meaning is that just as a lamp or similar object, by way of assisting the instruments of perception, is included within the category of instruments, so too the deities are merely assistants to the instruments and are not the experiencers.
The soul’s status as an enjoyer is due to its presiding over the instruments by means of unseen merit (adṛṣṭa), like the owner of a chariot;

whereas the gods’ presiding is due to their knowledge of how to assist the instruments, like a charioteer. Thus, there is no establishment of the matter through any other means via the soul alone. Furthermore, the inference that the gods are the enjoyers in this body by virtue of their presiding is sublated by the scriptural statement: "Indeed, evil does not reach the gods."

Therefore, it is established that since the scriptural statement "for one sees forms with the eye" teaches merely the instrumentality [of the sense organ], there is no contradiction with those scriptural passages teaching the dependence on presiding deities, such as "Fire, having become speech... and so forth.
"Those [others] are the sense organs (indriya) because they are designated as such, except for the Best (the Prāṇa).
Regarding the inquiry into the presiding deities when the sense organs exist,
he offers a rebuttal to the objection that those [deities] do not exist apart from the functions of the vital breath (prāṇavṛtti).
Those [others] are the sense organs (indriyas), because they are designated as such, with the exception of the "best" one.

Stating a doubt based on scriptural texts regarding both the difference and non-difference of the sense organs from the vital breath (prāṇa), the author presents the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) beginning with the words "And the principal... and so forth.

"Come now, let us all become the very nature of this chief vital breath (mukhya-prāṇa)"—having thus resolved, speech and the other organs became so; such is the meaning of the scriptural text regarding non-difference.
They are non-different from the vital breath, because they are denotable by the term "prāṇa."
He says "like the vital breath" (prāṇavat), [introducing the word] "vital breath.
He explains the three words as the meaning of the proposition: "those vital breaths are other than the pre-eminent one."
"Regarding the phrase *tattvāntarāṇy eva* (they are indeed distinct principles):
in the [sūtra] *tadvyapadeśāt*, the word *tat* refers back to the difference that was previously asserted.

He then applies those words of the sūtra once more for the purpose of establishing the reason—that they are distinct because they are designated by two non-synonymous terms, namely *prāṇāḥ* and *indriyāṇi*."
By the words beginning with "ka" [the author] shows that because the sūtra faces in all directions (*viśvatomukha*), its dual purpose is merely an ornament and not a defect.

By this, two defects are dispelled: the necessity of supplying an unstated proposition (*pratijñādhyāhāra*) and the fact that the word "tat" refers to a distinction (*bheda*) not previously introduced.
He raises the objection of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) regarding the proof of a difference in entities based on a difference in words— starting with "But surely" (*nanu*).
The meaning is that the mind (*manas*), like the vital breath (*prāṇa*), would also have to be distinct from the sense organs (*indriya*).
The general rule is that a difference in the designations of things occurs because of a difference in their non-synonymous designations, provided they are independent designata.
However, this rule is set aside in the case of the mind (*manas*) due to its sublation by such traditional texts as "the six organs, with the mind as the sixth.
But since there is no such sublating factor in the case of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the general rule remains established; thus he provides the resolution.

By the words "Truth," etc., the mention of a distinction between the mind (*manas*) and the senses (*indriya*) should be understood according to the maxim of the "cow and the bull" (*gobalīvardanyāya*).

Some maintain that, according to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), because the mind is the material cause of valid cognition (*pramā*), it is intended to be a non-sense-organ (*anindriya*) like the self (*ātman*); therefore, there is no sublation of the general rule.

Furthermore, because of the designation of a separate birth in the passage, "From this [Being] are born the vital breath (prāṇa), the mind, and all the sense organs," he states that there is a distinction between independent entities:
"And this is a difference in designation.

The meaning is that within a single sentence, the word *indriya* applies to the vital breath (*prāṇa*) due to their identity, yet does not apply to it for fear of tautology; thus, there is a contradiction. //17//
Because of the scriptural teaching of difference. (BS 2.4.18)

Thus, the reason has been explained by the statement that [the two] are spoken of through distinction, through non-synonymous designations, and through the designation "ordinary person" (*pṛthagjana*).
By the sūtra stating "because of the mention of distinction," the reason given is the difference in context; therefore, there is no tautology.

Those gods, whose nature consists of the functions of the senses and mind according to the scriptures, [undertook] the *udgītha* rite for the sake of conquering the *asuras*, whose nature consists of evil conduct.

First, they said to Speech, which was occupied [with its own function], "Sing the Udgītha for us for the sake of destroying the Asuras. Having consented, saying "So be it," the Asuras destroyed Speech as it was singing by means of defects such as falsehood. In this manner, when all the sense organs had been seized by evil, then—breaking off the context with the word "then" (atha)—they spoke to the one residing in the mouth (*āsanya*), that is, the principal vital breath (*mukhya-prāṇa*). To him they said: "Sing that..."
"Sing that!"—by means of that vital breath (*prāṇa*), which has risen upward, is devoid of objects, and is free from the defect of attachment, the Asuras were destroyed.
Thus, by the statement of the chief *prāṇa* as the destroyer of the Asuras, the existence of difference [between the individual self and the supreme Self] is established; so he says:
"Those... (*te ha...*) [Note: The phrase *te ha...* refers to the opening of the subsequent section of the text.]
The meaning is that Prajāpati created those other three for himself, for his own sake. //18//
And because of their distinctness. (BBs 2.4.19)
And he says that there is a difference because of the possession of contradictory attributes:
"and because of their distinctness.
Death is the fault of attachment.
"Speech held its vow" means that it remained steadfast.

Because of the contradiction arising from the many distinct characteristics [of speech and the other organs], their becoming the form of Prāṇa must be explained as consisting in their having a state of existence dependent upon Prāṇa.

This very point is the basis for the figurative application (*lakṣaṇā*) of the word "Prāṇa" to the sense organs in the Śruti, which refers back to it with the words: "Therefore, they are designated by this name."
Thus, it is established that there is no contradiction between the scriptural texts concerning difference and non-difference. //19//
But the fashioning of names and forms belongs to Him who performs the tripartition, because of the teaching [in scripture]. (BS 2.4.20)

The two activities of "origination" (*utpatti*) and "producing" (*utpādanā*) are well known as belonging respectively to the object and the agent. Among these, the contradiction with the scriptural texts regarding the origination of the world was refuted by the preceding two chapters;
now, the contradiction with the scriptural texts regarding producing is being refuted.
In this regard also, that the production of the subtle elements belongs solely to the Supreme Lord is not disputed in the scriptures.
However, since there is a conflict of scriptural statements regarding the production of gross elements, he says the following in order to refute that:
"But the fashioning of names and forms belongs to Him who makes the tripartition, because of the teaching.
It has been stated that the vital breath (prāṇa) is distinct from the instruments due to the distinction between name and form.

In connection with that, the question is considered as to by whom the formation of gross name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) is brought about; this is the intermediate transition (*avāntarasaṃgati*). "Process" (*prakriyā*) means the section (*prakaraṇa*).
He states the very act of seeing (*īkṣaṇa*):
With the words "Hanta" and so forth, the connection is as follows: "Come now, let me enter into the subtle deities.
The Śruti statement, "I shall make each one of those three deities threefold by means of fire, water, and food," is intended to indicate the process of quintuplication (pañcīkaraṇa).

Since the inclusion of ether and air is also stated in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, the purpose of the Supreme Deity is that the worldly activity of living beings will be established once the elements have been made gross. He states a doubt based on whether or not it is possible for the word "by the individual soul" (jīvena) to be connected with the phrase "I shall manifest" (vyākaravāṇi):
Regarding the word "therein" (*tatra*):

the result [of the discussion] is that in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), because the individual soul (*jīva*) alone is the creator of material things, Brahman’s status as the creator of all is not established; whereas in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), that is established.
He states the prima facie view, namely that the word "by the soul" (*jīvena*) is connected with the principal verb "I shall manifest" (*vyākaravāṇi*).
Regarding the phrase "it has been established" (*tatra prāptam*):

having raised the objection as to how the use of the first-person pronoun (*uttama-puruṣa*) is possible if the Supreme Deity is not the agent, he states that the designation of agency is metaphorical because of [the Deity's] status as the instigator, saying:
"Just as in the world... (*yathā loke*).
He establishes the conclusion with the words beginning "by the word 'tu'":
[it is] per form.
The meaning is "having entered.
By this, the incapacity of the individual soul (jīva) regarding the creation of the entire gross universe is indicated.

Furthermore, since the syntactic connection of words depends upon the fitness of their meanings, the construction is: "Having entered in the form of the individual soul, I alone shall evolve [the world]."
"But [I shall not declare it] by means of the individual soul.

Now, one might object: "In that case, since the act of entering has the individual soul as its agent and the declaration has the Lord as its agent, the suffix -kṛtvā would be grammatically incorrect due to the difference in agents. To this, he says:
"And there is no such thing as an 'individual soul' [independent of the Lord]."

In reality, however, it should be understood that because the sun itself is designated as the agent in the act of "entering" known as the state of reflection when it enters into water, so too, even regarding the entry by way of the individual self (jīvātman), the Lord alone is the agent; thus the scriptural statement is logical. Now, one might object: "If there is non-difference, why could the individual self itself not be the transformer? Anticipating this doubt, he says [the following] to show that this is not so, because that [self], which is distinct only through conceptual construction, lacks the capacity [for such agency] and because it would contradict scripture.
Regarding the term "Parameśvara":

since the creation of each of the great elements has already been described previously, it is here—in this sentence concerning evolution—that the creation of the stable material world is stated with specific effort. Thus, by rearranging the order of the words, he states the meaning of the Śruti as indicated by the Sūtra:
"preceded by the tripartition" (*trivṛtkaraṇapūrvakam*).
To the question, "Where has it been seen that the threefold nature was created by Īśvara? he says:
"And that...
Now, he states the sequence for the differentiation of names and forms:
Regarding the phrase "there [is] fire":

although it was stated in the passage "because of its origin from that" (*ataḥ prabhavāt*) that the creation of objects is preceded by the word of the Veda, there is no contradiction here; for while the creation of objects from the unmanifested word as remembered occurs [in general], what is stated here is the manifestation of the relationship with distinct names.

Now, one might object that since only fiery things like fire are cited in the scripture, the intention is not to convey that earth and water consist of the three elements (*trairātmakatva*). To this, he says:
And by this [phrase], "among them at the beginning," the word "among them" (tāsām madhye) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
The meaning is that whatever form, such as that of a pigeon, appears as if cognized through specific qualities like blackness and so forth, that is the collective form of the deities. //20//
Meat and so forth belong to the earth; the other two [classes of food] are according to their respective names. (BBs 2.4.21)

Having explained the external tripartition (*trivṛtkaraṇa*), [the author] introduces the next sūtra— beginning with "Of these" (*tāsām*)— to describe another internal tripartition that differs from what was previously stated.
The meaning is that, having entered the human body, each one becomes threefold, existing in the form of a triad of effects.

The meaning of the commentary is that, in order to dispel the objection raised by the subsequent sūtra, it first demonstrates the internal tripartition (*trivṛtkaraṇa*) which is the subject of that doubt.
Now, one might ask: "How can flesh and so forth, which consist of food (*annamaya*), be considered terrestrial?
To this, he says: "It is indeed the earth itself that has been tripartite."
The fact that the vital breath (prāṇa), which is air, is an effect of water should be understood as figurative. //21//
But on account of its preeminence, it is designated by that name; it is designated by that name. (BS 2.4.22)
Having thus stated the subject matter, he raises an objection regarding a fault— “here he says”—
and explains the Sūtra as a response to that:
Regarding the phrase "by the word 'tu'":
since one might ask for what purpose the term *vaiśeṣya* (distinction) is employed to denote an excess of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvādhikya*), he says:
"for the sake of establishing conventional usage" (*vyavahāraprasiddhyartham*).
Thus, it is established that there is no contradiction with Smṛti, logic, other doctrines, or Śruti regarding the Vedāntic purport concerning Brahman. //22//

Thus ends the fourth quarter of the second chapter in the *Bhāṣyaratnaprabhā*, a commentary on the *Śārīrakamīmāṃsā* composed by the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya Śrī Govindānanda Bhagavatpāda. //4//
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Resolution of Contradictions Regarding the Scriptures on the Subtle Body."
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "Non-contradiction," in the venerable Śaṅkara-bhāṣya on the Brahma-sūtras.
